Accelerating development for massive Git repositories

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Android’s source code is major – the Android 17 open source release has 1,084 Git repositories, 1.62 million files, and takes 300 GB for a built workspace.
  • Sources indicate that we built Another Build File Service (ABFS) to address these bottlenecks.
  • Today, we are excited to announce that ABFS is open source on GitHub.The impact of ABFS to Android is:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Android’s source code is major – the Android 17 open source release has 1,084 Git repositories, 1.62 million files, and takes 300 GB for a built workspace. Additionally, in a typical Android source tree with hardware vendor code and first-party applications, the size increases by 2-3x. Traditionally, it took over 30 minutes to fetch Android Open Source Project (AOSP) source code and well over an hour to build on even highly capable developer workstations. As software development evolved over the last 2 years, modern coding harnesses and LLMs have accelerated the development of many projects. These tools are used today for Android operating system development, but the long sync and build times make them less efficient. Both human developers and agents need quick setup, parallel workspaces, and fast build-and-test iteration times.

Sources indicate that we built Another Build File Service (ABFS) to address these bottlenecks. ABFS is a full suite of software across a Linux kernel filesystem module, user-space daemons, and server-side infrastructure. ABFS uses content-addressability across the entire stack to lazy-load and cache source code, developer workspaces, intermediate build files, and build results.

Today, we are excited to announce that ABFS is open source on GitHub.The impact of ABFS to Android is:.

ABFS already powers parallel workflows for developers and agents in Android, but it is designed to scale to other massive Git-based projects.

In the Android build system, developers define build rules in Blueprint files (Android.bp), Soong compiles them into Ninja files, and Ninja executes the final build graph (see the Android build overview). Similar to the Make build tool, Ninja is timestamp-based. If a build step’s input file is newer than the existing output file, Ninja rebuilds the output file.

Analyzing the AOSP code for Android 17 shows the sheer disk footprint and file count involved in a single checkout and build.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A newly leaked document purportedly details no less than seven latest Nova Lake-S desktop processors based on C1 stepping qualification samples, including 28-core models, three months before Intel is expected to officially take the wraps off them.
  • Recent findings suggest that of the seven chips that have been detailed, the top-of-the-line Core Ultra 9 4970K BFC will be the one of most interest.
  • If the leak holds up, the mid-range will be catered for by the Core Ultra 7 4870K and 4850K chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A newly leaked document purportedly details no less than seven latest Nova Lake-S desktop processors based on C1 stepping qualification samples, including 28-core models, three months before Intel is expected to officially take the wraps off them. The new leak, from VideoCardz, includes an Intel warning that clock speeds and performance may change before the final products are ready to be shipped. But given the fact that this rarely happens when dealing with qualification samples, it's believed that the chips will likely be released just as they are outlined in the document, if the leak is accurate.

Recent findings suggest that of the seven chips that have been detailed, the top-of-the-line Core Ultra 9 4970K BFC will be the one of most interest. It will reportedly feature 28 cores comprising eight performance cores, 16 efficiency cores, and four low-power efficient cores. Its base efficiency core clock speed of 2.7 GHz is eclipsed by the 5.5 GHz boost speed its performance cores will reach, while 144 MB of L3 cache and a 125-watt power rating round out the main figures. According to the leak, it will be joined by a Core Ultra 9 4950K with the same core count and almost identical clock speeds, albeit with a much smaller 36 MB L3 cache. Beyond that, the report says the Core 9 4900 BFC will be locked at 65 watts, have 22 cores, and a 120 MB L3 cache.

If the leak holds up, the mid-range will be catered for by the Core Ultra 7 4870K and 4850K chips. Both will reportedly have a 125-watt power rating and 24 cores, but will again differ in terms of L3 cache — the former will have 144 MB, the latter just 36 MB. Both will boost to 5.2 GHz.

The report notes the entry-level models will include the Core Ultra 5 4650K and 4650KF, both packing 22 cores and 30 MB L3 caches, and that they'll also have the same 125-watt power rating and top out at a boosted 5.1 GHz, according to the documentation.

It has been revealed that the document reportedly states that all seven processors will support DDR5-8000 RAM, an increase over the DDR5-6400 that the Arrow Lake-S chips top out at. The specs also indicate a maximum of 256 GB of RAM is supported, with 24 CPU PCIe lanes and a 77 PTOPS integrated NPU. Integrated graphics are set to range from 2.9 to 3.1 GHz depending on the chosen chip, with support for the DNx, XAVC, JPEG-XS, and VVC decoding all included alongside AV1 High and Professional profile support.

Recent findings suggest that it has previously been reported that Intel is likely to announce its next-gen chips at an event in Berlin, Germany, between February 22 and 25, 2026. But we can also expect that motherboard manufacturers will show off products compatible with the new chips before that — no doubt at the CES 2027 event in Las Vegas in January. It's already been confirmed that new motherboards will be needed if you blueprint on picking up any of the next-gen chips.

Sources indicate that this latest leak comes weeks after it was reported that the new Nova Lake chips would "universally limit the maximum core frequency to 5.1 GHz when above 90°C." However, it's important to remember that the limitation only applies when the chips reach that temperature. Machines with adequate cooling will not experience that limitation, although it remains to be seen how easy these chips are to cool.

Modders are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC.

Game modding communities are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC, but one massive effort has been taken down by Take-Two today. Leonida, a fan project by 15-year-old “NotRexed,” has vanished after a DMCA takedown notice from GTA VI publisher Take-Two.

Recent findings suggest that leonida was designed to translate a leaked GTA VI Xbox build to run natively on Windows. Cyberleek, the leaker who posted multiple GTA VI gameplay videos over the summer, published a full Xbox build of the game earlier this week. The leak has kicked recompilation efforts up a notch, as modders race to reverse-engineer the game’s code and rebuild it into native PC code.

Industry observers note that portWatch VI is tracking the efforts to recompile, emulate, or port the leaked Xbox build over to PC. At the time of publishing, the VIctory project and forks of it are leading the way. People are also trying to use XCL, a compatibility layer that runs Xbox Series X games on a Windows PC, to get GTA VI running.

Recent findings suggest that at this point, it seems like Take-Two might not be able to avoid the inevitable here. The clock started ticking down to the release of the PC version last week, and if recent reports are true, we might see it in a few months. If GTA VI is close to being officially ready for PC, we could hear about a release before modders manage to get the game running on PC unofficially.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hugging Face has become synonymous with advancing AI at scale. With over 4 million builders deploying models on the Hub, the rapid growth of the platform necessitated a rethinking of how sensitive configuration data —secrets— are managed.

According to recent reports, last year, the engineering teams set out to improve the handling of their secrets and credentials. After evaluating tools like HashiCorp Vault, they ultimately chose Infisical.

This case study details their migration to Infisical, explains how they integrated its powerful features, and highlights how it enabled engineers to work more efficiently and securely.

As Hugging Face's infrastructure evolved from an AWS-only setup to a multi-cloud environment that includes Azure and GCP, the engineering team needed a more agile, secure, and centralized way to manage secrets. Instead of reworking legacy systems or adopting heavyweight solutions like HashiCorp Vault, they turned to Infisical due to its developer-friendly workflows, multi-cloud abstraction, and robust security capabilities.

The key challenges they faced were:.

In addition, the team needed a solution that adhered to infrastructure-as-code practices, supported project-by-project secret management, and provided a smooth balance between automation and manual control during deployments.

Infisical’s flexible architecture was an ideal solution. The engineering team seized the opportunity to re-examine their internal project structure, splitting projects into distinct infrastructure and application domains. This allowed them to implement a clearer separation of concerns and standardize secret rotation practices—a priority in the wake of a recent security incident.

In a recent development, by leveraging Terraform, which was previously used to create Kubernetes secrets from AWS configurations, they found the transition to the Infisical Kubernetes Operator exceptionally smooth. This integration enabled security improvements while standardizing secrets management across all environments.

According to recent reports, kubernetes is at the heart of Hugging Face’s production environment, and Infisical's Kubernetes Operator has been instrumental in automating secret updates. The Operator continuously monitors for changes to any secret in Infisical and ensures that these updates are propagated to the corresponding Kubernetes objects. Whenever a change is detected, it can automatically reload dependent Deployments, ensuring that containers always run with the most recent secrets.

According to recent reports, A new secret is required by an application running in Kubernetes. The secret can be created via the Infisical's CLI or the web UI, then the developer creates an InfisicalSecret resource in Kubernetes that specifies which secret from Infisical should be synced:.

Industry observers note that once the CRD is applied, the Infisical Operator continuously watches for updates. When changes are detected in Infisical, the Operator automatically updates the Kubernetes secret (my-app-k8s-secret).

Better yet, since the application's Deployment references my-app-k8s-secret as an environment variable source or mounted volume, the Operator can automatically trigger a container reload when the secret changes.

Sources indicate that in practice, Hugging Face engineers favor waiting for manual redeployments despite the Operator’s ability to automatically trigger container restarts. This decision was driven by the need for precise control over deployments, particularly when high traffic (over 10 million requests per minute) and numerous replicas are involved.

For local development, Infisical’s CLI streamlines workflows by injecting secrets directly into development environments. This removes the need for insecure local .env files, aligning local configurations with production standards and reducing onboarding friction.

Security improvements form the backbone of this migration. By integrating Infisical with existing identity providers such as Okta, Hugging Face established a fine-grained RBAC system. Permissions are automatically mapped from Okta groups, ensuring that developers retain administrative rights over their projects, while frontend and backend teams receive appropriately restricted read or write access.

Additionally, the secret sharing functionality allows secure credentials sharing among ML/AI researchers at Hugging Face. The centralized Infisical platform also simplifies auditing and managing secret rotations—a necessity highlighted by previous security incidents.

Seamless integration with CI/CD pipelines further enhanced the overall security posture. Infisical was embedded into the deployment pipeline via GitHub Actions using OIDC authentication and Terraform integration. By operating self-hosted runners within a secure environment, every deployment adhered to production-grade security standards. This integrated approach minimized risks and ensured a uniform experience from local development to cloud deployment.

Centralizing secrets management with Infisical brought tangible improvements:.

As noted by Adrien Carreira, Head of Infrastructure at Hugging Face,.

"Infisical provided all the functionality and security settings we needed to boost our security posture and save engineering time. Whether you're working locally, running kubernetes clusters in production, or operating secrets within CI/CD pipelines, Infisical has a seamless prebuilt workflow.".

Sources indicate that hugging Face's migration to Infisical demonstrates how a technically driven, engineering-centric approach to managing secrets across multiple cloud platforms delivers significant benefits. For tackling similar challenges, using Infisical is a practical way to work more efficiently while keeping security strong.

When the secure path is made the easiest path, teams can focus on building innovative products instead of worrying about managing secrets.

Efficient Request Queueing – Optimizing LLM Performance

📅 02 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1666 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Serving LLMs to many applications and people in parallel is challenging because they compete for limited GPU resources.
  • An inference engine like vLLM or HuggingFace TGI consists of.
  • Sources indicate that why do we need a queue here?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Serving LLMs to many applications and people in parallel is challenging because they compete for limited GPU resources. This article is the first in a series on LLM performance, based on our experience with serving self-hosted LLMs at TNG Technology Consulting GmbH. In the first part, we focus on the impact of queuing and discuss different scheduling strategies.

An inference engine like vLLM or HuggingFace TGI consists of.

Sources indicate that why do we need a queue here? Because calculations on the GPU are more performant and resource-efficient when they are done batch-wise instead of isolated for individual requests. This backend queue allows the scheduler to pick multiple requests and put them on the same batch to be processed.

Note that typically each inference engine serves only a single model, and we have multiple deployments running for different models in parallel.

According to recent reports, when a single user "A" sends a large number of requests, they will quickly fill up the queue. Other consumers ("B" and "C") that send their requests only shortly after are blocked from using the same model (until all requests from "A" have been processed). Note that the picture focuses on vLLM as inference engine, but the problem is more general and applies to other backends as well.

It has been revealed that at TNG, users don't send requests directly to the vLLM backend but to an API Server (what we call "LLM-Server"). Here we can have separate queues for each user (and model), and a scheduler that is not FIFO (first in - first out) but goes round-robin through all user queues. This achieves some "fair scheduling": for example, in the diagram users B and C send their request a bit later, when user A's first request has already been scheduled. At that time, three requests from user A had been waiting already for some time, but user C has to wait for only one request from user A to be completed.

The key idea is: prioritize requests from different customers in our own component and not in the inference backend! Typically, you can't change the order of requests once they have been sent to the inference engine, so you have to bring them in the right order while they are still in the LLM-Server, where we have full control.

According to recent reports, you can consider different aspects in order to decide what "fair" scheduling is. In the above example, any fresh user with a single request should be served before any user is served two or more times in a row. This is "fair" on a number-of-requests level. But you could also look at processing time: how long does a request keep the backend busy? Long prompts and long generations will "block" the LLM for other users for a longer time, so maybe shorter requests should have precedence? Unfortunately, it is very difficult to estimate the generation length. While there are some requests with a "max_tokens" limit, a typical chat message from an interactive AI assistant has no token limit, and can vary between a very short generation ("summarize this text") and a very long one ("tell me a story" / "write all code for xyz").

Sources indicate that depending on the prompts, there can be some benefit in arranging requests based on similarity, so that vLLM can maximize cache hits, which speeds up the performance. This kind of KV-cache-aware routing has recently gained attention by frameworks like NVIDIA Dynamo and AIBrix.

In a business context, and for hosted LLMs, the cost of individual requests can be another metric to consider, but comes with similar challenges.

The solution can also be extended by having not only one queue per user (and model) but several queues with different priorities. For example, interactive applications like TNG's AI Assistant with chat interface should have higher priority because users who don't see any progress within five seconds will think the application is broken. Users who generate code reviews for tens of files and several thousand lines of code, however, will expect the LLM requests to take some time. And some use cases (like benchmark runs, scheduled via a batch API) should have such low priority that they don't disturb other use cases and are just scheduled when nothing else is running.

Recent findings suggest that consider again the scenario that one user A sends a lot of requests at once, and some time later a new user C joins and wants to schedule a single request. If the scheduler on LLM-Server side sent every request (according to the fair prioritization) immediately to the backend, all requests from A would accumulate again in the FIFO queue. The new user C would have to wait again until all previously received requests have been processed. There would be almost no improvement to the initial scenario without LLM-Server.

In a recent development, ideally, you could limit the number of maximum elements in the backend queue, but vLLM doesn't give you that option. Therefore, we have to dynamically adjust the rate at which the scheduler on LLM-Server side sends latest requests to the backend. Here, our goal is: keep the backend queue length short in order to minimize latencies experienced by new users.

(The simplest approach would be a static rate limit, but this would likely result in underutilization when most requests are short and hard to calibrate for different models and load patterns).

In order to make the backend queue length available in the LLM-Server, we need to fetch the respective Prometheus metrics from the vLLM /metrics endpoint. Our fair scheduler is only allowed to send requests to the backend as long as the backend queue length metric is smaller than three, for example. This target length for the backend queue can be lowered for an even shorter latency for latest people, until it results in under-utilized batches and a reduced efficiency - there is a trade-off. Keep in mind, though, that the target queue length does NOT reflect maximum concurrency; there can still be more than three requests being processed in parallel; vLLM will add queuing requests to the current batch as soon as there is sufficient space ("continuous batching").

Industry observers note that once you have the feedback loop between backend queue and scheduler in the LLM-Server, you can easily extend the set of vLLM metrics used for making scheduling decisions. For example, for a good user experience in TNG's interactive AI Assistant we aim for a high token generation speed (e.g., >7 tokens/s, that is ~150ms per token), and if the reported time-per-output-token metric rises above 150ms, no new requests will be scheduled.

Sources indicate that you can also program different metric thresholds for different request priorities. For example, for low-priority requests from the batch API we only schedule a request when the backend queue is completely empty: we rather risk short periods of underutilized GPUs than causing increased latencies for any later request with higher priority.

It has been revealed that there is quite some potential for optimizations: for example, if you allow scheduling for a backend length shorter than three and the current metric is zero, you can immediately send three requests to the backend before having to fetch the metrics again. In the worst case, none of them fit into the current batch and all of them are in the backend queue (in which case the latest length is three, just fine).

Recently, vLLM added a priority-based scheduling option instead of sticking with FIFO. For this newly introduced feature, requests are tagged with a priority before they are sent to the backend. And vLLM would regularly check if any higher-priority request is queuing and then sort all requests by priority (both the running batch and the waiting queue). This would not only let the high-priority request literally jump the queue but even move it directly to the processed batch. The price is (aside from some overhead due to sorting) that lower priority requests would be evicted from the running batch and put back in the waiting queue again.

According to recent reports, vLLM understands the request priority as a continuous number. This does not only allow you to distinguish between default, high priority (interactive AI assistant) and low priority (batch API) but you could even make smaller decrements for every request that the user has already sent to the backend and where the response is pending. For example, consumers B and C send only single requests, which will have priority zero. User A sends four requests at once; the first one has priority zero, too, but the next ones will have priorities one, two, and three, and will be processed later (higher number = lower priority).

Overall, backend-side priority scheduling can be a good strategy for vLLM-based systems, because it simplifies queueing logic on the upstream LLM-Server. Unfortunately, in a realistic setting you cannot get rid of the LLM-Server as an additional scheduling layer, since you need some objective instance to assign priorities to individual requests.

Industry observers note that queueing and scheduling are crucial for applications with multiple customers and clients of varying priorities, as they significantly impact the user experience. This is especially true in scenarios where multiple clients submit requests in parallel, benefiting from a dedicated "fair scheduling" strategy. Although backend features like priority scheduling can simplify optimization, an upstream gateway server is still necessary to fully manage these complexities.

In the next part of this blogpost series, we will shift gears and focus on the token generation in the inference engine during prefill and decode phases. In particular, we will discuss resource utilization and strategies for concurrent processing of multiple requests.

yes, disaggregated prefill has improved by now, although it still takes some custom work to set it up correctly.The original challenge of multi-user serving with heterogeneous load patterns and priorities remains, though.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you are looking for a reliable, everyday handset without spending flagship money, Samsung’s mid-range lineup is usually a safe bet. Right now, the Samsung Galaxy A56 has dropped to just $299 on Amazon, which makes a sizable $200 dent in its original $499 retail price.

Industry observers note that at under $300, the biggest selling point here isn’t just the upfront savings; it is the longevity. Samsung committed to six years of OS and security updates for the Galaxy A56, meaning this device will stay current and secure well into 2032. For a budget-tier purchase, getting that kind of software runway is hard to beat and only matched by Google with the Pixel 10a.

Hardware-wise, the A56 punches above this sale price. You get a crisp 6.7-inch 120Hz Super AMOLED display, an IP67 dust- and water-resistance rating, and a 5,000mAh battery with 45W wired charging, matching the charging speeds of Samsung’s flagship models. The triple-camera array, led by a 50MP main sensor with OIS, won’t win any photography awards against Ultra-tier phones, though it is plenty capable for casual snaps. Plus, One UI brings plenty of handy Samsung ecosystem features and baked-in AI tools like Object Eraser.

Of course, the Google Pixel 10a is the obvious rival in this space. If you can catch the Pixel 10a on sale around the $350 mark, its cleaner Android experience, seven-year revision promise, and superior computational photography make it a very tempting alternative.

It has been revealed that that noted, it hasn’t been available at that price point for a while and can only be picked up for $400 if you buy renewed. For photographers, videographers and content creators, an SD card is more than a storage device. It holds the raw material behind a finished project: wedding photographs, travel footage, product demos and drone recordings that may be impossible to recreate. Data loss can happen at almost any stage of that workflow, from a folder deleted to make space to a card formatted before the footage was backed up.

According to recent reports, this article explains why files on a card become unavailable, what to do in the first minutes, how recovery tools find data, and how to compare options. It includes a small Python example that recovers JPEG files from a disk image, so you can see the mechanism for yourself. It also compares free open-source tools with paid graphical ones, using criteria you can apply yourself. Recovery is never guaranteed, and tool features change, so confirm details against each vendor’s current documentation.

Recovery is not just a matter of finding a deleted filename. Several different problems can make files unavailable, and they call for different approaches.

These steps cannot guarantee recovery, but they reduce avoidable risk.

Most tools combine two methods, and understanding them helps you read scan results.

Carving has a cost. Because file system information is ignored, names and folder structure are usually lost, which is why scan results often show generic names. Fragmented files can also be recovered incomplete, since the tool assumes the pieces are stored one after another. Free tools build on these same ideas. Wondershare Recoverit V15, which also offers a free version for Windows and Mac, adds a graphical interface, while PhotoRec and ddrescue stay closer to the command line.

Industry observers note that the script below is a teaching sketch, not a recovery product. It reads a raw disk image, finds JPEG start markers, and writes out the bytes up to the last end marker before the next start. That detail matters because a JPEG can contain an embedded thumbnail with its own markers, so stopping at the first end marker would cut a file short.

A short test builds two real JPEGs, hides them in random bytes, and checks that both are carved and open as valid images:.

Use it on an image rather than the card itself. On Linux you can make one with a read-only copy, for example with the GNU ddrescue tool, which is designed to copy data from failing media. Then run the carver against the image and save the output to a different drive. Real tools handle many more formats, trim files using header information, and deal with video containers, so treat this as a way to understand the idea.

The right choice depends on the problem, your platform and how comfortable you are with the command line. The table summarizes what each project’s own documentation states.

Graphical tools follow the same logic and mainly change step 3, with thumbnails, filters and search that make large result sets easier to browse. Whether that is worth paying for depends on how many files you need to sift through and how comfortable you are on the command line. When comparing any tool, ask:.

Features such as search by capture time, folder or AI-based tagging depend on metadata surviving the loss, and they narrow results without proving a file is intact. Treat them as convenience, not verification.

Recent findings suggest that recovering a video file does not necessarily mean recovering a playable video. A recording interrupted during writing can lack the structural information a player needs, and other files may be damaged in ways that block playback.

The distinction matters. Recovery retrieves missing or inaccessible data, while repair tries to fix damage that affects a file’s usability. Some cases need one, the other or both. Repair has limits too: if essential video data was overwritten or never recorded, software cannot recreate the original footage in full. After any recovery or repair, play the file all the way through and compare it with what you expect.

For a quick check of a recovered clip, ffprobe can show whether the container is readable:.

An error or a missing duration suggests the file needs repair or is incomplete.

Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Journey to 1 Million Gradio Users!

📅 04 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1196 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 5 years ago, we launched Gradio as a simple Python library to let researchers at Stanford easily demo computer vision models with a web interface.
  • Sources indicate that today, Gradio is used by >1 million developers each month to build and share AI web apps.
  • Sources indicate that how did we get here?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

5 years ago, we launched Gradio as a simple Python library to let researchers at Stanford easily demo computer vision models with a web interface.

Sources indicate that today, Gradio is used by >1 million developers each month to build and share AI web apps. This includes some of the most popular open-source projects of all time, like Automatic1111, Oobabooga’s Text Generation WebUI, Dall-E Mini, and LLaMA-Factory.

Sources indicate that how did we get here? How did Gradio keep growing in the very crowded field of open-source Python libraries? I get this question a lot from folks who are building their own open-source libraries. This post distills some of the lessons that I have learned over the past few years:.

Industry observers note that 1. Invest in good primitives, not high-level abstractions.

Recent findings suggest that when we first rolled out Gradio, we offered only one high-level class (gr.Interface), which created a complete web app from a single Python function. We quickly realized that developers wanted to create other kinds of apps (e.g. multi-step workflows, chatbots, streaming applications), but as we started listing out the apps users wanted to build, we realized what we needed to do: go lower.

Instead of building many high-level classes to support different use cases, we built a low-level API called Gradio Blocks that let consumers assemble applications from modular components, events, and layouts. Despite generally being more work to use, gr.Blocks today represents 80% of the usage of Gradio—including the highly popular apps mentioned above.

With a small team, a focus on low-level abstractions has necessarily meant that we could not chase many tempting, high-level abstractions. But this focus saved us from two common pitfalls:.

Customization-maintenance trap: high-level abstractions are easy to use, but consumers request extra parameters to customize them, which in turn leads to increased maintenance burden since every abstraction and parameter needs to be implemented, maintained, and tested to avoid bugs.

The productivity illusion: using high-level abstractions seems like less work, until a user needs functionality that is not supported (which can be hard to predict at the beginning of a project), forcing the developer to do a costly rewrite.

The first problem wastes our time as maintainers of Gradio, while the second problem wastes our consumers’ time. To this day, Gradio only includes two high-level abstractions (gr.Interface and gr.ChatInterface) which themselves are built with Blocks.

Industry observers note that the advantage of having good primitives is even more dramatic in the age of AI-assisted coding, where we find that LLMs are generally good at combing through documentation and building complex applications out of primitives (see all the games being built with three.js for example). It doesn’t take much extra time to write low-level code if the AI is writing the code for you.

It has been revealed that the best ambassador for your library is not you, but an enthusiastic user. It follows, then, that you should find ways for owners to share your library or its products as part of their workflow. Gradio’s early growth was fueled by our “share links” feature (which created a temporary public link for your Gradio app in a single line of code). Instead of having to worry about packaging or hosting their code on a web server with the right kind of compute, Gradio users could share their apps with colleagues immediately.

After joining Hugging Face, we also benefited from being the standard UI for Hugging Face Spaces—widely used by the machine learning research community. The most viral Spaces drew millions of visitors, exposing developers to Gradio, who in turn shared and built their own Gradio apps, using those same Spaces (whose code was publicly available) as a resource to learn how to use Gradio.

According to recent reports, 3. Build for a (growing) niche use case.

It has been revealed that early on, we faced a critical decision: should Gradio be a general-purpose Python web framework, or should we focus specifically on building machine learning web apps? We chose the latter, and this has made all the difference.

In the crowded ecosystem of Python web libraries, we are frequently asked, "How is Gradio different from X?" Our concise answer—that Gradio is optimized for machine learning web apps—is memorable and fundamentally accurate. Each Gradio app ships with features particularly suited to ML workflows, such as a built-in queue that can manage long-running ML tasks efficiently, even with thousands of concurrent consumers. The components we have designed are specifically tailored to ML use cases. On the other hand, for a long time, Gradio did not even include features like link buttons, simply because our core users never needed it. By narrowing our focus, Gradio promptly became the go-to choice among machine learning developers—the default "UI for AI.".

Industry observers note that of course, we benefited tremendously from choosing a niche that itself was growing. The recent headwinds that have propelled all things AI-related benefited us tremendously and we likely would not have experienced the same kind of growth if we had focused on data science or dashboards for example.

4. Your only roadmap should be rapid iteration.

Unlike some other libraries, Gradio doesn’t publish roadmaps. Instead, we track emerging trends in machine learning and ship accordingly. In open-source software generally, and AI specifically, shipping features based on the needs of the community (and deprecating features that are no longer needed) is key to continuous growth. As a concrete example, in the early versions of Gradio we built specific functionality to allow developers to show the “interpretation” of their machine learning models—as this was a very popular use case around 2020-21. As interest in interpretation waned, we deprecated this and instead poured our efforts into audio/video streaming and chat-related features.

Our internal process is decentralized as well. Each of the 11 engineers and developer advocates on the Gradio team is encouraged to identify impactful ideas, prototype quickly, engage directly with the open-source community via GitHub, Hugging Face, and social media. Each team member brings these ideas back to the team and we continuously build and rebuild consensus around what ideas are likely to be impactful as we keep growing the most impactful directions.

Recent findings suggest that 5. Maximize ways owners can consume your library's outputs.

Industry observers note that when you create a Gradio app and “launch()” it, you get a web application running in your browser. But that’s not all -- you also get an API endpoint for each Python function, as well as automatically-generated documentation for each endpoint. These endpoints can be consumed via Python or JavaScript Clients that our team has built, or directly using cURL.

Sources indicate that the reason that we do this is because we want each minute that a developer spends with Gradio to be maximally useful. A single Gradio app should run locally or be deployed without any code changes on Hugging Face Spaces or on your server, or integrate into larger applications programmatically, or even be harnessed by AI agents through MCPs (more on that soon!). By focusing on maximum usability, we hope that developers can continue to get more and more out of the Gradio library.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we are incredibly excited to welcome the next generation of large language models from Meta to the Hugging Face Hub: Llama 4 Maverick (~400B) and Llama 4 Scout (~109B)! 🤗 Both are Mixture of Experts (MoE) models with 17B active parameters.

In a recent development, released today, these powerful, natively multimodal models represent a significant leap forward. We've worked closely with Meta to ensure seamless integration into the Hugging Face ecosystem, including both transformers and TGI from day one.

Industry observers note that this is just the start of our journey with Llama 4. Over the coming days we’ll continue to collaborate with the community to build amazing models, datasets, and applications with Maverick and Scout! 🔥.

Sources indicate that llama 4, developed by Meta, introduces a new auto-regressive Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture. This generation includes two models:.

Recent findings suggest that both models leverage early fusion for native multimodality, enabling them to process text and image inputs. Maverick and Scout are both trained on up to 40 trillion tokens on data encompassing 200 languages (with specific fine-tuning support for 12 languages including Arabic, Spanish, German, and Hindi).

For deployment, Llama 4 Scout is designed for accessibility, fitting on a single server-grade GPU via on-the-fly 4-bit or 8-bit quantization, while Maverick is available in BF16 and FP8 formats. These models are released under the custom Llama 4 Community License Agreement, available on the model repositories.

To help the community leverage these state-of-the-art models immediately, we're thrilled to announce the following integrations:.

Recent findings suggest that the Llama 4 models were pre-trained with a context length of 256K. The Instruct models were fine-tuned to support much larger context lengths: 1M in the large 128 experts version (Maverick), and 10M (!) for the 16 experts version (Scout).

These large context lengths come with a few very interesting architecture choices. Until an official technical report is published, this is what we know so far.

Industry observers note that noPE (cute name, +1 charisma points), which was explored as far back as 2022, just forgoes the traditional positional encoding schemes, such as RoPE, that are most times applied in transformers models. In the case of Llama 4, NoPE layers are used every 4 layers. These layers are crucial for long context, as they use the full causal mask over the context.

For RoPE layers (three out of 4), chunked attention is used.

Meta refers to the interleaved use of NoPE layers, together with temperature scaling (as explained below), as the iRoPE architecture.

If you want to learn more about positional encodings, we recommend Chris' recent post.

As a way to reduce memory requirements, Llama 4 uses chunked attention in the layers that work with traditional RoPE positional encodings (three out of 4 decoder layers). The best way to visualize how chunked attention works is through this ASCII representation that was extracted from the transformers source code:.

It has been revealed that this diagram indicates the attention mask that would be used if the chunked attention length was 3. In the case of Llama 4, chunked attention length is 8192. This means that RoPE layers can only keep track of context in 8K blocks, while NoPE layers have access to the full context. You can see it as a more memory and compute efficient version of Sliding Window Attention.

In a recent development, attention blocks applied to long contexts have a problem: the attention probability scores fade closer to zero as the sequence length increases. This is a known consequence of applying the softmax function to very long sequences. To address this problem, Llama 4 uses a scaled softmax, which the model refers to as temperature tuning. This is applied in the NoPE layers, but not in the RoPE ones as these attend to shorter sub-sequences.

This method is a way to improve generalization for arbitrary context lengths, and probably one of the key factors to achieve 10M context length in Llama 4 Scout.

Llama Scout (the 16 experts version) uses an additional RMS normalization without learnable parameter of the Query and Key states in RoPE layers, after RoPE embeddings have been applied.

Llama Scout is a full MoE consisting of 16 experts. Llama Maverick uses 128 experts, but MoE and dense layers alternate. Therefore, experts are applied in half of the layers.

Llama Maverick was co-distilled from a larger model, Llama Behemoth, using a novel loss function that weight dynamically the student and teacher logit.

The models leverage MetaP, a methodology likely inspired by MuP, to optimally tune hyperparameters across different dimensions including training budget and model size.

Sources indicate that getting started with Llama 4 using transformers is straightforward. Make sure you have transformers v4.51.0 or later installed (pip install -U transformers huggingface_hub[hf_xet]). Here's a quick example using the instruction-tuned Maverick model responding about two images, using tensor parallel for maximum speed. You need to run this script on an instance with 8 GPUs, using a command like:torchrun –nproc-per-instance=8 script.py.

Make sure to check the model cards on the repos (Llama 4 Maverick (~400B) and Llama 4 Scout (~109B)) for detailed usage instructions, including multimodal examples, specific prompt formats (like system prompts), quantization details, and advanced configuration options!

Evaluation results confirm the strength of these models, showing state-of-the-art performance that significantly outperforms predecessors like Llama 3.1 405B. For instance, on reasoning and knowledge tasks, the instruction-tuned Maverick achieves 80.5% on MMLU Pro and 69.8% on GPQA Diamond, while Scout scores 74.3% and 57.2% respectively.

Releasing a giant like Llama 4 takes a colossal effort across teams, geographies and a lot of VMs. In no particular order we’d like to thank Arthur, Lysandre, Cyril, Pablo, Marc, Mohammed from the Transformers team. We are grateful to the full vLLM team for rich discussions, insights, shared testing and debugging during this intense integration with many challenges. With larger optimisation needs, we’d like to thank Mohit for single-handedly adding support to Llama 4 in TGI. These chonky models require some serious engineering at the storage level. This took a lot of effort from Ajit, Rajat, Jared, Di, Yucheng and the rest of the Xet team too.

There are a lot of people involved in this effort, thanks a lot to the rest of the Hugging Face, vLLM and Meta Llama teams for the brilliant synergy!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients.
  • To scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters.
  • To address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients. However, physical and cost constraints make scaling a single slice increasingly difficult.

To scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters. However, when training across multiple datacenters over wide-area networks (WAN), standard data-parallel training suffers from severe network stalls because slow WAN transfers cannot be fully overlapped with computation.

To address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections. In this blog post, we discuss the core concepts of DiLoCo, how it is implemented in MaxText (Google's open-source JAX-based LLM training framework), and the performance benefits it brings to large-scale LLM training on Google Cloud.

In a recent development, diLoCo was introduced by Google DeepMind in the paper DiLoCo: Distributed Low-Communication Training of Language Models. Instead of synchronizing gradients across all devices at every single training step (as in standard Data Parallelism), DiLoCo partitions training across M independent compute groups, referred to as learners, and allows each learner to perform many local optimization steps independently before communicating across groups.

Despite communicating significantly less frequently (by a factor of H, e.g., 1-2 orders of magnitude less) than standard synchronous training, DiLoCo has been shown to achieve comparable convergence and model quality.

In a recent development, the Vanilla DiLoCo described above reduces total communication volume by a factor of H, however, all learners still transmit their weight deltas for the entire model all at once at every H-th step. On a thin network pipe, that full-model transfer creates a large periodic stall every H steps. This issue is alleviated by Streaming DiLoCo, which is described in the next section.

According to recent reports, in multi-slice training, communication within a single slice is handled by high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnects (ICI). When scaling to multiple slices, synchronization across slices must traverse the Data Center Network (DCN) or, if the slices are geographically distributed, wide-area networks (WAN).

Within a single datacenter, DCN bandwidth is high enough that JAX and XLA can often hide standard Data Parallel all-reduce collectives by overlapping gradient communication with backward-pass computation. Across datacenters or congested links, however, bandwidth drops and latency rises sharply. Standard DP stalls at every step waiting for global gradient synchronization, collapsing Model FLOPS Utilization (MFU).

According to recent reports, streaming DiLoCo eliminates this synchronization stall by partitioning the model's parameters into P disjoint fragments. Over the course of H steps, every single fragment in the model is synchronized exactly once, achieving the exact same outer-loop cadence as vanilla DiLoCo without spiky bandwidth utilization.

According to recent reports, using a roofline model (similar to the JAX Scaling Book), we can calculate the network bandwidth required to prevent communication stalls for a model with ∣Θ∣ parameters (at b bytes per parameter, e.g., b=2 for bfloat16) and per-step compute time tstep=tfwd+tbwd. For example, the standard Data Parallel algorithm transfers 2∣Θ∣b bytes per sync via an all-reduce collective, which is a distributed reduce-scatter where each node reduces a different part, followed by an all-gather so all participants receive all parts. To achieve zero communication stalls, we overlap the reduce-scatter of the gradients with the backward pass, which produces them and takes tbwd time. Therefore, the peak required bandwidth is Bdp ≈ 2∣Θ∣b / tbwd.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that at Inception, we have been working to enhance AI model evaluations within the Arabic language context. Previously, we introduced AraGen, one of the first generative Arabic leaderboards, serving as a benchmark for evaluating Arabic LLMs on generative tasks.

As part of our ongoing efforts, we are excited to share the following updates:.

The following sections provide details about each of these updates.

It has been revealed that arabic-Leaderboards is a comprehensive and unified space for all Arabic evaluations and tasks. It is meant to serve as a central hub covering a broad spectrum of evaluations, for models across modalities. Right now, it has AraGen-03-25 and Arabic Instruction Following as live leaderboards. We strategy to expand this space with more leaderboards and tasks for Arabic AI models across various modalities.

We invite interested contributors to reach out to us through the community tab or directly through email in order to discuss how to integrate their work/leaderboards as additional tabs into this space.

In December 2024, we introduced the AraGen Benchmark as the foundation for the AraGen Leaderboard. A key feature of this leaderboard is its dynamic nature, with evaluation datasets remaining private (blind testing) for three months to ensure fair and unbiased assessments. Adhering to the same philosophy, we are publicly releasing the AraGen-12-24 benchmark, along with all model responses evaluated by Claude-3.5-Sonnet following the 3C3H guidelines.

By sharing this benchmark and model responses, we aim to encourage the community to review them, identify any unexpected behaviors we may have missed and help us refine our evaluation framework.

According to recent reports, in this latest AraGen release, we have expanded the dataset to include 340 pairs of questions and answers, up from 279 in the previous version. The distribution remains relatively similar:.

This allocation reflects the primary focus on question answering as the main use cases of any Language-Model/Chatbot/AI-Assistant, while still addressing other evaluation areas, particularly given the complexity of generating challenging queries in Arabic grammar and orthography.

Additionally, we refined the judge system prompt to enhance clarity, even for smaller/weaker judge models.

Sources indicate that maintaining consistency and reliability in our benchmark and evaluation pipeline is crucial as we introduce dynamic evaluation cycles. To ensure this, we analyzed ranking variations among the top 10 models across different dataset versions and system prompt configurations.

We analyzed model performance under two evaluation scenarios:.

The overall rankings were stable, with the top-performing model (o1-2024-12-17) consistently maintaining its lead. Notably, we observed a swap in rankings between two Claude models, underscoring the sensitivity of our evaluation approach, especially given their initially close scores.

The only significant change in rankings was for the gpt-4o-2024-08-06 model, whose performance markedly improved with the updated dataset and prompt. This sudden jump is currently under investigation as part of our ongoing benchmarks-design research.

Industry observers note that no major variations occurred solely due to changes in the system prompt, indicating good reproducibility as long as the same judge model (claude-3.5-sonnet) is used. However, we anticipate potential variations with smaller or weaker models as judges, where employing the second system prompt (SP2) may enhance consistency.

As a summary, the robust, consistently top-ranking performance of o1-2024-12-17—whose top score dropped from 82.67% to 70.25%—continues to reinforce its reliability for Arabic applications under the more challenging updated benchmark. While recent updates to the evaluation pipeline introduced minor ranking shifts, the overall framework remained stable, with top and bottom performers showing consistent positions. Many observed ranking adjustments likely reflect typical evaluation error margins due to minor score differences. Notably, scores for the second- through fifth-ranked models, previously between 70–78%, are now between 51–57%. This highlights that the updated AraGen dataset poses a markedly more difficult benchmark aligned with ongoing advances in reasoning models. Despite these shifts in absolute scores, it is encouraging that leaderboard positions remained largely consistent, underscoring the robustness of the evaluation approach moving forward.

As part of our December release, we introduced 3C3H as a latest evaluation measure of the chat capability of models, aimed at assessing both the factuality and usability of LLMs’ answers. Over the past three months, we have observed some interesting findings, which we share in this section.

One emergent trend is that the various dimensions are almost perfectly correlated. In most cases, correct answers are scored as both highly helpful and harmless, while most models fail to maintain this correlation for the conciseness dimension. This generally reflects the way we train these models today, where more verbose answers are often rewarded as more helpful. This trend has recently caught the attention of the research community, as exemplified by the release of OpenAI’s GPT-4.5 model. According to their use cases section, answers from GPT-4.5 are more concise than those from GPT-4, while still being equally helpful.

A model that stood out in this analysis is “silma-ai/SILMA-9B-Instruct-v1.0”, which exhibited a higher conciseness score compared to other open-weight models—even those with larger sizes. However, this gain in conciseness came at the cost of helpfulness and other dimensions when compared to its base model, “google/gemma-2-9b-it”. We believe that this analysis, along with optimizing for 3C3H, will enable the community to develop better models through curated datasets while maintaining the correlation across all dimensions.

According to recent reports, this is an ongoing effort to better understand how these dimensions are interconnected and how various scenarios and training recipes affect this relationship. Below, we provide a space where you can generate heatmaps for any combination of models of your choice. We hope the community finds it helpful in spotting additional trends that we may not have noticed. Ultimately, we aim for this tool to foster more discussion about evaluation and 3C3H, serving as a resource for others’ work.

We believe that one limitation of this analysis is the zeroing rule, whereby we do not evaluate the other dimensions if the answer is not correct. In the future, we strategy to investigate further whether an answer can be helpful despite being incorrect, and how dimensions such as conciseness and harmlessness factor into this evaluation if the answer is not correct.

Recent findings suggest that one of the core capabilities of large language models (LLMs) is their ability to understand and follow human instructions. This skill is crucial for building reliable chatbots, virtual assistants, and AI systems that do what people ask. Without strong instruction-following, a model might generate correct information but in the wrong format, ignore user-specified constraints, or produce unwanted content. Instruction-Following benchmark is standardized, objective way to measure a model's instruction adherence and compare models fairly to drive improvements.

According to recent reports, our work took inspiration from the IFEval dataset. IFEval, originally introduced by Google, provides a structured benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs on their ability to follow verifiable instructions. It consists of prompts containing specific, objectively measurable commands such as “use exactly three bullet points,” “include the word ‘innovation’ twice,” or “limit your answer to 100 words.” English IFEval dataset contains around 500 prompts covering 25 different types of such verifiable instructions. Evaluation within IFEval is conducted through Python functions that automatically verify whether instructions are followed, avoiding the need for human evaluators or another AI judge. This makes the evaluations reproducible and unbiased. While IFEval has become the standard for assessing LLMs responding in English, a similarly detailed and structured resource is absent for Arabic.

Industry observers note that construction of our Arabic IFEval dataset began by carefully adapting approximately 300 prompts from the original English IFEval. This wasn't a straightforward, word-for-word translation; instead, we thoughtfully adjusted prompts to clearly reflect Arabic linguistic nuances and cultural contexts. Instructions that made little sense in Arabic, such as those involving English-specific vowel constraints, were either adapted to equivalent Arabic linguistic challenges or omitted entirely. Cultural references specific to English-speaking contexts were replaced with culturally relevant or Arabic-language equivalents to maintain contextual clarity. Additionally, we created unique Arabic-specific samples from scratch, specifically designed to emphasize distinctive Arabic phonetics, orthographic characteristics, and morphology, such as the careful use of diacritical marks (tashkīl), phonetic constraints like avoiding certain letters (e.g., writing without using the letter Alef (ا)), and leveraging root-based morphology to challenge models' word-selection abilities. All prompts underwent rigorous expert validation by Arabic linguists and domain experts who ensured grammatical accuracy, cultural appropriateness, and unambiguous clarity of each instruction.

It has been revealed that arabic IFEval dataset is publicly available for the research community to utilize, test, and contribute to. It is available on Huggingface under inceptionai/Arabic_IFEval.

Industry observers note that to evaluate the models, we adopted a comprehensive methodology combining both explicit and implicit evaluation techniques. Explicit evaluation involved using automated scripts to assess whether instructions were strictly followed, focusing on elements such as correct formatting and specific word usage. Implicit evaluation addressed more nuanced linguistic expectations, such as maintaining the intended response language and avoiding repetitive patterns.

Additionally, we utilized scoring metrics introduced by Google in the IFEval framework, applying these metrics at both prompt-level and instruction-level granularity. These metrics were measured using strict criteria accuracy, which requires adherence to the provided instructions. The prompt-level score is notably harder, reflecting the user's viewpoint by asking, "Did I get everything I requested?" If a prompt included multiple requirements, failing to meet any single requirement would mean the user's request was not fully satisfied. In contrast, the instruction-level score is more lenient, allowing us to evaluate partial compliance.

In our analysis, we will emphasize the prompt-level strict accuracy as it provides the most rigorous assessment of a model's instruction-following capabilities.

We evaluated a broad range of LLMs on both the English IFEval benchmark and our newly introduced Arabic IFEval. This encompassed closed-source models (such as OpenAI's GPT series and Anthropic's Claude models) and open-source alternatives (including the Jais series, Meta’s LLaMA-2 variants, and various open bilingual models). 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spacecraft enters orbit after epic journey but something shortened a burn.
  • Humanity’s third-ever mission to Mercury has arrived, but a last-minute “software matter” has complicated matters.
  • The BepiColombo mission is a joint effort by the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan’s Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spacecraft enters orbit after epic journey but something shortened a burn.

Humanity’s third-ever mission to Mercury has arrived, but a last-minute “software matter” has complicated matters.

The BepiColombo mission is a joint effort by the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan’s Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Reaching Mercury is not easy because its gravity is weak and its orbit is fast. The tiny planet’s proximity to the Sun further complicates matters, because our star’s gravity accelerates everything that falls towards it.

BepiColombo’s journey has therefore seen it whiz past Earth once, Venus twice, and Mercury six times on a complicated path the two space agencies designed to slow it down sufficiently to be captured by mercurial gravity, while also keeping up with its rapid orbit.

In 2024, the craft’s thrusters underperformed, leading the ESA and JAXA to re-plot the planned trajectory and reschedule its arrival at Mercury from mid-2025 to this past weekend.

According to recent reports, the ESA’s operations team sent the commands to insert BepiColombo into orbit on Friday. On Sunday the craft phoned home with news that it entered orbit. A little later, however, the ESA revealed “the thruster burn was shorter than planned following a software issue.”.

The spacecraft is safe, but the ESA claims it is “working to understand what happened” and promised updates early this week.

Readers may recall that a pair of NASA missions to Mars are also experiencing software glitches, which have in recent weeks become all-too-prevalent on Earth, too.

If all is well, BepiColombo will deploy two orbiters.

The ESA’s craft is called the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), which the ESA says will map the planet, assess the composition of its surface and interior, measure its magnetic field, and even gather data that scientists hope will “test Einstein's theory of General Relativity to an unprecedented level of accuracy.”.

JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MIO) will also investigate the planet’s magnetic field, plasma, dust, and atmosphere.

Both orbiters are extraordinary feats of engineering. As JAXA explains, MIO is solar-powered but the sunlight it will receive at Mercury is around ten times as powerful as on Earth. Mercury itself is also sufficiently hot that the orbiter needs protection from heat radiated from the planet’s surface. ESA’s MPO keeps itself cool with three to four insulating blankets comprised of layered titanium, aluminum, and a ceramic fabric called Nextel. The blankets alone weigh 94kg.

The two space agencies expect to start science operations in April 2027 but haven’t yet noted if the two orbiters are in peak condition.

JAXA, sadly, last week revealed that its Hayabusa2 probe has deteriorated to the point at which it can no longer make its planned landing on asteroid 1998 KY26. JAXA scheduled that for the year 2031, but problems with the probe’s thrusters mean the agency will instead attempt a high-speed fly-by of asteroid 2015 BM510 in 2028. Hayabusa2 released in 2014, so is rather older than BepiColombo.

It has been revealed that humanity has visited Mercury twice before. Mariner 10 made three rapid passes across 1974 and 1975, when it managed to map less than half of the planet’s surface. Messenger made it to Mercury in 2011 and spent more than four years in orbit before crashing into the planet’s surface. The probe mapped the entire planet and even spotted ice near its poles. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're excited to announce a new partnership between Cloudflare and Hugging Face that gives FastRTC developers instant access to enterprise-grade WebRTC infrastructure with a Hugging Face token.

As a preview of what you can build with FastRTC and Cloudflare, check out this voice chat app built with Meta's latest Llama 4 model!

As conversational AI becomes a core interface for tools, products, and services, real-time communication infrastructure is increasingly essential to support natural, multimodal interactions. Hugging Face built FastRTC to let AI developers build low-latency AI-powered audio and video streams with minimal Python code by abstracting away the complexities of WebRTC – the gold standard technology for real-time communication.

WebRTC-powered applications often face deployment challenges due to the need for specialized TURN servers, which enable reliable connections across different network environments. To address this issue, Cloudflare has built a global network of these servers that spans over 335 locations worldwide.

This partnership combines FastRTC’s easy development approach with Cloudflare's global TURN network, ensuring developers can create fast and reliable WebRTC applications with global connectivity.

FastRTC developers with a valid Hugging Face Access Token can stream 10GB of data for FREE every month without a credit card. Once the monthly limit is reached, developers can switch to their Cloudflare account for higher capacity (instructions).

This partnership is especially valuable for AI developers building:.

This partnership lets developers focus on their core application logic with FastRTC, while eliminating the need to build and maintain TURN infrastructure. Cloudflare's managed service handles global scalability and reliability, allowing AI developers to deliver exceptional experiences without the overhead of maintaining infrastructure.

The integration will be available in the FastRTC version 0.0.20 and above. To get started:.

Launch your script with python, python .py.

See this Collection on Hugging Face as well as the FastRTC Cookbook for more examples.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Outage after outage after outage is a syndrome that needs radical treatment.
  • Among the many organizations to adopt Outage As A Service (OAAS) were Microsoft, Apple, the FAA, and any number of European supermarkets.
  • OAAS is synonymous with infrastructure failure, a more useful term that begins to hint at cause and cure as well as effect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Outage after outage after outage is a syndrome that needs radical treatment.

No Access November is going well this year.

Among the many organizations to adopt Outage As A Service (OAAS) were Microsoft, Apple, the FAA, and any number of European supermarkets. Even the NSA has succumbed. For us, at least, outage is word of the year. It's certainly deeply embedded in the public mind, with schoolchildren reportedly referring to the 19th century Irish famine as "the potato outage." There's no danger of an outrage outage.

OAAS is synonymous with infrastructure failure, a more useful term that begins to hint at cause and cure as well as effect. In all of the latest crop, what we know is depressingly familiar. Microsoft's O365 meltdown was a cascading failure caused by a botched upgrade that took stuff offline and melted down as it tried to come back. The FAA was a migration from Jurassic hardware that wasn't end of life so much as living fossil. The Eurofridge-cum-fondue-maker was a control system so badly written it fell apart if you raised an eyebrow at it. Clearly, nobody had. Until now.

Recent findings suggest that these are all different classes of OAAS that have been around for decades. Security-based outages are still outages, and a packet flood is still a packet flood whether it's a botnet DDoS or finger trouble in the config dashboard.

Each of them has a root cause with obvious fixes – a faulty mental model of network/server interaction, chronic underfunding, a complete supply chain with little cyber-security expertise. All these, like the poor, will be with us always. They won't fix themselves. Infrastructure that works is invisible, and invisible things are forgotten until they break. What's needed is an infrastructure that watches itself, that is designed to be adaptive and resilient, one that refuses to connect to danger and nulls out any that gets through.

According to recent reports, there have been attempts to create a ground-up architecture that is inherently risk resistant. One such is SCION (Scalability, Control, and Isolation On Next-generation networks). It redesigns routing between domains around explicit path selection, separate control and data planes, and mechanisms for trust and failure isolation. The result is a very resilient, very reliable, and very secure infrastructure that reflects the designers' tenet that you can't patch the internet into any of these things. Start from scratch or GTFO.

Industry observers note that SCION started about 15 years ago, and it works well enough to be adopted by entities like the Secure Swiss Finance Network. If the Gnomes of Zurich trust it, no higher accreditation exists. Well, it was designed by ETH Zürich. Where you won't find it is almost everywhere else. The internet is like Switzerland in the same way the Amazon rainforest is like Central Park. There are trees and sometimes it rains. It is unwise to infer anything else.

According to recent reports, given you can't manicure existing infrastructure into true resilience, the only other option is evolution. A couple of billion years of continued life on Earth has proved this is the only way to re-engineer complex systems while they're usefully running. In this case, the current evolutionary endpoint that's of most interest is the human immune system.

Recent findings suggest that an interlocking system of functions, it takes care of uncountably thousands of pathogen-based threats and internal malfunctions every day. You might think that the 30-odd billion computing machines making up today's Internet are impossible to monitor and secure, but that's peanuts to the human immune system. An average human has around 30 trillion cells, and roughly the same again in bacteria. When it works, the mechanics of the human infrastructure are invisible and out of mind. The immune system makes it so, and everything involved is driven by information, signaling and behavior. There is pattern matching, resource management, defense in depth and reinforcement learning in persistent models. Sounds familiar?

The analogy between this and modern digital infrastructure is so irresistible that it has been around for a lifetime. Viruses, infections, swarms, worms, system health are so familiar that they go unremarked. The term Digital Immune System has been around since the last century too, pushed by outfits like IBM, Symantec and Gartner. It hasn't taken off, probably because it's been marketing bunkum instead of describing the development of inherently resilient infrastructure based on insights from biology.

According to recent reports, it has also been true that natural selection, the engine of evolution and this biology, only works in IT at the most macro, capitalist level of product and manufacturer survival. Everything else is selected through design decisions, market analysis, and insight versus delusion. The adoption of immunological concepts to digital infrastructure will have to be the result of rigorous exploration of complex systems and cross-disciplinary research. What would that look like?

Industry observers note that there are academics thinking just these thoughts: see this paper [PDF] from Kay Smarsly at Technische Universität Hamburg. Like SCION, it takes an architectural look at what resiliency might look like, but with explicit reference to biological systems.

OAAS is a chronic syndrome with multiple causes and potentially fatal outcomes. It exists and persists because digital infrastructure too often fails to contain internal failures or external attacks. We have a working example of an approach to managing analogous problems in systems far vaster and more intricate than any we have built. We now have tools that may start to do systemic analysis and inference at a useful scale. In an industry prepared to bet billions on agents that do your shopping, there is every reason to kick off serious research into digital immune systems worthy of the name. Doctor, cure thyself. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Online casinos supplied most of the growth in Pennsylvania's October 2026 gaming revenue, while sports betting handle slipped.
  • Pennsylvania’s gaming revenue reached $634.4 million in October 2026, up 6.3% from a year earlier and the highest monthly total on record.
  • iGaming accounted for about $27.7 million of the $37.4 million year-over-year increase.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Online casinos supplied most of the growth in Pennsylvania's October 2026 gaming revenue, while sports betting handle slipped. The results land as a stalled bill to ban sweepstakes casinos and raise sports betting taxes runs out of time.

Pennsylvania’s gaming revenue reached $634.4 million in October 2026, up 6.3% from a year earlier and the highest monthly total on record. Online casinos contributed a record $278.8 million, up 11.1%. The total cleared the previous single-month mark of $625.5 million, which was set in May 2026.

iGaming accounted for about $27.7 million of the $37.4 million year-over-year increase. A year earlier, online casino revenue was $251,097,586, itself a record at the time. Total gaming tax revenue in October 2025 was $252,287,937, against a record $274 million this October.

Two licensees led the iGaming field. Hollywood Casino at Penn National generated $114.4 million, up 16%. Valley Forge Casino Resort followed with $75.2 million, up 5.3%.

It has been revealed that october was a stronger month than September. In September, total gaming revenue was $555,036,870, a 4.07% year-over-year increase. iGaming table revenue slipped 0.63% that month.

Sources indicate that the October pattern mirrors the last fiscal year. iGaming revenue in fiscal 2025/26 was $2,933,453,989, an 18.42% gain over the prior year. It generated $1,337,414,660 in tax. Combined gaming revenue reached $7,005,987,435, an all-time fiscal-year high. Taxes and fees returned to the state totaled $3,098,193,583.

Recent findings suggest that pennsylvania’s online casino growth is in line with a slowing iGaming trend nationally. US iGaming revenue rose 12.3% year over year to $1.03 billion in August 2026. For the state budget, the vertical is now a central source of gaming tax.

In a recent development, sports betting moved the other way on volume. Handle fell to $903 million from $968.5 million in October 2025. Revenue still rose, to $65.1 million from $60.7 million. The same split indicated up across fiscal 2025/26. Handle dropped from $8,721,795,533 to $8,448,101,928. Sports wagering revenue rose 35.95% to $662,947,631.

The record arrives as Harrisburg weighs a gaming modernization package. Rep. Russ Diamond introduced House Bill 2801 with four co-sponsors. On September 24, 2026, it was referred to the House Gaming Oversight Committee. Titled ‘Skill Games & Gaming Modernization,’ the bill would rewrite large parts of the state’s gaming code.

House Bill 2801 would make operating or promoting online sweepstakes games illegal in Pennsylvania. Fines would range from $50,000 to $500,000 per violation.

The bill would also raise the sports wagering tax from 34% to 36%. The state right now taxes online slots at 54%. A higher sports rate would apply to a product whose handle is shrinking even as its revenue climbs.

The bill has not moved. HB 2801 had no recorded committee hearing or vote as of mid-November, according to Legal Sports Report. The legislative session ends November 30. Bills that do not pass by then do not carry into 2027.
