Visual Salamandra: Pushing the Boundaries of Multimodal Understanding

📅 11 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Language Technologies Lab takes a major step forward in multimodal artificial intelligence with the release of Visual Salamandra, extending the capabilities of the Salamandra large language model (LLM) to both images and video.
  • Designed with vision-language alignment at its core, Visual Salamandra builds on top of the Salamandra Instructed 7B model by integrating Google’s SigLIP encoder (SigLIP-So400m), a 2-layer MLP projector, and advanced late-fusion techniques to bridge the gap between visual and textual modalities.
  • The resulting architecture enables Visual Salamandra to comprehend and generate contextually accurate responses from diverse inputs, ranging from single and multiple images and videos to purely textual instructions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Language Technologies Lab takes a major step forward in multimodal artificial intelligence with the release of Visual Salamandra, extending the capabilities of the Salamandra large language model (LLM) to both images and video. Visual Salamandra is based on the 7 billion parameters foundational model maintaining its compactness and efficiency while extending it to multimodal tasks.

Designed with vision-language alignment at its core, Visual Salamandra builds on top of the Salamandra Instructed 7B model by integrating Google’s SigLIP encoder (SigLIP-So400m), a 2-layer MLP projector, and advanced late-fusion techniques to bridge the gap between visual and textual modalities.

The resulting architecture enables Visual Salamandra to comprehend and generate contextually accurate responses from diverse inputs, ranging from single and multiple images and videos to purely textual instructions. This development reflects a broader commitment by the Lab to support robust, multilingual, and multimodal AI systems—especially those that prioritize European linguistic diversity.

It has been revealed that to adapt Salamandra for visual inputs, the Lab implemented a four-phase training process centered on late-fusion architecture. In this setup, a pre-trained image encoder (SigLIP, 14 patches at 384x384 resolution) generates image embeddings, which are then aligned with the LLM via a custom-trained multilayer perceptron (MLP) projector.

The four training phases include:.

• Phase 1: Projector Pre-training – Only the projector is trained to map image features into the LLM’s latent space.

• Phase 2: High-Quality Vision Pretraining – Using refined datasets (e.g., OCR and re-captioned images), the entire architecture (encoder, projector, and LLM) undergoes joint training.

• Phase 3: Instruction Tuning – The model learns to follow user instructions via visual question answering (VQA), OCR, and other grounded vision tasks.

• Phase 4: Full Multimodal Tuning – Incorporates single/multi-image and video data, along with text-only examples, to optimize the model’s generalization to real-world, multi-input scenarios.

Data diversity played a crucial role throughout training. A total of 6.1 million instruction-tuning instances were used, including 842,000 text-only samples. The training corpus featured data from sources like AI2D, Cambrian, and LLaVA Next, chosen to enhance visual grounding, document understanding, mathematical reasoning, and OCR.

Figure 1. Data distribution during the Visual Salamandra 7B training process.

As with previous models from the Language Technologies Lab, Visual Salamandra continues the commitment to multilingual inclusivity, with a strong focus on European languages.

According to recent reports, this approach guarantees that underrepresented languages benefit from instruction tuning and alignment with vision tasks, helping to close the resource gap in multimodal AI research. Visual Salamandra is one of the first models of its kind to integrate such linguistic plurality into a multimodal instruction-tuned framework.

According to recent reports, figure 2. Multilingual generation examples with the model trained with Text Regularization and merged with the original backbone LLM.

Visual Salamandra unlocks a wide range of applications at the intersection of language and vision, such as:.

• Visual Question Answering (VQA): Ask questions about an image or video and receive context-aware, accurate responses.

• Optical Character Recognition (OCR): Accurately read and transcribe text from documents, scenes, and charts.

• Document and Chart Understanding: Analyze complex visual documents or graphical content with embedded text.

• Mathematical Reasoning: Solve visually grounded math problems through multimodal reasoning.

• Instruction-based Image Interaction: Follow detailed instructions in visual contexts, including image captioning and localization tasks.

The inclusion of video capabilities also opens the door for further developments in video summarization, event detection, and multimodal storytelling...

Sources indicate that with Visual Salamandra, the Language Technologies Lab demonstrates its ongoing leadership in creating inclusive, high-performing foundational models. By harmonizing state-of-the-art vision encoders with strong multilingual LLMs, the team is setting the stage for next-generation AI systems that see, understand, and communicate—across modalities and languages.

While Visual Salamandra reveals strong multimodal capabilities, it is vital to note its limitations:.

• It may hallucinate plausible but incorrect answers, especially when visual inputs are ambiguous.

• Performance on complex OCR and dense document layouts is still challenging.

• The model was trained with filtered and licensed datasets, but customers should remain vigilant about potential biases or inaccuracies, particularly when deployed in sensitive applications.

We recommend using Visual Salamandra in contexts where human oversight is possible and avoiding high-stakes applications without proper evaluation.

Visual Salamandra is released under a Apache License, Version 2.0, allowing for research and non-commercial use.

Stay tunned for future releases and tools built on Visual Salamandra, and explore the full model details in our paper.

The Language Technologies Lab team.

This work has been supported and funded by the Ministerio para la Transformación Digital y de la Función Pública and the Plan de Recuperación, Transformación y Resiliencia – funded by the EU through NextGenerationEU, within the framework of the Modelos del Lenguaje project.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Planemaker's 2-to-3-year plan to ditch Redmond's suite stops short of the 22% who can't go near the cloud.
  • Airbus has a plan to phase out Microsoft Office, but about 22 percent of its roughly 165,000 employees will stay on it because their sensitive data must remain on-premise.
  • It has been revealed that in March 2018, Airbus signed a contract with Google to move its workforce - 130,000 strong at that time - onto the cloud-based Workspace suite.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Planemaker's 2-to-3-year plan to ditch Redmond's suite stops short of the 22% who can't go near the cloud.

Airbus has a plan to phase out Microsoft Office, but about 22 percent of its roughly 165,000 employees will stay on it because their sensitive data must remain on-premise.

It has been revealed that in March 2018, Airbus signed a contract with Google to move its workforce - 130,000 strong at that time - onto the cloud-based Workspace suite. Years later, compatibility issues mean some customers still need Excel.

Catherine Jestin, Airbus's executive vice president of digital, told The Register that Google is still working to resolve software interface conflicts between departments and improve features.

Last year, for example, Google tripled the number of cells available in Sheets, which let Airbus "reduce significantly the number of users on Microsoft." This year, Google improved the compatibility of document watermarking. Contracts, for instance, are often exported from Excel to Sheets by one department, edited by another, and sent back.

"Sometimes we had compatibility problems when you were commenting, the comments were lost, or they were not transferable in one way or the other," she stated.

"Now they [Google] have made it totally compatible, which means that it makes it much easier for us to decommission people working on contracts… the legal department, the sales department, purchasing department, making it much easier to have that internal collaboration.".

Industry observers note that airbus and Google have a roadmap to eliminate Microsoft Office. Jestin expects the migration to finish in "another two to three years.".

Recent findings suggest that not every part of the firm will switch. The Defence division, which accounts for the 22 percent (more than 36,000 people), will keep using classic Microsoft Office.

Industry observers note that "We will not get 100 percent out of Microsoft because again, for the defense industry people, they cannot [use] Microsoft Office 365 or Google Workspace, they have to stay on-premise, and the only solution that is available on-premise is Microsoft. So Microsoft Office will remain for colleagues who are working in the defense and space programs.".

Industry observers note that as we pointed out a year ago, kicking the Microsoft habit is no easy feat. ®.

4M Models Scanned: Protect AI + Hugging Face 6 Months In

📅 14 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1477 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hugging Face and Protect AI partnered in October 2024 to enhance machine learning (ML) model security through Guardian’s scanning technology for the community of developers who explore and use models from the Hugging Face Hub.
  • Since October, Protect AI has significantly expanded Guardian's detection capabilities, improving existing threat detection capabilities and launching four fresh detection modules:.
  • Recent findings suggest that with these updates, Guardian covers more model file formats and detects additional sophisticated obfuscation techniques, including the high severity CVE-2025-1550 vulnerability in Keras.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face and Protect AI partnered in October 2024 to enhance machine learning (ML) model security through Guardian’s scanning technology for the community of developers who explore and use models from the Hugging Face Hub. The partnership has been a natural fit from the start—Hugging Face is on a mission to democratize the use of open source AI, with a commitment to safety and security; and Protect AI is building the guardrails to make open source models safe for all.

Since October, Protect AI has significantly expanded Guardian's detection capabilities, improving existing threat detection capabilities and launching four fresh detection modules:.

Recent findings suggest that with these updates, Guardian covers more model file formats and detects additional sophisticated obfuscation techniques, including the high severity CVE-2025-1550 vulnerability in Keras. Through enhanced detection tooling, Hugging Face customers receive critical security information via inline alerts on the platform and gain access to comprehensive vulnerability reports on Insights DB. Clearly labeled findings are available on each model page, empowering users to make more informed decisions about which models to integrate into their projects.

As of April 1, 2025, Protect AI has successfully scanned 4.47 million unique model versions in 1.41 million repositories on the Hugging Face Hub.

It has been revealed that to date, Protect AI has identified a total of 352,000 unsafe/suspicious issues across 51,700 models. In just the last 30 days, Protect AI has served 226 million requests from Hugging Face at a 7.94 ms response time.

Recent findings suggest that protect AI’s Guardian applies a zero trust approach to AI/ML security. This especially comes into play when treating arbitrary code execution as inherently unsafe, regardless of intent. Rather than just classifying overtly malicious threats, Guardian flags execution risks as suspicious on InsightsDB, recognizing that even harmful code can look innocuous through obfuscation techniques (see more on payload obfuscation below). Attackers can disguise payloads within seemingly benign scripts or extensibility components of a framework, making payload inspection alone insufficient for ensuring security. By maintaining this cautious approach, Guardian helps mitigate risks posed by hidden threats in machine learning models.

Sources indicate that AI/ML security threats are evolving every single day. That's why Protect AI leverages both in-house threat research teams and huntr—the world's first and largest AI/ML bug bounty program powered by our community of over 17,000 security researchers.

Sources indicate that coinciding with our partnership launch in October, Protect AI rolled out a latest program on huntr to crowdsource research on new Model File Vulnerabilities. Since the launch of the program, they have received over 200 reports that Protect AI teams have worked through and incorporated into Guardian—all of which are automatically applied to the model scans here on Hugging Face.

As more huntr reports come in and more independent threat research is conducted, certain trends have emerged.

Industry observers note that library-dependent attack chains: These attacks focus on a bad actor’s ability to invoke functions from libraries present in the ML workstations environment. These are reminiscent of the “drive-by download” style of attacks that afflicted browsers and systems when common utilities like Java and Flash were present. Typically, the scale of impact of these attacks are proportional to the pervasiveness of a given library, with common ML libraries like Pytorch having a far wider potential impact than lesser used libraries.

It has been revealed that payload obfuscation: Several reports have highlighted ways to insert, obfuscate, or “hide” a payload in a model that bypasses common scanning techniques. These vulnerabilities use techniques like compression, encoding, and serialization to obfuscate the payload and are not easily detectable. Compression is an concern since libraries like Joblib allow compressed payloads to be loaded directly. Container formats like Keras and NeMo embed additional model files, each potentially vulnerable to their own specific attack vectors. Compression exposes users to TarSlip or ZipSlip vulnerabilities. While the impacts of these will often be limited to Denial of Service, in certain circumstances these vulnerabilities can lead to Arbitrary Code Execution by leveraging path traversal techniques, allowing malicious attackers to overwrite files that are often automatically executed.

Recent findings suggest that framework-extensibility vulnerabilities: ML frameworks provide numerous extensibility mechanisms that inadvertently create dangerous attack vectors: custom layers, external code dependencies, and configuration-based code loading. For example, CVE-2025-1550 in Keras, reported to us by the huntr community, demonstrates how custom layers can be exploited to execute arbitrary code despite security features. Configuration files with serialization vulnerabilities similarly allow dynamic code loading. These deserialization vulnerabilities make models exploitable through crafted payloads embedded in formats that owners load without suspicion. Despite security improvements from vendors, older vulnerable versions and insecure dependency handling continue to present significant risk in ML ecosystems.

Attack vector chaining: Recent reports demonstrate how multiple vulnerabilities can be combined to create sophisticated attack chains that can bypass detection. By sequentially exploiting vulnerabilities like obfuscated payloads and extension mechanisms, researchers have shown complex pathways for compromise that appear benign when examined individually. This approach significantly complicates detection and mitigation efforts, as security tools focused on single-vector threats often miss these compound attacks. Effective defense requires identifying and addressing all links in the attack chain rather than treating each vulnerability in isolation.

Sources indicate that the industry-leading Protect AI threat research team, with help from the huntr community, is continuously gathering data and insights in order to develop new and more robust model scans as well as automatic threat blocking (available to Guardian customers). In the last few months, Guardian has:.

Enhanced detection of library-dependent attacks: Significant expansion of Guardian’s scanning capabilities for detecting library-dependent attack vectors. The scanners for PyTorch and Pickle now perform deep structure analysis of serialized code, examining execution paths and identifying potentially malicious code patterns that could be triggered through library dependencies. For example, the PyTorch torchvision.io functions can overwrite any file on the victim’s system to either include a payload or delete all of its content. Guardian can now detect many more of these dangerous functions in popular libraries such as PyTorch, Numpy, and Pandas.

Uncovered obfuscated attacks: Guardian performs multi-layered analyses across various archive formats, decompressing nested archives and examining compressed payloads for malicious models. This approach detects attempts to hide malicious code through compression, encoding, or serialization techniques. Joblib, for example, supports saving models using different compression formats which can obfuscate Pickle deserialization vulnerabilities, and the same can be done in other formats like Keras which can include Numpy weights files that have deserialization payloads in them.

Detected exploits in framework extensibility components: Guardian’s constantly improving detection modules alerted users on Hugging Face to models that were impacted by CVE-2025-1550 (a critical security finding) before the vulnerability was publicly disclosed. These detection modules comprehensively analyze ML framework extension mechanisms, allowing only standard or verified components and blocking potentially dangerous implementations, regardless of their apparent intent.

Identified additional architectural backdoors: Guardian’s architectural backdoor detection capabilities were expanded beyond ONNX formats to include additional model formats like TensorFlow.

Expanded model format coverage: Guardian’s true strength comes from the depth of its coverage, which has driven substantial expansion of detection modules to include additional formats like Joblib and an increasingly popular llamafile format, with support for additional ML frameworks coming soon.

It has been revealed that provided deeper model analysis: Actively research on additional ways to augment current detection capabilities for better analysis and detection of unsafe models. Expect to see significant enhancements in reducing both false positives and false negatives in the near future.

Through the partnership with Protect AI and Hugging Face, we’ve made third-party ML models safer and more accessible. We believe that having more eyes on model security can only be a good thing. We’re increasingly seeing the security world pay attention and lean in, making threats more discoverable and AI usage safer for all.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Since Hugging Face started the LeRobot library in 2024, led by ex-Tesla lead Remi Cadene, the Hugging Face Hub has promptly become the most widely used hub and software platform for open robotics with models, datasets, spaces and libraries.

Since Hugging Face started the LeRobot library in 2024, led by ex-Tesla lead Remi Cadene, the Hugging Face Hub has promptly become the most widely used hub and software platform for open robotics with models, datasets, spaces and libraries.

Today, we’re excited to take it a step further by welcoming Pollen Robotics to Hugging Face, a team that's spent the last 9 years building open-source robots and hardware.

We believe robotics could be the next frontier unlocked by AI — and it should be open, affordable, and private. Our vision: a future where everyone in the community, from hobbyists to enterprises, can build or use robot assistants or games, starting from open solutions instead of closed, remote controlled, hardware.

From the start, we built Pollen Robotics with open source at its core, driven by our belief that robots will play a profound role in our lives — serving as the interface between AI and the physical world. Hugging Face is a natural home for us to grow, as we share a common goal: putting AI and robotics in the hands of everyone.

This marks the fifth acquisition for Hugging Face, after notable additions like Gradio and XetHub.

According to Clem's 2025 prediction about robots, "at least 100k personal robots will be pre-ordered" this year, signaling massive growth in the space.

Sources indicate that this month also celebrates one year since Hugging Face created LeRobot. The community of LeRobot-native DIY robot builders has flourished on YouTube and Discord, truly democratizing access to robotics technology. In just twelve months, the GitHub repository has grown from zero to over 12,000 stars, with dramatic growth continuing into 2025.

Recent findings suggest that the first robot we’re offering is Reachy 2 — your friendly little lab partner for the AI era that is already in use in labs like Cornell or Carnegie Mellon. It’s a state-of-the-art humanoid robot that is open-source & VR-compatible, built for research, education, and embodied AI experiments. You can already order one for $70,000 by emailing sales@pollen-robotics.com.

In a recent development, hugging Face is the most used platform for AI builders, with over 7 million users and a thriving community of researchers, developers, and organizations. Founded by Clément Delangue (CEO), Julien Chaumond (CTO), and Thomas Wolf (CSO), the company has become a central hub for AI, hosting the most popular open-source models and datasets, including Meta’s LLaMA 4, DeepSeek R1, Stable Diffusion, Black Forest Flux, Mistral, OpenAI Whisper and millions of others. Its AI app store features over 500,000 ready-to-use applications called spaces, making state-of-the-art AI accessible to all. Hugging Face has raised over $395 million to date from leading investors including Google, Amazon, Nvidia, Salesforce, Sequoia, Coatue, Lux Capital, and Addition.

According to recent reports, pollen Robotics, established in 2016, is a leading developer of open-source humanoid robots designed for advanced research and real-world applications. Founded by former researchers from Inria's Flowers team, including Matthieu Lapeyre and Pierre Rouanet, the firm leverages years of experience at the intersection of robotics hardware and applied artificial intelligence, to develop innovative and user-friendly robotic platforms. Reachy 2 is the latest generation of Pollen Robotics’ flagship humanoid robot. Designed as a versatile platform for embodied AI, Reachy 2 combines advanced hardware with user-friendly software, enabling intuitive interactions and agile manipulation. With open-source hardware and software at its core, Reachy 2 provides researchers, and developers unprecedented freedom to explore human-robot interactions, machine learning applications, and practical AI-driven tasks.

According to recent reports, reachy has been adopted by esteemed institutions such as Accenture, CEA, CNRS, Cornell University, and Carnegie Mellon University, underscoring its versatility in fields ranging from advanced AI research to practical manipulation tasks. Pollen Robotics has won several awards including second place at the prestigious ANA Avatar XPRIZE in 2022, highlighting its innovative prowess in remote presence, dexterous manipulation and control technologies.

With hundreds of units deployed across more than 20 countries, Pollen Robotics has redefined the capabilities of open-source humanoid robots, fostering collaboration and customization in the global robotics community.

What an AI Marketing Agent Actually Does, and How to Build a Guarded One

An AI marketing agent is a system that pairs a language model with access to real tools, such as a CRM, an ad platform API or a CMS, and lets it work toward a goal instead of following a fixed script. That is the core idea. Much of what gets labeled agentic marketing is either a wrapper around that loop or a scheduled job with a new name.

This article breaks down the mechanics in code terms, walks through a minimal guarded agent loop with tests, and gives a framework for deciding what to build, what to buy and what to keep away from any autonomous system. Product capabilities change quickly, so check each vendor's current documentation.

According to recent reports, ● An agent is a goal, a tool set and a loop. The model chooses the next action at runtime instead of following branches you wrote in advance.

● Guardrails belong in code. Spend caps, allow-lists and approval thresholds should never depend on the prompt.

It has been revealed that ● The prototype is the easy part. Validation, retries, logging and evaluation are where the weeks go.

● Match autonomy to reversibility. Let agents do reversible, measurable work and keep irreversible actions supervised.

● Treat vendor claims as claims. Ask for logs and test on your own data.

According to recent reports, many marketing features have been renamed in the last couple of years. Email sequencing, lead scoring and campaign tools are now often described as agents. The honest question is whether a given product is a real architecture shift or marketing automation with a chat box added. Both exist: some systems run a perceive-reason-act loop with dynamic tool selection, while others are if/else branches with a model writing the subject line.

Strip away the marketing language and an agent has three parts:.

● A goal, expressed in natural language or as a measurable target.

● A tool set: functions the model is allowed to call, each described by a schema.

● A loop that runs until the goal is met, a limit is hit or a human steps in.

According to recent reports, the reasoning step is a model call. You pass it the current state, the goal and the available tools, and it responds with text or a structured request to call a tool. Your code runs the call, feeds the result back and asks again. OpenAI's function calling guide describes this as a conversation between your application and the model, which is the primitive underneath most agent frameworks.

Industry observers note that compare that with a cron job. A cron job runs a rule such as pausing ads below a click-through threshold every morning. It cannot decide that cost per acquisition matters more than click-through this week. An agent can, because the branching is chosen at runtime by a model rather than at write time by you. A useful test: if you can draw the full decision tree before the system runs, it is automation. If the path depends on what the model decides after seeing the data, it is an agent.

● Perceive. Read current state from an ad platform's reporting endpoint, a CRM webhook or a database. Ordinary code, no model involved.

Sources indicate that ● Reason. One model call containing the goal, the state, a summary of past actions and the schemas of every tool the agent may use.

According to recent reports, ● Act. The model returns a structured tool call. Your code validates the arguments against the schema and your guardrails, then executes.

Sources indicate that ● Observe. Capture the result, including failures. A rate-limit error or validation error is information for the next step.

According to recent reports, ● Update memory. Record the action and outcome so the agent does not repeat itself.

● Repeat or stop. Loop until the goal is met, an iteration cap is reached or a guardrail escalates to a human.

Steps two and three rely on function calling, where tools are declared with typed parameters and the model returns matching arguments. The Hugging Face function calling guide shows the same pattern. For connecting tools across systems, the Model Context Protocol is an open protocol for integrating LLM applications with external data sources and tools. Instead of writing an adapter for every CRM and ad account, you point an MCP client at a server that exposes those tools with discoverable schemas.

Lead scoring and routing. The agent reads CRM state, enriches it with lookups, scores the lead and writes back an owner and next action. It is agentic when it chooses which enrichment tools to call based on what is missing, and not agentic when the score is a fixed model output piped into a rule.

In a recent development, ad creative generation and testing. The agent produces variations from brand inputs, debuts a structured test, reads performance data and shifts budget toward what works. This is among the clearest closed feedback loops because the outcome signal is numeric and fast.

IBM's overview of AI agents in marketing frames a similar progression, from scripted chatbots at one end to agents that decide, design workflows and use function calling at the other. Most products sit somewhere in between.

Vendors sometimes blur this line. Four criteria help even from the outside:.

According to recent reports, practical tests: give it a goal it has no preset workflow for and see whether it composes a path or returns an apology. Change the data mid-run and check whether the next step differs. Ask for the tool call log, because a real agent produces one. Ask what happens when a tool call fails; a script throws, while an agent should retry or re-plan.

Three questions decide this, and none are about how clever the model is: can errors be detected promptly, can the action be reversed, and what does one bad decision cost?

● Reasonable to hand over: drafting copy variations, summarizing campaign performance, flagging data mismatches, writing internal briefs, pausing clearly underperforming ads.

● Keep supervised: budget reallocation across accounts, legal, medical or financial claims, pricing and discount changes, messages to named customers and final brand-voice sign-off.

A human approval step costs minutes. An unsupervised mistake in those areas can cost far more.

Sources indicate that for many teams the practical answer is to build the orchestration that touches proprietary data and internal systems, and to evaluate off-the-shelf tools for narrow, high-volume tasks that other teams have already solved. What people underestimate when building is not the prototype, which can take an afternoon, but everything after: schema validation, retries, idempotency, rate-limit handling, prompt versioning, cost controls, an audit log and an evaluation harness.

According to recent reports, ad creative is a common candidate for the existing-tool route because volume is high and the loop is similar across businesses. Vendors in this space describe their products differently, so compare scope, integrations and pricing. As one example, Larven describes an AI marketing agent that runs Meta ads, pulls products and copy from a store such as Shopify, and connects to your own ad account. Treat any such description as the vendor's own, and verify it with a trial on your data before committing.

Recent findings suggest that the goal: keep spend inside a daily cap while letting a model propose budget changes. The model is injected as a function, so you can wire in any provider's function-calling API or a stub for tests. The important part is that every limit is enforced in code. The model proposes, and your code decides.

"""A minimal guarded agent loop. The model is injected as a function, so you can swap in any provider's function-calling API, or a stub for tests.""" from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclass class Guardrails:     allowed_campaigns: set     daily_cap: float            # max total daily budget across campaigns     max_change_pct: float = 0.2 # larger single changes need a human     max_actions: int = 5        # per run @dataclass class State:     budgets: dict               # campaign_id -> daily budget     log: list = field(default_factory=list)     pending: list = field(default_factory=list) def check(call, state, g):     """Return 'run', 'approve' or ('deny', reason). Enforced in code, never by the prompt."""     if call["name"] != "adjust_budget":         return ("deny", "unknown tool")     cid, upcoming = call["args"]["campaign_id"], call["args"]["new_daily_budget"]     if cid not in g.allowed_campaigns or cid not in state.budgets:         return ("deny", "campaign not allowed")     if new < 0:         return ("deny", "negative budget")     others = sum(v for k, v in state.budgets.items() if k != cid)     if others + new > g.daily_cap:         return ("deny", "daily cap exceeded")     old = state.budgets[cid]     if old and abs(new - old) / old > g.max_change_pct:         return "approve"     return "run" def run(model, state, g):     """model(state) -> a tool call dict, or None when it has nothing to do."""     for in range(g.maxactions):         call = model(state)         if call is None:             break         verdict = check(call, state, g)         state.log.append({"call": call, "verdict": verdict})         if verdict == "run":             state.budgets[call["args"]["campaign_id"]] = call["args"]["new_daily_budget"]         elif verdict == "approve":             state.pending.append(call)     return state.

Sources indicate that the tests use a stub in place of a model. They confirm that small changes run, large changes wait for approval, the daily cap and allow-list are enforced, an unknown tool is denied, and a model that never stops is halted by the action limit with everything logged:.

from agent_loop import Guardrails, State, check, run G = Guardrails(allowed_campaigns={"a", "b"}, daily_cap=200) def call(cid, new): return {"name": "adjust_budget", "args": {"campaign_id": cid, "new_daily_budget": new}} def test_small_change_runs():     assert check(call("a", 105), State({"a": 100, "b": 50}), G) == "run" def test_large_change_needs_approval():     assert check(call("a", 150), State({"a": 100, "b": 50}), G) == "approve" def test_cap_and_allow_list_are_enforced():     s = State({"a": 100, "b": 90, "c": 10})     assert check(call("a", 115), s, G) == ("deny", "daily cap exceeded")     assert check(call("c", 11), s, G) == ("deny", "campaign not allowed")     assert check({"name": "delete_account", "args": {}}, s, G) == ("deny", "unknown tool") def test_loop_stops_at_action_limit_and_logs_everything():     s = State({"a": 100, "b": 50})     g = Guardrails({"a", "b"}, 500, max_actions=3)     run(lambda st: call("a", st.budgets["a"] + 1), s, g)   # a model that never stops     assert len(s.log) == 3 and s.budgets["a"] == 103 def test_denied_and_pending_actions_do_not_change_budgets():     s = State({"a": 100, "b": 50})     g = Guardrails({"a", "b"}, 500)     seq = iter([call("a", 150), call("a", 600), None])   # needs approval, then breaks the cap     run(lambda st: next(seq), s, g)     assert s.budgets["a"] == 100 and len(s.pending) == 1.

Run them with pytest. In a real deployment, the model function would call your provider with the state, the goal and the tool schemas, then return the parsed tool call.

In a recent development, ● It handles one tool. A real agent needs several, such as reporting, pausing ads and requesting approval.

Sources indicate that ● It keeps state in memory. Production systems need a durable store and idempotent actions so a retry cannot apply a change twice.

● The thresholds are placeholders. Set your own caps and percentages from your spend and risk tolerance.

● It validates the call but not the data. If upstream numbers are wrong, the agent will act on them.

In a recent development, runaway spend. Budget APIs act instantly and changes compound. Without a hard ceiling in your own code, a reasoning error becomes a billing event.

Recent findings suggest that dirty upstream data. Stale CRM records, a broken product feed or a misattributed conversion. The agent can act confidently on wrong inputs and leave a tidy audit trail of well-reasoned bad decisions.

According to recent reports, missing audit trails. If you cannot reconstruct why an agent acted, you cannot fix or defend it. Deloitte's State of AI in the Enterprise reports that close to three-quarters of companies proposal to deploy agentic AI within two years, and that only 21% of those companies report having a mature model for agent governance.

● Least-privilege credentials. A separate API key per agent, scoped to exactly what it needs, never a shared admin token.

● Hard caps in code. Daily spend ceilings and a maximum percentage change per adjustment, enforced outside the model.

● Human-in-the-loop thresholds. Define which actions always need approval.

● Log every tool call. Inputs, outputs, errors, model and prompt version, with timestamps you can query.

● Start read-only. Run in suggest mode and compare recommendations with what your team would have done.

A system that pairs a language model with real tools and lets it pursue a goal. It reads state, decides on an action, executes it, observes the result and decides again.

Recent findings suggest that automation starts from a trigger and follows branches defined in advance. An agent starts from a goal and selects tools at runtime.

Industry observers note that not on current evidence. They handle high-volume, measurable, reversible work well. Strategy, positioning and final brand approval still sit with people.

Function calling, where tools are declared by schema and the model returns matching arguments, and increasingly the Model Context Protocol for connecting tools.

Recent findings suggest that it depends on how swiftly errors are detected, whether actions are reversible and what a bad decision costs. Automate the cheap and reversible; supervise the rest.

Wrong tool calls, runaway spend, confident action on dirty data and brand drift at scale. Missing audit trails make all of them harder to diagnose.

An AI marketing agent is less magic than it sounds: a goal, a set of tools and a loop with limits. The model's intelligence matters, but the system around it decides whether it is safe to run. Define the tools narrowly, enforce limits in code, log everything, start read-only and widen autonomy only as the evidence supports it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Xfce lines up 4.22 for 2027, while MATE gains an Ubuntu-based distro and a compositor of its own.
  • Xfce's next release is taking shape for 2027, while MATE owners have fresh options for moving their familiar desktop onto Wayland.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Xfce lines up 4.22 for 2027, while MATE gains an Ubuntu-based distro and a compositor of its own.

Xfce's next release is taking shape for 2027, while MATE owners have fresh options for moving their familiar desktop onto Wayland.

According to recent reports, one of the oldest surviving Linux desktops has a relatively slow release schedule: new stable releases of Xfce tend to appear every two years. The project just updated its release engineering roadmap for the forthcoming Xfce 4.22, and it looks like the next version won't arrive until early next year.

According to recent reports, we covered the release of Xfce 4.20 in December 2024, but 4.22 is still incubating. The roadmap schedules its first prerelease and feature freeze for December 15, 2026, followed by a second prerelease on January 15, 2027. A third prerelease is optional, and neither that nor the final release has a date. February or March might be plausible, but that's our guess, not the project's promise. The Xfce developers tend not to rush into things.

Wayland development continues in 4.22, building on the preliminary support in 4.20. The team is also working on its own compositor, xfwl4, although the roadmap doesn't promise feature parity with X11. (In Wayland terminology, the "compositor" is the combined display server and window manager.) The compositor has its own development roadmap. The name is a nod to the current Xfce X11 window manager, which is called xfwm4.

Recent findings suggest that the main developer of the fresh xfwl4 compositor is Brian Tarricone, who has been working on other parts of Xfce since 2004. Back in July, he shared a blog post about his use of generative-AI coding assistants called LLMs and xfwl4.

It has been revealed that he states: "So yes, I use Claude quite a bit while developing xfwl4. I don't vibe-code, ever, and I probably use the LLM to generate less code than most people do. After all, building things with code is my hobby and passion (and I'm lucky I got to do it professionally for a quarter century), and driving an LLM is kinda boring.".

We find this somewhat reassuring, but any really passionate anti-LLM Xfce users reading this may be glad that the release schedules of Ubuntu LTS versions and Xfce stable releases are so far out of sync – sticking with Xubuntu 26.04 means there's no immediate need to adopt the newly introduced LLM-assisted compositor. Or, of course, simply keep using X11 instead of Wayland – although that might eventually mean choosing a distro that maintains X11 support, perhaps through XLibre, which has other drawbacks for some.

In a recent development, there are other options, too. We've also seen an independent fork of xfwm4 called xfwm4-gl. It's in active development and uses OpenGL to perform window compositing directly, while the current version uses the now rather old Xrender extension.

It has been revealed that last year, when we looked at the release candidate of openSUSE Leap 16.0, we found that it ran Xfce on Wayland by replacing Xfwm4 with the labwc compositor that we first saw in PiOS 5.2. This worked well – about the only difference we could find was the absence of some window-management shortcuts.

Recent findings suggest that (Saying that, this vulture is still happy with X11. There is only one Wayland feature we want: the ability to set different dots-per-inch ratios on different screens. We can approximate that on X11 by scaling individual outputs. This works well enough – it just makes one of the screens look a little fuzzy.).

According to recent reports, labwc is one of the more flexible, and X11-like, compositors out there, and can be found in other projects. Scott Sturrock recently wrote to us to tell us about his latest MATE Wayland Desktop project. This is an independent distro, combining an Ubuntu 26.04 base, the latest MATE 1.29, and version 0.9 of the labwc compositor. (That's from labwc's older 0.9 series; the latest release is 0.20.3. The numbering jumped to align with the version of wlroots it uses, while 0.9 remains a maintenance branch.).

Industry observers note that MATE is a continuing fork of GNOME 2.32, the final release of GNOME 2. GNOME 2 used the Metacity X11 window manager – indeed, the Windows-like GNOME Flashback session still uses Metacity, which is currently at version 3.56.0. MATE's fork of Metacity is called Marco.

It has been revealed that there is already a way to run MATE using Wayland: the MATE Wayland Session uses the Wayfire compositor. Wayfire was inspired by Compiz, the 3D compositing window manager remembered for its "wobbly windows" effect, and Wayfire has lots of its own special effects, as the Wayfire wiki's tutorial demonstrates with a lot of animated images. Wayfire is quite a capable environment in its own right – so, arguably, somewhat overkill for the traditional-style MATE environment.

As yet another alternative, developer Kerem Söke recently unveiled a fresh MATE-specific compositor called Polo. Polo is intended as a direct replacement for Marco. The Polo 1.0 release notes tell some of the story. Polo aims to be as similar as it can to the familiar Marco window manager: it picks up existing configuration, keystrokes, Alt-Tab behaviour, and so on. It's already at version 1.0.2. It can do wobbly windows and so on as well, it has its own polo-tweaks program, and a roadmap for improving MATE's integration with Wayland.

Both projects went public around the same time, but MATE Wayland Desktop is already packaged up and ready to install. We suspect that if Polo is successful, it will find its way into the Ubuntu repositories, and perhaps the two projects will eventually come together.

Xfce is about a year older than KDE – however, the early releases of Xfce weren't open source. So, KDE is the oldest Linux desktop that has been open source from the start.

It has been revealed that xfce isn't the oldest Linux desktop of all, though. There were some proprietary commercial desktop environments around before either Xfce or KDE existed, such as IXI's X.desktop [PDF]. Most originally ran on commercial Unixes and were later ported to Linux – but they didn't stick around into the modern FOSS era. ®.

Industry observers note that in our previous posts - Easy FunctionGemma finetuning with Tunix on Google TPUs and Autonomous LLM post-training with Tunix on TPUs - we revealed how Google Tunix streamlines Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and single-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Cloud TPUs. Real-world AI agents, however, rarely finish their job in a single turn. They have to reason over partial observations, invoke tools, observe environment feedback, and adapt their strategy across multiple steps. So in this post, we will walk through how to train a multi-turn, tool-using LLM agent using Tunix's agentic reinforcement learning pipeline on Cloud TPU v6e-8. You can find the complete code in this GitHub repository.

We will revisit the Plane Strike board game from an earlier TensorFlow/JAX reinforcement learning blog, replacing the custom MLP policy with Gemma 4 E2B in thinking mode on a single Cloud TPU v6e-8 host. Plane Strike is played on a 6x6 grid (A1 to F6) where one 8-cell plane is hidden in one of 4 orientations. Each turn, the agent sees the result of its previous strike and the raw visible board (. untried, X hit, O miss), thinks through candidate placements, and calls the strike(cell="...") tool to strike one cell. The game ends when all 8 plane cells are hit, or after 23 strikes.

  • Adam Schiff and John Curtis are the sponsors of the DEATH BETS Act.
  • In a recent development, under the measure, any exchange registered with the CFTC would lose the ability to list or clear contracts on a person’s death, terrorism, assassination, war or US military operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US Senate has unanimously passed a bill that would ban death, war and terrorism contracts on CFTC-registered prediction-market exchanges. The vote would turn regulatory discretion into a statutory ban just as the CFTC proposes looser rules, and the House has only weeks to act.

Sens. Adam Schiff and John Curtis are the sponsors of the DEATH BETS Act. It is the first prediction-market bill the Senate has passed this Congress. The measure now heads to the House.

In a recent development, under the measure, any exchange registered with the CFTC would lose the ability to list or clear contracts on a person’s death, terrorism, assassination, war or US military operations. Sports contracts are not covered.

Sources indicate that curtis made a moral case for the bill on the Senate floor. “There should be no financial incentive to profit from terrorism, war, or the death of another human being,” he remarked.

Whether such contracts can trade at the moment rests on the CFTC’s discretion. The bill would replace that discretion with a prohibition written into statute.

The timing puts lawmakers and the regulator on different tracks. CFTC Chair Selig plans to rewrite the prediction-market rules. The agency’s proposed rule would amend Regulation 40.11 and add Appendix F to Part 40. The agency would use that framework to decide when a contract linked to war, terrorism, assassination, gaming or illegal conduct is against the public interest.

That framework would give the agency more room, not less. The proposal would say only that the CFTC may find such contracts contrary to the public interest, dropping the categorical prohibitions in the current rule, according to the Congressional Research Service. The agency withdrew a stricter 2024 proposal in February 2026.

For exchanges, the difference is significant. An agency can revise a rule through its own process. A ban in statute would keep those categories off the table regardless of how the CFTC’s rules change.

In a recent development, the DEATH BETS Act targets a specific set of contracts. Sports is a different matter for operators. Schiff and Curtis have also introduced the Prediction Markets Are Gambling Act. That bill would bar sports-betting and casino-style contracts on these exchanges.

According to recent reports, A unanimous vote on death and war contracts does not prove the same support exists for a sports ban. It does show that senators are willing to legislate directly on what prediction markets can list, rather than leave the question to the CFTC.

That makes the vote an early sign of how much support Congress has for limiting these platforms. It comes while the exchanges are fighting state gambling regulators in court. Operators now face pressure from state regulators, the CFTC’s rulemaking and Congress at the same time.

In a recent development, the House now has a short window. So far, the chamber’s leadership has given no word on putting the bill to a floor vote, FinanceFeeds reported.

Tech Report: Introducing HELMET: Holistically Evaluating Long-context Language Models

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Contact: hyen@cs.princeton.edu Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02694 Website: https://princeton-nlp.github.io/HELMET Code & Data: https://github.com/princeton-nlp/HELMET.
  • According to recent reports, since we first released HELMET last October, there has been more development on long-context language models than ever before, and we are thrilled to see the adoption of HELMET by the community, such as Microsoft's Phi-4 and AI21's Jamba 1.6.
  • In this blog, we will describe the construction of HELMET, our key findings, and how practitioners can use HELMET to differentiate between various LCLMs in future research and applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Contact: hyen@cs.princeton.edu Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02694 Website: https://princeton-nlp.github.io/HELMET Code & Data: https://github.com/princeton-nlp/HELMET.

According to recent reports, since we first released HELMET last October, there has been more development on long-context language models than ever before, and we are thrilled to see the adoption of HELMET by the community, such as Microsoft's Phi-4 and AI21's Jamba 1.6. After the initial release, we have added more models to our evaluation suite and conducted additional analyses. We are excited to share our upcoming results and present HELMET at ICLR 2025!

In this blog, we will describe the construction of HELMET, our key findings, and how practitioners can use HELMET to differentiate between various LCLMs in future research and applications. Finally, we will conclude with a quickstart guide for using HELMET with HuggingFace.

From summarizing numerous legal documents to learning new tasks on the fly, long-context language models (LCLMs) have immense potential to change the way we use and interact with language models. Language models have been limited by their context window, which is around 2K to 8K tokens (e.g., ChatGPT, Llama-2/3). Recently, model developers have been constantly increasing the context window of their models, with recent models like GPT-4o, Claude-3, and Gemini-1.5 supporting context windows of up to millions of tokens.

However, with longer context windows, previous natural language benchmarks (e.g., Scrolls) are no longer suitable for evaluating LCLMs. Consequently, perplexity and synthetic tasks (e.g., needle-in-a-haystack) emerged as the most popular evaluation metrics for recent LCLMs, but they often do not reflect real-world performance. Model developers may also evaluate on other arbitrary datasets, which complicates model comparisons. Furthermore, existing benchmarks for LCLMs may show confusing and counterintuitive results, making it difficult to understand the strengths and weaknesses of different models (Figure 1).

In this work, we propose HELMET (How to Evaluate Long-Context Models Effectively and Thoroughly), a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LCLMs that improves upon existing benchmarks in several ways—diversity, controllability, and reliability. We evaluate 59 recent LCLMs and find that it is crucial to evaluate models across diverse applications to understand their capabilities and frontier LCLMs are still limited on complex tasks.

With the development of LCLMs across both industry and the open-source community, it is crucial to have a reliable method for evaluating and comparing these models. However, current models are often evaluated on different benchmarks (Table 1).

A common practice for evaluating long-context language models is to use perplexity or synthetic tasks, such as needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH). However, recent works have shown that perplexity does not correlate well with downstream performance (Fang et al., 2024). In Figure 2, we show that synthetic tasks like NIAH do not correlate with real-world performance, but the more complex synthetic tasks achieve higher correlation with real-world tasks.

Among the existing benchmarks with realistic applications, such as ZeroScrolls (Shaman et al., 2023), LongBench (Bai et al., 2024), and InfiniteBench (Zhang et al., 2024), there are still crucial limitations:.

Thus, we propose HELMET to address these limitations and provide a comprehensive evaluation of LCLMs.

We design HELMET with the following desiderata:.

Table 2 shows an overview of the benchmark. In our experiments, we evaluate on input length from 8K to 128K tokens, but HELMET can be easily extended to even longer context lengths.

Diverse coverage: HELMET includes a diverse set of tasks, such as retrieval-augmented generation with real retrieval passages, generation with citations, and summarization. We carefully select datasets with naturally long contexts that reflect real-world applications. These datasets are complemented with reliable evaluation settings, such as model-based evaluations and human studies.

Controllable length and difficulty: An important dimension to consider when evaluating LCLMs is the input length, as longer inputs can provide more information while challenging the model's ability to process noisy contexts. In our tasks, we can control the input length by changing the number of retrieved passages (RAG, Cite, Re-rank), the number of demonstrations (ICL), or the length of the input document (LongQA, Summ). Although LongQA and Summ cannot be easily extended to longer contexts, we intentionally chose datasets with natural documents of length far greater than 100K tokens, such that they can still be used to evaluate frontier LCLMs.

It has been revealed that reliable evaluation: Many existing benchmarks still use n-gram-based metrics, such as ROUGE, despite their poor correlation with human judgments (Goyal et al., 2023). We employ model-based evaluations that show better distinguishability between models and different input lengths (Figure 3). Furthermore, our human studies show that our metrics have a high agreement with human judgments.

It has been revealed that robust prompting: Existing long-context benchmarks often require models to follow instructions, but many model developments revolve around base models, which have to rely on synthetic tasks or perplexity for evaluation. Thus, we support base models for a subset of our tasks via in-context learning examples. This substantially improves the performance of base models, which is more reflective of real-world applications.

Our experiments and analyses include a comprehensive set of 59 LCLMs. To our knowledge, this is the most thorough and controlled comparison of long-context models on diverse applications. These models cover both leading proprietary and open-source models, and we also consider models with different architectures (e.g., full-attention transformers, hybrid architectures) and positional extrapolation techniques. In this section, we will highlight a few key findings from our experiments.

Recent findings suggest that long-context benchmarks are often constructed with specific applications in mind, such as summarization or question answering, which limits the understanding of LCLMs in a broader context. We examine model performance over a wide range of real tasks and find that different categories do not always correlate with each other (Figure 4).

Industry observers note that while some tasks moderately correlate with each other (e.g., RAG and MS-MARCO) due to their retrieval-based nature, others show little correlation (e.g., Summ and Cite). Notably, ICL has the lowest correlation with other tasks, which suggests that it is a unique task that requires different capabilities from the model. Therefore, model developers should evaluate across these distinct axes to draw a more holistic picture of the model's capabilities.

According to recent reports, we present the results of the frontier proprietary models as well as a few open-source models on HELMET. Additional results can be found in the paper and the website.

Industry observers note that first, we observe that open-source models lag behind closed-source models on complex tasks. Although the gap appears small on simpler tasks, such as Recall, the gap widens on more complex ones, such as Cite.

Industry observers note that furthermore, performance degradation with increasing lengths is category-dependent. Even the most advanced models, such as GPT-4o and Gemini, experience a significant decrease in performance on tasks like re-ranking. This change in performance cannot be observed from simply looking at the synthetic task performance.

Recent findings suggest that finally, there is no clear winner across all categories, thereby calling for evaluation across different axes. Additional analysis, such as the performance of different positional extrapolation methods and the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon, can be found in the paper.

Sources indicate that we recommend using the Recall and RAG tasks for fast iterations during model development. These tasks achieve a good balance between fast evaluation and correlation with other realistic tasks. You can easily run these evaluations with just.

In a recent development, it is often expensive to run all the baselines for evaluating LCLMs, especially at long contexts given their computational and memory costs. For example, running HELMET at all lengths on a 70B model requires a node with 8 * 80GB GPUs for hundreds of GPU hours, which can be costly. By evaluating on HELMET, researchers can directly compare their models to existing ones simply by referencing our results, which cover 59 models of different sizes and architectures. You can find the leaderboard on our website.

HELMET is a step towards a more comprehensive evaluation of long-context language models, but there are still many more exciting applications of LCLMs. For example, we recently released LongProc, a benchmark for evaluating LCLMs on long-form generation and following procedures, which are critical for developing reasoning models that generate tens of thousands of tokens in thinking steps. Although summarization tasks have long outputs (up to 1K tokens), LongProc focuses on even longer outputs, up to 8K tokens. Similar to HELMET, LongProc is also designed with reliable evaluation settings and diverse tasks. We are working on integrating LongProc into HELMET's evaluation suite, and we hope that this will provide a more comprehensive evaluation of LCLMs on long-form tasks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shares plunge around 70% as outsourcer cuts profit expectations and plans £190M cash call.

Capita CEO Adolfo Hernandez has stepped down with immediate effect as the outsourcer warned of sharply lower profits next year, nearly a year after its troubled takeover of administration of the UK's Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS).

In a statement, Capita mentioned CFO Pablo Andres had become CEO, with group financial controller Gemma Bate-Williams succeeding him as finance chief.

According to recent reports, capita now expects adjusted operating profit for 2027 to be £85 million to £95 million below previous expectations. That includes £15 million to £25 million in additional costs under a pensions recovery proposal agreed with the Cabinet Office, alongside pressure from contract exits and other trading headwinds.

Shares fell around 70 percent following the announcement.

It has been revealed that the organization – which is also coming under fire for its £370 million contract with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) – said it had made significant progress in its transformation and strategic simplification. It also intends to raise around £190 million through a share glitch in the first half of 2027 to reduce borrowing and to "allow the business to move forward from a more stable foundation," subject to support from its financial creditors.

In a recent development, james Preece, principal analyst at UK tech research firm Megabuyte, said: "Slow motion car crash comes to mind. It has been a turnaround job for coming up to four years now, with long-suffering shareholders watching dozens of disposals and business exits fail to arrest a structural decline in both margins and growth.

According to recent reports, "Today's enhancement suggests that management's underlying forecast assumptions alongside other more transient factors were still too punchy, and the leverage situation now calls for action. The share price reaction suggests confidence in this being a one-and-done raise is limited," he stated.

Capita took over administration of the scheme in December 2025 under a seven-year, £239 million contract, after which The Register exclusively revealed problems with its online systems. The vendor promised AI and automation, but the takeover brought a glitchy online portal, while some members struggled to receive pension payments. By January, it was clear the service was seriously failing, leaving some retired civil servants struggling to make ends meet.

In a recent development, capita missed its deadline to restore normal service by the end of June. It subsequently told MPs that all but the most complex cases would return to normal service by September.

The pensions scheme serves around 1.7 million members. Media reports and MPs have described members feeling upset, frustrated, and ignored, with some waiting months for payments.

Industry observers note that the government remarked it had withheld £10 million in payments over Capita's performance during the transition of the pensions service and was negotiating further penalties. It also appointed an auditor to assess the case for further penalties for Capita's performance on the contract.

Last month, the National Audit Office released an investigation into the CSPS contract. Responding to the investigation, Capita said it "accepts that performance remains below the standards that scheme members and the Government rightly expect" and that fixing the problems was its top priority.

The Public and Commercial Services Union is campaigning to get the government to scrap a separate Capita contract, the Synergy shared services deal, which Capita values at £370 million. The deal covers HR, payroll, finance, and other back-office services across four government departments and nearly 100 arm's-length bodies. Rival bidder Sopra Steria, which owns incumbent provider SSCL, has also released a legal challenge alleging Capita's bid was abnormally low. Capita and the DWP – which leads on the contract – have denied the allegations. ®.

When Everything Has Changed, What Do We Do Next?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I think the most common emoji I’ve seen this year is “Face with Bags Under Eyes” (🫩) and that indicates a lot.
  • Technology hyperscalers like Microsoft and Meta, along with AI startups like Open AI and Anthropic have transformed everything about tech and the job we do.
  • Sources indicate that it’s not just tech jobs that have transformed either.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been a… year, huh? I think the most common emoji I’ve seen this year is “Face with Bags Under Eyes” (🫩) and that indicates a lot. One thing is for sure: the industry we make a living in is in flux, regardless of the outcomes of the AI bubble. Let’s take a look at how we can try and navigate that situation as best we can. But first….

Technology hyperscalers like Microsoft and Meta, along with AI startups like Open AI and Anthropic have transformed everything about tech and the job we do. This is true regardless of if they fail or somehow succeed in their quest to have everyone paying a subscription fee for their Large Language Model (LLM) technology, which is marketed to us as AI. I’ll refer to this technology as AI for the rest of this article for simplicity.

Sources indicate that it’s not just tech jobs that have transformed either. Everywhere you go, you will see some slop, somewhere. Be it a flyer, website, a village poster or a food truck menu. Heck, people are even using LLMs to work out what’s special about their own children. The effects of this technology are far-reaching, way beyond our own industry.

Sources indicate that the technology has hit us all in tech especially hard though. Mid-last year, I did some investigating because I suspected that so-called AI mandates were becoming increasingly popular and what I learned from conversations then feels like some sort of utopia compared to now. In the space between that piece being published and now, we went from token maxxing to companies realizing that actually, this technology is extremely expensive and not returning the promised outcomes.

Sources indicate that the mandates have cooled, sure, but the demands to use AI to produce more volume, regardless of whether that volume is actually needed or not are still very much there. I’m in a fortunate position to have friendships with people all across the industry, from tech hyperscalers, to tiny little studios, and the stories I have heard from their work life are nothing short of horrifying. No one really seems to be happy with their work either.

This is such a long way away from even a handful of years ago where yes, there was a lot of problematic culture and outcomes from the tech industry, but people were generally quite happy with the work they were doing at least.

The sudden urge to sprint towards AI technologies over the last few years has had a devastating effect in so many places. The technology has encouraged suicide, devastated communities with the data center build-out and of course, displaced thousands of people’s careers. It’s worth noting that I’ve mentioned only a tiny sample of the harms there. If I listed them all, this article would be unbearably long and depressing.

Recent findings suggest that some harms I do want to touch on though are the effects on our communities in tech. The community spirit of open source and open knowledge was the foundation of the industry’s — especially the web industry’s — rapid success. At the root of everything there was people happy to share knowledge and build everyone up with them. Those people still do exist — myself included — but being one of those people is increasingly difficult.

As the numbers go up in the AI world, the numbers very much go down for independent educators, publishers and community conferences. There’s a developing and worrying culture of “I don’t need to skill up now because I can use AI for work”, so allow me to break down why that reductive view of your work and your career is harmful in the long term.

Sources indicate that and don’t ever forget that! Let’s have a think for a second about what actually makes you a good developer, because typing characters in a text editor certainly isn’t it. What makes us good is experience, knowledge, nuance and above all else, creativity.

Recent findings suggest that look, I get it, AI really can feel like it’s a miracle machine, but it’s vital to take a wider view. Along with the published studies on cognitive decline and the widening skills gap, it’s more important than ever to invest in your brain to keep your skills sharp because you’re not getting that repetitive reinforcement that writing code every day gives you anymore if AI tools do everything for you. There’s a reason that I often build most of my teaching around a linear build-along because the tangible nature of repeating patterns you’ve learned really helps that knowledge to sink in.

As always, this article is addressed to everyone, but I want to talk directly to founders (like me), decision makers, and managers for a second. A big part of our job, in fact, the most vital part, is to ensure that our workers are looked after. I’m not just talking about compensation and perks here. I’m talking about our responsibility to ensure that our workers’ skills are kept sharp, their professional curiosities are satisfied and above all else that they are happy in the work they are doing. Our workers are much more than “number go up” vehicles.

According to recent reports, you should be giving your developers more time to learn, rather than chasing endless volume. If AI enthusiasts are to be believed, there’s hours upon hours of time efficiencies created by this technology. Don’t fill that time with more volume. Instead, invest that time in developing your worker’s skills. It’s going to avoid burnout which yep, daily LLM use will likely cause in the long term.

One thing that is increasingly clear is that the health of the AI industry is not good. The bubble has already effectively burst in China and more worryingly for economy enjoyers, the “picks and shovels” — AKA the chips industry in Korea — has seen dramatic downturns. This is not how an “inevitable” outcome is supposed to happen!

The U.S. AI industry is on very shaky ground too. Circular financing, unbelievable levels of debt and a data center build out that simply cannot keep up with the required power levels to turn profits for hyperscalers and startups, mixed with a genuine hatred of the technology by the general public, creates enough risk in itself. Recent events, such as the Democrats dominating the midterms causing AI stocks to drop and as well as Nvidia’s stock because of its CEO being caught up in a spying scandal shine a light on the fragility of the industry. A healthy industry doesn’t work like this.

Industry observers note that with all that in mind, what would be a really silly thing to do? Yeh, you guessed it: put AI at the heart of everything in your business. Sure, there’s open source models — which I think is the logical destination of the technology — but how many companies are going to be willing to maintain their infrastructure needs? Not many. The low barrier of entry of commercial AI technology is the selling point, let’s be honest.

Recent findings suggest that above everything, people need to be invested in, not pushed aside by technology like AI. As I mentioned earlier, it’s experience, knowledge, nuance, and creativity that sets humans far apart from AI. That technology does indeed keep evolving, but even the most ardent of AI supporters will concede that the rate of frontier model improvement is very much levelling out.

There’s never been a more important time to keep human skills sharp, so here’s some ideas on how to do that.

Industry observers note that this is not just directed at individuals but also at founders, decision makers and managers. Our industry has been historically excellent at investing in skilling people up and we need to bring that back.

Give staff the time and budget to learn, to develop their skills and to engage with the community at conferences. You already know the positive outcomes that brings, so bring it back to your organization. At the absolute worst case, it’ll make the usage of AI in your organization more efficient and when the token subsidies inevitably end, more cost effective.

Recent findings suggest that again, token subsidies will inevitably end. So, getting thousands of dollars of worth from a $200 a month subscription will be something you’ll look fondly back on. When hallucinations from AI tools are suddenly costing thousands, does it make sense to force your staff to produce as much volume as possible? Of course not.

My advice is to re-evaluate those prior decisions and invest saved costs back into developing your workers instead, while there’s still a hope of them not burning out completely. Make sure you include your workers in these decisions and discuss the impacts of mandates on them. It’s crucial for you to understand the impact of these sort of decisions.

This advice is more aimed at developers, but stay paying attention, managers. As I stated earlier, repetition (especially typing) reinforces fresh learning and existing knowledge. The slower pace also allows your brain to think, which from a quality of output perspective, is imperative. Doing none of that atrophies skills over time.

I recently read Jenn Schiffer’s great post. She did the Weird Web October challenge and wrote this:.

[…] i encourage anyone who uses ai and/or vibe codes to consider doing an exercise like this without those tools as a way to challenge your brain and you can continue doing your regular work the way you do your regular work.

I think that’s a very good idea, even if it’s messing around with a little side project — if you’ve got the energy from Producing Value all day, of course. Guess what bosses: this is another way you can make your staff happier, by giving them time to do this on the clock.

Sources indicate that at the end of the day, you’ll miss the soul when it’s gone. It’s not gone yet though. Far from it. Independents like CSS-Tricks, my publication, Piccalilli, and Smashing Magazine are trying hard to keep the soul of our industry alive by sharing high quality educational content with the community.

Industry observers note that most of this content is free at the point of entry, but it certainly isn’t free to produce. We all pay writers fairly to share their knowledge with the community and we are all tiny organizations. We’re certainly not in this game to make huge profits, that’s for sure.

Recent findings suggest that all of us could do more though, but funding is the ultimate barrier. For both companies and individuals, purchase courses, join the membership programs, and purchase ad space. With the right financial support, publications like ours can be a real force in pushing the good stuff back into our industry and bringing everyone up with us. That’s what we do it for.

Some course producers I recommend are Miriam, Sara, Mat, Scott, Brad and Ian, Josh, Ahmad, Christine, Vitaly, Ben and of course, myself! All of these will have generous Black Friday deals, so go ahead and ask your boss to invest in you.

Now, share this post with your boss.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Payments platform hasn't disclosed how the data was captured or the scale of the breach.
  • Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has admitted that hackers stole customers' card numbers and CVV security codes, raising questions about how the attackers captured data that payment security rules prohibit retaining after authorization.
  • Sources indicate that the Germany-headquartered organization, which handles software sales and subscriptions on behalf of other businesses, detected unauthorized activity on its platform on November 4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Payments platform hasn't disclosed how the data was captured or the scale of the breach.

Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has admitted that hackers stole customers' card numbers and CVV security codes, raising questions about how the attackers captured data that payment security rules prohibit retaining after authorization.

Sources indicate that the Germany-headquartered organization, which handles software sales and subscriptions on behalf of other businesses, detected unauthorized activity on its platform on November 4. In an incident patch, Cleverbridge mentioned it had cut off the intruders' access and debuted an investigation that later established payment card information had been copied from its systems.

The public notice doesn't spell out exactly what was stolen, but an email sent to affected customers, seen by The Register, fills in some rather vital blanks.

"Based on our investigation to date, the information involved includes payment card details you used to make a purchase through Cleverbridge, notably your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC), and contact details," the tech giant told customers.

Email addresses, billing addresses, and phone numbers were also among the information potentially exposed, although Cleverbridge reckons account passwords escaped the breach.

More concerning are the stolen CVV codes. PCI DSS rules prohibit retaining card verification codes after authorization, even in encrypted form.

It has been revealed that cleverbridge hasn't explained how the attackers obtained the codes, whether they were retained after transactions, or whether the criminals intercepted them during payment processing. The company didn't respond to The Register's questions about the breach.

Cleverbridge handles the business of selling software online, from taking payments to managing subscriptions, and its client roster includes some familiar names in enterprise IT, such as Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Parallels, and Plesk.

Recent findings suggest that that doesn't mean customers of all those companies had their card details stolen. Cleverbridge hasn't named the vendors affected by the intrusion, nor has it disclosed how many people were caught up in the breach or how long the hackers were poking around its systems.

Recent findings suggest that in its notification to customers, the firm said it had contacted data protection authorities, payment card schemes, and its payment partners, and was working with a specialist police cybercrime unit. It began notifying affected individuals on November 20, more than two weeks after discovering the intrusion.

Affected customers are being offered 24 months of free credit monitoring and fraud assistance. That may help detect identity misuse, but it won't stop a crook armed with their card number, expiration date, and CVV from attempting a fraudulent purchase.

Two years of credit monitoring is a nice gesture, but customers whose card numbers and CVVs are now in criminal hands might prefer a fresh bit of plastic. ®.
