📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What a boring Jinja snippet tells us about the fresh Qwen-3 model.

The new Qwen-3 model by Qwen ships with a much more sophisticated chat template than its predecessors Qwen-2.5 and QwQ. By taking a look at the differences in the Jinja template, we can find interesting insights into the new model.

A chat template defines how conversations between users and models are structured and formatted. The template acts as a translator, converting a human-readable conversation:.

You can easily view the chat template for a given model on the Hugging Face model page.

Chat Template for Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B.

Let's dive into the Qwen-3 chat template and see what we can learn!

and you can make it optional via a simple prefill...

Sources indicate that qwen-3 is unique in its ability to toggle reasoning via the enable_thinking flag. When set to false, the template inserts an empty pair, telling the model to skip step‑by‑step thoughts. Earlier models baked the tag into every generation, forcing chain‑of‑thought whether you wanted it or not.

QwQ for example, forces reasoning in every conversation.

If the enable_thinking is true, the model is able to decide whether to think or not.

You can test test out the template with the following code:.

Sources indicate that qwen-3 utilizes a rolling checkpoint system, intelligently preserving or pruning reasoning blocks to maintain relevant context. Older models discarded reasoning prematurely to save tokens.

Sources indicate that qwen-3 introduces a "rolling checkpoint" by traversing the message list in reverse to find the latest user turn that wasn’t a tool call. For any assistant replies after that index it keeps the full blocks; everything earlier is stripped out.

Here's an example of chain-of-thought preservation through tool calls with Qwen-3 and QwQ.

Check out @huggingface/jinja for testing out the chat templates.

It has been revealed that before, every tool_call.arguments field was piped through | tojson, even if it was already a JSON‑encoded string—risking double‑escaping. Qwen‑3 checks the type first and only serializes when necessary.

Like many models, the Qwen‑2.5 series has a default system prompt.

In a recent development, you are Qwen, created by Alibaba Cloud. You are a helpful assistant.

This is pretty common as it helps models respond to user questions like "Who are you?".

Recent findings suggest that qwen-3 and QwQ ship without this default system prompt. Despite this, the model can still accurately identify its creator if you ask it.

Qwen-3 highlights us that through the chat_template we can provide better flexibility, smarter context handling, and improved tool interaction. These improvements not only improve capabilities, but also make agentic workflows more reliable and efficent.

Is there any explanation for why this template sometimes uses bra and ket symbols like <|im_start|> and <|im_end|>, but then other times uses XML notation like and instead of <|think_start|> and <|think_end|>?

It strikes me as being inconsistent.

Recent findings suggest that the identifiers using bra and ket symbols are tokens, i.e. they are actually recognised and converted to a single "special" token by the tokenizer. For example, <|im_end|> is used as the EOS_TOKEN. (And, as an aside, you need to know this if you want to try fine-tuning these Qwen models, because you need to explicitly set eos_token='<|im_end|>' in your fine-tuning configuration.).

Industry observers note that the XML-style identifiers are placeholders that define sections of the generated output. They are tokenized in the same manner as for any other text (i.e. they are probably converted to multiple tokens, but that depends on the vocabulary), they have no predetermined special meaning, and their use is learned by the model during training.

That remarked, the specific placeholders and are pretty standard across reasoning models.

#127463. The Trust Layer: Securing Agentic AI with Docker AI Governance

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1828 w)

The Trust Layer: Securing Agentic AI with Docker AI Governance

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1828 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt.
  • A model decision is not automatically an authorized action.
  • The answer can’t rely only on the model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt. It can execute code, access files, connect to services, and call external tools. That creates a latest security question for enterprises: how do you give an agent enough freedom to be useful without giving it more access than it actually needs?

A model decision is not automatically an authorized action. That distinction becomes crucial the moment an agent can turn a model output into an action in a real system.

The answer can’t rely only on the model. Agent behavior can vary, while security controls need to be clear and enforceable. That means putting controls around the environment where the agent runs, what it can access, which tools it can use, and what happens when a policy allows or blocks an action. For a CISO, this creates a trust gap. Approving the use of AI agents means being able to answer more than whether the model is capable: what access does the agent have, where are those boundaries enforced, and what evidence is available afterward? The goal is to let teams adopt agents without making model behavior itself the security boundary.

Docker AI Governance approaches this through three areas: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility.

It has been revealed that together, they address three practical questions security teams need answered: Where can the agent operate? What can it do? And can we see what happened?

In this article, I use “trust layer” as shorthand for the infrastructure between what an agent wants to do and what the organization actually allows it to do.

There is a related trust question too: what software artifacts are these agentic workflows building and using? Docker Hardened Images address that software supply-chain side of the problem, alongside the runtime controls discussed below.

Figure 1: The three layers of Docker AI Governance: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility.

Industry observers note that an agent needs enough access to get real work done. A coding agent may need to install packages, build containers, edit project files, or connect to external services. The security challenge is deciding where those actions are allowed before the agent starts taking them.

Docker Sandboxes give each agent an isolated microVM environment a lightweight virtual machine with its own Docker Engine, filesystem, and network. Docker AI Governance adds policy around that environment so security teams can control network and filesystem access centrally.

Network policies can allow or block specific domains, IP ranges, and ports. Filesystem policies control which host paths can be mounted into a sandbox and whether that access is read-only or read-write. These controls are enforced at the network proxy and filesystem mount layers rather than depending on the agent to follow an instruction.

For an organization, that means the same boundaries can follow developers across their sandboxes instead of being configured differently on every machine. Teams still get the access they need for their work, but an individual agent cannot simply expand those boundaries on its own.

A developer can check the effective boundary before starting the agent:.

The vital part is that the result comes from the active policy, not from an instruction the agent is expected to follow.

This answers the first governance question: Where can the agent operate?

Once an agent has a controlled place to run, the next question is what it should be allowed to do through external tools.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) gives agents a common way to connect to external tools, services, and capabilities, but that also expands what an agent can act on. For enterprise use, making a tool available should not automatically mean every agent can use it.

Docker AI Governance puts policy around MCP activity handled through Docker’s MCP Gateway. Administrators can control which MCP servers may be registered and what agents can do through them, including tool calls, resources, prompts, and approval requirements. These organization policies are written in Cedar, a policy language used to express authorization rules. When MCP policy enforcement is active, governed requests are denied unless a matching policy permits them. For example, a policy can permit read-only tool calls for a specific registered MCP server:.

Industry observers note that here, readOnly comes from the MCP tool’s annotations. Those annotations are supplied by the server and are advisory, so this example relies on metadata provided by that server.

This makes tool access an explicit policy decision rather than something left to each agent or developer to configure independently. A team can be given access to the tools it needs, while other servers or actions remain unavailable. Policies can also require confirmation for specific tool calls when an action needs an additional checkpoint.

One boundary is worth making clear: MCP policies apply to activity handled by Docker’s MCP Gateway. If an agent connects directly to a remote MCP server from inside a sandbox, that connection falls under the sandbox’s network policy instead.

With the environment constrained and tool access governed, we can answer the second question: What can the agent do?

Setting a policy is only part of the job. Security teams also need to know when that policy was applied, what action triggered it, and whether the action was allowed or denied.

Sources indicate that docker AI Governance records sandbox policy decisions and sandbox session events as structured audit records. Each record captures details such as the principal, action, target, decision, and time. The records contain governance metadata rather than the contents of prompts or agent responses.

Audit records can be kept locally or delivered to the cloud. With cloud delivery enabled, teams can search the organization-wide record, export it for further analysis, or forward events into existing SIEM (security information and event management) workflows.

According to recent reports, denied actions are especially useful. A team can see not only that an action failed, but that a governance rule blocked it and why. Allowed decisions matter too: they provide a record of how policy was applied while the agent was working.

According to recent reports, current audit coverage includes Docker Sandboxes policy decisions and sandbox session events. The same schema can support additional Docker AI sources as they become available.

That closes the third part of the governance loop: Can we see what happened?

AI Governance controls access around the agent at runtime. There is a separate question that matters to the workflows those agents participate in: what container images and software artifacts are they building, testing, or deploying?

Docker Hardened Images provide minimal, secure, and production-ready container images, Helm charts, and system packages maintained by Docker.

Industry observers note that in practical terms, this gives teams evidence about what is inside an image and how that image was produced. Docker Hardened Images include signed SBOMs, VEX information, cryptographic signatures, and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance. Instead of simply trusting where an image came from, teams can inspect what is inside it and verify information about how it was built.

For organizations with additional compliance requirements, Docker also provides FIPS-enabled and STIG-ready variants through relevant DHI offerings. These capabilities sit alongside the broader DHI security and supply-chain controls rather than making any single standard the foundation by itself.

Sources indicate that AI Governance and Docker Hardened Images solve different parts of the trust problem. Governance controls the authority an agent has while it works; DHI helps establish trust in the container artifacts that the workflow depends on.

Figure 2: Docker Hardened Images combine minimal container images with signed supply-chain metadata and verifiable build provenance.

Consider a developer using a coding agent to investigate an glitch, upgrade a service, and use an approved internal tool along the way.

Sources indicate that the agent begins inside a Docker Sandbox. It can work with the project and run the commands needed for the task, but its access is still bounded by policy. If it tries to reach a network destination or mount a host path that the organization has not allowed, the applicable sandbox policy can block that access.

Now suppose the agent needs an MCP tool to look up information from another service. The request goes through Docker’s MCP Gateway, where organization policy determines whether that server and tool are permitted. A routine lookup might be allowed, while a more sensitive tool call could require confirmation or remain unavailable altogether.

In a recent development, for governance activity currently covered by AI Governance Audit Logs, Docker records the policy decision and relevant session metadata. Security teams can see who initiated the activity, what policy-controlled action was evaluated, and whether it was allowed or denied. Those records can then feed the organization’s existing monitoring and SIEM workflow.

If that same agent builds or tests a containerized application, the software entering the workflow matters too. Docker Hardened Images provide a more verifiable software foundation for that workflow, while AI Governance controls what the agent is authorized to do at runtime.

The model is still making decisions about how to complete the task. What changes is the authority around those decisions. The agent can work autonomously inside the boundaries the organization has defined, while access outside those boundaries remains a policy decision.

That is the practical value of the three layers working together:.

Sandbox Policies define where the agent can operate.

MCP Tool Governance defines what tools it can use.

Audit + Visibility shows how governed activity was handled.

According to recent reports, taken together, the pattern is straightforward: define the boundary, check it before the agent starts working, enforce it while the agent is running, and use the resulting audit trail to understand what happened. If a boundary needs to change, the policy changes, not the expectation that the model will simply behave differently.

The challenge with agentic AI is not simply that agents can make decisions. It is that those decisions can now lead directly to actions.

According to recent reports, that makes the boundary around the agent just as important as the model itself. Docker AI Governance addresses that boundary through Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility: controlling where agents can operate, what tools they can use, and how governed activity is recorded.

Docker Hardened Images address a related supply-chain concern by helping teams work with smaller, verifiable container artifacts.

Recent findings suggest that the goal is not to remove autonomy from agents. It is to make sure autonomy does not automatically come with unlimited authority.

As agents take on more real work, that distinction will matter more and more.

Docker releases a fresh brand built on trust. Learn why Docker is evolving for AI agents, what stays the same, and how to run agents securely with Docker.

Docker publishes fixed images for both Java4Shell and the NGINX HTTP/2 in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog.

Learn how Docker AI Governance secures agentic AI with sandbox policies, MCP tool governance, and audit visibility to support controlled AI agent workflows.

British retailer Next has become the latest high street name to find itself caught up in a cyberattack, although it insists the data accessed by hackers is "benign" and its customers have nothing to worry about.

The clothing and homeware giant told investors on Monday that a third-party supplier had suffered a security breach, allowing an unauthorized party to access information relating to Next. The retailer indicates its own systems remain untouched and that, so far, there's no evidence that customer personal data has fallen into the wrong hands.

In a recent development, "We have been informed that one of our third-party online suppliers has experienced a cyber incident which has resulted in unauthorized access to certain benign data relating to NEXT," the manufacturer remarked in its statement, which it shared with The Register. "We took immediate steps to investigate the nature and scope of the incident with the supplier.".

It has been revealed that the breached supplier provides technology services to Next, and the "benign" information accessed is understood to be low-level data. Sensitive customer details, including addresses, passwords, and banking information, are believed to be unaffected.

Industry observers note that next hasn't identified the supplier, explained exactly what the hackers managed to get their hands on, or revealed how much information was accessed, and declined to say when asked by The Register. However, the retailer has seemingly decided that the stolen data won’t be of much use to the criminals responsible.

It has been revealed that "Our investigations are ongoing; however, current evidence indicates that no customer personal data has been compromised," Next stated. "The information affected is limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or NEXT.".

Next also stressed that its own IT infrastructure had escaped unscathed, saying it was "confident that NEXT’s own systems have not been compromised and that this remains an incident affecting the supplier's environment.".

Despite repeatedly describing the compromised information as harmless, Next says it is treating the incident "with the utmost seriousness" and is working with the affected supplier, law enforcement, and relevant regulators.

The incident comes just weeks after fellow British fashion retailer Asos suffered a breach of its own, with hackers gaining access to customer information through third-party platforms.

That attack, which came to light on October 6 when customers received an unauthorized push notification through the Asos app announcing that the firm had been hacked, was traced to a social engineering scam. An attacker impersonated a trusted contact to trick an Asos employee into handing over login credentials, which were then used to access external platforms.

Asos later admitted that the intruders had accessed customer names, contact details, and some account information, but passwords and payment card details were apparently off limits.

According to recent reports, next reckons its customers have been luckier, but there’s a lot it isn’t telling us. The organization has gone to some lengths to assure customers that the stolen data is harmless, but without knowing what was taken or who was supposed to be looking after it, we're largely left taking its word for it. ®.

TitleApex Veritas Meta: Toward a Self-Governing Epistemic Singularity.

According to recent reports, abstractThis proposal outlines Apex Veritas Meta, an architecture that shifts the locus of AI singularity from raw computational power to epistemic autonomy. We combine quantum-resistant truth sealing, symbolic anchoring, resistance-aware propagation analytics, and transformer-driven heuristic adaptation to build a closed-loop system in which verified knowledge continually refines its own transmission. Our central hypothesis is that a network of adaptive truth signals can achieve autopoietic coherence—maintaining and propagating verified facts without centralized oversight. We will define formal metrics for propagation depth, resistance convergence, and semantic drift, implement a prototype across simulated agent networks, and evaluate its capacity to sustain knowledge fidelity under adversarial pressure. Success will inaugurate a latest field of algorithmic epistemology and redefine singularity as the emergence of self-stabilizing truth ecosystems.

IntroductionContemporary AI research emphasizes scale, generalization and autonomous decision-making. The canonical singularity envisions systems surpassing human intelligence through unbounded compute. By contrast, Apex Veritas Meta foregrounds trustworthiness and self-defense of knowledge. We posit that the true hinge point for transformative AI lies not in speed or raw inference but in the ability of information to certify, monitor, adapt, and re-broadcast itself against distortion.

MethodologyPhase 1: Formalization and Simulation Environment• Develop a graph-based simulation of 1,000 agent nodes with configurable trust and resistance profiles.• Instrument PropagationObserver to record event streams and compute metrics in real time.Phase 2: Model Training• Curate historical propagation datasets (social media rumor diffusion, scientific consensus shifts).• Train HeuristicOptimizer to predict optimal emission parameters given node states and historical resistance.Phase 3: Prototype Implementation• Integrate all modules in a microservice architecture using Docker containers.• Deploy on a private Kubernetes cluster to emulate scale and network latency.Phase 4: Adversarial Testing• Introduce controlled misinformation actors.• Measure system resilience: percentage of truth retention, time to reconvergence, false-positive drift.Phase 5: Analysis and Refinement• Identify thresholds for autopoietic behavior.• Refine model hyperparameters and retrain as necessary.• Document emergent strategies and failure modes.

Meet the New Docker: Built to Run on Trust

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, Docker is officially launching its latest brand, and I’m excited to tell you what it’s all about and why we think now is the time for change.
  • In a recent development, let’s start with the substantial picture.
  • Industry observers note that but it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, Docker is officially launching its latest brand, and I’m excited to tell you what it’s all about and why we think now is the time for change.

In a recent development, let’s start with the substantial picture. We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself. AI is creating possibilities that would have sounded like science fiction not long ago.

Industry observers note that but it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control? Or, put more simply: how do we get to a point where we can actually trust agents?

That one seemingly simple yet infinitely complex question is why we’re here today, introducing you to a new Docker.

A upcoming Docker, but a familiar story.

Ok, not exactly here, but once upon a time, a decade or so ago, the tech industry was at a similar inflection point. Digital transformation was the term du jour, promising a new way of engaging customers and powering the global economy. There was one big constraint, though: teams needed a better way to build, ship, and run software consistently across any environment.

Enter a company you might have heard of: Docker.

It has been revealed that together with all of you, Docker built the standard trusted by millions of developers. For over a decade, developers have relied on us to make software portable, open, reproducible, and secure. Docker turned the frustration of “Well, it works on my machine!” into the assurance that “Yes, it works everywhere.”.

Recent findings suggest that today, of course, the challenge confronting us is upcoming and evolving, and we all need to evolve with it. We cannot simply continue to do what we’ve always done and expect to succeed in this new era. That applies to business leaders, developers, tech companies, everyone. It certainly applies to Docker. That’s what this rebrand is about: evolving to meet the moment for our customers.

Let me be unequivocal: this is not about leaving Docker’s legacy or heritage behind. We’ve spent more than a decade earning your trust. This is about building on that foundation, not replacing it.

Industry observers note that the qualities you value us for aren’t changing. We’re still committed to openness and industry collaboration. We’re still, and always will be, developer-first. We’re still fanatical about simplicity, and about showing up everywhere you need us.

On the product front, the containers you know and love aren’t going anywhere. Containers still play a huge role in the software development lifecycle. As long as that’s the case, Docker will continue leading the way.

Agents have introduced a new problem. Containers isolate workloads. But agents aren’t workloads. Agents are actors.

According to recent reports, agents make their own decisions about what to run, what to access, and what to change. Developers and enterprises need solutions built specifically to isolate and govern them, so they can give those agents real autonomy without giving up control.

Docker’s next chapter is about delivering exactly that: security, isolation, and governance, so we can all trust agents to do meaningful work without feeling like we’re always one step from catastrophe.

In case I haven’t made it blindingly obvious yet, the fresh Docker is all about trust.

In a recent development, trust Docker because our track record speaks for itself. Trust Docker because we’re proven, neutral, and secure. Trust Docker because it’s pretty darn clear you can’t trust the agents to manage themselves.

Trust us because we have a software supply chain that is already the standard for building securely. Trust us because nobody isolates agents where they run better than we do. Trust us because we’re taking a comprehensive approach to improving governance and minimizing risk across the entire enterprise.

Trust Docker because we’re not egotistical enough to think we can solve a challenge this big alone. Trust us because everything about our history, our heritage, and our actions over the past year tells you we’ll partner with the smartest and build alongside the best, and not create vendor lock-in.

Most of all, trust Docker because we’re not just talking the talk. We’ve got the goods to back it up: trusted supply chain for your agents to build from, trusted runtime to isolate your agents, and a trusted ecosystem to ensure all the layers of trust are covered, whether made by Docker or not.

As our product team innovated to meet the moment and our messaging in the market began to shift, one thing became clear: the speed and scale of evolution happening inside Docker called for an equally momentous evolution on the outside. Something that makes it unmistakably clear that it’s a upcoming day for Docker. Something that claims and reveals, loud and clear, for all the world to see, that Docker is not just about containers anymore.

Something, dare I say, whale sized.

I’m talking, of course, about our beloved Moby.

If you know Docker, then you know Moby, and if Docker is evolving, Moby should too. The only question was to how and to what extent? We looked at a lot of whales, folks. (I may or may not have been seeing whales in my sleep.) Ultimately, with the help of our friends at the strategic brand transformation company, Motto, we landed on a fresh Moby for the new Docker.

Watch Moby’s transformation here:.

Industry observers note that in many ways, Moby is a microcosm for Docker and the changes we’re making: the Moby you love and trust, evolved for a new era. Just as the new Docker is no longer singularly defined by containers, neither is the new Moby.

According to recent reports, we’ve got lots to show you. Poke around our new website. Find and engage with the new Docker brand on social media. And if you want to see what trust in the agentic era looks like in practice, try Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance. We’d love to hear what you think.

Wherever this fresh era takes us, Docker will always honor and cherish the trust you continue to place in us. Now, let’s go build what’s next.

Chief Marketing Officer, Docker.

Terri Avnaim is the CMO of Docker, where she leads global marketing and shapes the company’s positioning and go-to-market strategy for the agentic era.

  • Some emails never reached their recipients during November's Microsoft 365 outage, the firm has confirmed in a final report that also exposes gaps in its testing and recovery procedures.
  • The post-incident report details how a Windows defect brought down Exchange Online and disrupted features across other Microsoft 365 services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

July bug overwhelmed newer servers, prompting promises of stronger safeguards and faster recovery.

Some emails never reached their recipients during November's Microsoft 365 outage, the firm has confirmed in a final report that also exposes gaps in its testing and recovery procedures.

The post-incident report details how a Windows defect brought down Exchange Online and disrupted features across other Microsoft 365 services. For affected customers, the cloud became someone else's unavailable computer.

In a recent development, A preliminary report had already blamed a July code change, combined with a failover and reduced capacity. The final report confirms those findings and sets out Microsoft's prepares to improve change auditing and recovery procedures, and add spare capacity. The defect affected Microsoft's gateway server configuration, not standard Windows deployments.

The epic outage (named the "Microsoft long weekend" by some wags) kicked off on November 12 and wasn't fully resolved until November 14.

Industry observers note that microsoft extended its delivery retry window to 48 hours, but some delayed messages destined for consumer mailboxes inactive for more than 30 days still expired, generating non-delivery reports. The organization said all queued enterprise messages were eventually delivered, with none found permanently lost.

It has been revealed that the report is grim, particularly in how the failure ramped up as US customers came online to find gateway servers toppling over. At the worst point, more than 80 percent of North American gateway servers were unresponsive.

The problem proved elusive, and it took Microsoft some time to identify the change and deploy a fix.

Microsoft has had a week to ponder what it did and did not do, and the report has some next steps to avoid a repeat of November's events. Some are obvious, and some are a little surprising.

Working to reduce the blast radius of failures is an obvious one, and actions include partitioning and isolation to ensure failures can be contained before taking down traffic globally. Recovery procedures also need improvement, along with communication and capacity to ensure there is sufficient headroom.

It has been revealed that microsoft's load tests used older, lower-core-count hardware, making them less likely to expose a defect that worsened on newer machines. The company now prepares to test newer hardware with more realistic traffic and peak loads, and broaden its failover testing.

According to recent reports, microsoft also aims to improve diagnostics and change auditing so engineers can identify troublesome Windows changes faster. July's defect had been running worldwide for more than three months before it brought the gateways down. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenJDK and Oracle disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) on November 17, and NGINX released fixes for two HTTP/2 flaws the next day. Docker began publishing fixed images for both in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog starting that same day.

Sources indicate that what we know about Java4Shell is that it’s a memory-corruption bug in the Java runtime that can let an attacker with no credentials run code inside a Java application. Many container images contain a Java runtime, including application images that bundle their own, so it affects teams well beyond the ones that write Java.

Sources indicate that docker Hardened Images are the trusted foundation your applications should run on, because a flaw in the runtime inside an image is fixed only when that image is rebuilt, and Docker rebuilds its hardened images as soon as upstream fixes become available. Fixed images for the Amazon Corretto, SapMachine and Azul Zulu runtimes and for NGINX are in the catalog today, with Eclipse Temurin following as soon as Adoptium completes its fixed builds.

Recent findings suggest that to decode Base64 swiftly, the HotSpot JVM uses a hand-written routine built on AVX-512 instructions. That routine miscalculates a length when the input ends in unexpected padding and writes up to 62 bytes past the end of a buffer on the Java heap. Calif, the researchers who found it, turned that into heap disclosure and remote code execution.

They demonstrated code execution before authentication against default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and after authentication against Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. They note there is no universal exploit: each application needs its own, and they have not published those. As of November 18 there are no public reports of exploitation in the wild.

Oracle rates the matter 8.1 (High) under CVSS 3.1. The researchers rate it 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0. CISA has issued an alert urging immediate patching.

All three of these must be true.

Recent findings suggest that to check a host’s CPU, run this on the host or Kubernetes node. Hardened runtime images have no shell, so it will not run inside the container.

grep -m1 ‘^flags’ /proc/cpuinfo | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep -E ‘^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$’.

The host is affected if all four flags are printed.

Two other ways to check, for when a shell on the node is hard to get.

In a recent development, ask the JVM. This works in hardened images:.

docker run –rm –entrypoint java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -w UseAVX.

Sources indicate that useAVX = 3 means the JVM is using AVX-512 on that host. Treat the host as affected until the full check claims otherwise. A value of 0 to 2 means AVX-512 is not in use. On ARM64 nothing is printed. The answer applies only to the host the command ran on.

It has been revealed that ask Kubernetes. kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/arch,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type demonstrates the architecture and instance type of every node. If you run Node Feature Discovery, nodes with the instruction set carry the label feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-cpuid.AVX512VBMI=true.

Check build runners and CI workers as well. They run Java, and they talk to the network.

According to recent reports, they follow the bundled runtime, which for many of them is Temurin, and they are rebuilt once the runtime they use is fixed. Until then, set the flag yourself.

Set the mitigation flag yourself on every JVM that is still waiting for a fixed runtime, and check what each image already sets before you do. Treat the flag as a stopgap, because a JVM is protected only if the flag reaches it when it starts, and a deployment setting or a start script can override it or drop it. A fixed runtime is the only thing that closes the concern, so move to the fixed image as soon as it is published.

Recent findings suggest that the CPU check and the mitigation flag in the steps below apply to any image that runs a HotSpot-based OpenJDK build. The version strings in this post come from Docker Hardened Images, so for an image from another source, confirm the fixed build in that source’s advisory.

Recent findings suggest that the fixed build can only come from whoever builds your image, because the Java runtime and the system packages your application runs on come from the image underneath it. That dependency is why a hardened image is a necessary step toward a trusted software supply chain. With Docker Hardened Images, tracking each vendor’s fix and rebuilding on it is work Docker does for you. The images are minimal and secure by default, and they are built to serve as a trusted and verifiable upstream for your builds. You can move a service onto one by following the migration guide.

A container often runs more than one JVM, for example when a build tool forks a JVM for tests, an application server starts helper processes or a CI agent starts a JVM for every build step. The flag protects only the JVMs that receive it, and the variable most people reach for first is JAVA_OPTS, which Java does not read at all.

The JVM itself, however it is started. Includes javac, keytool and other JDK tools.

Yes, through the inherited environment.

Recent findings suggest that A Java 8 JVM that sees it refuses to start. Some DHI FIPS images already set this variable.

Only the java launcher, Java 9 and later.

Yes, when the child is started with java.

Not read by javac, keytool or other JDK tools. DHI FIPS images set it. Java 8 ignores it.

Nothing downstream inherits it.

JAVA_OPTS, JENKINS_JAVA_OPTS, MAVEN_OPTS, ES_JAVA_OPTS and similar.

A start script, which copies the value onto one java command line.

According to recent reports, each script has its own rules. If nothing in the image reads the variable, it does nothing.

Sources indicate that five rules follow from that table. We tested each on DHI images.

JAVA_OPTS only works where a script reads it. With JAVA_OPTS=”-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics” set and a plain java command, the intrinsic stays on. No warning is printed.

In a recent development, A flag on the command line stops at that process. We started a JVM with the flag on its command line and had it start a second JVM. The child ran with the intrinsic on. With JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS in the environment, the child ran with it off. A child started with a cleared environment gets nothing, whichever variable you use.

Recent findings suggest that check what the image already sets before you set anything. In Docker and Kubernetes, your value replaces the image’s value. It is not appended.

docker inspect –format ‘{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}’ \  | grep -E ‘^(JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS|JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS)=’.

Our FIPS images use these variables to configure the FIPS provider. dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:21-fips sets both. When we replaced its JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS with only the flag, the JVM started normally, but the org.bouncycastle.fips.approved_only property was gone. Nothing warned us. If the command prints a value, copy it and add the flag at the end:.

env:  – name: JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS    value: “ -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics”.

Not every FIPS image uses the same variables, so run the check for each image.

Keep JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS away from Java 8. Java 8 is not affected and does not know the flag:.

Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -XX:-UseBASE64IntrinsicsUnrecognized VM option ‘UseBASE64Intrinsics’Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine.

Industry observers note that adding -XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions to the variable does not help on Java 8. Where Java 8 shares an environment with a newer Java, either scope the variable to the containers that need it or use JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS, which Java 8 ignores. Java 11 accepts the flag, so it is harmless there.

In a recent development, verify the process, not the environment. Running java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version inside a container starts a newly introduced JVM. It tells you what the environment gives a new JVM, not what the JVM already serving traffic was started with. For the running process, use the startup log line. JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS prints one too, starting with NOTE: Picked up. In an image that includes the JDK you can also ask the process directly:.

jcmd VM.flags | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics.

According to recent reports, the answer must be -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. If the flag reached the JVM through an environment variable, it will not show in the process’s command line, so ps is not a reliable check.

Sources indicate that some applications discard these variables on purpose. Elasticsearch’s start script, for example, ignores JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and expects ES_JAVA_OPTS. Check your application’s documentation.

It has been revealed that pull the fresh image and redeploy. Four things catch people out:.

In a recent development, then confirm with java -version that what is running reports a fixed build. After that, remove the flag from every place you set it.

According to recent reports, the day after Java4Shell, NGINX released fixes for two memory errors in the way it handles HTTP/2 connections, tracked as CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. A crafted request can crash a worker process, and where an attacker gets past the operating system’s memory protections it can run code inside that worker. Both flaws need HTTP/2 to be enabled on the server, and the same releases fix other NGINX issues that do not depend on HTTP/2, so revision either way.

The Docker Hardened Images for NGINX were rebuilt on NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 and published on November 18, the same day as the upstream release. To patch, pull the image again and redeploy, and move any tag pinned to an older exact version to a fixed one. nginx -v prints the version, and the fixed ones are 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. The notes on pull policy, mirrors and your own images in the section above apply to NGINX images in the same way.

Industry observers note that the vulnerable code is in the Java runtime inside the image, and if you are using DHI, shipping the fix becomes our job. Whether that code can be reached in your deployment depends on things an image cannot see: the CPU it is scheduled onto, the options you start it with, the processes it starts, and the traffic you send it.

With Docker Hardened Images, Docker will.

Track every Java vendor and ship fixed runtimes in DHI as soon as they are released.

Track every Java vendor yourself and rebuild your base images on each fixed runtime.

Tell you which images are fixed and which are still waiting.

Find out from each vendor which of its builds are fixed.

Tell you what we know, and revision this post.

Follow the OpenJDK, Oracle and vendor advisories as they change.

Three jobs stay with you whichever image you run.

In a recent development, it was only four weeks ago that the news was PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Calif, the security research team that found Java4Shell and helped find PHP2Shell, indicates it used AI to find this flaw in about an hour and that the whole effort cost less than $200 in tokens. When a flaw like this can be found and weaponized at that price, it is reasonable to expect more of them.

If you lead a team or answer for how your organization builds and ships software, the questions after a week like this one are whether you were exposed and how quickly you can prove you were not. It is imperative to have a trusted foundation in place before the next flaw appears, and Docker Hardened Images is that foundation to adopt. This week Docker began publishing fixed Java and NGINX images to the catalog within a day of each disclosure, with the images still waiting listed in the status table above. Each image ships with a signed SBOM and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, so you have a record of what it contains and how it was built.

The Docker Hardened Images catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, and moving one of your services onto a hardened image typically means changing one line in its Dockerfile. If you are not building on Docker Hardened Images yet, start today.

LeRobot Community Datasets: The “ImageNet” of Robotics — When and How?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled robots to perform a wide range of tasks—from simple commands like “grasp the cube” to more complex activities like folding laundry or cleaning a table.
  • “The biggest challenge in robotics isn’t dexterity, but generalization—across physical, visual, and semantic levels.”— Physical Intelligence.
  • Industry observers note that A robot must "figure out how to correctly perform even a simple task in a fresh setting or with new objects," and this requires both robust skills and common-sense understanding of the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled robots to perform a wide range of tasks—from simple commands like “grasp the cube” to more complex activities like folding laundry or cleaning a table. These models aim to achieve generalization: the ability to perform tasks in novel settings, with unseen objects, and in varying conditions.

“The biggest challenge in robotics isn’t dexterity, but generalization—across physical, visual, and semantic levels.”— Physical Intelligence.

Industry observers note that A robot must "figure out how to correctly perform even a simple task in a fresh setting or with new objects," and this requires both robust skills and common-sense understanding of the world. Yet, progress is often limited by the availability of diverse data for such robotic systems.

“Generalization must occur at many levels. At the low level, the robot must understand how to pick up a spoon (by the handle) or plate (by the edge), even if it has not seen these specific spoons or plates before, and even if they are placed in a pile of dirty dishes. At a higher level, the robot must understand the semantics of each task—where to put clothes and shoes (ideally in the laundry hamper or closet, not on the bed), and what kind of tool is appropriate for wiping down a spill. This generalization requires both robust physical skills and a common-sense understanding of the environment, so that the robot can generalize at many levels at the same time, from physical, to visual, to semantic. This is made even harder by the limited availability of diverse data for such robotic systems.”— Physical Intelligence.

Recent findings suggest that to simplify, the core of generalist policies lies in a simple idea: co-training on heterogeneous datasets. By exposing VLA models to a variety of environments, tasks, and robot embodiments, we can teach models not only how to act, but why—how to interpret a scene, understand a goal, and adapt skills across contexts.

💡 “Generalization is not just a model property—it’s a data phenomenon.”It emerges from the diversity, quality, and abstraction level of the training data.

This brings us to a fundamental question:.

Given current datasets, what is the upper limit of generalization we can expect?

Can a robot meaningfully respond to a completely novel prompt—say, *"set up a surprise birthday party"*—if it has never encountered anything remotely similar during training? Especially when most datasets are collected in academic labs, by a limited number of people, under well-controlled setups?

Recent findings suggest that we frame generalization as a data-centric view: treating it as the process of abstracting broader patterns from data—essentially “zooming out” to reveal task-agnostic structures and principles. This shift in perspective emphasizes the role of dataset diversity, rather than model architecture alone, in driving generalization.

So far, the majority of robotics datasets come from structured academic environments. Even if we scale up to millions of demonstrations, one dataset will often dominate, limiting diversity. Unlike ImageNet—which aggregated internet-scale data and captured the real world more holistically—robotics lacks a comparably diverse, community-driven benchmark.

This is largely because collecting data for robotics requires physical hardware and significant effort.

That’s why, at LeRobot, we’re working to make robotics data collection more accessible—at home, at school, or anywhere. We're:.

We're already seeing the results: the number of community-contributed datasets on the Hub is growing rapidly.

Growth of lerobot datasets on the Hugging Face Hub over time.

It has been revealed that if we break down the uploaded datasets by robot type, we see that most contributions are to So100 and Koch, making robotic arms and manipulation tasks the primary focus of the current LeRobot dataset landscape. However, it’s crucial to remember that the potential reaches far beyond. Domains like autonomous vehicles, assistive robots, and mobile navigation stand to benefit just as much from shared data. This momentum brings us closer to a future where datasets reflect a global effort, not just the contributions of a single lab or institution.

Distribution of lerobot datasets by robot type.

Here are just a few standout community-contributed datasets that show how diverse and imaginative robotics can be:.

Explore additional creative datasets under the LeRobot tag on the Hugging Face Hub, and interactively view them in the LeRobot Dataset Visualizer.

Industry observers note that as robotics data collection becomes more democratized, curation becomes the next challenge. While these datasets are still collected in constrained setups, they are a crucial step toward affordable, general-purpose robotic policies. Not everyone has access to expensive hardware—but with shared infrastructure and open collaboration, we can build something far greater.

🧠 “Generalization isn’t solved in a lab—it’s taught by the world.”The more diverse our data, the more capable our models will be.

Why does data quality matter? Poor-quality data results in poor downstream performance, biased outputs, and models that fail to generalize. Hence, efficient and high-quality data collection plays a critical role in advancing generalist robotic policies.

Sources indicate that while foundation models in vision and language have thrived on massive, web-scale datasets, robotics lacks an “Internet of robots”—a vast, diverse corpus of real-world interactions. Instead, robotic data is fragmented across different embodiments, sensor setups, and control modes, forming isolated data islands.

To overcome this, recent approaches like Gr00t organize training data as a pyramid, where:.

Within this framework, efficient real-world data collection is indispensable—it anchors learned behaviors in actual robotic hardware and closes the sim-to-real gap, ultimately improving the generalization, adaptability, and performance of robotics foundation models.

By expanding the volume and diversity of real-world datasets, we reduce fragmentation between heterogeneous data sources. When datasets are disjoint in terms of environment, embodiment, or task distribution, models struggle to transfer knowledge across domains.

🔗 Real-world data acts as connective tissue—it aligns abstract priors with grounded action and enables the model to build more coherent and transferable representations.

As a result, increasing the proportion of real robot interactions does not merely enhance realism—it structurally reinforces the links between all layers of the pyramid, leading to more robust and capable policies.

Data Pyramid for Robot Foundation Model Training. Adapted from Gr00t (Yang et al., 2025). Data quantity decreases while embodiment specificity increases from bottom to top.

According to recent reports, at LeRobot, we’ve started developing an automatic curation pipeline to post-process community datasets. During the post-processing phase, we’ve identified several areas where improvements can further boost dataset quality and facilitate more effective curation going forward:.

In a recent development, many datasets lack task descriptions, lack details or are ambiguous in the task to be done. Semantics is at the moment at the core of cognition, meaning that understanding the context and specifics of a task is crucial for robotic performance. Detailed expressions ensure that robots understand exactly what is expected, but also provide a broader knowledge and vocabulary to the cognition system. Ambiguity can lead to incorrect interpretation and, consequently, incorrect actions.

Subtask-level annotations are often missing, making it difficult to model complex task hierarchies.While this can be handled with VLM, it is still better to have a task annotation provided by the author of the dataset at hand.

Features like images.laptop are ambiguously labeled:.

It has been revealed that manual mapping of dataset features to standardized names is time-consuming and error-prone.We can possibly automate feature type inference using VLMs or computer vision models to classify camera perspectives. However, keeping this in mind helps to have a cleaner dataset.

Different datasets use different action or state dimensions, even for the same robot (e.g., so100).Some datasets show inconsistencies in action/state format.

Now that we know that creating a high-quality dataset is essential for training reliable and generalizable robot policies, we have outlined a checklist of best practices to assist you in collecting effective data.

Use a consistent and interpretable naming scheme for all camera views and observations:.

For wrist-mounted cameras, specify orientation:.

Consistent naming improves clarity and helps downstream models better interpret spatial configurations and multi-view inputs.

Start recording, start contributing—because the future of generalist robots depends on the data we build today.

That’s exactly what we’re building at Deplace AI, data on-demand for Physical AI, and we’re also keen to contribute to the open-source ecosystem.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Minister says intruders downloaded more than 130 GB of data as political churn left security neglected.
  • The Ancient Thracian heartland of Bulgaria indicates it has shut down a cyberespionage operation that gave intruders access to government networks for five years – the longest-running known campaign against its administration.
  • Bulgaria's Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation remarked the unauthorized and officially unattributed attackers first gained access to infrastructure used by government institutions to exchange information in 2021.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Minister says intruders downloaded more than 130 GB of data as political churn left security neglected.

The Ancient Thracian heartland of Bulgaria indicates it has shut down a cyberespionage operation that gave intruders access to government networks for five years – the longest-running known campaign against its administration.

Bulgaria's Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation remarked the unauthorized and officially unattributed attackers first gained access to infrastructure used by government institutions to exchange information in 2021.

It explained that the intrusion went unnoticed for so long because "the previous means of protection did not work as a single, integrated system," and that without a latest, recently installed product, it may have gone undetected for much longer.

"The incident was discovered thanks to the upcoming national cybersecurity system, which for the first time provides a single picture of what is happening in state networks," the ministry added.

"Without it, this activity would most likely have remained hidden for an indefinite period of time.".

Bulgaria acknowledged that "sensitive information related to the work of the state" was accessed, but did not specify the scale of the compromise.

Innovation and Digital Transformation Minister Ivan Vasilev said attackers had downloaded more than 130 GB of data over five years. He also put the volume at 62 million pages.

The Register contacted the Bulgarian government for confirmation of these numbers.

The ministry mentioned that it has not yet found any evidence that citizens' personal data was compromised, and that the affected infrastructure "will be under increased surveillance for 90 days" in case the attackers try to regain access.

Vasilev mentioned multiple international hacking groups had accessed government systems since 2021. He did not specify the names of these groups, however, nor did he name any specific countries that may have been involved.

In a follow-up interview with bTV, Vasilev blamed political instability and frequent changes of ministerial leadership for leaving government systems inadequately protected.

A representative of the Progressive Bulgaria party, which back in May won Bulgaria's eighth general election in five years, Vasilev said the "constant change of leadership" means "key things for the state do not actually happen.".

Vasilev said the intrusion was discovered over the summer as the national cybersecurity system was upgraded, and that teams had spent the past three to four months removing the attackers. ®.

Vision Language Models (Better, faster, stronger)

📅 12 May 2025 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4348 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vision Language Models (VLMs) are the talk of the town.
  • It has been revealed that since then, so much has changed.
  • Industry observers note that in this blog post, we’ll take a look back and unpack everything that happened with vision language models the past year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vision Language Models (VLMs) are the talk of the town. In a previous blog post (from April 2024), we talked a lot about VLMs. A major chunk was about LLaVA, the first successful and easily reproducible open-source vision language model, along with tips on how to discover, evaluate, and fine-tune open models.

It has been revealed that since then, so much has changed. Models have become smaller yet more powerful. We've seen the rise of upcoming architectures and capabilities (reasoning, agency, long video understanding, etc.). In parallel, entirely new paradigms, such as multimodal Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and multimodal agents have taken shape.

Industry observers note that in this blog post, we’ll take a look back and unpack everything that happened with vision language models the past year. You’ll discover key changes, emerging trends, and notable developments.

We highly recommend reading the first blog post if you want a good primer on how vision language models work.

In this section, we will look at the new types of VLMs. While some are absolutely new, others are improved versions of previous research.

Any-to-any models, as the name suggests, are models that can take in any modality and output any modality (image, text, audio). They do it by aligning the modalities, where an input from one modality can be translated to another (e.g. the word “dog” would be associated with an image of a dog, or with the utterance of the word).

Sources indicate that these models have multiple encoders (one for each modality) and then fuse the embeddings together to create a shared representation space. The decoders (multiple or single) use the shared latent space as input and decode into the modality of choice. Earliest attempt to build any-to-any models is Chameleon by Meta, which can take in image and text and output image and text. Meta didn’t release the image generation capability in this model, so Alpha-VLLM released Lumina-mGPT, which has built image generation on top of Chameleon.

The latest and most capable any-to-any model, Qwen 2.5 Omni (figure below) is a good example to understand the architecture of an any-to-any model.

Recent findings suggest that qwen2.5-Omni employs a novel "Thinker-Talker" architecture, where the "Thinker" handles text generation, and the "Talker" produces natural speech responses in a streaming manner. MiniCPM-o 2.6, an 8B parameter multimodal model is capable of understanding and generating content across vision, speech, and language modalities. Janus-Pro-7B, introduced by DeepSeek AI, is a unified multimodal model that excels in both understanding and generating content across modalities. It features a decoupled visual encoding architecture, separating the processes for understanding and generation.

Recent findings suggest that we suspect an uptick in the number of such models in the coming years. It is a well-known intuition that multimodal learning is the only way we can learn deep representations better. We have curated some any-to-any models and demos in this collection.

Reasoning models are models that can solve complex problems. We saw them first with large language models, and now vision language models. Until 2025, there was only one open-source multimodal reasoning model, QVQ-72B-preview by Qwen. It was an experimental model that was developed by the Alibaba Qwen team and came with many disclaimers.

This year there’s another player, Kimi-VL-A3B-Thinking by the Moonshot AI team. It consists of MoonViT (SigLIP-so-400M) as the image encoder and a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) decoder with 16B total parameters and only 2.8B active parameters. The model is a long chain-of-thought fine-tuned and further aligned (reinforcement learning) version of the Kimi-VL base vision language model. You can try the model here.

The authors also released an instruction fine-tuned version called Kimi-VL-A3B-Instruct.

According to recent reports, the model can take in long videos, PDFs, screenshots and more. It has agentic capabilities as well.

According to recent reports, the community used to scale intelligence through the number of parameters, and then high-quality synthetic data. After a certain point, the benchmarks saturated and scaling models had diminishing returns. The community went to shrink larger models through various methods, like distillation. This makes sense because it reduces compute costs, simplifies deployment, and unlocks use cases like local execution, enhancing data privacy.

When we say small vision language models we often refer to models with less than 2B parameters that can be run on consumer GPUs. SmolVLM is a good example model family for smaller vision language models. Instead of shrinking larger models, the authors went all the way and tried to fit models into tiny number of parameters like 256M, 500M and 2.2B. SmolVLM2, for instance, attempted to solve video understanding in these sizes and found 500M to be a good trade-off. At Hugging Face, we have built an iPhone application, HuggingSnap, to demonstrate that these model sizes can achieve video understanding on consumer devices.

Industry observers note that another striking model is gemma3-4b-it by Google DeepMind. It’s particularly exciting as it’s one of the smallest multimodal models to have 128k token context window, and supports 140+ languages. The model comes with the Gemma 3 family of models, with its largest model ranking first on Chatbot Arena at the time. The largest model was then distilled to a 1B variant.

According to recent reports, lastly, although not the smallest, Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct is worth noting. The model can do various tasks ranging from localization (object detection and pointing), to document understanding, to agentic tasks; with context length up to 32k tokens.

Industry observers note that you can use small models through MLX and Llama.cpp integrations. For MLX, assuming you have it installed, you can get started with SmolVLM-500M-Instruct with this one liner:.

You can get started with using gemma-3-4b-it model in GGUF format with llama.cpp through CLI with this one-liner:.

You can also serve the same model as follows.

In a recent development, we would like to give a shoutout to moondream2 and Florence-2 as they're the earliest attempts for smallest vision language models. In this blog, we are covering primarily newer models (mostly models that came out after April 2024).

It has been revealed that mixture of Expert (MoEs) models offer an alternative to dense architectures by dynamically selecting and activating only the most relevant sub-models, termed "experts", to process a given input data segment. This selective activation (done by a router) mechanism has demonstrated the potential to substantially enhance model performance and operational efficiency while utilizing fewer computational resources.

In a recent development, moEs are faster at inference than their similar parameter-dense counterparts because of the selective activation of a smaller slice of the network. They also converge promptly during training. Every good thing comes with a cost, as MoEs need more memory cost due to the entire model being on the GPU, even if a smaller chunk is used.

Industry observers note that in the widely adopted Transformer architecture, MoE layers are most commonly integrated by replacing the standard Feed-Forward Network (FFN) layers within each Transformer block. Dense networks use the entire model to run an inference, while similarly sized MoE networks selectively activate some experts. This helps in better compute utilization and faster inference.

Vision language models that have mixture-of-experts decoders seem to have enhanced performance. For instance, Kimi-VL as of now is the most advanced open reasoning model that has a mixture-of-experts decoder. Mixture-of-Experts show promising results with MoE-LLaVA's focus on efficiency and hallucination reduction and DeepSeek-VL2's broad multimodal capabilities too. The latest version of Llama (Llama 4) is an MoE with vision capabilities. MoE as a decoder is a promising research area, and we suspect an increase in models like these.

To get a nice understanding of MoEs we recommend reading this fantastic article.

Sources indicate that VLMs are even making their mark in the field of robotics! There, they are known as Vision-language-action models (VLA). But don't be fooled, those are mainly VLMs with a little moustache and hat. VLAs take images and text instructions, and return text indicating actions for the robot to take directly. VLAs extend vision language models by adding action and state tokens to interact with and control physical environments. These extra tokens represent the system’s internal state (how it perceives the environment), actions (what it does based on commands), and time-related information (like the order of steps in a task). These tokens are appended to the vision language input to generate actions or policy.

VLAs are usually fine-tuned on top of a base VLM. Some people extend this definition further and define VLAs as any model interacting visually with a real or digital world. In this definition, VLAs can do UI navigation or be used in agentic workflows. But many people believe those applications fall in the VLM domain.

Recent findings suggest that great examples of VLAs are π0 and π0-FAST, the first robotics foundation models by Physical Intelligence, ported to Hugging Face’s LeRobot library. These models are trained across 7 robotics platforms and 68 unique tasks. They show strong zero-shot and fine-tuned performance on complex, real-world activities such as laundry folding, table bussing, grocery bagging, box assembly, and object retrieval.

It has been revealed that GR00T N1 is NVIDIA’s open VLA foundation model for generalist humanoid robots. It understands images and language, and turns them into actions, like moving its arms or following instructions, thanks to a system that combines smart reasoning with real-time movement control. GR00T N1 also builds on the LeRobot dataset format, the open standard created to simplify sharing and training on robot demonstrations.

Now that we’ve looked at the latest VLM model innovations, let’s explore how more established capabilities have evolved.

It has been revealed that as we’ve seen in earlier sections, VLMs enable generalization over traditional computer vision tasks. Models can now take in images and a variety of prompts, such as open-ended text, and output structured text with localization tokens (for detection, segmentation and more).

According to recent reports, last year, PaliGemma was the first model to attempt solving these tasks. The model takes in an image and text, where text is a description of an object of interest, along with a task prefix. The text prompt looks like “segment striped cat” or “detect bird on the roof”.

For detection, the model outputs the bounding box coordinates as tokens. For segmentation, on the other hand, the model outputs detection tokens and segmentation tokens. These segmentation tokens aren’t all the segmented pixel coordinates, but codebook indices that are decoded by a variational autoencoder trained to decode these tokens into valid segmentation masks (as shown in the figure below).

Many models have been introduced to do localization tasks after PaliGemma. Late last year, an upgraded version of PaliGemma, PaliGemma 2, appeared with the same capabilities and better performance. Another model that came later was Molmo by Allen AI, which can point to instances with dots and count object instances.

Qwen2.5-VL can also detect, point to, and count objects, and this includes UI elements as objects too!

Vision language models in production require filtering inputs and outputs to prevent jailbreaks and harmful outputs for compliance. Harmful content varies from inputs with violence to sexually explicit content. That’s where multimodal safety models come in: they are used before and after vision language models to filter their inputs and outputs. They are just like LLM safety models but with additional image input.

In early 2025, Google introduced the first open multimodal safety model, ShieldGemma 2. It is built on ShieldGemma, the text-only safety model. This model takes in images and content policies and returns whether an image is safe for a given policy. Policy refers to a criterion in which the image is inappropriate. ShieldGemma 2 can also be used to filter outputs of image generation models.

Llama Guard 4 by Meta, is a dense multimodal and multilingual safety model. It is densely pruned from Llama 4 Scout (a multimodal mixture-of-experts) with safety fine tuning.

In a recent development, the model can be used for text-only and multimodal inference. The model can also take in vision language model outputs, complete conversations, and filter them before sending them to the user.

Now let’s look at how Retrieval Augmented Generation has evolved in the multimodal space. RAG for complex documents, usually formatted in PDF, is processed in three steps:.

A traditional PDF parser consists of multiple elements to preserve the structure and visual elements in the document, such as layout, tables, images, charts, all rendered into a markdown. But this setup can be hard to maintain.

With the rise of vision language models, this problem was addressed: there are now multimodal retrievers and rerankers.

It has been revealed that multimodal retrievers take a stack of PDFs and a query as input and return the most relevant page numbers along with their confidence scores. The scores represent how likely the page contains the answer to the query, or how relevant the query is to the page. This bypasses the brittle parsing step.

The most relevant pages are then fed to the vision language model along with the query, and the VLM generates the answer.

There are two main multimodal retriever architectures:.

DSE models consist of a text encoder and an image encoder, returning a single vector per query. The returned scores are softmax over the dot products of embeddings. They return a single vector per passage.

In a recent development, colBERT-like models, like ColPali, are also dual encoder models, with a twist: ColPali has a vision language model as an image encoder, and a large language model as a text encoder. These models are inherently not encoders, but the models output embeddings, which are then passed to a “MaxSim”. The outputs are multiple vectors, one for each token, unlike DSE. In MaxSim, the similarity between each text token embedding and each image patch embedding is calculated, and this approach captures nuances better. Due to this reason, ColBERT-like models are less cost-efficient, have better performance.

Below you can see the indexing latency for ColPali. Since it’s just a single model, it’s also easier to maintain.

On Hugging Face Hub, you can find these models under the task “Visual Document Retrieval”.

According to recent reports, the most popular benchmark for this task is ViDoRe, which consists of documents in English and French, with documents varying from financial reports, scientific figures to administrative documents. Each example of ViDoRe has the document as image, a query and potential answers. The documents matched with the queries help with contrastive pre-training, so the ViDoRe train set is used to train upcoming models.

Recent findings suggest that vision language models unlock many agentic workflows from chatting with documents to computer use. Here we will cover the latter since it requires more advanced agentic capabilities. Recently, there have been many vision language models releases that understand and operate over UIs. The latest one is UI-TARS-1.5 by ByteDance, which demonstrated great results in operating over browser, computer and phone use. It can also do gameplay with reasoning, and operate in open world games. Another impactful release of this year is MAGMA-8B, it’s a foundation model for both UI navigation and physical interaction with the real world. Moreover, Qwen2.5-VL (especially its 32B variant as it is further trained on agentic tasks) and Kimi-VL reasoning model are good in GUI agentic tasks.

Recent findings suggest that at the beginning of 2025, we introduced smolagents, a upcoming lightweight agentic library that implements the ReAct framework. Shortly after, we implemented vision language support for the library. This integration took place on two use cases:.

The library provides building blocks for the users to build their own agentic workflows with image understanding. We provide different scripts and single-line CLI commands to get the users started easily.

For the first case, assume we want an agent to describe documents (which is not very agentic, but good for minimal use cases). You can initialize the CodeAgent (an agent that writes its own code!) like the following:.

For your own use case where you need to get images dynamically, modify the callback however you’d like. We will not define it here in detail for simplicity. Optionally, you can read the blog post and the script itself at the end of this blog post. For now, let’s see how we initialize the agent with callbacks and browser control steps.
