It has been revealed that smolagents provides different model types, such as local transformers models, open-source models served using Inference Providers, or endpoints closed-source model providers. We encourage the use of open-source models as many agentic workflows at the moment require reasoning, which benefits from models with a large number of parameters. Qwen 2.5 VL as of April 2025 is a good candidate for agentic workflows, as the model is further trained on agentic tasks.

Most vision language models these days can handle videos, because videos can be represented as a sequence of frames. However, video understanding is tricky because of the temporal relationship between frames and the large amount of frames, so different techniques are used to select a representative set of video frames.

Since last year, the community has weighed on different approaches and tricks to solve this problem.

A good example is the LongVU model by Meta. It downsamples video frames by passing them to DINOv2 to pick the most similar ones to remove them, and then the model further refines frames by picking the most relevant frames according to the text query, where both the text and the frames are projected to the same space and similarity is calculated. Qwen2.5VL can handle long context and is adapted to dynamic FPS rates, as the model is trained with videos with different frame rates. Through extended multimodal RoPE, it understands the absolute time positions of frames, and can handle different rates and still understand the speed of the events happening in real life. Another model is Gemma 3, which can accept video frames interleaved with timestamps in text prompt, e.g. “Frame 00.00: ..”, and is very performant for video understanding tasks.

Sources indicate that preference optimization is an alternative fine-tuning approach for language models that can also be extended to vision language models. Instead of relying on fixed labels, this method focuses on comparing and ranking candidate responses based on preferences. The trl library offers support for direct preference optimization (DPO), including for VLMs.

In a recent development, below is an example of how a preference dataset for DPO of a VLM fine-tuning is structured. Each entry consists of an image + question pair and two corresponding answers: one chosen and one rejected. The VLM is fine-tuned to generate responses aligned with the preferred (chosen) answer.

An example dataset for this procedure is RLAIF-V, which contains over 83000 annotated samples formatted according to the structure described above. Each entry includes a list of images (usually one), a prompt, a chosen answer, and a rejected answer, just as expected by the DPOTrainer.There is a RLAIF-V formatted dataset, which is already formatted accordingly. Below is an example of a single sample:.

Once the dataset is prepared, you can use the DPOConfig and DPOTrainer classes from the trl library to configure and launch the fine-tuning process.Below is an example configuration using DPOConfig:.

Sources indicate that to train your model using DPOTrainer, you can optionally provide a reference model to compute the reward difference. If you’re using Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT), you may omit the reference model by setting ref_model=None.

Benchmarks have also evolved significantly over the past year. In our previous blog, we described MMMU and MMBench as two emerging benchmarks for evaluating Vision Language Models. With the rapid progress in the field, the models have saturated on these benchmarks, and we need better evaluation tools. To achieve this, we need tools that assess specific capabilities, on top of general purpose benchmarks.

Now, we highlight two general-purpose benchmarks that stand out: MMT-Bench and MMMU-Pro.

MMT-Bench is designed to assess VLMs across a wide range of multimodal tasks that require expert knowledge, precise visual recognition, localization, reasoning, and planning. The benchmark includes 31325 multi-choice visual questions from various multimodal scenarios, with image, text, video, and point cloud modalities. With 32 different meta-tasks with 162 subtasks, it covers a variety of tasks, including OCR, Visual Recognition, or Visual-Language Retrieval.

In a recent development, MMMU-Pro is a better version of the original MMMU benchmark. It also evaluates advanced AI models’ true understanding capabilities across multiple modalities.It is more complex than MMMU, e.g. it has a vision-only input setting and an increase in the number of candidate options from 4 to 10. The benchmark also incorporates real-world simulation, with vision-only questions derived from screenshots or photos captured within a simulated display, featuring varying backgrounds, font styles, and sizes to mimic real-world conditions.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CISA, F6 sound the alarm after PoC exploit made public.
  • Attackers are currently exploiting a critical vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-76466 in Cisco Expressway that allows them to remotely execute commands as root without any authentication, according to warnings from the US government and security researchers.
  • Sources indicate that CVE-2026-76466, which carries a 9.8 CVSS rating, affects Cisco Expressway-C and Cisco Expressway-E gateways configured in clusters, both virtual and physical appliances running vulnerable software.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CISA, F6 sound the alarm after PoC exploit made public.

Attackers are currently exploiting a critical vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-76466 in Cisco Expressway that allows them to remotely execute commands as root without any authentication, according to warnings from the US government and security researchers.

Sources indicate that CVE-2026-76466, which carries a 9.8 CVSS rating, affects Cisco Expressway-C and Cisco Expressway-E gateways configured in clusters, both virtual and physical appliances running vulnerable software. These provide firewall traversal, VPN-less remote access, and call routing for remote users connecting to voice, video, and messaging collaboration services.

The bug involves hard-coded authentication credentials and insufficient certificate validation in clustered Expressway deployments.

At the time, the networking vendor mentioned it wasn’t aware of any abuse of the vulnerability.

That all changed late last week, however, when Russian security firm F6 said it was investigating “the first observed case” of miscreants exploiting CVE-2026-76466, shortly after a public proof-of-concept exploit became available.

“The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices,” F6’s Cyber Defense Center stated on Thursday. “Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network. After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure.”.

Sources indicate that specifically, the criminals prepared custom Python code to scan the victim’s network and identify files and folders shared over the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. The scripts were also designed to interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories for credentials and other sensitive information.

The Python scripts used in the attack indicated that the operator used an AI assistant, according to F6.

The security shop also noted that one of the key indicators of compromise is a nodeup “wombat@127.0.0.1” entry in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices.

A day later, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-76466 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and told federal agencies to patch by Monday.

It has been revealed that cisco updated its advisory on Monday to acknowledge CISA’s addition, while noting that it has no direct evidence of active exploitation. The Register reached out to the networking and security vendor for additional details about the scope of the attacks, but did not receive any response. We will update this story as we learn more. ®.

Breaking: OpenAI Preprint Reports 9/4 Bound for Matrix Multiplication

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that openAI released a preprint reporting an upper bound of 9/4 for the exponent of matrix multiplication over the complex numbers.
  • The paper concerns ω, the asymptotic matrix-multiplication exponent: the infimum of the values τ such that, for every positive ε, multiplication requires O_ε(n^(τ + ε)) scalar arithmetic operations as n tends to infinity.
  • Industry observers note that an earlier preprint, submitted on August 17, 2026 by Emilien Dupont and co-authors, reports ω < 2.371177 and identifies 2.371339 as the previous best bound.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that openAI released a preprint reporting an upper bound of 9/4 for the exponent of matrix multiplication over the complex numbers. The manuscript is dated October 2, 2026, and the paper file’s initial repository commit is dated October 6, 2026.

The paper concerns ω, the asymptotic matrix-multiplication exponent: the infimum of the values τ such that, for every positive ε, multiplication requires O_ε(n^(τ + ε)) scalar arithmetic operations as n tends to infinity. Theorem 1.1 states that, for every positive ε, two n-by-n complex matrices can be multiplied using O_ε(n^(9/4 + ε)) arithmetic operations, with the algorithm and its constants allowed to depend on ε.

Industry observers note that an earlier preprint, submitted on August 17, 2026 by Emilien Dupont and co-authors, reports ω < 2.371177 and identifies 2.371339 as the previous best bound. Its approach enlarged the optimization setting, introduced a machine-learning-based optimization algorithm and refined it with AlphaEvolve. OpenAI’s reported 9/4 bound is below the earlier 2.371177 threshold, and its proof takes a different route: explicit tensor degenerations combined with Strassen’s spectral viewpoint, rather than a further optimization of the combination-loss framework.

It has been revealed that the proof represents bilinear algorithms as tensors, or trilinear coefficient arrays, whose three variable groups are called legs. A recurring obstacle is that useful tensor pieces can share variables, whereas a full direct sum requires independent variables on all three legs. The central construction therefore starts with blocks that are independent on two legs but share the third.

A finite Fourier projection supplies a tentative block label on the shared leg. The construction then uses a degeneration, a weighted reduction that retains terms of minimum total weight after fixed linear substitutions. Here, that weight is the square of the label mismatch, leaving exactly the correctly labeled blocks.

Proposition 3.1 uses 5M source copies to produce M fully independent blocks, each retaining an M-dimensional auxiliary dot product. The paper distinguishes those two multiplicities: the dot-product index does not label additional direct-sum blocks. Corollary 3.2 converts the separation into an entropy inequality, with the entropy term arising from counts of tensor-power words whose sector frequencies are fixed.

Strassen’s spectral framework supplies tensor characters, normalized numerical invariants that add on direct sums, multiply on tensor products and are monotone under restriction, meaning independent linear substitutions on each leg. Each character has value n^(3t) on n-by-n matrix multiplication for a positive parameter t. For polynomial multiplication with coefficient-vector lengths a and b, the paper defines a profile P(a,b) as a normalized geometric mean of character values under all six leg permutations, making it symmetric in the input lengths.

Evaluation at a+b−1 distinct points followed by interpolation gives the polynomial-multiplication tensor rank at most a+b−1; its output flattening, a matrix view of one leg against the other two, supplies the matching lower bound. The rank is therefore exactly a+b−1, supporting the upper bound P(a,b) ≤ (a+b−1)^(1/t), while the case a=1 gives P(1,b) = b.

It has been revealed that A determinant filtration then proves the discrete-concavity inequality 2P(a,b) ≥ P(a,b+1) + P(a,b−1), while a three-sector decomposition proves P(a,3h+a−1) ≥ 3P(a,h). Together, these properties force P(a,a) ≥ a^(4/3). Comparing that lower bound with the upper bound as a tends to infinity forces t ≤ 3/4 and therefore 3t ≤ 9/4. The detecting-character result, proved in the appendix, connects that uniform constraint on characters to the matrix-multiplication exponent.

To obtain an arithmetic algorithm, the proof fixes ε, chooses a smaller positive δ and selects a fixed matrix size u with an exact rank decomposition of length r < u^(9/4+δ). Applying that decomposition recursively to matrix blocks yields the stated O_ε(N^(9/4+ε)) cost, while padding handles arbitrary input dimensions.

Recent findings suggest that the coefficients are fixed once ε is chosen. The argument uses the complex arithmetic model, and the paper states that algebraic coefficients would lie in a single number field.

In a recent development, the authors state explicitly that the theorem concerns the asymptotic arithmetic exponent and that the proof does not specify a competitive finite matrix size. The reported result’s immediate contribution is therefore a tighter asymptotic upper bound, while the matrix size at which the recursive method could become competitive remains the central practical question.

Bluetooth brakes are broken as researchers find anyone can control them

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Security fixes are available for two Elecbrakes models, but an older controller remains vulnerable and unpatched.
  • Imagine something as mission-critical as the brakes on a trailer being vulnerable to unauthorized control.
  • Anyone within Bluetooth range of an unpatched Elecbrakes trailer controller could potentially trigger its brakes or apply more braking force than intended, without needing to authenticate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Security fixes are available for two Elecbrakes models, but an older controller remains vulnerable and unpatched.

Imagine something as mission-critical as the brakes on a trailer being vulnerable to unauthorized control. One Australian manufacturer made the interesting choice of building Bluetooth into a trailer brake controller without adequately securing its critical braking functions.

Anyone within Bluetooth range of an unpatched Elecbrakes trailer controller could potentially trigger its brakes or apply more braking force than intended, without needing to authenticate.

The discovery comes courtesy of a pair of security researchers from Element Digital, Patrick Forck and Jeremy McCarthy. Their investigation began earlier this year when Forck was driving down the road and noticed that his physical Elecbrakes In-Car Remote had connected to someone else's trailer without pairing or prompting him.

“It had connected mid-drive, without pairing or a prompt, to a brake controller that wasn’t mine, on a trailer I’d never seen, belonging to a driver who had no idea,” the researchers wrote. That one-off connection triggered a full-scale investigation by the pair.

According to recent reports, for those unfamiliar with trailer brake controllers, these devices are commonly used on larger trailers. Australian manufacturer Elecbrakes sells such controllers in Australia and New Zealand. Depending on jurisdiction, trailers over a certain weight are required to have their own braking system, which Elecbrakes manufactures. Elecbrakes offers two versions that are designed to be easier to install than traditional controllers: One that’s mounted in a vehicle, and one that is mounted directly on a trailer. That trailer-mounted unit can receive Bluetooth commands from the Elecbrakes smartphone app or a separate in-car remote.

Given the importance of such control units to road safety, it’s easy to imagine how serious such a vulnerability could be if it proved to be easy to exploit, and boy, did it.

Forck and McCarthy admitted they’re infrastructure security guys, not software devs, so they turned to Claude Code to dissect a decompiled copy of the Elecbrakes app, which Claude was happy to oblige.

“What came back from the analysis was a map of the device’s entire Bluetooth GATT profile: 47 characteristics across four services, commands sent as plain unencrypted byte arrays, no checksums, no sequence numbers,” the researchers noted. To make matters worse, there was no authentication required for critical braking commands, even though other Bluetooth functions required pairing.

Claude then built a web app that ran in Chrome which was able to access the Bluetooth controls for a nearby Elecbrakes system, and they were able to modify practically every aspect of brake control on a unit owned by one of them.

Industry observers note that pairing failed on a few attempts, but not where it mattered: It allowed the connection without glitch for actual brake control. They sent a few bytes to the brake control characteristic, and were shocked.

“The electromagnetic hum at the brake drums was immediate and, frankly, a little sickening,” the pair mentioned. “It said yes to four bytes from a total stranger then energised several tonnes’ worth of brakes and reported back that it had done so, pleased with itself.”.

Further experiments managed to modify braking strength based on deceleration speed as well, making it so that the trailer acted unpredictably based on the amount of force a driver applied to stop their vehicle.

To say this is worse than a typical internet-connected device bug is to put it mildly - it even earned a trio of CVEs from CISA, with two of them scoring a CVSS of 9.6.

“The attack surface is ‘anyone within Bluetooth range,’ the skill required is ‘can write four bytes,’ and the victim selection is ‘optional,’ ” Forck and McCarthy stated. The fact AI was able to get them to that point in just a couple of days is even more concerning, they added.

It has been revealed that “This kind of research used to require a fairly rare and specific skill set,” the pair noted. “It now requires curiosity, a device you own, and an AI that can read bytecode faster than any human.”.

According to recent reports, luckily, they appear to have been dealing with a relatively responsive company in Elecbrakes - patches have been deployed for both the in-car and trailer-mounted models of their brake controllers. Installation is a manual process, we note, so if you own a controller from the company, be sure to stop and install the upgrade.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, Elecbrakes has a third controller out there that hasn’t been manufactured in several years, and it got skipped in the patching process. Owners of an ELBC2000 should be aware that their controller is still vulnerable, and there’s no patch available yet, as the vendor didn’t confirm that the ELBC2000 was vulnerable until the end of October, after it faced pressure from the researchers.

Following publication, the firm told us, "Elecbrakes takes the safety and security of its products seriously. Our engineering team reproduced and validated the cybersecurity vulnerability reported by the researchers. A safety risk assessment considered the likelihood of injury under specific scenarios. It concluded that, when a user is actively connected to their own controller through the Elecbrakes app or remote in line with product instructions, the cybersecurity vulnerability identified in the research is not present." ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that today we are happy to introduce a fresh blazing fast OpenAI Whisper deployment option on Inference Endpoints. It provides up to 8x performance improvements compared to the previous version, and makes everyone one click away from deploying dedicated, powerful transcription models in a cost-effective way, leveraging the amazing work done by the AI community.

Sources indicate that through this release, we would like to make Inference Endpoints more community-centric and allow anyone to come and contribute to create incredible inference deployments on the Hugging Face Platform. Along with the community, we would like to propose optimized deployments for a wide range of tasks through the use of awesome and available open-source technologies.

The unique position of Hugging Face, at the heart of the Open-Source AI Community, working hand-in-hand with individuals, institutions and industrial partners, makes it the most heterogeneous platform when it comes to deploying AI models for inference on a wide variety of hardware and software.

According to recent reports, the upcoming Whisper endpoint leverages amazing open-source community projects. Inference is powered by the vLLM project, which provides efficient ways of running AI models on various hardware families – especially, but not limited to, NVIDIA GPUs. We use the vLLM implementation of OpenAI's Whisper model, allowing us to enable further, lower-level optimizations down the software stack.

In this initial release, we are targeting NVIDIA GPUs with compute capabilities 8.9 or better (Ada Lovelace), like L4 & L40s, which unlocks a wide range of software optimizations:.

CUDA graphs record the flow of sequential operations, or kernels, happening on the GPU, and attempts to group them as bigger chunks of work units to execute on the GPU. This grouping operation reduces data movements, synchronizations, and GPU scheduling overhead by executing a single, much larger work unit, rather than multiple smaller ones.

Sources indicate that last but not least, we are dynamically quantizing activations to reduce the memory requirement incurred by the KV cache(s). The computations are done in half precision, bfloat16 in this case, and the outputs are being stored in reduced precision (1 byte for float8 vs 2 bytes for bfloat16) which allows us to store more elements in the KV cache, increasing the cache hit rate.

There are many ways to continue pushing this and we are gearing up to work hand in hand with the community to improve it!

Whisper Large V3 shows a nearly 8x improvement in RTFx, enabling much faster inference with no loss in transcription quality.

We evaluated the transcription quality and runtime efficiency of several Whisper-based models—Whisper Large V3, Whisper Large V3-Turbo, and Distil-Whisper Large V3.5—and compared them against their implementations on the Transformers library to assess both accuracy and decoding speed under identical conditions.

Industry observers note that we computed Word Error Rate (WER) across 8 standard datasets from the Open ASR Leaderboard, including AMI, GigaSpeech, LibriSpeech (Clean and Other), SPGISpeech, Tedlium, VoxPopuli, and Earnings22. These datasets span diverse domains and recording conditions, ensuring a robust evaluation of generalization and real-world transcription quality. WER measures transcription accuracy by calculating the percentage of words that are incorrectly predicted (via insertions, deletions, or substitutions); lower WER indicates better performance. All three Whisper variants maintain WER performance comparable to their Transformer baselines.

To assess inference efficiency, we sampled from the rev16 long-form dataset, which contains audio segments over 45 minutes in length—representative of real transcription workloads such as meetings, podcasts, or interviews. We measured the Real-Time Factor (RTFx), defined as the ratio of audio duration to transcription time, and averaged it across samples. All models were evaluated in bfloat16 on a single L4 GPU, using consistent decoding settings (language, beam size, and batch size).

You can deploy your own ASR inference pipeline via Hugging Face Endpoints. Endpoints allows anyone willing to deploy AI models into production ready environments to do so by filling in a few parameters. It also features the most complete fleet of AI hardware available on the market to suit your need for cost and performance. All of this directly from where the AI community is being built. To get started, nothing easier, simply choose the model you want to deploy:.

Running inference on the deployed model endpoint can be done in just a few lines of code in Python, you can also use the same structure in Javascript or any other language you're comfortable with.

Here's a small snippet to test the deployed checkpoint quickly.

With this blazing fast endpoint, it’s possible to build real-time transcription apps. Try out this example built with FastRTC. Simply speak into your microphone and see your speech transcribed in real time!

Spaces can easily be duplicated so please feel free to duplicate away. All of the above is made available for community use on the Hugging Face Hub in our dedicated HF Endpoints organization. Open challenges, suggest use-cases and contribute here: hfendpoints-images (Inference Endpoints Images) 🚀.

Amazon scoops up AI accelerator tech to keep chips busy at all times

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Not the whole startup - just its tech and the brains behind it.
  • Amazon has agreed to buy AI optimization technology from an Israeli startup in a bid to speed up its inference operations.
  • Industry observers note that the house of Bezos on Monday announced a deal to purchase proprietary AI acceleration tech from Decart AI, known as the Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), for an undisclosed amount.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Not the whole startup - just its tech and the brains behind it.

Amazon has agreed to buy AI optimization technology from an Israeli startup in a bid to speed up its inference operations.

Industry observers note that the house of Bezos on Monday announced a deal to purchase proprietary AI acceleration tech from Decart AI, known as the Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), for an undisclosed amount. Amazon also plans to bring Decart’s three founders and their engineering team into the fold.

Recent findings suggest that decart’s DOS is designed to push AI hardware closer to its maximum performance across different AI models and hardware platforms. The company claims that most AI chips live their lives without reaching their full potential – practically a sin in this age of increased hardware costs and limited availability – and DOS aims to fix that by operating between the model and the chip, optimizing kernels, compilers, and runtimes for the underlying hardware “so every core stays busy.”.

DOS is hardware-agnostic, with Decart saying it supports Nvidia GPUs, Google TPUs, and, most critically for our purposes here, AWS Trainium chips.

“More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost,” Peter DeSantis, Amazon SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, and quantum computing, mentioned in the announcement. “That's the pillar Trainium and our AI efforts are built on, and from our earliest work with Decart, we knew they … would help us push it even further.”.

Decart doesn’t offer much in the way of details about its proprietary AI-maxxing tech, but claims it can reduce latency, improve throughput, and reduce the costs associated with training and inference runs.

An Amazon spokesperson clarified to The Register that the deal is an asset purchase and not a full firm acquisition, with Amazon only acquiring DOS and the tech behind it as well as personnel. As for what may become of Decart after the deal, that’s unclear. Amazon told us to reach out to Decart to learn what may happen to any remaining employees and the company’s other technology, but we didn’t hear back.

Along with offering its optimization stack, Decart has a couple of different AI models: Lucy, a live video model marketed toward advertisers, live streamers, and the like; and Oasis, a world model AI marketed toward companies working on embodied AI applications.

Decart’s non-DOS assets weren’t mentioned in the press release, and per the Amazon spokesperson we talked to, that means they weren’t part of the deal. We can’t imagine that the Decart team is too upset about the potential abandonment of those models, though: While neither tech giant has disclosed a price, Bloomberg claims its sources value the deal at around $7.5 billion.

If Bloomberg's figure is accurate, that would make this deal one of the most expensive in Amazon’s history, right between its $3.9 billion acquisition of One Medical and its $8.5 billion purchase of film studio MGM. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that kaggle and Hugging Face customers are part of one AI community.
  • Beginning today, Kaggle is launching an integration that enhances visibility and discoverability for Hugging Face models directly on Kaggle.
  • Sources indicate that you can navigate from Hugging Face models to Kaggle and vice versa.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that kaggle and Hugging Face customers are part of one AI community. That’s why we’re excited to announce our plans to bring our platforms and communities closer to better serve AI developers everywhere.

Beginning today, Kaggle is launching an integration that enhances visibility and discoverability for Hugging Face models directly on Kaggle.

Sources indicate that you can navigate from Hugging Face models to Kaggle and vice versa. Start by visiting a Hugging Face model page like Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B. To use it in a Kaggle Notebook, you can click on “Use this model” and select “Kaggle” to open up a Kaggle notebook with a pre-populated code snippet to load the model. You can do the same from a Hugging Face model page on Kaggle by clicking the “Code” button.

In a recent development, when you run a notebook on Kaggle that references a model hosted on Hugging Face Hub, we will automatically generate a Hugging Face model page if one doesn’t exist already. You don’t need to make any special changes to your code. Additionally, when you make your notebook public, it will automatically show on the “Code” tab of the Kaggle model page.

In a recent development, discover Hugging Face models and explore all the community examples in public notebooks in one place on Kaggle at https://www.kaggle.com/models. As more Hugging Face models are used on Kaggle, the number of models and associated code examples you can explore for inspiration will grow.

When browsing Hugging Face models on Kaggle, we want to make it easy for you to navigate back to Hugging Face to explore additional details, metadata, community usage in Hugging Face Spaces, discussion, and more. Simply click “Open in Hugging Face” on the Kaggle model page.

If you use a private Hugging Face model in your Kaggle notebook, authenticate via your Hugging Face account as normal (add your HF_TOKEN in the “Add-ons > Secrets” menu in the notebook editor). A Hugging Face model page won’t be generated on Kaggle.

If you want to access a consent-gated model in your Kaggle notebook, you’ll need to request access to it using a Hugging Face account and follow the prompts on your browser's Hugging Face model page as normal. Hugging Face has documentation to guide you through this process. Otherwise, the integration will work the same as for non-gated models.

Sources indicate that we’re actively working on a solution to seamlessly use Hugging Face models in Kaggle competitions that require offline notebook submissions. While this will take a few more months to complete, we believe the wait will be worth it.

You can read Kaggle’s position on “AI Competitions as the gold standard for empirical rigor for GenAI evaluation” to understand why it’s so vital for us to get this part of the integration right! But tl;dr – Kaggle is highly sensitive to data leakage and its impact on model contamination. Our goal is to design this integration to preserve the integrity of our competitions and their vital role in the industry, while enabling seamless access for Kaggle competitors to build with the best models from Hugging Face!

We’d love to hear your feedback in the meantime - share your thoughts and ideas here!

Certis and the Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) declared a three-year memorandum of understanding on November 25, 2026 to jointly develop and test Physical AI, robotics and drone technologies in live security and facilities operations. The MOU also covers engineering talent development and ambitions for commercial deployment.

Sources indicate that the agreement pairs SUTD’s research in autonomous systems and robotics with Certis’s technology integration and deployment experience across security, facilities management, aviation and the built environment. It builds on the organizations’ first partnership in 2024, which focused on raising AI literacy among security professionals.

According to recent reports, certis reports that it has deployed robots in live operations since 2019 and operates more than 60 robots across 30 Singapore sites for security patrols, cleaning and concierge services. Mozart, its proprietary AI orchestration platform, brings autonomous systems and frontline teams together.

Recent findings suggest that joint research will cover autonomous navigation in complex environments, sensor fusion and perception systems, edge computing, human-robot teaming and fleet management. The partners will also adapt autonomous systems for tropical urban environments and develop tailored drone and unmanned-system technologies for security, inspection and facilities operations.

Heavy rain, heat and humidity can degrade sensor performance and battery life, according to the partners, making local testing key before systems are deployed at scale. Environmental adaptation consequently sits alongside autonomy and fleet coordination in the planned development work.

In a recent development, the partners will set up a framework for demonstrations, trials and field validation. Solutions may be tested at SUTD facilities, including its DIVE \| Physical AI facility, and in Certis’s operational environments, allowing capabilities to be assessed against real conditions and refined before wider deployment.

“The challenge is translating advances in technology into solutions that can operate reliably and at scale,” remarked Raahul Kumar, Certis’s chief executive for international and robotics and chief strategy officer.

The partners expect the first joint projects to begin in the first half of 2027, initially addressing autonomous aviation security screening operations such as loading capabilities and unattended baggage handling systems.

The MOU provides for SUTD students to gain practical experience through internships, capstone projects, research attachments and field deployments with Certis. Structured internship-to-employment pathways and work-study arrangements remain to be developed. Certis will contribute operational expertise through guest lectures, workshops, industry challenges, case studies and mentoring.

Beyond research and education, the partners plan to engage industry and government stakeholders to identify pilot deployment opportunities. Their stated ambition is to turn jointly developed technologies into commercially viable solutions that can be deployed at scale.

For both partners, the practical test is whether the 2027 aviation-security work can turn that combination of research, field validation and training into systems ready for broader operational use.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Still slinging hardware – now with added AI and attendant risks or opportunities.

Dell and HPE this week both told investors they’ve become “different companies.”.

Sources indicate that the two hardware giants made that assertion on their respective earnings calls this week. HPE went first, on Monday, when CEO Antonio Neri declared “We are now a fundamentally different company” after acquiring Juniper Networks and creating products “built to capitalize on the next phase of AI.”.

On Tuesday, Dell’s chief operating officer and vice chairman Jeff Clarke declared “We are now a different company” because the Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) has become the source of “the vast majority of our profit and growth.”.

HPE’s claim to having changed is perhaps more credible on the face of it, given that its acquisition of Juniper means it has become more of a networking player.

It has been revealed that dell hasn’t made significant additions to its hardware portfolio, but there’s a significant difference in its sources of revenue, which three years ago was just about evenly split between its infrastructure and client devices. In its Tuesday announcement, Dell revealed ISG revenue grew 198 percent year over year to $42 billion, while CSG racked up three percent growth to $12.9 billion – meaning Dell is now predominantly an infrastructure manufacturer.

Clarke remarked he’s seen some companies deferring their PC purchases to buy AI hardware instead, and said Dell is re-assigning parts it ordered to build PCs and using them for servers instead.

Dell exited its Q3 with a backlog of $32 billion worth of AI servers and is clearly aware that investors might worry that’s not a useful metric because some buyers’ dreams of operating neoclouds have struck financial or regulatory barriers. Clarke assured investors that Dell is “highly selective about the partners we work with”.

“Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance, and access to land and power.”.

Recent findings suggest that HPE also has wrinkles in its AI business, because buyers won’t stand for fat margins and that’s dented the company’s profits a little. Neri was able to point to AI-related revenue also rising sharply, up 68.6 percent year over year to $11.3 billion, while overall revenue climbed 50 percent to reach $14.5 billion. Networking grew at a more relaxed 12 percent.

The CEO remarked HPE expects better growth ahead, because new server purchases create demand for networks and storage. He also pointed to HPE having the opportunity to sell its networking kit to other OEMs who build AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems. HPE predicted its next quarter will see revenue reach $14.0 billion to $14.6 billion, up 51 to 57 percent year over year.

Dell is also optimistic that AI buyers will spend on kit beyond servers and GPUs and updated its full-year revenue outlook to $202 billion, $10 billion above its previous forecasts and up 78 percent year over year. ®.

The Transformers Library: standardizing model definitions

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TLDR: Going forward, we're aiming for Transformers to be the pivot across frameworks: if a model architecture is supported by transformers, you can expect it to be supported in the rest of the ecosystem.
  • It has been revealed that transformers was created in 2019, shortly following the release of the BERT Transformer model.
  • Sources indicate that transformers now supports 300+ model architectures, with an average of ~3 fresh architectures added every week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TLDR: Going forward, we're aiming for Transformers to be the pivot across frameworks: if a model architecture is supported by transformers, you can expect it to be supported in the rest of the ecosystem.

It has been revealed that transformers was created in 2019, shortly following the release of the BERT Transformer model. Since then, we've continuously aimed to add state-of-the-art architectures, initially focused on NLP, then growing to Audio and computer vision. Today, transformers is the default library for LLMs and VLMs in the Python ecosystem.

Sources indicate that transformers now supports 300+ model architectures, with an average of ~3 fresh architectures added every week. We have aimed for these architectures to be released in a timely manner; having day-0 support for the most sought-after architectures (Llamas, Qwens, GLMs, etc.).

Over time, Transformers has become a central component in the ML ecosystem, becoming one of the most complete toolkits in terms of model diversity; it's integrated in all popular training frameworks such as Axolotl, Unsloth, DeepSpeed, FSDP, PyTorch-Lightning, TRL, Nanotron, etc.

Recent findings suggest that recently, we've been working hand in hand with the most popular inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TGI, ...) for them to use transformers as a backend. The value added is significant: as soon as a model is added to transformers, it becomes available in these inference engines, while taking advantage of the strengths each engine provides: inference optimizations, specialized kernels, dynamic batching, etc.

As an example, here is how you would work with the transformers backend in vLLM:.

That's all it takes for a new model to enjoy super-fast and production-grade serving with vLLM!

Read more about it in the vLLM documentation.

It has been revealed that we've also been working very closely with llama.cpp and MLX so that the implementations between transformers and these modeling libraries have great interoperability. For example, thanks to a significant community effort, it's now very easy to load GGUF files in transformers for further fine-tuning. Conversely, transformers models can be easily converted to GGUF files for use with llama.cpp.

The same is true for MLX, where the transformers' safetensors files are directly compatible with MLX's models.

Industry observers note that we are super proud that the transformers format is being adopted by the community, bringing a lot of interoperability we all benefit from. Train a model with Unsloth, deploy it with SGLang, and export it to llama.cpp to run locally! We aim to keep supporting the community going forward.

Sources indicate that to make it easier for the community to use transformers as a reference for model definitions, we strive to significantly reduce the barrier to model contributions. We have been doing this effort for a few years, but we'll accelerate significantly over the next few weeks:.

As a model user, in the future you should see even more interoperability in the tools that you use.

This does not mean that we intend to lock you in using transformers in your experiments; rather, it means that thanks to this modeling standardization, you can expect the tools that you use for training, for inference, and for production, to efficiently work together.

As a model creator, this means that a single contribution will get your model available in all downstream libraries that have integrated that modeling implementation. We have seen this many times over the years: releasing a model is stressful and integrating in all notable libraries is often a significant time-sink.

By standardizing the model implementation in a community-driven manner, we hope to lower the barrier of contributions to the field across libraries.

We firmly believe this renewed direction will help standardize an ecosystem which is often at risk of fragmentation. We'd love to hear your feedback on the direction the team has decided to take; and of changes we could do to get there. Please come and see us over at the transformers-community support tab on the Hub!

According to recent reports, awesome news! Transformers being the default access point for as many models on day 0 as well as in being able to use the inference engine of choice is an epic goal!

if a model architecture is supported by transformers, you can expect it to be supported in the rest of the ecosystem.

Industry observers note that it's interesting, but it seems regardless of the TLDR, Llama.CPP maintains its own implementation and so won't benefit from any "day-0 support" for new architectures in Transfomers. I was kind of hoping Llama would get straight Transformer compatibility for a moment.

It's not clear what, if anything, is changing there.

You're entirely correct that llama.cpp maintains its own implementation; we've been working hand-in-hand with the team to get better intercompatibility however: export between frameworks on both sides (from transformers to llama.cpp, and vice-versa).

Additionally, with the frequent VLM releases happening recently, we've been working directly with @ngxson to have the implementations day-0 (or week-0) in llama.cpp when the implementation already exists in transformers.

We won't have "automatic day-0 support" as the two libs have different backends; but we can still try by making the two more compatible, reducing the time needed to get there.

It has been revealed that thanks @lysandre . Apologies if I sounded overly negative at all, it's a very good goal.

Industry observers note that since I doubt Llama.cpp would implement Transformers directly as VLM did (although that would be nice), perhaps an in-between project is possible using the low-level C bindings Llama provides. I believe that's how llama-cpp-python and similar work.

Then again I'm not sure how much benefit there is, but food for thought.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, drawing from our experience with BitNet, Falcon-Edge introduces and validates an latest pre-training paradigm that delivers a full-scope output from a single training process, simultaneously yielding both non-quantized and quantized model variants.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this blogpost, we present the key highlights and rationales about the Falcon-Edge series - a collection of powerful, universal, and fine-tunable language models available in ternary format, based on the BitNet architecture.

According to recent reports, drawing from our experience with BitNet, Falcon-Edge introduces and validates an latest pre-training paradigm that delivers a full-scope output from a single training process, simultaneously yielding both non-quantized and quantized model variants. This comprehensive approach produces a non-BitNet model in bfloat16 format, the native BitNet model, and a pre-quantized BitNet variant specifically engineered for effortless fine-tuning, enabling users and developers to precisely tailor these models to their specific applications and needs.

Industry observers note that available now in two sizes—1 Billion and 3 Billion parameters—each size comes in both base and instruction-tuned models. Discover the Falcon-Edge series on our dedicated Hugging Face collection.

Industry observers note that large Language Models (LLMs), by design, are inherently large and resource-intensive. As demand grows to deploy these models efficiently on edge devices, research into model compression has accelerated. Recent efforts, such as those by DeepSeek and Llama 4, explore training with reduced precision formats—down to FP8—to improve deployment scalability. On the other hand, many state-of-the-art methods emphasize post-training quantization. In contrast to these approaches, BitNet introduces a fundamentally different paradigm: unlike reduced-precision training which still relies on floating-point formats, and post-training quantization which adjusts weights after full-precision training, BitNet operates with the lowest possible precision — ternary weights ({-1, 0, 1}) — directly during training, enabling an end-to-end ultra-efficient model design.

These ternary weights are paving the way for a “matmul-free” LLM design that is notably faster and remarkably memory-efficient in practice. The primary challenge of this innovative approach is the necessity for pre-training BitNet models, which can be computationally demanding and costly for typical consumers.

It has been revealed that leveraging the learnings from pre-training data strategies from our center, we pre-train our model on an internal data mixture for approximately 1.5 Tera Tokens. We use the classic WSD learning rate scheduler for pre-training.

We evaluate our models (base and instruct versions) on the former Hugging Face leaderboard v2 benchmark and report the normalized results below in comparison with other models of similar size:.

Additional results (leaderboard v1) on comparing our instructed models with Microsoft’s new BitNet model:.

Falcon-Edge demonstrates on-par and better performances than models of comparable sizes on the leaderboard v2 tasks, demonstrating that it is possible to train powerful BitNet models on desired domains while being competitive enough on other tasks.

If we look closer at the formula of the BitNet linear layer for inference (in terms of Python code):.

The normalization activation_norm_quant quantizes the activations in int8 format, then the activation is computed back in half precision by diving it by x_scale. Since the model has been trained with fake 8-bit activation quantization, we argue that it is possible to approximate that:.

Therefore, instead of quantizing the model post-training, injecting the weight scale after quantizing the weights should lead to a good enough “approximation” of the non-BitNet version of the model:.

We confirm this by running end-to-end evaluations on the bfloat16 variant of our 1B and 3B base models and below are the results:.

The bfloat16 counterparts of the models can be loaded directly via Hugging Face transformers by passing revision="bfloat16" in the from_pretrained function:.

Recent findings suggest that to the best of our knowledge, except from the most recent release from Microsoft previous BitNet releases only focus on releasing the final quantized model, making it usable only for inference. Similarly to the release from Microsoft, we propose to extend the accessibility of research and application of BitNet models by releasing their pre-quantized weights. That way, users can either perform fine-tuning on their target domain, or do continuous pre-training of the BitNet checkpoint as long as nn.Linear layers are replaced by BitnetLinear layers, and by making sure to quantize the model post training in BitNet format. Since the weights corresponds to the pre-quantized weights, performing text generation without replacing the nn.Linear layers with BitnetLinear layers will produce gibberish output.

The pre-quantized weights can be downloaded via Hugging Face's transformers library by specifying the revision argument to be prequantized:.

It has been revealed that this way, we will help fostering an ecosystem around first powerful 1-bit fine-tunes by the community. We provide to community the tools to get easily started and fine-tune their own version of powerful BitNet models by packaging all needed utility methods for performing fine-tuning on the pre-quantized weights on a Python package called onebitllms that we will cover in the next section.

In this release, we also introduce onebitllms - a lightweight Python package that can be plugged into your favorite LLM fine-tuning tools in order to fine-tune any pre-quantized BitNet model. At this time of writing onebitllms exposes these main functionalities:.

Currently, only full-finetuning is supported through this framework, while in this release the model sizes are relatively small, supporting Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning (PEFT) methods for BitNet models remains an exciting and impactful open question for upcoming BitNet models.

To get started, simply install the package directly through pip or from source, and take a look at examples/ folders inside the source code.

With this package, we hope to accelerate research and development around ternary format LLMs, and hope to see many derivations of Falcon-Edge and other future powerful BitNet models developed by the community.

We believe this release opens up multiple interesting directions - among all the possible follow up directions, we currently think that the following open questions will make BitNet models much more impactful in the near future:.

Nutanix CEO Rajiv Ramaswami has decided to step down from the job once the company’s board can find his successor.

Ramaswami confirmed his decision on Tuesday and in conversation with The Register noted he doesn’t have another job lined up, isn’t sure what he will do next, fancies sitting on boards or advising startups, but will take a break after Nutanix finds its next leader.

The CEO moved from VMware to Nutanix in 2020 and characterized his time at the company as writing its “second chapter.” The first, he explained, saw Nutanix focus on hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) and a limited group of workloads, especially desktop virtualization, while struggling to make a profit.

Recent findings suggest that in chapter two, Nutanix redefined HCI as “hybrid cloud infrastructure” by enabling its stack to run on-prem or in public clouds, and by adding support for containers alongside VMs. Ramaswami took credit for stabilizing Nutanix’s finances while leading the expansion of its platform and for keeping net promoter scores high while the firm grew.

It has been revealed that the CEO added that Nutanix’s decision to end its devotion to virtualized storage and start to support external arrays was also part of chapter two. Ramaswami stated he hopes to expand the number of storage vendors Nutanix supports beyond Dell, Everpure, and NetApp, until it works with all major array suppliers.

Chapter 3, he said, will be making Nutanix an AI platform, “by catering to a whole new set of ecosystems.”.

Ramaswami told The Register he had been thinking about moving on for some time and raised it with the board in recent weeks. In the letter he wrote to Nutanix staff, the CEO said the manufacturer's board has begun the search for a successor and said he will remain at his post until a replacement is found and then “continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time.”.

News of the CEO’s planned departure came on the same day Nutanix revealed its Q1 results, which saw 15 percent revenue growth to $772.4 million. The tech giant added 410 customers in the quarter, the slowest growth for several years. Ramaswami said high hardware costs remain “a headwind” for Nutanix, but said the company continues to win customers seeking an alternative to VMware. He also pointed to the largest latest customer win for the quarter coming from a financial services outfit that uses Dell external storage, a significant score because two years ago Nutanix could not have competed for that business.

Nutanix forecast slightly faster growth for the rest of its financial year, suggesting it is not ready to ride AI’s rocket to riches. Investors knocked about ten percent off the firm’s share price in after-hours trading, sending it to around $50, roughly double what it was when Ramaswami took over as CEO, but below $79-plus peaks in late 2025. ®.

If you head over to Azure AI Foundry today, you will find a vastly expanded collection of 10,000+ Hugging Face models you can deploy in a couple clicks to power AI applications working with text, audio and images. And we’re just getting started!

2 years ago, Microsoft and Hugging Face started a collaboration to make open models more easily accessible on Azure - back then the Hub was home to 200,000 open models.

According to recent reports, with now close to 2 million open models on Hugging Face, covering a wide diversity of tasks, modalities, domains and languages, it was time to take our collaboration to the next level. The new collaboration revealed today creates a framework for mutual success to vastly expand how Azure customers can benefit from Hugging Face.

"Open source is how AI moves faster—with transparency, choice, and community at its core. This collaboration represents our commitment to that momentum. By combining Hugging Face’s vibrant model ecosystem with Azure’s secure, enterprise-grade infrastructure, we’re giving developers the freedom to pick the best model for the job—and helping organizations innovate safely and at scale.”.

-- Asha Sharma, Corporate Vice President at Microsoft.

Making more open models easily accessible to Azure customers, for secure deployment alongside company private data, will enable enterprises to build AI applications and agents while being fully in control of their technology and data.

We’re enabling companies to take control of their AI destiny, deploying the best open models securely within their Azure account, to build AI applications they can trust and verify.

-- Clement Delangue, CEO and cofounder at Hugging Face.

Industry observers note that let’s head over to Azure AI Foundry, and select the Model Catalog. Here you can now find over 10,000 models under the Hugging Face Collection.

Models in the Collection include the most popular, trending models on Hugging Face for a wide range of tasks to work with text, audio and images - including text generation, feature extraction, fill-mask, translation, identifying sentence similarity, image classification, image segmentation, text to image generation, image to text conversion, automatic speech recognition and audio-classification.

To make the Hugging Face Collection on Azure AI Foundry enterprise-ready, we are only featuring models:.

In addition, Microsoft and Hugging Face will continuously test inference containers for vulnerabilities to maintain and patch them as needed.

Now let’s say you want to deploy for instance the popular Microsoft Phi-4 Reasoning Plus open model.

First, let’s select the model in the Hugging Face Collection in Azure AI Foundry, and click the “Deploy button”. The form allows you to select a VM, instance count and deployment parameters, and start the deployment process with just another click!

Now, if you prefer browsing models on the Hub, you can also start from the model page - the “Deploy on Azure ML” option will take you to the same deployment option within Azure AI Machine Learning Studio.

We are really excited about all the upcoming Hugging Face models and modalities now directly available within Azure AI Foundry, but we’re not going to stop there!

In the weeks and months to come, you can expect a rolling thunder of updates:.

If you’re on Azure, it’s time to build with open models!

In a recent development, siemens revealed on November 24, 2026 an expanded automation portfolio for AI-powered autonomous production at SPS 2026 in Nuremberg, including a goods-unpacking robot under development and AI agents for planning and engineering. Siemens expects the planner to reduce manual planning effort by 70%.

The portfolio is built around goal-based automation: manufacturers specify the outcome they want, and industrial AI determines how to achieve it or carries out the work through AI agents. “The next productivity leap will come from automating tasks that were impossible to automate before,” said Rainer Brehm, president of automation at Siemens.

Recent findings suggest that the shop-floor example is at Siemens’ Electronics Factory Erlangen, where the manufacturer is developing an AI-based robot application to unpack incoming goods. Electronics deliveries vary so widely in packaging type and size that fixed robot programs cannot handle them, leaving the work largely manual. The application is designed to open cartons and remove component reels for further processing.

Cameras capture the workspace in real time, while AI-based robot foundation models interpret the scene and determine the required actions. Siemens provides the automation and control systems, industrial PCs, software orchestration, and manufacturing expertise drawn from its own facilities. That combination addresses the central limitation of a fixed program: the robot must adjust its steps to each delivery instead of repeating one predetermined sequence.

The Autonomous Production Planner is being introduced within Intelligence Center X, Siemens’ industrial AI orchestration software. Several AI agents collaborate to create production schedules and optimize them against defined key performance indicators. Each schedule is checked in a physics-based digital twin before release to production, putting a simulation test between an agent-generated plan and factory execution. Siemens also expects the planner to lower costs by up to 20%.

It has been revealed that the Eigen Engineering Agent, connected to the TIA Portal engineering software, can now adapt automation code and verify it through simulation. Creating safety configurations remains a future capability. For process industries, the agent is now available with SIMATIC PCS 7, Siemens’ distributed control system, where it analyzes existing control logic, checks or creates Continuous Function Charts, and automatically creates control modules from engineering data. Siemens says these functions can accelerate engineering and help companies apply expertise across projects.

It has been revealed that during production, the Industrial AI Suite connects AI models running on Industrial Edge to SIMATIC S7 controllers through PROFINET. This enables real-time inference within machine automation and supports uses such as AI-based motion control. Production data can also be used to retrain, validate, and redeploy models on-premises, creating a closed loop from deployment and operation to continuing model improvement.

Industry observers note that standardized device information supplies another layer. Siemens is making Asset Administration Shell data available for more than 120,000 hardware products, allowing software tools and AI-enabled workflows to access and process product information directly. The standardized data also supports digital engineering and digital-twin workflows.

Security accompanies that expansion of AI into control systems. Siemens is progressively preparing relevant industrial products for applicable requirements of the EU Cyber Resilience Act, which sets cybersecurity requirements relevant to its industrial products and customers’ machines. It is also supporting machine builders as they prepare their machines for requirements applicable from December 11, 2027.

According to recent reports, the portfolio’s near-term significance is the connection between AI-generated decisions and the industrial systems that validate and execute them. Its current limits are also clear: the Erlangen unpacking application remains under development, and the planner’s benefits are expectations, making simulation validation, accessible device data, and cybersecurity central to the move toward more autonomous production.

Recent findings suggest that fibre optics are run across power lines are typically a design known as ADSS - All Dielectric Self Supported. They run multiple fibres in multiple cables held together by a Kevlar mesh and then UV stabilised PVC as a covering.

Look at Aerial Cables in the following link https://www.thefoa.org/tech/re... [thefoa.org].

They are substantial(6-10mm) stiff black armored cables that contain a metal wire cable for strength and toning. They are typically suspended on the lower level of electrical poles, like telephone copper, or cable TV wires.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four more critical vulns, including another unauthorized access flaw in vCenter.

VMware has issued its third critical security advisory in a week, this time to warn of four critical flaws and address a total of 23 issues.

Recent findings suggest that VMSA-2026-0011 landed on November 24, just five days after two other advisories. VMware’s FAQ for the new advisory includes the following remarks:.

Because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing this VMSA comes on the heels of VMSA-2026-0009, and atop a major holiday in the United States.The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure environment amidst modern, AI-assisted threats is paramount to us.

Make of that what you will as you ponder how and when to patch the four critical flaws, including the 9.8-rated CVE-2026-123903, which allows a malicious actor to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to vCenter, the management tool VMware owners rely on to manage hosts and VMs.

This is the third 9.8-rated authentication problem VMware has fixed in vCenter since July.

According to recent reports, two of the other critical flaws in this new advisory allow an attacker to run code on an ESX host, earning the bugs a 9.8 rating. CVE-2026-123910 makes that possible thanks to a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123911 is a use-after-free vulnerability.

In a recent development, the other critical flaw, CVE-2026-123912, can result in a guest escape from VMware’s desktop Workstation and Fusion desktop hypervisors. It’s also present in VMware’s ESX hypervisor, but attackers thankfully can’t escape that product’s sandbox. This one’s easy to mitigate because the problem is in a USB controller that consumers can turn off.

Most of the other flaws require installation of updated software.

In a recent development, there’s a little good news in that some of the software updates VMware issued last week include fixes for the newly disclosed flaws. But there are still plenty of fresh fixes to apply, across ten products: ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware tools, Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, the Telco Cloud Platform, Telco Cloud Infrastructure, and the VMware Avi Load Balancer.

Industry observers note that VMware’s advisory thanks external researchers for finding and reporting most of the flaws. The Broadcom business unit is known to be a member of Project Glasswing, the Anthropic-run effort to use the Mythos model to find flaws that has seen many vendors dramatically increase the number of patches they produce.

Sources indicate that in past years, VMware has often published considerably more than this year’s 11 security advisories. With five weeks left in the year, perhaps vAdmins need to worry Christmas might also get complicated. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

nanoVLM is the simplest way to get started with training your very own Vision Language Model (VLM) using pure PyTorch. It is lightweight toolkit which allows you to launch a VLM training on a free tier colab notebook.

We were inspired by Andrej Karpathy’s nanoGPT, and provide a similar project for the vision domain.

It has been revealed that at its heart, nanoVLM is a toolkit that helps you build and train a model that can understand both images and text, and then generate text based on that. The beauty of nanoVLM lies in its simplicity. The entire codebase is intentionally kept minimal and readable, making it perfect for beginners or anyone who wants to peek under the hood of VLMs without getting overwhelmed.

According to recent reports, in this blog post, we cover the core ideas behind the project and provide a simple way to interact with the repository. We not only go into the details of the project but also encapsulate all of it so that you can quickly get started.

You can start training a Vision Language Model using our nanoVLM toolkit by following these steps:.

Here is a Colab notebook that will help you launch a training run with no local setup required!

As the name suggests, a Vision Language Model (VLM) is a multi-modal model that processes two modalities: vision and text. These models typically take images and/or text as input and generate text as output.

Recent findings suggest that generating text (output) conditioned on the understanding of images and texts (inputs) is a powerful paradigm. It enables a wide range of applications, from image captioning and object detection to answering questions about visual content (as shown in the table below). One thing to note is that nanoVLM focuses only on Visual Question Answering as the training objective.

If you are interested in learning more about VLMs, we strongly recommend reading our latest blog on the topic: Vision Language Models (Better, Faster, Stronger).

"Talk is cheap, show me the code" - Linus Torvalds.

In this section, we’ll guide you through the codebase. It’s helpful to keep a tab open for reference as you follow along.

Below is the folder structure of our repository. We have removed helper files for brevity.

Recent findings suggest that we model nanoVLM after two well known and widely used architectures. Our vision backbone (models/vision_transformer.py) is the standard vision transformer, more specifically Google’s SigLIP vision encoder. Our language backbone follows the Llama 3 architecture.

The vision and text modalities are aligned using a Modality Projection module. This module takes the image embeddings produced by the vision backbone as input, and transforms them into embeddings compatible with the text embeddings from the embedding layer of the language model. These embeddings are then concatenated and fed into the language decoder. The Modality Projection module consists of a pixel shuffle operation followed by a linear layer.

According to recent reports, pixel shuffle reduces the number of image tokens, which helps reduce computational cost and speeds up training, especially for transformer-based language decoders which are sensitive to input length. The figure below demonstrates the concept.

All the files are very lightweight and well documented. We highly encourage you to check them out individually to get a better understanding of the implementation details (models/xxx.py).

This model isn't intended to compete with SoTA models, but rather to demystify the components and training process of VLMs.

In this blog post, we walked through what VLMs are, explored the architecture choices that power nanoVLM, and unpacked the training and inference workflows in detail.

It has been revealed that by keeping the codebase lightweight and readable, nanoVLM aims to serve as both a learning tool and a foundation you can build upon. Whether you’re looking to understand how multi-modal inputs are aligned, or you want to train a VLM on your own dataset, this repository gives you a head start.

If you try it out, build on top of it, or just have questions we’d love to hear from you. Happy tinkering!

I’ve been working on a fork of Nano-vLLM called Nano-vLLM-v1, which re-engineers the core architecture to closely reproduce the vLLM v1 scheduler and introduces Chunked Prefill for better performance.

The goal was to build a lightweight, readable, yet highly efficient inference engine that stays true to the original vLLM design while being easy to understand and extend.

Check it out here: https://github.com/slwang-ustc/nano-vllm-v1/tree/main.

It has been revealed that I’d love for the community to try it out, give feedback, or contribute! The code is designed to be readable and modular, making it easy to experiment with upcoming features or optimizations.

If you’re interested in lightweight, high-performance LLM inference without the complexity, give it a star ⭐ and let me know what you think!

At its November 25, 2026 Tech Day, XPENG presented IRON as a “qualified work partner”, detailing autonomous commercial-work functions, onboard AI and safety systems for the humanoid while inviting purchase or partnership inquiries.

Seven IRON robots were gathered for the Tech Day presentation, with multilingual interaction among the features highlighted in XPENG’s official event post. The humanoid stands 170 cm tall, weighs 62 kg and has 76 whole-body degrees of freedom. Its full-coverage bionic skin and flexible muscles sit over a skeleton combining lightweight magnesium-aluminum alloy with high-strength steel. The accompanying product presentation concentrates on what the robot can do during a workday.

XPENG says its work-service model combines schedule management, autonomous task planning, downloadable skill packages, whole-machine over-the-air updates and knowledge accumulation. The initial roles are shopping guidance and tours, with broader commercial settings in view. Designed for 24/7 service, IRON can recharge itself and return to work; a 20-minute charge supports 1.5 hours of work. That makes self-managed charging a necessary part of the availability pitch, since the robot must move between tasks and power without staff intervention.

Recent findings suggest that deployment also relies on local navigation. After being taken through an unfamiliar site once, IRON can generate a local map, navigate without a network connection, accept visual calibration through a phone app and share maps with other robots. XPENG rates its three in-house Turing chips at 2,250 TOPS of effective computing, with full-stack models running on the robot for millisecond-level responses and offline reasoning. The on-device architecture therefore pairs offline navigation with local reasoning, reducing dependence on a network connection during work.

It has been revealed that for physical tasks, XPENG lists more than 1,500 tactile contact points across the body, with over 80% tactile coverage in core areas. Each hand has 21 degrees of freedom, 375 tactile sensors and support for 33 categories of everyday manipulation. Those sensing and hand specifications provide the hardware basis for the shopping-assistance and broader commercial roles described above.

According to recent reports, XPENG states its safety design spans psychological, physical, interaction, information and quality safety. Sensitive face and voice data are isolated on-device, and the communications system has dual-channel redundancy. For loss of balance, IRON is designed to recover or, when a fall is predicted, bend its knees and choose a direction to reduce damage. The solid-state battery specification adds cell energy density of at least 300 Wh/kg, supporting the smaller and lighter battery design.

It has been revealed that XPENG reports more than 1,000 automotive-grade tests, approximately 50 million mechanical-durability tests on assemblies, over 20 million leg-and-foot impact tests and more than 10 million dexterous-hand grasp-durability tests. A roughly 50,000-square-metre data factory covers more than 250 scenarios and 15 job categories for real-robot training. Together, the testing and training infrastructure shows the scale of the effort to make job behavior repeatable across environments rather than dependent on a single demonstration.

As background, XPENG’s September 9, 2026 release said its humanoid production line had been commissioned and an IRON had completed automated final assembly before walking off autonomously. Core processes were more than 80% automated. The proposal then was scale production by the end of 2026, commercial deployment beginning in XPENG stores and campuses, and launch and delivery in China and overseas in 2027.

The official IRON inquiry form collects purchase and partnership interest, and the product page invites global partners to help build a robotics ecosystem. The Tech Day material therefore has a commercial function beyond the event showcase.

It has been revealed that the remaining qualification is substantial: XPENG cautions that the displayed performance, functions and appearance may differ from the final mass-production product. The disclosure establishes a detailed operating model and validation program, but leaves the central commercialization test unresolved: whether those capabilities remain consistent during daily work in the production version.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Criminal masterminds claimed to work for ‘Weihua’ or to have source code from ‘oscic’ instead of Cisco.

A US jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei stole tech from American companies, laundered money, and violated sanctions by building major internet infrastructure for Iran, but didn’t operate an illegal racket to get that done.

Recent findings suggest that this case kicked off in 2020, when the US Department of Justice claimed entities Huawei operated in America violated federal law. The indictment led to a trial on a dozen criminal matters that has played out over the last three months in the Eastern District Court of Newly introduced York.

The trial ended on Tuesday when a jury found Huawei and three subsidiary companies guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) and substantive violations of that law, plus money laundering conspiracy.

The Department of Justice’s celebration of the decision notes Huawei was found to have stolen Cisco’s source code, after prosecutors showed evidence that “Huawei engineers left Cisco’s notes about the Cisco code, referred to Cisco using its name backwards ‘ocsic’ and described that portions of the code remained as they existed in the ‘ocsic’ code.”.

Another item of evidence apparently indicated a Huawei staffer photographing Fujitsu equipment while wearing a fake employee badge for a company called “Weihua” – cunningly reversing the two syllables of “Huawei.”.

Another allegation the jury accepted involved Huawei staffers signing a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) ahead of a visit to T-Mobile to inspect a robot the telco created to test mobile devices.

Huawei staff ignored that NDA so thoroughly that they “sent photographs and technical details of the robot back to China” so the Chinese company could make its own robot. “When that data was not sufficient, a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DoJ notes.

According to recent reports, the feds say the Chinese company also “lied about its activities in Iran to banks to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and access to U.S.-dollar clearing services, which enabled Huawei to be a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services — in part because of its lies.”.

Huawei has issued a statement noting that the jury found it not guilty of racketeering and insisting the charges on which it was found guilty are “without legal or factual merit.”.

“The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades,” the statement adds.

Sentencing will take place in September 2027.

The presiding judge will likely consider the fact that in 2017, US authorities fined Chinese telco equipment maker ZTE $900 million just for selling to Iran, then added an additional $1.4 billion penalty to lift a ban on doing business in the USA.

Washington has already banned Huawei from selling its telco products and personal devices in the USA. Lawmakers have little appetite to let the Chinese company return to the American market after spending billions to help American telcos replace the Huawei kit with locally made alternatives. ®.
