Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers

📅 21 May 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Large diffusion models like Flux (a flow-based text-to-image generation model) can create stunning images, but their size can be a hurdle, demanding significant memory and compute resources.
  • Before we dive into the technical details of how various quantization backends in Hugging Face Diffusers work, why not test your own perception?
  • It has been revealed that we created a setup where you can provide a prompt, and we generate results using both the original, high-precision model (e.g., Flux-dev in BF16) and several quantized versions (BnB 4-bit, BnB 8-bit).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Large diffusion models like Flux (a flow-based text-to-image generation model) can create stunning images, but their size can be a hurdle, demanding significant memory and compute resources. Quantization offers a powerful solution, shrinking these models to make them more accessible without drastically compromising performance. But the massive question always is: can you actually tell the difference in the final image?

Before we dive into the technical details of how various quantization backends in Hugging Face Diffusers work, why not test your own perception?

It has been revealed that we created a setup where you can provide a prompt, and we generate results using both the original, high-precision model (e.g., Flux-dev in BF16) and several quantized versions (BnB 4-bit, BnB 8-bit). The generated images are then presented to you and your challenge is to identify which ones came from the quantized models.

Often, especially with 8-bit quantization, the differences are subtle and may not be noticeable without close inspection. More aggressive quantization like 4-bit or lower might be more noticeable, but the results can still be good, especially considering the massive memory savings. NF4 often gives the best trade-off though.

In a recent development, building on our previous post, "Memory-efficient Diffusion Transformers with Quanto and Diffusers", this post explores the diverse quantization backends integrated directly into Hugging Face Diffusers. We'll examine how bitsandbytes, GGUF, torchao, Quanto and native FP8 support make large and powerful models more accessible, demonstrating their use with Flux.

Sources indicate that before diving into the quantization backends, let's introduce the FluxPipeline (using the black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev checkpoint) and its components, which we'll be quantizing. Loading the full FLUX.1-dev model in BF16 precision requires approximately 31.447 GB of memory. The main components are:.

It has been revealed that bitsandbytes is a popular and user-friendly library for 8-bit and 4-bit quantization, widely used for LLMs and QLoRA fine-tuning. We can use it for transformer-based diffusion and flow models, too.

All benchmarks performed on 1x NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU.

Industry observers note that note: When using PipelineQuantizationConfig with bitsandbytes, you need to import DiffusersBitsAndBytesConfig from diffusers and TransformersBitsAndBytesConfig from transformers separately. This is because these components originate from different libraries. If you prefer a simpler setup without managing these distinct imports, you can use an alternative approach for pipeline-level quantization, an example of this method is in the Diffusers documentation on Pipeline-level quantization.

For more information check out the bitsandbytes docs.

According to recent reports, torchao is a PyTorch-native library for architecture optimization, offering quantization, sparsity, and custom data types, designed for compatibility with torch.compile and FSDP. Diffusers supports a wide range of torchao's exotic data types, enabling fine-grained control over model optimization.

For more information check out the torchao docs.

Quanto is a quantization library integrated with the Hugging Face ecosystem via the optimum library.

Note: At the time of writing, for float8 support with Quanto, you'll need optimum-quanto<0.2.5 and use quanto directly. We will be working on fixing this.

For more information check out the Quanto docs.

GGUF is a file format popular in the llama.cpp community for storing quantized models.

For more information check out the GGUF docs.

FP8 Layerwise Casting is a memory optimization technique. It works by storing the model's weights in the compact FP8 (8-bit floating point) format, which uses roughly half the memory of standard FP16 or BF16 precision. Just before a layer performs its calculations, its weights are dynamically cast up to a higher compute precision (like FP16/BF16). Immediately afterward, the weights are cast back down to FP8 for efficient storage. This approach works because the core computations retain high precision, and layers particularly sensitive to quantization (like normalization) are typically skipped. This technique can also be combined with group offloading for further memory savings.

For more information check out the Layerwise casting docs.

It has been revealed that most of these quantization backends can be combined with the memory optimization techniques offered in Diffusers. Let's explore CPU offloading, group offloading, and torch.compile. You can learn more about these techniques in the Diffusers documentation.

Note: At the time of writing, bnb + torch.compile also works if bnb is installed from source and using pytorch nightly or with fullgraph=False.

Recent findings suggest that model CPU Offloading (enable_model_cpu_offload): This method moves entire model components (like the UNet, text encoders, or VAE) between the CPU and GPU during the inference pipeline. It offers substantial VRAM savings and is generally faster than more granular offloading because it involves fewer, larger data transfers.

bnb + enable_model_cpu_offload:.

Recent findings suggest that group offloading (enable_group_offload for diffusers components or apply_group_offloading for generic torch.nn.Modules): It moves groups of internal model layers (like torch.nn.ModuleList or torch.nn.Sequential instances) to the CPU. This approach is typically more memory-efficient than full model offloading and faster than sequential offloading.

FP8 layerwise casting + group offloading:.

Note: torch.compile can introduce subtle numerical differences, leading to changes in image output.

According to recent reports, torch.compile: Another complementary approach is to accelerate the execution of your model with PyTorch 2.x’s torch.compile() feature. Compiling the model doesn’t directly lower memory, but it can significantly speed up inference. PyTorch 2.0’s compile (Torch Dynamo) works by tracing and optimizing the model graph ahead-of-time.

Explore some benchmarking results here:.

You can find bitsandbytes and torchao quantized models from this blog post in our Hugging Face collection: link to collection.

Here's a quick guide to choosing a quantization backend:.

Quantization significantly lowers the barrier to entry for using large diffusion models. Experiment with these backends to find the best balance of memory, speed, and quality for your needs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, XPENG unveiled WorldGPT on November 24, 2026, a world action model that predicts physical scenes and prepares machine actions. It was trained across six embodiments, or machine types: cars, boats, drones, single-arm robots, dual-arm robots and humanoids. The system belongs to XPENG’s Turing World Model family.

Sources indicate that the WorldGPT project site indicates the model starts with about one second of video from one or several cameras and a text instruction. It can then generate multi-camera video of the next few seconds, actions such as steering, joint motion or thrust, depth and segmentation outputs, and a plain-language explanation of its decisions. The same weights handle every supported machine, replacing separate perception, simulation and action pipelines with one model.

In a recent development, XPENG’s argument is that these machines share physical problems despite having different controls. A car must judge distances and anticipate surrounding vehicles, while a robotic arm must locate an object and adjust its movements to grasp it. Developing a separate model for each machine splits the available data and repeats development work.

Sources indicate that worldGPT instead learns in a shared pixel space. Steering angles cannot transfer directly to robot arms, and joint angles cannot transfer directly to drones, but camera images provide a common input through which each embodiment’s data can teach the others. The model then produces actions appropriate to the machine it is controlling.

In a recent development, worldGPT’s architecture separates the large model from deployment on individual machines. The cloud-based teacher learns across embodiments and is designed for distillation, the transfer of its knowledge into smaller, specialized student models that run on individual machines. A latest embodiment adds its data to the teacher rather than requiring another complete model stack.

XPENG claims this arrangement could reduce development costs, improve data efficiency and simplify extensions to new machines. It places WorldGPT within a broader physical AI strategy spanning intelligent vehicles, humanoid robotics and autonomous mobility.

XPENG reports 12 first-place results on public benchmarks across autonomous driving, robotic manipulation, visual understanding and video generation as of November 12, 2026. Four are in driving, including NAVSIM v2 results for standard and challenging scenarios. The reported average success rate for robotic manipulation is 95.2% across 50 single-arm tasks. Its other first-place results cover CV-Bench and two BLINK subtasks; WorldGPT also has the highest overall VBench 2.0 score and a tie for first on WorldOlympiad.

It has been revealed that the project site qualifies those comparisons: they do not control for training data, and VBench 2.0 is marked as self-evaluated with prompt rewriting. A technical report is listed as coming soon, so the current technical disclosures are the announcement and project page.

The site also hosts 32 demonstration clips across the supported machines. Each begins with real camera footage, while the following video is WorldGPT’s prediction; a real recording plays alongside for comparison. Separate demonstrations start from the same recorded moment and change the instruction, showing how the generated future and planned action change with it.

In a recent development, worldGPT’s broader implication is a shift from building separate AI stacks for each machine toward training a shared foundation and adapting it for deployment. The benchmark results describe its reported breadth; the teacher-to-student handoff is the mechanism on which XPENG’s projected gains in development cost and data efficiency depend.

Falcon-Arabic: A Breakthrough in Arabic Language Models

📅 21 May 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1219 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we are excited to introduce Falcon-Arabic, a 7B parameter Language Model that sets a new benchmark for Arabic NLP.
  • Falcon-Arabic redefines the boundaries of what is possible for Arabic Language Models.
  • In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed Artificial Intelligence, powering tools for translation, content creation, virtual assistance, and more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Check out our official blogpost (EN, AR).

Industry observers note that we are excited to introduce Falcon-Arabic, a 7B parameter Language Model that sets a new benchmark for Arabic NLP. Built on the Falcon 3 architecture, Falcon-Arabic is a multilingual model that supports Arabic, English, and several other languages. It excels in general knowledge, Arabic grammar, mathematical reasoning, complex problem solving, and understanding the rich diversity of Arabic dialects. Falcon-Arabic supports a context length of 32,000 tokens, allowing it to handle long documents and enabling advanced applications like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), in-depth content creation, and knowledge-intensive tasks.

Falcon-Arabic redefines the boundaries of what is possible for Arabic Language Models. It significantly outperforms other Arabic LLMs in its size category and even models up to four times larger across both Arabic-native models and those adapted from other languages. This makes Falcon-Arabic not only a state-of-the-art model in terms of performance, but also a uniquely efficient and accessible solution for developers and researchers working with the Arabic language.

In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed Artificial Intelligence, powering tools for translation, content creation, virtual assistance, and more. Yet much of this progress has focused on highly represented languages like English, leaving languages such as Arabic underrepresented. Arabic presents unique challenges it's morphologically rich, diglossic (spanning both Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and diverse regional dialects), and used across a vast and culturally varied population. Developing robust Arabic LLMs is essential to ensure Arabic-speaking communities are fully included in the AI revolution.

It has been revealed that with this goal in mind, we’re introducing Falcon-Arabic a specialized adaptation of the Falcon 3 model family, developed by the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in the UAE. The Falcon models have earned global recognition for their multilingual strength and open-source approach. Falcon-Arabic builds on this legacy, bringing advanced language understanding and generation to Arabic. By training the model to handle both Modern Standard Arabic and key dialects, Falcon-Arabic fills a critical gap in language technology enabling more natural, intelligent, and inclusive Arabic AI across the Gulf, Middle East, and North Africa.

Building Falcon-Arabic started with a strategic decision: rather than training a model from scratch, we chose to adapt a strong multilingual foundation. In the Arabic LLM landscape, three main approaches exist: training from scratch (e.g., Jais-native), adapting multilingual models (like Allam or Fanar), or using models that natively support Arabic alongside other languages (such as Qwen or LLaMA). Observing the Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard, it became clear that adapted and multilingual models consistently outperformed others in both efficiency and capability. To build on that momentum, we selected Falcon 3-7B, a model that strikes a practical balance between performance and resource efficiency within the Falcon 3 family developed by the Technology Innovation Institute (TII).

The core challenge was adapting Falcon 3-7B, which originally lacked Arabic support at the tokenizer and embedding level. We addressed this by extending the tokenizer’s vocabulary with 32,000 Arabic-specific tokens, and applying a novel embedding initialization strategy based on textual similarity. This technique mapped upcoming Arabic tokens to semantically related embeddings from the existing vocabulary, allowing the model to inherit prior knowledge and accelerate learning particularly around sentiment, abstract concepts, and reasoning patterns. This gave Falcon-Arabic a head start in understanding and generating high-quality Arabic text.

Industry observers note that with the tokenizer and embeddings in place, we began continuous pretraining on high-quality, 100% native Arabic datasets, avoiding the use of machine-translated content to minimize cultural bias and preserve linguistic authenticity. Training followed a multi-stage curriculum: early stages focused on general knowledge and dialect-rich Arabic content to stabilize the model and reinforce logical capabilities, while later phases emphasized math, code, and reasoning. The result is a model that not only speaks Arabic fluently across dialects, but also retains Falcon’s multilingual and reasoning strengths pushing the boundaries for Arabic-first AI.

Industry observers note that we evaluated Falcon-Arabic on OALL v2, the leading benchmark for Arabic Language Models. It includes six multiple-choice tasks such as Arabic MMLU (native and translated), Arabic Exams, Alghafa, MadinahQA, Aratrust and one generative benchmark, Alrage. Falcon-Arabic outperforms all existing Arabic LLMs in its size range and even surpasses models up to 4× larger. It leads in key benchmarks like Arabic MMLU, Exams, MadinahQA, and Aratrust, setting a new standard for Arabic-first Language Models.

The evaluation details (log probabilities, predictions and LLM as judge metrics) of Falcon-Arabic-7B-Base are available on https://huggingface.co/datasets/tiiuae/Falcon-Arabic-7B-Base-details.

It has been revealed that after finalizing the base model training, we performed a post-training alignment phase to fine-tune Falcon-Arabic’s responses according to human preferences. This phase began with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) using a combination of high-quality public datasets and internally collected native Arabic instruction data, covering a range of tasks and conversational scenarios.

In a recent development, to further enhance alignment, we applied Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) a reinforcement learning-based method that tunes the model to prefer outputs that humans rate as more helpful, safe, and relevant. This two-step process ensures that Falcon-Arabic Instruct not only understands Arabic well but responds in a way that aligns with real user expectations.

Sources indicate that as shown in the results plots, Falcon-Arabic Instruct leads the pack, outperforming all other Instruct-aligned Arabic LLMs in its size class and even models significantly larger across multiple benchmarks. The model demonstrates strong performance in both instruction following and open-ended dialogue, setting a upcoming standard for Arabic conversational AI.

The evaluation details (log probabilities, predictions and LLM as judge metrics) of Falcon-Arabic-7B-Instruct are available on https://huggingface.co/datasets/tiiuae/Falcon-Arabic-7B-Instruct-details.

Recent findings suggest that falcon-Arabic sets a latest benchmark for Arabic Language Models. With only 7B parameters, it delivers state-of-the-art performance outperforming models of similar size and even those several times larger across key benchmarks like Arabic MMLU, MadinahQA, and Aratrust. It combines fluency in Modern Standard Arabic, strong understanding of regional dialects, and robust reasoning and multilingual capabilities, making it ideal for a wide range of applications: from Arabic-first chatbots and educational tools to content generation, code assistance, and document understanding.

To give you a hands-on feel for what Falcon-Arabic can do, we built a simple demo that showcases its capabilities in machine translation even though the model hasn’t been fine-tuned specifically for that task. The tool runs purely on Falcon-7B-Arabic-Instruct, and the results are surprisingly strong across various translation directions. You can try it yourself through the demo linked just below. In fact, we used the same setup to translate this blog post into Arabic for our Arabic-speaking audience. Check it out here 🚀. And if you're curious to explore more, we also provide access to a live playground where you can interact with Falcon-Arabic Instruct and experience its performance across different tasks ✨.

Like all Large Language Models, Falcon-Arabic inherits some common limitations. These include occasional hallucinations (producing plausible but incorrect outputs), sensitivity to how prompts are phrased, and varying performance across very long contexts. While Falcon-Arabic is designed to reduce these concerns especially for Arabic tasks users should still apply critical thinking when interpreting results, particularly in high-stakes or fact-sensitive use cases.

If you find this work helpful for your research or projects, please consider citing it.

  • A study suggests extending the TV license to cover streaming services such as YouTube and Netflix could solve the BBC’s funding problems, netting it an extra £1.6 billion ($2 billion) per year by 2032.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Controversial move could save the BBC by bringing in more than a billion in extra funding each year.

A study suggests extending the TV license to cover streaming services such as YouTube and Netflix could solve the BBC’s funding problems, netting it an extra £1.6 billion ($2 billion) per year by 2032.

The British government is due to publish a white paper by the end of this year outlining its looks for the BBC's license fee and Royal Charter, which expires at the end of 2027.

One of the options is to extend the license so that it is needed to access streaming platforms like Netflix, Disney+, or Amazon Prime Video.

This is unlikely to prove popular, but if the fee was held at the current level (£180, $236 per year) it would generate up to £1.6 billion extra a year for the corporation and would better reflect how audiences watch television, according to entertainment industry research biz Ampere Analysis.

As any Brit knows, the BBC is funded primarily through the TV license, which is charged on a per household basis. A license is required to watch or record live TV on any broadcast channel, or access the BBC iPlayer for on-demand content. A license is not currently needed for on-demand streaming platforms.

The government is understood to believe the current license scheme is “outdated and no longer fit for purpose,” and is weighing several options to reform it. Scrapping it entirely looks unlikely for now: a committee found that other European countries that did so ended up with less stable funding for their public service broadcasters, and weaker independence from political interference.

TV licensing is controversial, with some people resenting having to pay the BBC just for the right to watch television. In response, the government has tried to limit fee increases, and made the license free for some elderly people. Together, these moved have reduced the BBC's funding, leading to service cuts and further. dissatisfaction.

Responding to a report by the National Audit Office (NAO) that found the BBC will remain under financial pressure despite widespread cuts, the National Union of Journalists (NUJ) urged the government to secure the broadcaster's future in the next charter renewal.

Industry observers note that "The BBC shouldn't be in this position. These cuts are the result of a decade of underfunding, with NAO identifying a 26 percent real-terms reduction in license fee income in the last nine years alone," remarked NUJ general secretary Laura Davison.

Many Brits no longer pay the license fee, preferring to watch only streamed content, or claiming that they do. Ampere says more than 90 percent of UK households watch live television, but only 84 percent of eligible households pay the fee, meaning a sizable number are freeloading. Extending the fee to cover on-demand and streaming services would close the loophole, it says.

According to recent reports, another option could see the license fee reduced to £150 ($196) in 2028, assuming perfect enforcement, analysts at Ampere say. They neglect to detail what this "perfect enforcement" mechanism consists of.

"Widening the remit of the license fee at current prices would significantly increase the BBC’s funding, strengthening its long-term financial position and ability to compete with local and global rivals," remarked Ampere Senior Analyst Sam Khoury.

"Alternatively, in the context of ongoing cost of living pressures in the UK, the government could opt to reduce the price of the fee payable by the extended pool of consumers. Coupled with a reformed enforcement mechanism that effectively reduces evasion, this would still improve the BBC's financial outlook relative to the status quo.".

Earlier this year, the government revealed that it was planning for a switch-off of the broadcast digital terrestrial television (DTT) service in the future.

This is again because of the rapidly changing nature of the TV landscape, with viewers shifting to online streaming, creating a hybrid landscape between IPTV, traditional DTT, satellite broadcasting, and cable.

Industry observers note that current licenses for DTT services expire at the end of December, 2034, but the government may choose to extend them to 2044. ®.

Falcon-H1: A Family of Hybrid-Head Language Models Redefining Efficiency and Performance

📅 21 May 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we are proud to introduce the Falcon-H1 series, a collection of six open-source models ranging from 0.5B to 34B parameters, each available in both base and instruction-tuned variants.
  • In this release, we feature six open-weight models: 0.5B, 1.5B, 1.5B-Deep, 3B, 7B, and 34B, along with their instruct versions.
  • Hybrid Architecture (Attention + SSM): We combine attention and Mamba-2 heads in parallel within our hybrid mixer block.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Check out also our official blogpost.

Today, we are proud to introduce the Falcon-H1 series, a collection of six open-source models ranging from 0.5B to 34B parameters, each available in both base and instruction-tuned variants. At the core of these models lies a hybrid architecture that combines the strengths of the classical Transformer-based attention mechanism with the State Space Model (SSM), known for its superior long-context memory and computational efficiency. This architectural innovation is further enhanced by fundamental advancements in training dynamics and data utilization, enabling Falcon-H1 models to deliver uncompromised performance that rivals the top Transformer-based models across all covered size tiers.

In this release, we feature six open-weight models: 0.5B, 1.5B, 1.5B-Deep, 3B, 7B, and 34B, along with their instruct versions. All our open-source models are with a permissive license based on Apache 2.0.

Hybrid Architecture (Attention + SSM): We combine attention and Mamba-2 heads in parallel within our hybrid mixer block. Importantly, the amount of attention and mamba heads can be adjusted independently, allowing for an optimal attention/SSM ratio. This hybrid design enables faster inference, lower memory usage, and strong generalization across tasks.

Wide Range of Model Sizes: Available in six scales—0.5B, 1.5B, 1.5B-deep, 3B, 7B, and 34B—with both base and instruction-tuned variants, suitable for everything from edge devices to large-scale deployments.

Multilingual by Design: Supports 18 languages natively, including Arabic (ar), Czech (cs), German (de), English (en), Spanish (es), French (fr), Hindi (hi), Italian (it), Japanese (ja), Korean (ko), Dutch (nl), Polish (pl), Portuguese (pt), Romanian (ro), Russian (ru), Swedish (sv), Urdu (ur), and Chinese (zh) — with scalability to 100+ languages, thanks to our multilingual tokenizer trained on diverse language datasets.

Sources indicate that compact Models, Big Performance: Falcon-H1-0.5B delivers performance on par with typical 7B models from 2024, while Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep rivals many of the current leading 7B–10B models. Each Falcon-H1 model is designed to match or exceed the performance of models at least twice its size, making them ideal for low-resource and edge deployments without compromising on capability.

256K Context Support: Falcon-H1 models support up to 256K context length, enabling applications in long-document processing, multi-turn dialogue, and long-range reasoning.

Exceptional STEM capabilities: Falcon-H1 models deliver strong performance in math and science domains thanks to the focus on high-quality STEM data during training.

Robust Training Strategy: Uses a high-efficiency data strategy and customized Maximal Upgrade Parametrization (μP) to ensure smooth and scalable training across model sizes.

When embarking on the Falcon-H1 series development, we chose to fundamentally rethink the training approach. While the field of LLM development has converged on many established practices that reliably produce strong models, these conventions were primarily validated on classical transformer architectures. The shift from pure attention mechanisms to a hybrid attention-SSM design represents a significant architectural change, making it uncertain whether these standard practices would remain optimal.

It has been revealed that given this uncertainty, we conducted an extensive experimentation phase, systematically revisiting nearly every aspect of model design and training methodology before launching our final training runs. While we will provide comprehensive details in our upcoming technical report, we'd like to share the key insights that shaped the Falcon-H1 models.

In a recent development, the hybrid attention-SSM models have a larger configuration space of all the parameters that define the model architecture. Our goal was to probe each of these configuration parameters to check its impact on model performance and efficiency. As a result, we reveal regions of model configuration space with an increased performance at a mild efficiency cost. We can roughly divide the hybrid model configuration space in the following 4 blocks:.

Capabilities of language models are known to come mainly from the training data, and that stays true for Falcon-H1 series. Besides the raw data prepared for the model, it is crucial how and when this data is shown during training. One such data strategy is commonly called curriculum learning, where simpler data is shown at the beginning of the training while the samples requiring more advanced reasoning are left for the end. Surprisingly, a completely opposite strategy worked best for us. Giving even the most complicated data, an advanced math problem or a long context sample, from the beginning of the training seems to give the model more time to learn features essential for handling the respective complex tasks.

Another key aspect is the scarcity of high-quality data. A common concern when training large models is brute force memorization of the data as opposed to its real understanding. To minimize the risk of such memorization, a common practice is not reusing data samples during training, or doing it at most a few times for the highest quality samples. A by-product of this strategy is data mixture being dominated by web samples that have disproportionally large volume compared to high-quality sources. We have found that the memorization effect might be a bit overestimated, and carefully estimating model's memorization window allows to reuse high-quality samples more often without any harm to model's generalization ability.

It has been revealed that classical μP is a technique heavily rooted in theory of neural networks but with a clear practical application: if one finds optimal training hyperparameters at a single base model size, it can be effortlessly transferred to other, typically bigger, model sizes using Mup scaling rules. We employed Mup hyperparameter transfer for the whole Falcon-H1 series, greatly reducing experimentation time and making it possible to train 6 models in parallel.

On top of that, we made the next step into inner workings behind μP to further boost the model performance. In a nutshell, each component of the model “wants” to train at its own intensity, and that intensity depends on the size of the component. μP scaling rules take into account this dependence through so-called ``μP multipliers'' to enable optimal hyperparameter transfer. However, classical μP uses trivial multipliers of 1 at the base model size, which corresponds to a nasusmption that intensity of all components are already optimal at the base size. We discard this assumption and tune the multipliers at the base model size. Specifically, we have divided model parameters into 35 fine-grained groups and performed a joint optimization of the respective 35 multipliers.

One of our first steps in working on Falcon-H1 series was treating and removing spikes that are known to be a serious issue for SSM-based models. The solution that has worked the best for us is placing dampening μP multipliers at a certain location of the SSM block. In addition to the smooth final model training, the removal of spikes is essential to get clean signals in the subsequent experiments.

Industry observers note that we have observed that many aspects of the training dynamics are linked together under a common theme of noise interpretation and control. This includes learning rate and batch size schedules, scaling of the learning rate with batch size, and the behavior of parameter norms. In particular, we have found the parameter norms to be mostly determined by the training hyperparameters rather than the model fitting the data. To take this into account, we have included weight decay, a hyperparameter that primarily controls parameter norms, into both the training schedule and μP multipliers.

Industry observers note that the current Falcon-H1 models were trained without reasoning-specific fine-tuning, yet they already demonstrate strong general instruction-following capabilities. To highlight their performance, we present a detailed comparison of Falcon-H1-34B-Instruct against other top-performing Transformer models of similar or larger scales, including: Qwen3-32B (non-thinking mode), Qwen2.5-72B, Qwen2.5-32B, Gemma3-27B, Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E (109B) and LLaMA3.3-70B. For full evaluation settings and methodology, please refer to the Falcon-H1 GitHub page.

Sources indicate that one of the standout features of the Falcon-H1 series is the strong performance of its compact models. Below, we compare 1.5B-scale instruct models. Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep-Instruct clearly outperforms leading models in its class, such as Qwen3-1.7B-Instruct. Even more notably, it performs on par with—or better than many 7B models, including Falcon3-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.

🔎 Note: Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep and Falcon-H1-1.5B were trained using identical settings; the only difference lies in their architectural depth and width.

It has been revealed that to give a picture of Falcon-H1 performance across languages, we provide average between Hellaswag and MMLU scores for 30B scale models and for a set of selected languages, including Arabic, German, Spanish, French, Hindi, Italian, Dutch, Portuguese, Romanian, Russian, and Swedish. It also demonstrates on-par performance in the other supported languages.

One of the standout features of Falcon-H1 is its ability to handle long-context inputs, an area where State Space Models (SSMs) offer significant advantages in terms of memory efficiency and computational cost.

According to recent reports, to demonstrate these capabilities, we evaluate Falcon-H1-34B-Instruct against Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct across a set of long-context benchmarks. We focus on three core task categories drawn from the Helmet benchmark suite - Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Natural Questions, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA; Recall tasks: JSON KV, RULER MK Needle, RULER MK UUID, RULER MV; Long Document QA tasks: ∞BENCH QA, ∞BENCH MC. These evaluations highlight Falcon-H1’s strength in scaling to longer sequences while maintaining high performance and efficiency.

In addition, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the Falcon-H1 series alongside leading Transformer-based models across 23 benchmarks, covering multiple domains and model scales. You can explore the interactive results below—simply select the benchmarks most relevant to your use case to view the corresponding aggregated performance scores (below is a screenshort of our interactive plot in the official blogpost).

We provide a detailed comparison of Falcon-H1-34B-Base with other leading base models at the same or larger scale, including Qwen2.5-72B, Qwen2.5-32B, Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E (109B) and Gemma3-27B.

🔎 Note: Qwen3-32B does not currently offer a base model checkpoint.

Below, we compare 1.5B-scale base models. Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep-Base clearly outperforms leading models in its class, such as Qwen3-1.7B-Base. Notably, it performs on par with Falcon3-7B, and even exceeds it on math and reasoning tasks, making it an excellent foundation for building small-scale reasoning-focused models.

For the base models, we also provide an interactive plot in our official blogpost showcasing their performance across 14 benchmarks, spanning multiple domains and various model scales (below is a screenshort of our interactive plot in the official blogpost).

Industry observers note that we compare input (prefill) and output (generation) throughput between Falcon-H1 and Qwen2.5-32B in the plots below. While Transformers are slightly faster at shorter context lengths, our hybrid model becomes significantly more efficient as the context grows—achieving up to 4× speedup in input throughput and 8× in output throughput at longer sequence lengths. Benchmarks were run using our Falcon-H1 vLLM implementation and the official vLLM implementation of Qwen2.5-32B.

Industry observers note that this performance gain highlights the scalability of the Falcon-H1 architecture. We attribute the throughput gap at small context lengths to the more mature optimizations of attention mechanisms, compared to current State Space Models (SSMs) implementations, in current inference pipelines.

⚙️ We invite the community to contribute to further optimizing SSM implementations — a promising direction for advancing the next generation of efficient LLMs.

In a recent development, 🔎 Note: Input throughput measures how fast models process tokens when reading/encoding text. Output throughput measures how fast they generate fresh tokens. The ratio line reveals Falcon-H1/Qwen2.5 performance comparison.

Recent findings suggest that in line with our mission to foster AI accessibility and collaboration, Falcon-H1 is released under the Falcon LLM license. We hope the AI community finds these models valuable for research, application development, and further experimentation. Falcon-H1 is a continuation of our efforts to create more capable and efficient foundation models. We welcome feedback and collaboration from the community as we continue to refine and advance the capabilities of these models.

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Automating Spark Upgrades with Codex Agents at OpenAI.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

Recent findings suggest that at QCon San Francisco 2026, Mouli Mukherjee, Engineering Manager for Data Infrastructure at OpenAI, argued that AI agents are most useful not for rebuilding a data platform, but for the open-ended operational work that is hard to turn into fixed playbooks. OpenAI’s platform runs at exabyte scale, with hundreds of thousands of datasets and a Spark fleet on millions of cores, and Mukherjee showed how Codex-driven agents can take on that kind of work when the right systems sit underneath them.

Industry observers note that mukherjee clearly distinguished between deterministic systems and agents. She stated that anything requiring consistent outputs for the same inputs, such as access control, configuration resolution, and data correctness guarantees, should remain within the realm of proper systems. Agents utilize these systems as tools and do not attempt to reimplement them. As she expressed:.

We should definitely build the systems where we want guarantees and guardrails.

Agents earn their place where failure modes and remediations cannot be fully enumerated in advance, such as debugging: follow the evidence, decide what to try next, and stay inside the tools’ guarantees.

In a recent development, the Spark upgrade outlines steps taken to ensure safety. The team first built a shadow-run service for testing, which reused production inputs and operated on a low-priority queue to avoid impacting live operations. They also implemented a configuration override service to prevent experiments from changing global settings and developed a validation skill to compare production and shadow runs. After these safeguards were in place, agents claimed jobs, debuted shadow runs, reviewed validation reports, classified errors, and transitioned jobs to the upcoming Spark version.

It has been revealed that mukherjee reported that the same primitives now cover more of routine platform operations. Agents can tune job efficiency continuously by inspecting query plans, trying a config change, comparing runs, and iterating. For lower-risk incremental library releases, the team sometimes skips the shadow step and promotes directly, trading capacity for higher rollback risk. Jobs that pass shadow validation but later fail in production can auto-roll back to the previous Spark version so pipelines keep running without manual intervention. On the support side, agents can search past incident reports, suggest runbook updates, trace why a table is stale through orchestrator and scheduler logs, and help users understand access-control denials, while permissions still enforce the user’s own credentials.

Mukherjee recommended starting with the repetitive, open-ended tasks where judgment matters and failure modes are too numerous to hard-code, building the safety mechanisms first, and only then letting agents operate inside those bounds so experimentation stays repeatable, observable, and reversible.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

The world's fastest computers have a problem: Keeping the work running

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1344 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I node what you did last summer: you went down when an HPC project was relying on you.
  • Frontier, Oak Ridge National Laboratory's exascale supercomputer, has thousands of processors working together on scientific problems.
  • In a recent development, an uncorrectable memory error can do it, or a maintenance mishap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I node what you did last summer: you went down when an HPC project was relying on you.

Frontier, Oak Ridge National Laboratory's exascale supercomputer, has thousands of processors working together on scientific problems. It also has a surprisingly ordinary way of ruining a researcher's day: one node going down.

In a recent development, an uncorrectable memory error can do it, or a maintenance mishap. Scott Atchley, chief technology officer at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, describes technicians accidentally rebooting the wrong node or risking a neighboring node's power supply while working in tightly packed racks.

The hardware fault can affect just one node, but a simulation running across thousands of processors can grind to a halt. Then comes a series of questions. How recently did the application save its progress? How much computation needs repeating? And how long before the scheduler lets the job run again?

According to recent reports, for operators, the challenge isn't just keeping the supercomputer running. It's keeping the science moving.

Sources indicate that on Frontier, a memory error can have an outsized audience. Atchley claims uncorrectable double-bit errors in high-bandwidth memory occurred about 1.5 times a day during the supercomputer's early bring-up.

Its predecessor, Summit, saw roughly one every two weeks. This sounds like a backward step, until you count the memory. Frontier has more than 16 times as much, giving bad bits considerably more places to hide.

It has been revealed that memory isn't the only problem. Problematic GPU firmware can crash a node, and so can a technician rebooting the wrong one. Interconnect faults add another way for a large job to come unstuck.

In a recent development, in a tightly coupled simulation using the Message Passing Interface (MPI) simulation, thousands of processes, or ranks, exchange data and participate in collective operations. If one rank disappears, the others cannot carry on as though nothing happened.

Clockwork.io CEO Suresh Vasudevan describes a similar dependency in synchronized GPU training.

According to recent reports, one failed GPU can bring a 1,024-GPU job to a pause. An underperforming GPU can be almost as troublesome: if one participant runs at 80 percent speed, others might have to spend time waiting for it.

The bigger the machine, the more ways there are for one small problem to become everybody's problem.

Since stopping every component from failing isn't an option, researchers need a way to preserve their work. That's where checkpointing comes in. The application periodically saves its state so that, when something goes wrong, the simulation can resume from an earlier point instead of starting from scratch.

The catch is that saving progress costs computing time, and doing it too often can become almost as wasteful as losing the work itself.

Sources indicate that vasudevan explains this with an example. If writing a checkpoint takes 30 seconds, saving every five minutes consumes roughly 10 percent of computing time. Stretch that interval to 50 minutes, and the overhead drops to about 1 percent. But a failure could wipe out considerably more work.

Atchley says the calculation depends on the job's size and expected failure rate. He uses an example of ten-hour mean time between failures for a full machine job on Frontier. Using half the machine would roughly double that interval. The Young-Daly checkpointing model helps find the balance between saving too frequently and risking too much work.

Researchers also have the scheduler to contend with. Frontier's standard batch queue limits larger jobs to 12 hours, with shorter limits for smaller jobs. Its extended queue permits jobs of up to 64 nodes to run for 24 hours.

Then there's storage. Checkpoints can be written to the Lustre-based Orion filesystem or node-local SSDs. The faster the data can be saved, the less time checkpointing steals from the actual science.

Before recovery can begin, someone has to notice the job has stalled. Vasudevan claims frameworks such as PyTorch can spend several minutes waiting before a hung process is recognized. Operators then have to sift through application logs and hardware telemetry to try to identify the offending GPU.

This can mean another encounter with the scheduler, which decides when replacement resources become available. Once allocated, the application still needs to load its libraries, initialize the runtime, and rebuild communication connections between processors.

And that's before the lost work enters the picture.

Restarting from a checkpoint means returning to the last saved state, potentially hours earlier, and repeating every calculation that has been completed since. The hardware may be back in action, but the simulation hasn't caught up.

Atchley states Frontier can launch a scheduled job in roughly 30 seconds. Restoring the application's data and getting back to useful computation takes longer.

According to recent reports, worse, researchers who lose their allocation may have to rejoin the queue. Depending on demand, Atchley claims, "it might take me a day or so before my job runs again.".

Recent findings suggest that keeping a supercomputer available is one thing. Making sure its processors are doing useful work is another, and the difference is measurable.

Sources indicate that A 2026 study by researchers Carlo Graziani, Bethany Lusch, and Bronson Messer examined computational efficiency using records of 331,640 jobs run on Frontier during 2024. Their model estimated that, even with optimally timed checkpoints, only 95.7 percent of allocated computing resources would go toward useful calculations.

In a recent development, the remaining 4.3 percent? Around 1.2 percent goes to writing checkpoints, 2.8 percent disappears into failures, and another 0.3 percent is spent restarting applications.

Skipping checkpoints altogether would be worse. The model puts useful computation at just 91.4 percent without proactive checkpointing, demonstrating that saving work has a cost, but losing it can cost considerably more.

Recent findings suggest that these efficiency figures are modeled estimates, not measurements of every source of lost productivity. They don't capture every delay from rejoining queues, stalled applications, or poorly performing components. The actual productivity bill can be harder to pin down.

This makes Frontier's reported 98.49 percent overall availability in 2024 an interesting contrast. The Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility's operational assessment measures how often the system was available to users.

Scale makes these losses expensive. An hour of wasted computation across 2,000 nodes represents 2,000 node hours gone, compared with just 100 node hours for a job using 100 nodes.

It has been revealed that saving checkpoints to local SSDs can speed things up, but there's a catch. If the node fails, the checkpoint stored on it can disappear too.

Atchley points to techniques such as Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's Scalable Checkpoint/Restart (SCR), which can copy checkpoint data to neighboring nodes. This gives applications another recovery point if the original node goes down.

Keeping spare nodes available can also shorten recovery time. Atchley claims researchers who reserve extra nodes will consume their computing allocation even if nothing breaks, which leaves fewer hours for useful computation.

According to recent reports, software developers are also trying to avoid the restart process altogether. Vasudevan describes techniques that attempt to transfer distributed application state to replacement hardware to allow synchronized workloads to continue without returning to an earlier checkpoint.

Some approaches can handle certain GPU and network failures through failover. These techniques depend on detecting faults quickly, preserving consistent application state, and having replacement resources available.

None of this makes failures disappear. Atchley notes that hardware improvements, including stronger memory protection, can address problems encountered on earlier machines. But as systems grow, newly introduced failure modes emerge.

The next generation of supercomputers may fix the faults that plagued their predecessors, but that doesn't mean they'll never break. Atchley explains that problems solved on one machine tend to give way to entirely new ones on the next.

Industry observers note that faster processors and more memory are only useful if scientists can keep their calculations moving. This makes fault detection and recovery every bit as vital as another headline-grabbing performance record.

Resilience research, Atchley admits, "is not sexy at all." But when you're dealing with machines of this size, "scale just amplifies everything." ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BlackSky Technology unveiled on November 24, 2026 that it had acquired EpochGeo, adding artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) tools that fuse multiple data sources to its real-time space-based intelligence business.

EpochGeo develops spatiotemporal AI/ML, which examines information across location and time, alongside data-management tools and mission-focused multi-source analytics. Its technology fuses sources including radio-frequency and signals intelligence for mission-critical defense applications. Those capabilities broaden BlackSky’s existing imagery and analytics business by supporting analysis across space-based and terrestrial inputs, with the stated aim of helping owners rapidly detect and respond to relevant changes.

BlackSky described the acquisition as a response to defense and national-security organizations investing in space-based intelligence and seeking to use AI to fuse diverse data sources, understand patterns and anticipate developments. The organization’s broader strategy is to deliver real-time intelligence on locations and events affecting national and economic security.

Sources indicate that founded in 2018, EpochGeo counts major U.S.-based defense prime contractors and the U.S. government among its customers. BlackSky will continue supporting those customers through existing contracts. The acquisition therefore includes established defense relationships alongside the analytics technology.

According to recent reports, blackSky CEO Brian O’Toole noted EpochGeo has developed and deployed mission-critical analytics with end users in secure operational environments, including support for U.S. combatant commands and international ministries of defense. “These are exactly the capabilities our largest customers are asking us to provide as an integrated extension to real-time imaging services,” he said.

According to recent reports, shortly after the acquisition’s closing, BlackSky intends to grant restricted stock unit awards to as many as 43 EpochGeo employees as an incentive to join the company in upcoming, non-executive roles. The awards would cover up to 565,000 shares of BlackSky common stock if all of the prospective employees agree to join.

The grants will use an inducement equity incentive strategy approved by BlackSky’s board on October 29, 2026 without stockholder approval under the Newly introduced York Stock Exchange’s employment-inducement exception. One-quarter of each award is scheduled to vest on December 10, 2027, followed by quarterly vesting of one-sixteenth of the underlying shares. Vesting remains subject to each recipient’s continued service through the applicable date.

BlackSky plans to make EpochGeo’s capabilities available through space-based intelligence and AI subscriptions or sovereign mission solutions, and to integrate them across its large-scale data contracts and mission programs. The stated goals are to increase the value customers derive from BlackSky’s collection capabilities, accelerate adoption of its analytics services and support more comprehensive situational-awareness and decision-support products.

According to recent reports, the acquisition links EpochGeo’s deployed defense analytics and customer relationships to those distribution channels. The central operational question is whether adding analytics that fuse radio-frequency and signals intelligence with other data to BlackSky’s existing imaging services will produce the broader analytics adoption the company is seeking.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that NEWLY INTRODUCED: tiny-agents now supports AGENTS.md standard. 🥳.

Inspired by Tiny Agents in JS, we ported the idea to Python 🐍 and extended the huggingface_hub client SDK to act as a MCP Client so it can pull tools from MCP servers and pass them to the LLM during inference.

Sources indicate that MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol that standardizes how Large Language Models (LLMs) interact with external tools and APIs. Essentially, it removed the need to write custom integrations for each tool, making it simpler to plug upcoming capabilities into your LLMs.

Industry observers note that in this blog post, we'll show you how to get started with a tiny Agent in Python connected to MCP servers to unlock powerful tool capabilities. You'll see just how easy it is to spin up your own Agent and start building!

Spoiler : An Agent is essentially a while loop built right on top of an MCP Client!

This section walks you through how to use existing Tiny Agents. We'll cover the setup and the commands to get an agent running.

First, you need to install the latest version of huggingface_hub with the mcp extra to get all the necessary components.

Now, let's run an agent using the CLI!

The coolest part is that you can load agents directly from the Hugging Face Hub tiny-agents Dataset, or specify a path to your own local agent configuration!

If you don't provide a path to a specific agent configuration, our Tiny Agent will connect by default to the following two MCP servers:.

The following example highlights a web-browsing agent configured to use the Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct model via Nebius inference provider, and it comes equipped with a playwright MCP server, which lets it use a web browser! The agent config is loaded specifying its path in the tiny-agents/tiny-agents Hugging Face dataset.

When you run the agent, you'll see it load, listing the tools it has discovered from its connected MCP servers. Then, it's ready for your prompts!

do a Web Search for HF inference providers on Brave Search and open the first result and then give me the list of the inference providers supported on Hugging Face.

In a recent development, you can also use Gradio Spaces as MCP servers! The following example uses Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct model via Nebius inference provider, and connects to a FLUX.1 [schnell] image generation HF Space as an MCP server. The agent is loaded from its configuration in the tiny-agents/tiny-agents dataset on the Hugging Face Hub.

Generate a 1024x1024 image of a tiny astronaut hatching from an egg on the surface of the moon.

Now that you've seen how to run existing Tiny Agents, the following sections will dive deeper into how they work and how to build your own.

Each agent's behavior (its default model, inference provider, which MCP servers to connect to, and its initial system prompt) is defined by an agent.json file. You can also provide a custom PROMPT.md in the same directory for a more detailed system prompt. Here is an example:.

According to recent reports, agent.json The model and provider fields specify the LLM and inference provider used by the agent. The servers array defines the MCP servers the agent will connect to. In this example, a "stdio" MCP server is configured. This type of server runs as a local process. The Agent starts it using the specified command and args, and then communicates with it via stdin/stdout to discover and execute available tools.

You can find more details about Hugging Face Inference Providers here.

Modern LLMs are built for function calling (or tool use), which enables users to easily build applications tailored to specific use cases and real-world tasks.

Industry observers note that A function is defined by its schema, which informs the LLM what it does and what input arguments it expects. The LLM decides when to use a tool, the Agent then orchestrates running the tool and feeding the result back.

InferenceClient implements the same tool calling interface as the OpenAI Chat Completions API, which is the established standard for inference providers and the community.

In a recent development, the MCPClient is the heart of our tool-use functionality. It's now part of huggingface_hub and uses the AsyncInferenceClient to communicate with LLMs.

The full MCPClient code is in here if you want to follow along using the actual code 🤓.

Key responsibilities of the MCPClient:.

​​Here’s a glimpse of how it connects to an MCP server (the add_mcp_server method):.

In a recent development, it supports stdio servers for local tools (like accessing your file system), and http servers for remote tools! It's also compatible with sse, which is the previous standard for remote tools.

The MCPClient's process_single_turn_with_tools method is where the LLM interaction happens. It sends the conversation history and available tools to the LLM via AsyncInferenceClient.chat.completions.create(..., stream=True).

First, the method determines all tools the LLM should be aware of for the current turn – this includes tools from MCP servers and any special "exit loop" tools for agent control; then, it makes a streaming call to the LLM:.

As chunks arrive from the LLM, the method iterates through them. Each chunk is immediately yielded, then we reconstruct the complete text response and any tool calls.

Once the stream is complete, if the LLM requested any tool calls (now fully reconstructed in final_tool_calls), the method processes each one:.

It first checks if the tool called exits the loop (exit_loop_tool). If not, it finds the correct MCP session responsible for that tool and calls session.call_tool(). The result (or error response) is then formatted, added to the conversation history, and yielded so the Agent is aware of the tool's output.

With the MCPClient doing all the job for tool interactions, our Agent class becomes wonderfully simple. It inherits from MCPClient and adds the conversation management logic.

The Agent class is tiny and focuses on the conversational loop, the code can be found here.

In a recent development, when an Agent is created, it takes an agent config (model, provider, which MCP servers to use, system prompt) and initializes the conversation history with the system prompt. The load_tools() method then iterates through the server configurations (defined in agent.json) and calls add_mcp_server (from the parent MCPClient) for each one, populating the agent's toolbox.

The Agent.run() method is an asynchronous generator that processes a single user input. It manages the conversation turns, deciding when the agent's current task is complete.

There are a lot of cool ways to explore and expand upon the MCP Client and the Tiny Agent 🔥 Here are some ideas to get you started:.

It has been revealed that pull requests and contributions are welcome! Again, everything here is open source! 💎❤️.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post will describe an algorithm for constructing an ANF/similar IR from a functional-like base language with no closure usage, and with no related excess space requirements. This algorithm is as far as I know not new, and has apparently been known in imperative compilation for a while. However, I admittedly have no source for this, nor have I seen it described for functional-like languages.

Thanks to Ryan Brewer and rpjohnst for their inspiration on this.

If you are only interested in code, please skip to Implementation.

First, let us describe our input and output languages. Our input language will look like this:.

This is meant to echo some simple functional programming language, and contains all the elements needed to demonstrate the algorithm.

According to recent reports, our output language will look like a lexically-scoped flat ANF-style construction, with all lets at the toplevel. The goal is to convert from our input ml to this language.

The notable addition is the Hole constructor in anf, the purpose of which will be described now.

Imagine we are trying to convert the term.

According to recent reports, when we arrive at the body of x, we have a conundrum. We need to put the conversion of y before x, so that using y is well-scoped. Hence, we must convert y before we can continue. How do we use this conversion, though? x's content needs to be put in the anf field of y's Let, so it's not clear how to both convert y before x and to use x's finished conversion in y.

Industry observers note that one "traditional" method of solving this is via continuations, where y is passed a closure representing "what to do next", after it converts its body. We can then put x's content in that closure, which will be invoked later. This has two main flaws:.

Recent findings suggest that recall that we left a Hole of anf option ref field in our anf type. I will denote a hole like this: [·]. The central idea is that our conversion of any given ml fragment will return:.

Consider this simplified example:.

When we convert x, this signals for the conversion of y. There are two steps to converting a let - we must first convert the "head" (2), and then the "body" (y).

Converting the head will result in something of form.

Recent findings suggest that note that the hole is left to be filled later. This way, the conversion of y's head need know nothing about its environment. We represent this in code via the Hole constructor, which contains a reference to a fragment that either may be empty (None) or filled (Some ...). The conversion of the body can then proceed by first generating the expected addition, binding it to nm so it may be referenced later:.

In a recent development, we now need to get this fragment into the proper lexical scope. We can do this by plugging it into the hole left by the conversion of the head:.

Then, returning this fragment, the name bound (y), and the reference to the inner hole, we can continue converting x; First, convert the head, using the name returned by the conversion of y:.

And finally plug it into the hole returned by y.

We are left with a final hole we can plug with Done to be explicit about the end of a control flow path. One disadvantage of this strategy is that it does generate many unneeded names. Most of these can be avoided by carefully special casing certain lets, and the rest can be eliminated via a simple folding pass.

Below is a sample implementation of this algorithm, in OCaml.

I recommend toying with the conversion yourself, using utop or similar. In the following, I will "clean up" the output slightly, as to not make it unreadable.

If we use our first example term:.

Industry observers note that we can then plug the returned hole, as described. Via some inspection, we can verify this is indeed correct, and conforms to our ANF-like form, as expected.

As mentioned earlier, the large amount of duplicate names can be mitigated through strategies such as special casing let _ = and folding passes.

Industry observers note that clearly, the algorithm does not use closures, or any indirect jumps. It does not allocate any more than needed for the representation of the output program; there is no excessive closure allocation. I do not currently have a good way to test performance on real-world large inputs, but I have no reason to believe it would not perform better than an equivalent higher-order version.

I believe this method should be extendable to CPS as well, although I have not tried as of the moment. The "usual" higher-order CPS conversion described in e.g. "Compiling with continuations, continued" looks quite similar to the higher-order presentation of ANF conversion, so I would be interested in whether it can be similarly massaged into a mutable form.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AutoPay login and vehicle records affected, alongside limited payment information and customer service emails.
  • London Gatwick Airport has warned customers that a breach of its drop-off payment service exposed personal information and, in limited cases, payment records.
  • A notification email seen by The Register identifies the affected system as AutoPay, operated by ParkPark and used by Gatwick's drop-off zone manager, Times24 UK Limited.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AutoPay login and vehicle records affected, alongside limited payment information and customer service emails.

London Gatwick Airport has warned customers that a breach of its drop-off payment service exposed personal information and, in limited cases, payment records.

A notification email seen by The Register identifies the affected system as AutoPay, operated by ParkPark and used by Gatwick's drop-off zone manager, Times24 UK Limited.

AutoPay lets drivers register their vehicle and payment details in advance so drop-off charges are collected automatically.

Gatwick told us it was unable to provide details about how many customers were affected by the breach, or how far back the affected records go.

The email stated most affected customers would have only some of the listed data exposed. The could include names, home addresses, cities, postcodes, contact details, and AutoPay login credentials such as email addresses and bcrypt-hashed passwords were affected.

Other records implicated in the breach include details of vehicles linked to AutoPay accounts, those vehicles' entry and exit times at Times24-managed parking locations, and vehicle registrations.

The email also states that payment records, including amounts, card types, card expiry dates, payment references, transaction statuses, transaction IDs, and drop-off locations and times were affected, but a Gatwick spokesperson remarked this applied only to "very limited cases.".

Again, in a minority of cases, "some limited emails between the customer service team and customers" were also exposed, the email stated.

It has been revealed that gatwick mentioned Times24 "immediately suspended" AutoPay after detecting the intrusion. The service remains disabled while the investigation continues.

Sources indicate that airport officials are overseeing the response with outside cybersecurity specialists. Gatwick warned of possible disruption to its website but stated flights were unaffected.

Customers can still use Gatwick's drop-off zones, although they'll have to use alternative payment methods, and all other airport services are still operating as usual.

The notification email urged customers to exercise caution when receiving communications from Gatwick, Times24, AutoPay, or ParkPark, especially those that ask for payment or bank details.

Times24, which operates across more than 200 car parks in the UK, did not immediately respond to our request for more information.

Dray Agha, senior manager at Huntress's tactical response division, warned that criminals could use the data for convincing scams long after news coverage of the breach has faded.

According to recent reports, "The real damage often comes after the breach," he remarked. "Criminals rarely use stolen data straight away; they'll wait until the headlines fade, then send a text about a 'parking fine' or an email offering a 'refund' that references a real booking. Even partial card details add a layer of credibility that makes people far more likely to hand over the rest.

"Gatwick customers should assume any unexpected message about their parking could be a scam, check directly with the airport, and keep a close eye on their bank statements over the coming months." ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This week at Dell Tech World, we confirmed the upcoming version of Dell Enterprise Hub, with a complete suite of models and applications to easily build AI running on premises with Dell AI servers and AI PCs.

If you go to the Dell Enterprise Hub today, you can find some of the most popular models, like Meta Llama 4 Maverick, DeepSeek R1 or Google Gemma 3, available for deployment and training in a few clicks.

But what you get is much more than a model, it’s a fully tested container optimized for specific Dell AI Server Platforms, with easy instructions to deploy on-premises using Docker and Kubernetes.

Meta Llama 4 Maverick can be deployed on NVIDIA H200 or AMD MI300X Dell PowerEdge servers.

We continuously work with Dell CTIO and Engineering teams to make the latest and greatest models ready, tested and optimized for Dell AI Server platforms as quickly as possible - Llama 4 models were available on the Dell Enterprise Hub within 1 hour of their public release by Meta!

The Dell Enterprise Hub now features ready-to-deploy AI Applications!

According to recent reports, if models are engines, then applications are the cars that make them useful so you can actually go places. With the new Application Catalog you can build powerful applications that run entirely on-premises for your employees and use your internal data and services.

The upcoming Application Catalog makes it easy to deploy leading open source applications within your private network, including OpenWebUI and AnythingLLM.

OpenWebUI makes it easy to deploy on-premises chatbot assistants that connect to your internal data and services via MCP, to build agentic experiences that can search the web, retrieve internal data with vector databases and storage for RAG use cases.

It has been revealed that anythingLLM makes it easy to build powerful agentic assistants connecting to multiple MCP servers so you can connect your internal systems or even external services. It includes features to enable multiple models, working with images, documents and set role-based access controls for your internal owners.

These applications are easy to deploy using the provided, customizable helm charts so your MCP servers are registered from the get go.

Dell Enterprise Hub is the only platform in the world that offers ready-to-use model deployment solutions for the latest AI Accelerator hardware:.

We work directly with Dell, NVIDIA, AMD and Intel so that when you deploy a container on your system, it’s all configured and ready to go, has been fully tested and benchmarked so it runs with the best performance out of the box on your Dell AI Server platform.

The newly introduced Dell Enterprise Hub now provides support for models to run on-device on Dell AI PCs in addition to AI Servers!

These models enable on-device speech transcription (OpenAI whisper), chat assistants (Microsoft Phi and Qwen 2.5), upscaling images and generating embeddings.

To deploy a model, you can follow specific instructions for the Dell AI PC of your choice, powered by Intel or Qualcomm NPUs, using the upcoming Dell Pro AI Studio. Coupled with PC fleet management systems like Microsoft Intune, it’s a complete solution for IT organizations to enable employees with on-device AI capabilities.

Industry observers note that dell Enterprise Hub offers an online portal into AI capabilities for Dell AI Server platforms and AI PCs. But what if you want to work directly from your development environment?

Introducing the newly introduced dell-ai open source library with a Python SDK and CLI, so you can use Dell Enterprise Hub within your environment directly from your terminal or code - just pip install dell-ai.

With Models and Applications, for AI Servers and AI PCs, easily installable using Docker, Kubernetes and Dell Pro AI Studio, Dell Enterprise Hub is a complete toolkit to deploy Gen AI applications in the enterprise, fully secure and on-premises.
