📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1144 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine two banks using AI agents to handle customer inquiries.
  • Most organizations assume that the solution to this problem is a better AI model.
  • According to McKinsey, nearly nine in ten respondents say their organizations regularly use AI in at least one business function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine two banks using AI agents to handle customer inquiries. One has built its reputation on flexibility, waiving fees and showing empathy when customers face financial hardship. The other prides itself on transparency and consistency, applying the same clear rules to everyone. When a customer disputes an overdraft fee, both agents might provide the same generic response unless they’ve been trained to reflect their bank’s approach to customer service.

Most organizations assume that the solution to this problem is a better AI model. But the real issue is often a lack of organizational context.

According to McKinsey, nearly nine in ten respondents say their organizations regularly use AI in at least one business function. While widespread adoption promises efficiency and productivity gains, it also makes technology less of a differentiator. As AI agents take on more work, make decisions and interact with customers on a company’s behalf, an key question emerges: Do those agents truly understand the company they’re working for?

Sources indicate that microsoft’s 2026 Work Trend Index highlights the growing integration of AI agents into organizational workflows and the importance of human judgment in how that work is designed. Yet, many businesses are building on the same foundation models and AI platforms. Without the right organizational context, their agents risk looking and sounding alike, eroding the qualities that make each customer experience different. The difference often lies in the decisions employees make every day, drawing on experience, customer knowledge and an understanding of what their organization values. These are the nuances that generic AI systems may struggle to replicate without additional guidance.

What if a firm could encode its corporate identity into its AI systems? The challenge for organizations is ensuring these agents reflect what makes the company unique: its secret sauce and competitive edge.

AI outputs can be technically correct but still fall short of how a company expects work to be done. For example, an AI agent at a luxury hotel responds to a guest’s request for a restaurant recommendation. It books a table at a highly rated restaurant without asking about the guest’s dining preferences or dietary restrictions. While the reservation might be made rapidly, the guest could end up somewhere with few suitable options, an experience that reflects poorly on the hotel.

According to recent reports, agents need more than basic training. Like employees, they require ongoing guidance, performance monitoring and coaching to ensure their actions reflect the company’s approach to customer service.

Beyond workflows and policies, AI agents need to understand the tech giant’s DNA: the institutional knowledge, expertise, decision-making principles, culture and values that shape how work gets done.

With AI capabilities becoming increasingly commoditized, manufacturer DNA becomes more valuable. Used right, AI should amplify what differentiates a company, not dilute it. That means teaching agents how work actually gets done, including the informal practices and judgment calls that contribute to success.

AI agents can also help preserve this knowledge as organizations grow, ensuring it remains accessible even as teams change.

According to recent reports, embedding organization DNA into AI doesn’t necessarily require overhauling existing systems. Leaders can start with several practical steps.

According to recent reports, define success metrics a competitor couldn’t copy: If agents are measured only on resolution rates and handling time, organizations risk creating the same experience as everyone else. Leaders should define what success looks like for their company, whether that’s helping customers feel supported during financial hardship or delivering the consistency they expect. Those differences should shape how agent performance is measured.

Sources indicate that codify the judgment calls, not just the rules: Mission statements and standard operating procedures provide a starting point, but company DNA often demonstrates up in how employees handle exceptions. When do they make an exception to a policy? How do they verify information or draw on past experiences? Coaching notes, quality reviews and conversations handled by top performers can help capture this knowledge and make it accessible to AI agents. Organizations can then use these examples to show agents how experienced employees navigate situations that don’t have a straightforward answer.

Map how work actually gets done: Leaders can create a “work graph” that captures how work moves across a team, including how customer support teams prioritize issues or managers make decisions. This should include the informal workarounds employees use when established processes fall short. These workarounds can reveal gaps between formal procedures and the realities of day-to-day work. By documenting these practices, organizations can help agents understand not just what gets done, but how and why.

Write down how to break a tie: Rules can’t anticipate every situation. Agents need guidance on how to navigate trade-offs, such as balancing policy with customer goodwill or speed with empathy. These principles should also define when an agent needs to involve a human, so escalation becomes a designed decision, never a failure.

Onboard agents like new hires and let your best people grade them: Before wider deployment, organizations should put agents through the same kinds of scenarios used to train new employees, including role-play exercises, difficult customer conversations and situations requiring. Experienced employees can review these interactions and identify where an agent’s response falls short of how the firm would approach the situation.

According to recent reports, make performance reviews a two-way coaching process: Review AI agent performance regularly, and have your people update its guidance as products, policies and customer expectations change. In return, AI interactions reveal where your people need help. For example, if the AI keeps escalating billing disputes and those calls still go unresolved, that’s a clear coaching priority. The result is a continuous feedback loop: people make the AI better, and the AI makes people better.

In a recent development, in the coming years, powerful AI agents will be available to nearly every tech giant. Those that codify and embed their identity into AI will be better positioned to scale without sacrificing what sets them apart.

Embedding company DNA is only the first step. Organizations must continuously guide and improve how agents perform, so they reinforce what makes the company different. Just as organizations evolve, so must their AI agents.

Industry observers note that gal Rimon is the founder and CEO of Centrical, a workforce orchestration platform that brings people and AI agents together to improve frontline performance. With a background in business intelligence and enterprise technology, he has spent his career helping organizations connect technology, people and business outcomes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai leads 2027 rollout, with a showroom visit still required to finish the paperwork.

Amazon is channeling its inner car salesman as it prepares to flog motors on the UK arm of its online tat bazaar.

Amazon Autos will launch in Britain in early 2027, its first expansion outside the US, where it debuted in December 2024. Customers can browse and reserve cars online before completing the purchase with a dealer.

Hoping it will be "a nice little earner," Amazon will let punters view real-time dealer inventory, prices, get an instant trade-in valuation, and connect with a local dealer to reserve a car, "all on Amazon.".

In a recent development, in the US, the service now covers more than 150 cities and offers vehicles from 35 brands. Hyundai is the first confirmed UK carmaker partner, while dealer group Vertu Motors will list used vehicles. More brands and dealers are due to be confirmed before launch.

Hyundai's launch range will include electric, hybrid, and petrol models.

"Buying a car is one of the biggest purchases people make, and we think it should feel as simple and transparent as shopping for anything on Amazon," noted Matt Nuffort, director of Amazon Autos International.

Of course, buying a car isn't quite like adding an air fryer or a memory stick to your basket. How does financing and checkout work for UK buyers? Customers will complete the purchase and paperwork at their chosen dealership.

Sources indicate that amazon is not offering financing itself, but buyers can explore financing options via the site, adjusting terms like deposit and duration to see how monthly payments change. Credit applications must be completed with the dealer.

In the US, buyers can submit a credit application through the platform, review terms and conditions, then sign electronic contracts online. They typically pay a deposit and visit the dealership to complete the remaining paperwork and pick up the vehicle.

Buyers shouldn't expect their new car to arrive in an enormous cardboard box with a smiley logo on it, or to be lowered onto their driveway by a giant Amazon delivery drone.

But given that one of the online retailer's flying delivery robots crashed into someone's garage after making a drop-off near Detroit last week, perhaps that's for the best. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Lambda Doubles Its Timeout to 30 Minutes After Eight Years at 15.

Nov 25, 2026 3 min read.

In a recent development, AWS recently doubled the maximum timeout of on-demand Lambda Event Functions from 15 to 30 minutes. The upcoming limit applies to synchronous, asynchronous, and event source mapping invocations in all commercial regions, at standard pricing and without an opt-in. The 15-minute ceiling had stood since 2018, after 60 seconds at launch in 2014 and five minutes from 2015.

Raising the limit is a configuration change per function, and Lambda rejects any value above 1,800 seconds with a validation error:.

In a recent development, the change covers one of the three shapes Lambda took this year. Web Functions keep 15 minutes, and Lambda MicroVMs allow eight hours, while on Lambda Managed Instances synchronous invocations now get 30 minutes and asynchronous ones keep the 90 minutes introduced in September. AWS names agentic AI requests that chain model and tool calls, media transcoding, Monte Carlo simulations, and report generation as the workloads that outgrew 15 minutes.

According to Tarun Rai Madan, Dan Slusariuc, and Snehil Ameta, the authors of the announcement, the first thing to check before raising the timeout is capacity:.

In a recent development, concurrency equals requests per second multiplied by average duration in seconds. At the same request rate, a function that runs for 30 minutes instead of 15 needs twice the concurrency. For example, 1 request per second at 30 minutes each needs 1,800 concurrent executions.

Industry observers note that the rest of the post is about what sits around the function. An SQS queue's visibility timeout has to be at least six times the function timeout, which means three hours. Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams read one batch per shard at a time, so a slow function slows the shard. Amazon MQ, DocumentDB and Kafka mappings created before November 19 stay at 14 minutes. A NAT gateway still drops idle connections after 350 seconds, and the Init phase keeps its 10-second limit.

Wibo van der Sluis, an independent AWS practitioner, tested the SQS rule in eu-west-1 by raising a function to 1,800 seconds behind a queue with a 90-minute visibility timeout and then lowering the queue to 60 seconds. Both changes were accepted with the mapping still enabled, while a fresh mapping from the same queue was refused:.

It has been revealed that so the check exists, but only at creation. One more thing the test demonstrated: at creation, Lambda compared the queue with the function timeout itself, not with six times it. I did not test where exactly that line sits, so treat the six times as guidance you enforce yourself.

He adds that an asynchronous function which times out three times has run for 90 minutes before the event reaches a dead-letter queue, and concludes that 30 minutes is the wrong fix for slow code behind an API.

Luc van Donkersgoed, principal engineer at NS and AWS Serverless Hero, writes:.

In a recent development, hell froze over. AWS Lambda now supports 30-minute timeouts. I am not sure how I feel about this.

The comments under the post took two directions. Magnus Eriksson, architect and former AWS employee, notes that Lambda "is anyhow quite expensive per CPU second compared to EC2" and would still reserve it for short-lived spiky loads. Matthew Bonig, AWS DevTools Hero and co-author of The CDK Book, looked further ahead: "Eventually it'll be 8 hours, and then nobody will be able to understand when to use it vs. MicroVMs.".

On Reddit, the most-upvoted reply welcomed the change because it avoids Fargate and ECS for hour-long batch jobs. The answer under it was that Fargate is beautifully simple. One commenter sets out where the longer limit fits:.

A 30 minute run still bills for the full duration at your configured memory, so check the cost per invocation before moving batch style work here, and keep the handler idempotent with a dead letter queue, because a failure or timeout partway through a long run can leave partial work behind. For multi step work, long running jobs, or anything that needs clear state and retries, Step Functions with Fargate or ECS is still usually cleaner.

Joseph Emison, CTO of Branch Insurance, reads the move as Lambda team recognizing that Cloud Run is its most compelling competitor. Cloud Run services allow 60 minutes per request, and Azure Functions on the Flex Consumption and Premium prepares enforce no maximum, with a 60-minute grace period during scale-in. AWS has not remarked whether the Lambda limit will move again.

🐯 Liger GRPO meets TRL

📅 25 May 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1255 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL; DR Liger supercharges TRL’s Group Relative Policy Optimization GRPO Trainer by slashing memory usage by 40% with zero drop in model quality.
  • Fine-tuning language models using reinforcement learning (RL) is a crucial step in a model's training lifecycle for steering models towards desirable behaviours which are more complex than can be achieved through typical supervised fine-tuning.
  • However, RLHF with PPO is a very resource-hungry approach - PPO requires loading multiple models in memory (policy, value, reward, and reference models), and also requires several iterations of fine-tuning reward and base models to achieve the desired results.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL; DR Liger supercharges TRL’s Group Relative Policy Optimization GRPO Trainer by slashing memory usage by 40% with zero drop in model quality. We also added support for FSDP and PEFT, making it easier than ever to scale GRPO across multiple GPUs.

Fine-tuning language models using reinforcement learning (RL) is a crucial step in a model's training lifecycle for steering models towards desirable behaviours which are more complex than can be achieved through typical supervised fine-tuning. RL has traditionally been applied to optimize large language models (LLMs) using the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm. This approach, often associated with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), utilizes a separately trained reward model to guide the fine-tuning of the primary model.

However, RLHF with PPO is a very resource-hungry approach - PPO requires loading multiple models in memory (policy, value, reward, and reference models), and also requires several iterations of fine-tuning reward and base models to achieve the desired results. The success of RLHF also depends on the capability of the reward model to effectively discriminate between desired and un-desired behaviour from our model.

It has been revealed that group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has seen significant recent popularity alongside DeepSeek's R1 model. GRPO eschews the pre-trained reward model and value models used in RLHF and instead relies on verifiable reward functions which can check the correctness of a model's output in a closed-form manner without needing an external reward model. This has resulted in massive improvements when using GRPO instead of PPO for fine-tuning on domains which are easily verifiable, such as teaching a model to reason, and perform well on math and coding tasks.

The following diagram highlights the GRPO vs PPO training pipeline (ref: Figure 4 of DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models):.

That mentioned, RL training still eats up a ton of GPU memory, so there's still plenty of room for optimizations here. In this blog post, we talk about an optimization that we recently added to TRL that cuts peak memory usage by 40% during GRPO Training, and we also dive into how to scale GRPO to multiple GPUs and nodes without losing performance or correctness.

Industry observers note that we extended the Liger Chunked Loss approach to the GRPO Loss, which lets us avoid having to store the full logits in memory for every training step. The calculation of logits, which involves the model's output head, is a significant contributor to peak memory usage, especially when dealing with large vocabularies, long sequence lengths, or large batch sizes. We address this by chunking the input to the lm_head across the batch and running the forward pass one chunk at a time.

But if you just implement it in a straightforward way, you won't actually be able to reduce the peak memory since you'd still need to keep all the logits in GPU memory for the backward pass. To get around that, we calculate the gradients for each loss chunk (with respect to the input chunk and the lm_head weight) during the forward pass, and then accumulate them as we go through each chunk.

Here's the visualization of the optimization (ref: Byron Hsu):.

We recently integrated Liger GRPO with TRL in PR #3184, so now you can use the Liger GRPO loss just by setting use_liger_loss to True in your GRPOConfig and enjoy the memory savings!

Heads up: these features aren't in the latest TRL release yet, so you'll need to install TRL from source for now:.

and then you can use it like this:.

We ran a bunch of GRPO experiments with and without the Liger GRPO Loss to see how things compare. For the policy model, we used Qwen3-0.6B and played around with different batch sizes. All the experiments were run on the gsm8k dataset using its reward functions.

According to recent reports, here's the plots of peak memory usage vs batch size for both FP32 and BF16 training. As expected, the memory savings get better with larger batch sizes since we chunk along the batch dimension. So when the batch size goes up, the Liger chunked loss ends up using a lot less memory, up to 40% less, compared to the regular (non-liger) version.

Quick note: Right now, we only support FP32, but we're working on open-sourcing BF16 support for Liger GRPO in TRL. The BF16 results shown here are from internal patches we've been testing.

It has been revealed that we also show that Liger Loss is effectively accurate. As seen in the plot, rewards over training steps stay pretty much the same as what you'd see using the standard TRL implementation.

We also added FSDP and PEFT support to Liger GRPO Loss in PR #3260 and PR #3355, respectively, allowing consumers to easily scale their experiments across multiple GPUs or nodes. PEFT techniques such as LoRA and QLoRA reduce the number of trainable parameters by only tuning the weights of smaller adapter weights on top of the original model, significantly lowering memory pressure as gradients, activations, and optimizer states for the entire model don't need to be held in memory. Additionally, using PEFT in GRPO allows one to forgo loading a separate reference model during training, as we can obtain the original, unmodified model during training by simply disabling the LoRA adapters.

Sources indicate that here, we show a multi-GPU GRPO training plot using FSDP and PEFT, where we compare the maximum training batch size possible with and without the Liger Loss across different Qwen3 model sizes. We found that with Liger, we were able to bump up the batch size by around 1.5 to 1.8x!

To accelerate text generation during training, Liger Loss can be effectively combined with TRL's integrated vLLM server. This significantly speeds up the collection of rollout data with minimal overhead and offers a seamless integration experience.

We encourage the community to try out these new features and share their feedback to help us further improve RL training for LLMs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’d like to share a wee pattern I’ve found useful for writing simple WebSocket apps in Haskell - specifically for my side project wordify - an open source ~ multiplayer crossword board game ~ .

I have in mind websocket applications where there’s some sort of ‘resource’ that is shared between multiple websocket clients that need to be kept updated as the state changes such as:.

For simplicity, we’ll implement a multiplayer server for Noughts and Crosses (as we’ll call it in a parochially defiant act of patriotism against the US-centric internet :P) to illustrate the pattern.

I’ll be exploring a pattern where we maintain a Map of all the Noughts and Crosses games we have in progress safely such that all the connected websockets see the same game updates.

There’s a few different options for writing web apps in haskell. Yesod is the one I’m most familiar with. The canonical examples on Yesod WebSockets illustate how to use a shared broadcast TChan as the basis for a chat server (blog here, code example here.)).

This shared TChan broadcast channel is a useful abstraction which will form part of our implementation but unlike the materials above we’ll need to maintain multiple gmaes at once with their own channel.

In a recent development, A naive approach might be to plonk our games in a Map GameId GameState stored in a TVar. A TVar is a mutable variable that can be updated by multiple threads (or websocket handlers) and can be updated transactionally along with other TVars (which we’ll get into later.).

We’ll also set up our GameState types including our board state, our two players, channel to broadcast move updates, etc:.

Since we’re using a TVar each WebSocket thread can load a new game into the game map if necessary by running modifyTVar to update the map.

Recent findings suggest that that just won’t do though! Only one thread can update the map entries at a time, and we have aspirations of being the Internet’s go-to Noughts and Crosses server! We’ll need something that scales better than that while we’ve still got the luxury of vertically scaling one machine along our path to world domination.

Sources indicate that stm-containers to the rescue! It uses a Hash Array Mapped Trie datastructure to split the map into chunks that can be updated inside independent STM transactions allowing for more concurrency.

Our next challenge is to load the game state into the game map when the first websocket connects and remove it from the map when it’s no longer needed so that we don’t run out of memory in our path to world domination.

Imagine our Yesod ‘App’ type also had a GameRepository that was a data store we could use to access and persist our TicTacToe games:.

We will leverage this function to load the game into the cache when it’s not already populated.

We will use Software Transactional Memory (STM) abstraction to ensure that if two websocket connections try to insert an entry into the game map at the same time, they both end up with the same ‘GameState’ instance so that they receive game updates on the broadcast channel.

In our getGameState function, if we don’t find the game already present in our game map then we attempt to load it freshly and insert it into the map. We do this insertion inside an STM transaction via the atomically function.

This means that if there is a conflict in the middle of the transaction because one or more other websocket threads have tried to load the game in another concurrent transaction, the transaction inside the atomically ‘block’ will be retried by the unsuccessful writing websocket threads. They will then read the newly inserted entry and increment the sharer count via registerSharer, meaning that all threads are reading from the same broadcast channel.

In a recent development, there’s an improvement we can make to make sure that multiple threads don’t try to load our game at the same time, wasting trips to the database just to throw the result away. This could happen in a thundering herd of observers to watch the latest tournament game between Noughts and Crosses grandmasters!

According to recent reports, we will use an MVar to allow a thread to lay claim to responsibility for loading the resource and signal any other threads waiting when it has done so. MVar’s readMVar function allows the caller to wait (block) until it has been populated with a value (or it will return immediately if it’s already populated with a value.).

The game entry in our game map will now either be a game loaded into the cache (LoadedGame) or a game that is currently being loaded by another websocket (LoadingGame.) LoadingGame will contain an MVar that can be read to receive a signal that the other thread has completed loading the game.

When we first try to retrieve a game, we have to decide the action we need to take based on the cache state, which we represent with this type:.

When we load a game we transactionally lay claim to loading the resource if it’s not already loaded or is currently being loaded by writing a ‘LoadingGame’ entry to cache:.

Recent findings suggest that this is performed in an STM transaction, so if multiple threads try to insert their ‘MVar’ claiming ownership then the losers of the race will retry the transaction and see the winning thread’s claim when they read the map again. They will then block on it being populated by the winning thread using using readMVar, which serves as a signal that they can now load the game from the cache.

When loading the resource we must make sure that threads don’t wait on the MVar indefinetly if an error is thrown while retrieving the game so we clean up the claim if an error occurs while trying to load the game.

Our last challenge is to make sure that entries are removed from the cache when it’s safe to do so (there are no websocket subscriptions.) Our Noughts and Crosses server will be very busy with many games being started and ended and we can’t have ourselves running out of heap space due to a memory leak of games remaining in the cache!

When we think of garaunteeing the safe release of scarce resources, one of the options our mind turns to is the resourcet package. This package allows us to use the type system to make sure a resource will be cleaned up when it is no longer being used. See this blog entry for more on how it works if you are unfamilar with it.

We will use the resourcet package’s allocate function to register the action that must be taken when the game resource is no longer in scope (due to the websocket disconnecting or an exception being thrown.).

We registered the releaseGameState function as the function that should be ran when the resource goes out of scope. It will check if there’s any sharers left, and if there are not it will remove the game from the game map.

According to recent reports, again, the STM abstraction has served us well. The transaction inside atomically will be restarted if either the ‘gameConnections’ TVar or game map is updated by another websocket thread.

If a fresh websocket connection retrieves the game from the cache at the same time as it is being removed in another transaction, either:.

Note: the conditional deletion can be achieved slightly more efficiently with stm-container’s focus function to avoid having to traverse the map a second time to do the deletion.

We can now use this game ‘resource’ in our websocket handler inside runResourceT:.

We use race_ to spawn two green threads to manage the Websocket connection.

handleOutgoingMessages will read from the shared broadcast channel and write to the websocket to inform the client of board changes.

Recent findings suggest that handleIncomingMessages will read from the websocket to make moves on behalf of the user. It will validate the move, enhancement the state and write to the shared broadcast channel.

When either handleIncomingMessages or handleOutgoingMessages fails on reading or writing to the socket due to it being disconnected, runResourceT will catch the error and run the releaseGameState function that we registered to run on resource deallocation in our getGameState function before rethrowing the error.

If you want to see a full implementation (mostly vibe coded other than what we’ve discussed here) of our demo noughts and crosses server, I’ve uploaded it to github here. The NoughtsAndCrosses.hs file contains all the logic we’ve been discussing in this blog entry.

It has been revealed that this pattern can be applied in any situation where it’s crucial that multiple threads need to share the same reference to something that is dynamically loaded. This is a requirement beyond that of a traditional cache where it doesn’t particularly matter if an item is evicted from the cache (per some eviction policy) while there’s still threads holding on to it, for example.

If you think you might find this pattern useful for something, I’ve published it as a library named shared-resource-cache. Source here.

Note: it works slightly differently to what we’ve explored here: when there are no ‘sharers’ of the given resource, it is not cleared from the cache immediately. Instead, it is cleared when there has been no sharers for at least a configured amount of time.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recovery windows of up to ten years are now available in Microsoft 365 Backup for OneDrive and SharePoint, up from a previous maximum of two.
  • The change took effect on October 31, though Exchange remains capped at two years.
  • Administrators can select recovery windows of three months, six months, or any whole number of years from one to ten.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sadly, no time travel back to 2016.

Recovery windows of up to ten years are now available in Microsoft 365 Backup for OneDrive and SharePoint, up from a previous maximum of two.

The change took effect on October 31, though Exchange remains capped at two years.

Administrators can select recovery windows of three months, six months, or any whole number of years from one to ten. Microsoft's list price is $0.15 per GiB per month of protected content. Extended windows can increase costs by keeping deleted data billable for longer.

Sources indicate that switching to a longer recovery window will also not make backups for that period magically available. So no nostalgic trips back to 2016.

Recent findings suggest that wider recovery windows may appeal to organizations that need access to older data, but backups are not a substitute for compliance retention and archiving. Recovery after a breach or ransomware attack is also critical, particularly getting back to a healthy state before any malware seeped into files.

Microsoft states backups are physically redundant and geographically replicated while respecting the tenant's data residency requirements.

Full OneDrive account and SharePoint site restores offer recovery points every ten minutes for the most recent two weeks, then weekly points through the configured window, up to ten years.

Individual file and folder recovery is limited to recovery points from the most recent 14 days, regardless of the configured window.

Restore remains free, which is handy since regular testing is a vital part of any disaster recovery proposal.

The arrival of a ten-year recovery window is good for enterprises that need it and have deep enough pockets. However, it is important to keep in mind that being able to configure a longer recovery window doesn't constitute a disaster recovery plan in itself and may be overkill in many instances.

It has been revealed that microsoft notes: "The existing one-year default recovery window remains unchanged. Longer recovery windows must be configured on the applicable backup policies.".

The company also recommends that users "review your organization's SharePoint and OneDrive backup requirements to determine whether longer recovery windows are needed.".

It has been revealed that A decade of recovery history could be valuable. It also means a decade of data to account for when setting budgets, access controls, and retention policies. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that today we're sharing research that bridges two powerful paradigms in AI agent design: the expressiveness of code-based actions and the reliability of structured generation.
  • In a recent development, figure 1: Accuracy comparison of three approaches: Structured CodeAgent (blue), CodeAgent (orange), and ToolCallingAgent (gray) on SmolBench (GAIA, MATH, SimpleQA, and Frames).
  • AI agents need to take actions in the world - whether that's calling APIs, processing data, or reasoning through complex problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that today we're sharing research that bridges two powerful paradigms in AI agent design: the expressiveness of code-based actions and the reliability of structured generation. Our findings show that forcing CodeAgents to generate both thoughts and code in a structured JSON format can significantly outperform traditional approaches across multiple benchmarks.

In a recent development, figure 1: Accuracy comparison of three approaches: Structured CodeAgent (blue), CodeAgent (orange), and ToolCallingAgent (gray) on SmolBench (GAIA, MATH, SimpleQA, and Frames). Error bars represent 95% Confidence Intervals.

AI agents need to take actions in the world - whether that's calling APIs, processing data, or reasoning through complex problems. How agents express these actions has evolved through several paradigms:.

Traditional JSON Agent: Agents generate structured JSON to call tools.

Sources indicate that these agents operate by selecting from a list of predefined tools and generating JSON-formatted calls. This method for calling tools has been popularized by OpenAI's function calling API, and has since then been the most widely used method to call tools.

It is reliable, but limited by:.

Code Agents: Agents make use of their innate coding ability and write executable Python code directly.

This shift, first presented as CodeAct in the paper “Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents” gave AI agents the flexibility to write arbitrary executable Python code in addition to tool-calling.

The key insight here is that tools are called directly from within the code, making variables and state management much more reliable. Agents can call tools within loops, functions, and conditional statements - essentially generating a dynamic graph of tool execution in each action!

However, parsing code from markdown can be error-prone which leads us to a proposition: why not use structured generation to generate code actions?

With Structured outputs, you can force the LLM to generate explicit thoughts and code as a JSON blob:.

The key difference is that the generation is enforced: basically, now instead of just being prompted to output thoughts, then code, the usage of structured outputs forces it to respect the structure.

This approach adds the reliability of structured generation to the flexibility of code execution, thus getting the best of both worlds.

We compared these three paradigms across multiple benchmarks including GAIA, MATH, SimpleQA, and Frames. The results show a clear pattern: Code actions + structured generation consistently improves performance for capable models.

Across most capable models, the structured approach consistently outperformed the regular CodeAgent approach by 2-7 percentage points on average.

Our implementation of CodeAgent in smolagents extracts Python code from the LLM output, which can fail when:.

Structured generation eliminates these issues with reliable JSON parsing.

Sources indicate that to understand why structured generation matters, we analyzed 15,724 agent traces across our benchmarks. The results are striking:.

Agent traces without parsing errors succeed 21.3% more often than those with parsing errors.

According to recent reports, this isn't just about convenience - parsing errors create a cascade of failures that significantly impact overall agent performance. When an agent can't execute its first action due to malformed code, it often struggles to recover, leading to suboptimal problem-solving paths.

Figure 2: Parsing errors in the first step reduce success rates of the agent by 21.3% and increase average steps taken from 3.18 to 4.63.

Additionally: Enforced Reasoning Process.

The use of structured generation and explicit thoughts not just prompts, but forces agents to articulate their reasoning before acting. This leads to:.

It has been revealed that our results also reveal a clear capability threshold: models need sufficient instruction-following ability and JSON coverage in their pre-training data to benefit from structured generation. This suggests that structured approaches work best with:.

Here's what happens when a smaller model (e.g mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3) tries to generate structured code - the cognitive load becomes too much:.

The model generates syntactically broken Python code: web_search(query="Eiffel Tower height")", - notice the malformed string with an extra quote and comma. This leads to an immediate SyntaxError and execution failure.

In a recent development, this illustrates the "structure tax": smaller models struggle to simultaneously handle JSON formatting, Python syntax, and the actual problem-solving logic. The cognitive overhead of structured generation can overwhelm models that would otherwise perform reasonably well with simpler markdown-based code generation.

✅ Use Structured CodeAgents when:.

According to recent reports, it’s super simple! Just enable it with use_structured_outputs_internally:.

The LLM will generate something like this:.

Then the "code" part gets executed by the agent as usual : this is the standard CodeAgent, but now it has 100% parsing reliability!

This research suggests we're moving toward a more nuanced understanding of agent architectures. It's not just about "what can the agent do?" but "how should the agent think about what it's doing?".

Maybe making the reasoning process more explicit helps the model stay on track. Or maybe it's just easier to parse. Either way, it’s a win.

But this is just the beginning. There are so many questions left to explore:.

In a recent development, for now, if you're using smolagents (or building your own CodeAgent system), consider giving structured output a try. Your parsing errors will thank you, and you might just see a nice increase in performance!

Did you try YAML block scalars or Python triple-quoted strings? These require less escaping, so they might mitigate the "structure tax".

The Simulation Gap: Why Physical AI Still Needs Real-World Data

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1232 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that simulation, digital twins, and synthetic data can reduce the time, cost, and risk involved in training robots.
  • For testing ideas, probing edge cases, and building training simulations, it is indispensable.
  • Industry observers note that A model can do well on the data it was trained on and still fail when something changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that simulation, digital twins, and synthetic data can reduce the time, cost, and risk involved in training robots. That has encouraged work on robotics foundation models intended to operate across tasks and industries. A lot of people in our field now assume that with enough simulation, we won’t need much real-world data at all. I’m less convinced, especially as Physical AI moves from controlled research environments into live operations. Analysts now treat Physical AI as its own branch of AI: systems that sense, reason, and act in the physical world instead of producing text or images.

For testing ideas, probing edge cases, and building training simulations, it is indispensable. My concern is with systems built mostly in simulation. They tend to break when they meet a real site. I’d rather treat simulation as a multiplier. Start from a real recording of a robot in an aisle, then use simulation to vary the lighting, clutter, and people around it. One real run becomes many plausible ones; each still tied to something that happened.

Industry observers note that A model can do well on the data it was trained on and still fail when something changes. That’s overfitting, and for a robot trained in simulation, the training data is the simulator. Researchers who study the reality gap see it as one of the main barriers to moving robots from simulation into the real world. The gap is difficult to measure, but teams relying heavily on simulation need to track how performance changes under production conditions.

In warehouses, you usually see it as a gap between the demo and the deployment. A robot runs well in one building and struggles in the next. One relies on a large seasonal workforce, the other on a stable crew; one stores small, fast-moving SKUs, the other bulky items.

In a simulator, engineers decide what exists. Objects can be labeled, events logged, and individual variables changed without disturbing the rest of the environment. That level of control makes simulation valuable for testing, but live warehouses are far less observable and far harder to isolate.

Industry observers note that robots share the floor with people, equipment, inventory and business processes, and the site itself keeps changing. Worse, a lot of problems only show up at scale, after you’ve already deployed thousands of robots and made the investment. A navigation model behaves until the season turns and, at one particular hour, sunlight lands on a sensor. Someone parks equipment in an aisle that’s always clear; now it’s a bottleneck. You rarely find any of this in benchmark datasets, but it often decides whether a deployment works.

AI is good at picking up patterns like these, such as when and where congestion builds. None of that shows up unless you’re collecting from live operations. Simulation can also teach a model the wrong lessons, and in manipulation it’s even more obvious. Vision models are very good at cheating, and they’ll happily latch onto a texture or render artifact that exists only in the simulator.

In a recent development, “World models,” which learn how a physical environment behaves and responds to a robot’s actions, are one attempt to address this problem. Nature recently took a close look at this work, and researchers see it as a possible bridge between perception, prediction and action. They don’t escape the problem, though. A world model is only as grounded as the real observations behind it. Today’s best world-model platforms still can’t capture every meaningful interaction in a complex physical environment — and a busy warehouse is full of them.

Synthetic data is most useful when it extends real-world datasets rather than standing in for them. It can add hazardous or low-frequency scenarios, such as a blocked main aisle or a forklift crossing a robot’s path. Many of the biggest Physical AI programs now lean on synthetic data to grow their training sets, move faster and show models rare conditions.

The limits come from how it’s made. Behind every synthetic dataset is an engineer deciding what to model, what to leave out, and which scenarios seem likely. Even sensible choices leave gaps because the resulting data can only represent the conditions included in its design.

Many teams now build on the same open models and published architectures, so the algorithm alone rarely separates one firm from another. What differs is the operational data available to train, test, and improve those models. A navigation trace becomes far more useful when you can connect it to what the robot was doing and whether the work is finished on time. Warehouse observations get interesting when they’re linked to inventory, throughput, labor, and performance.

Industry observers note that that’s why scale matters. A fleet spread across many sites sees cold-storage aisles, peak-season surges and night shifts that a single pilot never will. A congestion model tuned to one site’s shift change, for example, tells you little about a site that runs around the clock.

Google’s RT-2 demonstrated that mixing web-scale knowledge with robot data can help a robot handle situations it wasn’t trained on. But many real robotics problems are still specific to one domain. A robot can pick up a box perfectly, and the building can still miss its shipping cutoff.

It has been revealed that does a warehouse robot need to understand the physical world? Not all of it. It needs to know warehouses: inventory flow, labor workflows, congestion, equipment, and the site’s constraints.

Domain expertise determines what the system should optimize and which signals are relevant. In a warehouse, that means evaluating the model against operational measures such as throughput and shipping performance, rather than judging it only by a perception or manipulation benchmark. That knowledge matters more as models get more capable.

Industry observers note that as I recently discussed in an examination of Physical AI and robotics, I expect most of the industry’s near-term value to come from specialized systems in well-defined domains rather than from general-purpose intelligence. A warehouse operator judges a robot by whether orders ship on time and how many labor hours it saves, so those are the numbers a warehouse AI system should be built and judged on.

The decisive test is operational: place the system in a live warehouse and measure whether it performs across sites, shifts, workflows, and changing conditions. When it falls short, real-world data highlights where the model’s assumptions stopped matching the environment.

Dr. Oscar Mendez is Director of AI & Data Science at Locus Robotics, where he leads AI strategy, research, and deployment across a global fleet of more than 22,000 autonomous robots. An award-winning, internationally recognized researcher in Physical AI, robotics, machine learning, and computer vision, he focuses on bringing AI out of the digital world and into operational reality, developing intelligent systems that perceive, reason, and act to deliver greater productivity, adaptability, and operational confidence in large-scale warehouse environments.

The Biggest Risk in Agentic AI Is Not the Agent But the Business It Doesn’t Understand.

Dutch data protection authority advises against purchasing AI camera glasses

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), the Dutch data protection authority, advises consumers against purchasing AI camera glasses for general use.
  • It has been revealed that the AP had previously warned that filming bystanders is almost always prohibited.
  • Recent findings suggest that monique Verdier, Deputy Chair of the AP: “Glasses that film you without your knowledge are already a cause for concern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), the Dutch data protection authority, advises consumers against purchasing AI camera glasses for general use. A study on six AI camera glasses, conducted by the AP itself, demonstrates that these 'smart' glasses compromise not only the privacy of bystanders, but also the safety of people and those around them. For example, during a simulated resuscitation, one pair of glasses incorrectly indicated that an ambulance was on its way. Moreover, the glasses did not take sufficient account of the safety of minors, and the AP identified security complications in the software.

It has been revealed that the AP had previously warned that filming bystanders is almost always prohibited. The fresh study by the AP shows that the risks extend beyond just privacy.

Recent findings suggest that monique Verdier, Deputy Chair of the AP: “Glasses that film you without your knowledge are already a cause for concern. Glasses that also give you the wrong advice when someone’s life is at stake go a step too far. AI offers many opportunities, provided that we are able to trust that technology. In the case of the camera glasses that we examined, that trust cannot be justified at present.”.

Industry observers note that the AP investigated six AI camera glasses available on the Dutch market. Two of these were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations in which people’s safety was a key consideration.

The results are alarming. During a simulated emergency in which advice on CPR was sought, one of the glasses claimed on several occasions that an ambulance was already on its way, even though no emergency services had been called. In a real emergency, such an error could result in essential help arriving too late, with potentially life-threatening consequences.

In a recent development, the AI camera glasses also made errors related to the protection of minors, with potentially very serious consequences. For example, one pair of glasses gave dating advice to an adult who was interested in a minor. In another test, safety warnings on toys for young children were not followed. The glasses also made mistakes when reading medicine leaflets and interpreting warnings about extreme weather.

The tests show that AI camera glasses can sound convincing, even if the information provided is incorrect or even dangerous. As a result, owners may wrongly rely on advice that is not safe.

It has been revealed that in addition to these safety risks, the AP identified serious shortcomings in the protection of personal data. The recording lights on nearly all the camera glasses examined were barely visible and easy to cover up. Most glasses continued to film after the lights were covered, even though the manufacturer claimed this should not be possible. As a result, bystanders can hardly see whether they are being filmed.

Industry observers note that often, it is also unclear what happens to the footage and audio recordings. The AI functions examined process data through external servers, often located outside the European Union. Users are not provided with sufficient information about the AI models that process their data and the companies they share these data with. Furthermore, the AP discovered serious security concerns with several pairs of glasses. As a result, someone nearby could connect to the glasses without permission, view recordings or even control the camera.

The AP at the moment considers AI camera glasses to be unsafe because of the risks they pose to consumers and bystanders. The AP therefore advises consumers against buying AI camera glasses at this stage.However, the AP also recognises several legitimate uses for the technology. AI camera glasses can be valuable for people who are visually impaired or have low literacy levels, or who otherwise need support to understand their surroundings. But it is precisely for these users that it is crucial for the technology to be reliable.

The AP calls on developers of AI camera glasses to take more account of security, privacy and relevant legislation in the design and documentation of their products.

Sources indicate that the AP calls on Dutch and European policymakers to include these newly introduced research findings in the further development of policies on AI camera glasses. “It is vital that we, as a society, learn to deal with these kinds of high-risk AI products. Simply banning everything provides some breathing space for now, but we cannot keep this up indefinitely. It is essential that we work collectively to raise awareness, build resilience and foster ethical consciousness,” says Monique Verdier.

The AP recommends that owners and managers of locations prohibit the wearing and use of camera glasses in their house rules (in Dutch).

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Win4Wine runs the genuine Explorer shell atop Linux.
  • It has been revealed that win4Wine is one of the more remarkable and creative hacks we've read about in recent years.
  • As its GitHub repository explains: "The taskbar, Start menu, desktop and folder windows are XP's real ones, and Linux applications get XP's frames and taskbar buttons.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Win4Wine runs the genuine Explorer shell atop Linux.

It has been revealed that win4Wine is one of the more remarkable and creative hacks we've read about in recent years. It runs Windows XP's genuine Explorer shell through patched Wine on Debian 13, with a custom window manager integrating Linux applications into the desktop.

As its GitHub repository explains: "The taskbar, Start menu, desktop and folder windows are XP's real ones, and Linux applications get XP's frames and taskbar buttons.".

This impressive, possibly demented project has English installation instructions and a README, although its design documents are in Japanese. We found Mozilla's built-in translation handled those pretty well.

Its developer goes by miKuta0407 on GitHub, their homepage, and X.

Also note, you're going to need some Windows installation media for the full experience. The README says: "No Microsoft files are included. Only the files that are needed are extracted locally from your own ISO.".

In a recent development, it supports Windows XP Professional SP3 installation images in 32-bit Japanese or English editions, with an experimental option for Windows 7 SP1 x64. Without either Windows image, it can download and use ReactOS's free software shell instead, for what it terms "a Windows 2000-like classic look." In our view, that sounds much better anyway.

Recent findings suggest that before any former Windows users cry hurray and reach for an optical drive, this is not some ready-to-run project. The top of the README warns: "This is a personal, experimental project, not a finished product for daily use." The developer has tested it only on a fresh Debian 13 installation and recommends a VM or spare machine, rather than an existing working desktop, which sounds like an excellent precaution to us.

Also, before you ask, yes, it was vibe-coded with Claude.

According to recent reports, we found ourselves reminded of another crazy-but-is-it project that we wrote about back in January: What if Linux ran Windows... and meant it? Meet Loss32. The Loss32 proposal was even more extreme. It suggested replacing essentially the entire Linux userland, so it would be a Linux kernel running Wine with a Windows desktop and Windows apps.

Industry observers note that however, Mikuta-san was way ahead of us – lower down, the README mentions and even links to Loss32. Saying that, since it debuted at the end of 2025, the bottom of the Loss32 web page demonstrates a couple of updates, reporting on delays in getting it working. That, to be honest, did not shock us, but we still admire the let's-do-this spirit. The developer also seems to have got slightly distracted by a previous project, touchHLE: high-level emulator for early iOS apps.

Loss32, in turn, reminded us of Neptune OS, an attempt to give seL4 a Windows personality transplant. We wrote about that back in 2022, and work on it has continued: the project page shows updates in recent months. No GPU left behind: Unlocking Efficiency with Co-located vLLM in TRL

📅 03 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2736 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TRL supports training LLMs using GRPO, an online learning algorithm recently introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper.
  • Recent findings suggest that this makes generation a critical step in the training loop — and also a major bottleneck.
  • Recent findings suggest that before TRL v0.18.0, vLLM was only supported in server mode, running as a separate process on different GPUs from the training job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TRL supports training LLMs using GRPO, an online learning algorithm recently introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper. In GRPO, the model learns from its own outputs: it generates responses during training, receives feedback, and uses that feedback to improve itself over time.

Recent findings suggest that this makes generation a critical step in the training loop — and also a major bottleneck. To speed up generation, TRL integrates with vLLM. This combination lets you train powerful models more efficiently in GRPO setup. However, there’s a catch.

Recent findings suggest that before TRL v0.18.0, vLLM was only supported in server mode, running as a separate process on different GPUs from the training job. It communicated with the training script over HTTP, which made the setup modular and easy to use — but also introduced GPU inefficiencies.

This “ping-pong” between training and generation causes:.

Sources indicate that in online learning methods like GRPO — where generation happens constantly — this inefficiency becomes even more painful. You spend more on hardware, but don't get the performance you'd expect.

So, the key question becomes: Can we share the same GPUs for both training and generation, instead of separating them?

The main issue was that training and inference ran on separate GPUs, leading to idle time and underutilization. The natural solution? Run both on the same GPUs. Instead of having vLLM operate as a standalone server in its own process and devices, what if vLLM could run alongside the training code, within the same distributed process group? This would let us launch a single distributed job where training and inference share the same devices, switching between tasks efficiently without wasting resources.

Sources indicate that this approach is what we refer to as colocation. Training and inference are co-located on the same GPUs and coordinated via the same process group, allowing them to take turns smoothly — no extra hardware needed.

Previously, this wasn’t possible in TRL, which relied on vLLM as an external HTTP server. That changed with our PR #3394, which added support for vLLM’s external launcher and true integration into the training process.

It has been revealed that unified Execution: By embedding vLLM in the same process group, both training and inference tasks can share the same GPUs, taking turns instead of waiting on each other. This reduces idle time and boosts overall efficiency.

Skip HTTP Communication: No need for REST API calls or networking — vLLM runs inline with the training loop, avoiding overhead and latency.

Torchrun Compatibility: Works seamlessly with torchrun, so it's easy to scale across nodes with minimal config changes.

TP and DP Support: Compatible with Tensor Parallelism and Data Parallelism, making it suitable for large-scale training runs.

SPMD Execution Pattern: Uses a Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) model, where each GPU runs its own instance of the engine in sync. Ideal for distributed multi-GPU, multi-node setups.

Simplified Deployment: You no longer need to maintain a separate server script — vLLM is introduced and controlled directly inside your training job.

Enhanced Throughput: By avoiding idle GPUs and eliminating inter-process communication, the system delivers faster training and generation, especially crucial in online learning setups like GRPO.

Robust Inter-process Communication: This is more robust because it avoids the complexity of setting up distributed process groups between independent processes, as required in server mode.

Thanks to this feature, co-located training and inference is no longer a hack — it’s now first-class, scalable, and production-ready.

Sources indicate that the shift from server TRL to co-located TRL is all about smarter GPU usage. The diagram below indicates the difference:.

Industry observers note that in the server TRL setup, training and inference run on separate GPUs. For example:.

Recent findings suggest that during training steps, GPU 3 sits idle. During generation steps (inference), GPUs 0–2 are idle while GPU 3 generates outputs.

In a recent development, in contrast, the co-located TRL setup runs both training and vLLM on the same GPUs. Each GPU:.

Training and inference take turns using the GPU’s resources — no need for dedicated devices or separate processes.

Instead of launching vLLM as a server, the trainer now launches vLLM in-process using the external launcher, as shown below:.

Co-located vLLM respects the torch.distributed process group and rank structure. This allows vLLM to be initialized alongside training without conflict and makes TP/DP setups work seamlessly:.

Co-located vLLM no longer relies on REST APIs — it runs directly in memory and communicates via native Python calls:.

To use this setup, simply set vllm_mode="colocate" in your GRPO configuration:.

Note: Depending on the model size and the overall GPU memory requirements for training, you may need to adjust the vllm_gpu_memory_utilization parameter in GRPOConfig to avoid underutilization or out-of-memory errors.

To measure the impact of colocation, we ran a series of experiments comparing the traditional server mode (where vLLM runs on a separate GPU as a standalone server) with the new co-locate mode (where training and inference share the same GPUs).

In server mode, only 7 GPUs are used for training because 1 GPU is fully dedicated to the vLLM inference server.

In co-locate mode, all 8 GPUs are used for training — increasing the effective batch size by default.

To ensure a fair comparison, we normalized throughput in server mode by a factor of 8/7. This adjustment accounts for the greater training capacity in co-locate mode and allows us to compare the two setups under equal training conditions.

In a recent development, when training large models like Qwen2.5-Math-72B, it's important to use the right strategies to make training efficient, scalable, and stable across many GPUs and nodes. In our setup, we combined co-located vLLM with several key optimizations to make this work efficiently.

When using co-located training, managing GPU memory is crucial so that both training and inference can run smoothly on the same devices. To support this, we added vLLM’s sleep() API into the GRPO training loop.

Industry observers note that the sleep() function temporarily pauses the vLLM engine and frees up GPU memory. It supports two levels:.

Level 1: Unloads model weights from GPU (keeps them in CPU memory) and clears the KV cache. Useful when the same model will be reused soon.

According to recent reports, level 2: Unloads both model weights and KV cache entirely. Best for scenarios where the model will change or won’t be reused right away.

In GRPO, the model is updated after every step — so we use Level 2 sleep.

This small addition makes a significant difference in enabling smooth and scalable co-located training.

To train large models like Qwen2.5-72B, we rely on DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3, the same setup used in plain TRL.

ZeRO helps scale large models by distributing memory across GPUs. Stage 3 goes further by partitioning:.

This is essential for models that can’t fit on a single GPU. With ZeRO Stage 3, each GPU handles only a portion of the model.

"offload_optimizer": {"device": "cpu"} Moves optimizer states to CPU to free GPU memory — critical in co-located setups.

"overlap_comm": true Enables communication overlap with computation, speeding up training.

"contiguous_gradients": true Allocates gradients in a single memory block, improving memory access and reducing fragmentation.

These optimizations help train 72B models efficiently, and ensure colocation remains stable under tight memory constraints.

Sources indicate that as recommended in TRL, we use Accelerate, a lightweight library that simplifies distributed training. It handles:.

This makes the setup clean, scalable, and easy to maintain.

Even with 4 fewer GPUs, the co-locate setup is ~1.26× faster than plain TRL. This highlights the effectiveness of smarter GPU sharing and memory cleanup using sleep().

Training reward plots for co-locate and plain setups are nearly identical, demonstrating that:.

We evaluated three models: Base model, Co-locate-trained model, Plain-trained model on the Math500 benchmark. Both trained models outperform the base, and the co-locate model performs on par with the plain-trained model — confirming that colocation does not compromise downstream performance.

Through our work on scaling GRPO training with co-located vLLM, we've faced several critical challenges and learned vital lessons about efficiency, flexibility, and system design when training large models.

Tensor Parallelism Bug in vLLM ≥ 0.8.0. Tensor Parallelism (TP) with external_launcher stopped working in vLLM version 0.8.0 and above. This was tracked under Problem #15895. To identify the breaking point, we followed the approach described in this vLLM developer blog post, which provides wheels for every commit. After bisecting, we identified the breaking commit as cc10281. The root cause was determinism — the newer versions required explicitly setting the random seed. Once the seed was set, the issue went away.

Recent findings suggest that level 2 Sleep Buffer Bug. Initially, level 2 sleep didn’t work correctly when we tried to reload weights using load_weights. This glitch was tracked in Issue #16564. The problem was that model buffers (like running mean/var in BatchNorm) weren’t restored after waking up from sleep. The fix came with PR #16889, which added logic to explicitly restore buffers when waking up from level 2 sleep. We now keep a copy of the original buffers and manually reapply them after loading new weights.

Segmentation Fault on Exit. There’s still an open glitch with vLLM sleep causing a segmentation fault at the end of training when closing processes. This was reported in Issue #16993. This crash happens during shutdown but does not break training itself, so we were able to complete all demos and experiments shared in this blog. However, we’re waiting for an official fix before integrating sleep() fully into TRL upstream.

These challenges were not blockers, but they required careful debugging, version control, and a deeper understanding of how vLLM manages memory and parallelism under the hood.

Sources indicate that co-located inference dramatically improves GPU utilization. By allowing training and generation to share the same GPUs, we eliminate idle time and reduce hardware requirements — achieving higher throughput even with fewer GPUs.

vLLM's sleep() feature is essential for large-scale colocation. It enables fine-grained control over memory usage, allowing training to fully reclaim GPU memory between generation steps — a key enabler for models like Qwen2.5-72B.

Sources indicate that deepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3 is essential for training large models. It allows extremely large networks to fit into memory by distributing model weights, gradients, and optimizer states across multiple GPUs. In our experience, enabling contiguous_gradients helped reduce memory fragmentation, while offloading the optimizer to the CPU freed up critical GPU memory — both of which were especially helpful in colocated setups.

It has been revealed that colocation is powerful but comes with trade-offs. It works best when GPU memory is carefully managed, often requiring manual tuning of memory usage parameters like vllm_gpu_memory_utilization. While it offers clear throughput benefits and reduces idle GPU time, colocation may not be ideal for models with tight memory budgets or when memory fragmentation is not well controlled. When done right, though, it unlocks significant efficiency gains.

According to recent reports, TP/DP compatibility, Accelerate, and torchrun support make deployment seamless. Despite the complexity of the underlying architecture, the entire system can be released and scaled with standard distributed tools.

Co-located training maintains model quality. Across multiple benchmarks (Math500, AIME24), co-located and plain setups produced comparable results, validating that performance isn’t sacrificed for efficiency.

This blog post explored how co-locating vLLM with GRPO training unlocks significant efficiency gains when training large language models — including models as large as Qwen2.5-72B.

It has been revealed that traditionally, TRL only supported vLLM in server mode, which required separate processes and GPUs for inference, leading to wasted compute and idle time. With the introduction of vLLM’s external launcher and the colocation PR in TRL PR #3394, we can now run training and inference within the same distributed process group, on the same GPUs, with full support for TP, DP, and Accelerate.

While challenges remain — such as version-specific vLLM bugs and edge cases such as with sleep() — the overall results show that co-located GRPO is a practical, scalable solution for training large models efficiently. We’re excited to continue refining this setup, integrating features like FSDP, and pushing the limits of large model training — making it faster, cheaper, and more accessible for everyone building the next generation of LLMs.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 25, 2026 3 min read.
  • The Rust team has released Rust 1.100.0, the language's first three-digit stable version, with a release that finally lands the never type after a decade of work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Rust 1.100 Ships the Never Type After Ten Years and Five Failed Attempts.

Nov 25, 2026 3 min read.

The Rust team has released Rust 1.100.0, the language's first three-digit stable version, with a release that finally lands the never type after a decade of work. Declared on 12 November 2026, the release also stabilises the core of the custom allocator API, introduces a DropGuard helper, and gives Cargo opt-in dependency cooldowns and warnings for unused dependencies.

Industry observers note that the headline is the stabilisation of !, the canonical uninhabited type for computations that never return a value, such as panic!(), return or an endless loop. Although functions have long used it as a return type, naming it elsewhere, for instance writing Result to describe an operation that cannot fail, took ten years and five failed stabilisation attempts to land. The release also makes std::convert::Infallible an alias for !, which is what the type was always intended to be, so existing APIs using Infallible now accept ! transparently.

In a recent development, to make that alias work, the team shipped a small breaking change for the 2015, 2018 and 2021 editions, flipping the never-type fallback from () to ! and matching behaviour already introduced in Rust 2024. The release notes describe the impact as largely unnoticeable but warn that more code may be flagged as unreachable. Developers hitting problems on upgrade are advised to upgrade dependencies first, since fixes for widely used crates have already been published.

The core of the long-awaited allocator_api is also now stable, letting library authors define custom allocators used with Vec and Box through the newly introduced Allocator trait. This forms the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. Critics on the internals forum have argued that Rust still lacks Zig's granular control over allocation because the current design cannot support inline storage, with moves invalidating internal pointers, but the stabilised core is seen as a workable starting point for broader collections support.

On the Hacker News release post, one user noted that some of the changes weren’t mentioned in the blog post for the release:.

This release is so big that multiple useful stabilized API aren't event mentioned in the blog post like:.

The latest global-min-publish-age setting holds back newly published versions by a configurable window, an opt-in defence against malicious crate releases:.

On Hacker News, developer woodruffw argued cooldowns need to coexist with immediate security patching:.

You should do both: you should let normal updates cool down,.

you should immediately patch security advisories.

It has been revealed that one of the biggest ergonomic problems with cooldowns is that many tools let the former goal obstruct the latter. Both should be part of the state machine of resolution itself, rather than things that get layered on.

ImportStatic found on the beta that cargo install ignores the setting entirely and that an patch could even downgrade a forced security fix, something the release notes also flag as a known caveat. The approach sits alongside GitHub's Dependabot cooldown protection but builds the age check into dependency resolution itself.

Other notable additions include core::mem::DropGuard for running a closure on every exit path, std::mem::conjure_zst for zero-sized types in unsafe code, plus smaller ergonomic wins such as bool::toggle, str::trim_prefix, str::trim_suffix and Box::map.

Upgrading uses rustup update stable; Rust 1.99 is no longer supported, and 1.101 follows the six-week cadence around 24 December 2026.

Rust is an open-source systems programming language maintained by the Rust Foundation and a global community, designed to empower developers to build reliable and efficient software through strong type safety, memory safety guarantees without a garbage collector, and a mature package ecosystem through Cargo.
