📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Learning Out Loud (Under Near-Existential Pressure).

Industry observers note that laura Savino discusses the psychological friction of AI adoption for senior engineers & architects. She explains how shifting from static expertise to learning in public lowers anxiety, accelerates tooling fluency, and prevents burnout. Leaders will discover actionable strategies to support their teams, debunk tech zealotry, and foster an adaptive engineering culture that thrives during upheaval.

Laura Savino a software engineer at Adobe Photoshop. She brings her background in education and humanities to technical topics, creating talks that spark ongoing conversations.

Software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community. A practitioner-driven conference, QCon is designed for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors, and project managers who influence innovation in their teams.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Laura Savino: Several friends and colleagues have come to me to tell me recently that they are pregnant with their first child, and have taken comfort from a really odd bit of perspective that I've given them, because I have two lovely kids, two very much wanted and uneventful pregnancies. I hated being pregnant. Every so often, I look around a crowd of people, and I'm like, everyone here is the result of a pregnancy, and it creeps me out. It's beautiful. It's a miracle of life. It is also not my jam. The thing that made me willing to do it at all and that gave me great comfort along the way was actually the myth of the frog. This frog is swimming around in water that starts at a comfortable temperature, but is slowly heated through to a boil, and if you do it gradually enough, the frog won't really notice that its environment is no longer like anything it's ever experienced before, and the frog is eventually cooked.

This odd myth gave me a lifeline of hope, because if that frog can adapt to extreme, unprecedented conditions, so can I. Because the difficult parts usually come on gradually, day by day. If having a child started with the eighth-month pregnancy discomfort, very few of us would do it. It would be banned as inhumane torture if we could instantly make people eight months pregnant.

Some of you are like, "It's 9:00 in the morning. We're at a software conference. Can we please not talk about spontaneous advanced gestation? It is a repulsive idea." When we see a person eight months pregnant who got there gradually, the way we all luckily do, we just think, how nice. It's not repulsive at all, it's beautiful. It's usually obvious that they're just handling it like champions. It turns out the frog thing is thoroughly debunked. At a certain point, ectotherms change locations to keep themselves safe. The myth works to reassure me and my pregnant friends because of the way I frame it. It's not that the thing gets worse and worse slowly, and you don't notice and eventually are cooked. It's that you yourself change. You adapt. Yes, your context becomes more and more difficult, but if you're committed to sticking it out, you flex some increasingly creative coping strategies and skills, you become able to handle it. You worry about eighth month after you've figured out the seventh month and the sixth month, you'll be fine.

According to recent reports, let's tangent from there. I have these two amazing kids, one is 8. We've had Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse on repeat in our house this past month. There's this one scene that captures me. A newly bitten Spider-Man is trying to learn to thwip, that's the technical term, and he's doing it while being chased by an evil giant robo-scientist through the trees, so Spider-Man is like dodging trees, and he yells, "Whoa, whoa, I can't do this yet." His trainer quips, "Everyone knows that the best way to learn is under intense, life-threatening pressure." Another anecdote. My friend TJ. TJ is an all-around delightful person, but their rarest trait and the highest compliment that I can reach for is that they are a functional programming language aficionado and are not an asshole about it. These days we're all a little or a lot more on board with the functional aspects of Rust and Kotlin and Swift, and strongly preferring pure functions is just mainstream now.

Side Effect punk is dead. Remember Haskell, the language? Remember when there was a whole functional programming dogma with true believers, with the hyper-conviction of the newly converted, and there were memes about monads. If your brain could follow certain logical compressions, you were with it. You were good. You were likely to survive, and everybody else was getting left in the imperative rubble. When I learned TJ appreciated Haskell, I was like, but you're so chill about it. They were like, it's a really interesting tool. This was the first time that I'd met a functional programming enthusiast that I could relate to.

It has been revealed that I am Laura Savino. I'm a developer on Photoshop, somewhat on the iOS UI, but also on the C++ library that supports real Photoshop PSD file editing on your phone. Before I became a software engineer, I thought I was going to be a language teacher. I was for a minute. I took master's-level courses in things like how to teach American English pronunciation, how to design a test that tests what you want it to evaluate, which is hard. I taught English in France and French in Seattle, and English again at that time in South Korea, and eventually learned to code. Fast-forward several years, and here I am on the QCon London stage. Today's talk, I hope, will start to shift your identity from someone who's good at doing a specific thing to someone who's good at learning near anything. I'm taking it as an anthology of vignettes with research for structural support. In rough order of appearance, so you have a sense of time passing. There will be cabinet-making, teen vampires, December-born horses, a Zen priest, football kits, awkward dance floors, and a puppy. I will provide a slide with references at the end, so you can settle in.

I started with three stories, one about a frog, one about Spider-Man, and one about these monad pushers, and this is not exactly an un-telegraphed reveal that these stories map shockingly neatly onto the onslaught of AI. The first one, the frog metaphor that comforted me so much in my pregnancy, part of what makes the AI transition so disorienting is that we're being asked, many of us, to take it on. Like, now, now, now, the water is plasma, and you frogs will get in there, and you will like it. If you're not already orchestrating, you're so far behind, you might as well take up goat herding, because the goats are more your speed. For Spider-Man, a significant reason the AI transition is so daunting is that many people's livelihoods are directly tied to how well we adapt. It's fine. The robot arm's chasing us, they're motivating. We all just ducked in here for a minute to throw them off our trails.

Lastly, about my chill friend, it's tough out there because of all the zealots. I think most of them are not actually assholes. I genuinely believe they're mostly just excited, and they cannot imagine a reasonable person in possession of all the facts who's not exactly as excited as they are. They respond by either assuming you're an unreasonable person or giving you more facts, and I'm not sure which is worse. The ultimate well-meaning zealot is the Chris Traeger character on Parks and Rec played by Rob Lowe. This character is intense, precise, and painfully optimistic. There's this one scene where he states he's logged 65,000 miles running in his lifetime, and his goal is to run to the moon. Some AI enthusiasts are giving a little Chris Traeger running to the moon. We recognize they're telling us about something healthy and good, and they may even have our best interests at heart, but no part of me wishes I had my running shoes on so I could join him to the moon. How do we bring people with us?

Sources indicate that I experienced a massive at-the-time transition in Cocoa, in the Apple development community that did this well. See, it was possible for a long time to go into Apple development with a great deal of hubris. You were an Apple developer. You knew all the tricks and tips. You'd hand-molded a lock and knit release cycles. Back of the cabinet here means, sure, no one's going to see this part of the code, but we're still going to make it just so because we take pride in our work. For a minute there, you could be confident that your deep UI kit and Objective-C knowledge meant that significant companies would pay you and a team of three or four devs and a crack designer, absolute truckloads of cash to write them an app because everyone needed apps and no one knew how to write them except us. It was a really good time to be an Apple developer.

Then Apple dropped Swift, brand latest language. You're welcome, everyone. Soon all our new APIs will be in this brand-new language that you have to use. We were willing to give up our semicolons. No one likes those, but they ripped away our square brackets too. This was one of those watershed community moments. One perspective I really liked at the time was, we're knocked back to being beginners again, and we like it. We're on even footing. We're learning together. Isn't this exciting? The change electrified us in good and bad ways. On the good side, I distinctly remember watching people who'd shipped indie software on CDs, people who were intimately familiar with why NSString is prefixed that way because they used to code in NEXTSTEP. These developers dived headfirst into the new language. I was sitting around with The Omni Group folks, like OmniFocus, OmniGraffle, these are Apple ecosystem legends, with our laptops out in the hotel lobbies of San Francisco, just trying to figure out, what can I do with this new language? On the less good side.

Swift was announced in June, and on my production app, we had an intern who waited several weeks till late July, before Xcode, our IDE was even out of beta, the intern added Swift to the project just for fun. The tool chain support was abysmal. I couldn't exactly embrace the beginner's mind when I was trying to ship a feature and couldn't even type because my IDE kept lagging out with this message. It was frustrating and not at all production ready because the tool chain was literally in beta. On the whole, with the benefit of rose-colored nostalgia, it was good. Most super senior principal developers, these pinnacles of technical excellence, were having to relearn how to get the eighth element out of a string, like just rookie stuff. The behaviors that got rewarded were the ones where people learned in public. The people who learned the most were the ones who asked the most questions, who'd notice when they didn't understand something and say, this is something I don't understand.

Sources indicate that how interesting? They'd post forum questions and ask each other how things worked. They would post early code samples where they did not look like geniuses who knew all the answers, but just enthusiastic rookies who wanted to learn. You know how much people love correcting people on the internet, so anyone who posted something inaccurate got told about it real quick. How do you be ok with that, though? How do you psychologically handle going from the expert hot commodity to a total noob and keep up decent spirits while you do it?

My friends, has anyone considered the old standby straight-up denial? I don't think any of us are in first-order denial about AI where we refuse to accept that it exists or is changing things, but for myself, I am absolutely deep in second-order denial where you acknowledge the basic facts of the thing, but you deny the implications of those facts. Sure, the technology is here, but I am not ready to face its implications. I usually try to add a lot of details when I'm giving a talk, but here, I am going to kindly draw a veil and let the camera discreetly pan away because you do not need me to share my particular doomsday flavors. Besides, it weakens the denial. Denial can also stem from a fear that you or those you love lack the skills or resources to handle the consequences of a change. That's real.

Apparently, denial can have protective effects, though. This one study, "The role of denial in recovery from coronary heart disease," found that people who were in deep denial actually had better short-term outcomes than the ones who were actually facing reality. If you had deeper denial, you'd spend less time in intensive care and have fewer heart-related symptoms while you were in hospital. This rings true for me. Even if I've decided a thing is key to me, even when it's well-aligned with my values, if I face the full implications of how hard it's going to be, I will probably not do it. I might say, I don't have to exercise at the gym. I'm just going to put my shoes on and show up and we'll just see what happens. Denial can work to get us to start down a hard road and give us hope long enough to adapt to this ever-changing water.

Protective denial, it's incredibly common. We're also all going to die someday, but memento mori has somehow fallen out of fashion. If you want to sit in second-order denial with me for a little longer, that's ok. For a little longer, because the heart patients with serious denial had worse outcomes long-term. They didn't follow their medical advice, because why would they? They were fine. They got re-hospitalized more. Denial is not sustainable. If a little self-misdirection is what it takes to follow your values to stay in the room and not make a down payment on a yacht, go ahead, indulge. Let me suggest another indulgence, brain candy. When I was trying to improve my Spanish, I read the Twilight books, and I'm guessing most of you haven't read them or won't admit to having read them, because they're cloying vampire, werewolf, romance novels written for pre-teens. My Spanish became tan brillante como el pelo de Eduardo a la luz del sol, because brain candy, in the domain you're trying to learn, is just like the little carrot thrown down the path to convince the recalcitrant, what, I'm supposed to be good at this part of you, to at least look over and start to think about how to maybe head down this otherwise daunting path.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes you truly need to lower the stakes mentally just so you can push through. Get out of that intense, life-threatening pressure. Solve an actual problem that only you have. Make some tool, make some toy, make a flatulence app with your 8-year-old, something real, but where no one will evaluate you on the outcome because evaluation changes us. We don't learn so we can achieve the task we care about, we learn to pass the test assigned to us. This is bad even if you're an excellent test taker.

I took a break from my French major one summer to spend eight weeks in an intensive Japanese language study in northern Japan, where they promised to teach us the equivalent of two university semesters of Japanese. I was very good at French at that point. I had just breezed through a pair of graduate seminars and my placement test in the Japanese program put me in the very lowest level class. I'd only taken two basic Japanese classes by this point, but I just still felt like, "Hello, don't you know who I am? I'm good at languages. Why am I in the beginner's class with these people who can barely put a sentence together?" Granted, I couldn't say, do you know who I am, in Japanese, which is maybe a sign that their class placement was somewhat valid, but I had a demonstrated skill in a fundamentally different but still related area.

In a recent development, some of us are feeling this way about computing right now. I'm good at computers. I am a senior professional programmer. I once learned Python in an afternoon. If this new computing skill is hard for me, either is something is wrong with the system or something is wrong with me. Don't you know who I am? For me in Japan, my identity was so caught up in being good at languages that I worked hard to avoid ever making a mistake, not just on coursework, but asking the bus driver for a transfer ticket. I wanted my Japanese to be perfect. I actually learned the most about learning that summer on a weekend excursion, just me and a classmate, where we stayed at a family-run Buddhist temple out in the countryside. I won't go into the expectation thrashing experience of preparing myself for a solemn weekend of meditation and instead watching sumo wrestling on TV with a priest and his family, but the larger foundation-shattering surprise was the way my classmate spoke to our Japanese hosts and that she would just say things.

She'd trip over words. She'd mess up her verb endings. My grammar wasn't great, but I could recognize a bunch of mistakes even if I couldn't correct them. I was so deep in this prove to everyone that I'm good at this mentality that if I didn't know how to say something properly, I'd keep quiet so I didn't embarrass myself. Amy, though, just talked. They're like laughing, conversing. The priest gets another beer. What stuck with me long after I forgot all the extra kanji I learned that summer, is that interacting imperfectly builds fluency. You get early feedback before unwanted behaviors are calcified. Find your version of a Zen retreat where you can just play with the tools with no expectations of evaluation. You'll develop facility and fluency that much faster.

Another way to fail when something's not a test. Many years ago, as I was just learning to code, like mapping out how to do red-black trees on a whiteboard level, I went out with some friends and some friends of friends to rent a karaoke room. One of these friends of friends turned out to be an engineering manager at Microsoft, which is a hazard of where I live in Seattle. I remember the fear and dread and shame that I felt when I was unable to successfully navigate the karaoke interface via any of the in-room remote controls. See, I saw this as my chance to prove my technical prowess and maybe get hired on at Microsoft. Why would the engineering manager consider my resume if I couldn't even modify the output settings of a retro karaoke system? I don't remember what any of us saying, but I do remember holding that remote in my hand and thinking that I was never going to get a job in tech.

Now we're all looking back at 15 years ago me and inwardly shouting, everybody knows these systems are hard. Just try, don't give up, it's fine. We have so much compassion. What is your tool today that you're like, I still don't have this thing working. What are they all going to think of me? I better hide it and fake it and just play it cool. If you have that mental block, lower the stakes, make a tool, make a toy, something unspeakably inane that is tailored to exactly your interests. It can lower the activation energy required to take that next step towards learning.

Another way I make daunting things feel more approachable is thinking of them as a practice round. Picture this, every Sunday morning, I'm at a former aircraft hangar that's been turned into an indoor kids' sports hell hole arena. There are five football fields, a dozen simultaneous kid classes, there's adult workout classes, there's birthday rooms, plus an enormous bouncy house situation. I promise you whatever you're picturing, there are more bouncy houses. There's screaming and there's tears and there's kids running and begging for snacks, and I'm paying to be here. I went to great effort to dig the 4-year-old's soccer uniform out of his dirty laundry hamper and convince him to leave the house and convince him to leave the car. My reward for that is sitting on an uncomfortable bench drinking truly some of the worst coffee in Seattle. I want to paint for you this picture of aggressively, brightly colored despair, because what you need to appreciate is that it was a massive deal for me to change perspectives.

Recent findings suggest that because I realize that if you see this not as a whole collection of circumstances designed to maximize my suffering, but hundreds of families who each separately fought through the chaos that is having a child on a chilly, damp weekend morning and got them to leave the house. If we could see in a little heads-up display what people overcame to get through that door, we would be walking around high-fiving and pouring each other pints. Nobody mentions all these hurdles. They just act like, yes, kids are wearing their kits here on time, relatively few boogers, as if they didn't execute a dozen fancy maneuvers to get there. If I don't tell someone that I struggled to get my kid there dressed, I won't hear their advice. Yes, my kid sleeps in her football kit. Sunday mornings have become my time to bask in the glory that not only have all of us made it through a gauntlet, but we've also successfully identified flaws in our own getting-out-of-the-house systems.

We're basically red teaming our own lives. How did you do at getting out of the house without yelling and tears? C-minus. How will you do at learning from what went wrong? Are you committed to bringing better snacks next time? The point isn't how well you executed the thing today, but how well you've internalized and applied the changes for next time. Put the snacks in the car right now, and today counts as a success.

Industry observers note that when I was deciding whether to take this job I had at Photoshop, I called up a friend for advice, because I had two offers for very different jobs, one that I was sure I would be good at, that they would be lucky to have me, and the other was a stretch. It was on Photoshop, where I'd have to brush up on modern C++ and L1 caches and deal with real legacy code. My friend mentioned that if I had the appetite to learn the new thing, the hard thing, that I should do it now. Because at some point, he said, you're like, I don't want to learn a whole new paradigm again. I've been there. I've done that. I'm good. This advice was perfect when I was choosing my destiny, and learning modern C++ was supposed to be my last significant career challenge. Now, very few of us have a choice about whether to invest a ton of energy in learning this new thing.

In a recent development, I have to somehow generate energy for learning or hit burnout real hard. I feel like maybe external energy building works for salespeople. Like I could just shout, are you ready? Let's get pumped. Everyone would be like, yes, let's go. We're engineers who got to where we are by taking skepticism to an art form. How many people have looked at some shiny newly introduced tech, mentioned, no, and then just watched it crumble off into the sunset? No amount of like, rah, rah, do it, is going to convince us in all of the do it, learn, go. It's like being told by a scowling Simon Cowell to do a heartfelt interpretive dance. You're not at your best. How do we, the hopeful skeptics who do believe in a better future, in spite of it all, how do we generate energy to learn? Let's actually start by not spiraling, perhaps, by not leaking happiness.

In a recent development, one way I patch the leak is comparing current me to past me, because I'm obviously better than I was 10 years ago, aren't you? Think of you 10 years ago, and the glimmers of what you most value now that we're just starting to show. We were all goobers then compared to us now. Yet, we are all deeply discounting how much wiser we will be in the next 10 years, because we've got it figured out now. This is an actual studied phenomenon with a whole name, the end of history illusion. More specifically, we see the present as the moment where we have finally become the person we'll be for the rest of our lives.

It has been revealed that more published sources. Just this year, Dr. Maya Shankar published a really timely book called "The Other Side of Change." I feel like she gets us as software people today, because she was well on the path to becoming a professional violinist when she had a career-ending injury, at which point she went into the field of psychology. She eventually became the behavioral sciences advisor to the UN. She did all right. I am clinging to her perspectives like a lifeline. She adds to this end of history idea, not about years, but any large change, when we imagine what it will be like to navigate an unexpected change and its aftermath, we tend to assume that we'll be the same person from beginning to end. Research shows that we greatly underestimate how much we'll change in the future, even though we fully acknowledge that we've changed considerably in the past.

Sources indicate that am I just going to keep reading you quotes? Yes, I am. Because these are literally professional studiers of brains, and they stated this better than I can. You can think of this as the audiobook interlude. "The unique stresses and demands of being thrust into a newly introduced reality can uncover unexpected insights about ourselves and the world around us. These insights, coupled with the experience of the change itself, can transform us in extraordinary ways." I hear that, and I externally nod. Like, yes, maybe I'll grow on the other side of whatever this unprecedented time is. Also, a small part of me throws an absolute foot-stomping fit. I do not want to. I've barely got it together with the current state of things, and now you're coming at me with, think of all the personal growth you'll get. Like, no, I'm sorry. How many people are actively fantasizing about goat-herding careers right now?

According to recent reports, there is some comfort in knowing that the person who will undergo the full experience will be different from the person we are in this very moment. We will become new people on the other side of change in ways we are capable of shaping. I still don't want to. I don't. I remind myself to take a breath, or six, because, see, the frog is facing physical challenges and doesn't have biohacking tools there in its pot. Our challenges are all in our minds, for better or worse. As my favorite book series says, my head is where 90-plus percent of my problems are. We believe in neuroplasticity. We can change and grow our minds from the inside out. I promise this is related, but did you know in the competitive equine sports world, all horses have the same official birthday? In the Northern Hemisphere, they all turn one year older on January 1st.

Industry observers note that that means that if your horse was born on Upcoming Year's Eve, for juvenile racing purposes, they'll be considered 2 years old when they turn 366 days. You can see how a 700-day-old 2-year-old race horse would have an advantage. Breeders often arrange for foals to be born as close to January 2nd as they can. Football in the States has the same effect, actually, where a statistically improbable number of professional footballers are born in the first quartile of the year. Few parents strategy their kids' births around the football season for some reason. There's something to be said for always being a little ahead of your peer group. You literally win more. If the kids on your football team look up to you because they're barely 6 while you're nearly 7, and coaches look to you to lead the team's comeback when they're behind 3-0, you develop leadership skills and confidence from a very early age.

I am on the other side. I came to technology late, so I got used to seeking coding advice from literal teenagers from day one of my first professional programming job. Since then, every team I'm on, I've been in the middle quartile in terms of raw technical Leet code acumen. Before anyone starts DMing me about imposter syndrome and telling me to believe in myself, I'm going to stop you, because I'm on the Photoshop engineering team, and I'm solidly in the middle of the pack. It's like being in the bottom third of Man City players, like, I'm one of the worst world-class athletes. Like, it's fine. I'm no slouch. I just keep moving up to better and better leagues. Because I started out behind and have stayed in the middle, I've never developed an ego around being the fastest prototyper or the most effective algorithm tuner. I have learned how to learn.

Industry observers note that there's this famous study on which learning tasks people will take if given the option to improve their skills. One task is advertised as majorly effective, the other as so-so. It turns out the researchers could easily influence which participants chose which task. See, in the ineffective task, people could try and fail privately, and the highly effective one involved practicing in front of the group so everyone saw your mistakes. Clearly different paths with different risks and outcomes, and you all might have a sense of which group you would tend towards. How would a researcher influence you to pick one over the other? They gave people reading material about the malleability of the particular skill, debating in this case. One group read that debate is mostly an innate skill, the other that anyone can do it. It just takes training. It takes practice. The people who were in the inborn skill group, they did not participate in the activity that would help them improve, because then everybody would see that they lacked the skill.

According to recent reports, the trainable skill group people were like, ok, let's go. Who cares if other people see that I can't do this yet? Showing people you're ignorant of something today can and should be super low stakes. It goes along with believing in neuroplasticity. This study is out of Carol Dweck's research about growth mindset, which had a whole Silicon Valley trend moment. I think it's not as trendy now, but the research is still solid. People who believe that their traits and abilities can significantly change are more likely to engage in behaviors that improve them. One problem that I ran into face first, like a very clean plate glass door one, is that when you start paying attention to whether you have a growth mindset and realize that without the researcher's priming that you would definitely be in the group that's like, better make sure no one finds out I'm a terrible debater.

It has been revealed that it throws you extra, because you, by definition, don't really believe that you can change how fixed your mindset is. These research scientists, I have to believe them because they approach this problem with rigor and with science at Stanford. They say quite plainly that cherished traits can be developed. I want to be better at believing in change and in neuroplasticity, so I'm working on it.

It has been revealed that part of my identity has become someone who learns out loud, and I've modeled learning out loud in public. The first time a principal engineer on the Photoshop team wanted to show me how to use a fresh AI tool to bolt a tricky feature onto our existing architecture, I recorded our screen share session and posted it for the rest of the team because seeing a tool used in a real-world context is always more instructive than the demo-worthy vacuum. Especially because, like all my comrades who brought their kids to weekend morning soccer practices, we each come to AI and use AI in completely different ways. My favorite take on this is from Dr. Cat Hicks. She is a research psychologist studying software teams and gets riled up in a very data-driven way when people talk about things like measuring team effectiveness. She emphasizes that none of us are having the same experience.

"When you have a highly adaptive, dialogical tool," which means the user is in dialogue with the tool, "where the user is shaping the context and wielding progressive disclosure to probe very different parts of its capabilities, different people will continue to get very different answers. Until we get real about the personalized, adaptive nature of this." People are each running their own individual experiments with new tools, and if we don't tell each other what our own tool uses look like, no one will know that you can put your kid to bed already wearing their football kit. This is not the time to experiment alone until your output seems to resemble other people's. Plus, even if I just complain about a tool, I usually get some really good alternative suggestions. Even though we've all transcended onto this higher plane of mental abstractions, there is still value in showing your actual footwork. Where did your tool fall over? Why did you keep using it anyway?

I actually literally do this in a surprising social context. Otherwise, awkward dance floors. Specifically at weddings or oddly corporate events that have decided to have a dance floor. Basically, collections of people of very mixed abilities who don't know each other super well and yet are celebrating something important together. I pride myself on understanding the assignment to look like I am enjoying myself in a way that invites other people in. I am very specifically not dancing like no one's watching. I am dancing like there's no downside to looking like a goon. I actually want people to see me and think, what a goon? That actually looks fun. Then I, as an enthusiastically mediocre dancer, will also have more fun because more people will be dancing. I also do this in socio-professional groups. I run a biweekly hallway track meeting for Photoshop developers where we just get together and talk off the record about our most recent formal meeting.

Sometimes there's a lull in the conversation. I'll just jump in with an inane comment, sometimes a spicy question, just to let people know we aren't here trying to impress each other. I'll set the bar and then open the door and get out of the way because I love hearing experienced people hash things out. Being mediocre in public can invite people out with you. It brings out other intermediate-level folks. It brings out some shy experts because you've made it obvious that the bar for participation is one that they can easily clear. Now you're in a group of people sharing information and refining ideas before they've fully calcified, and you make each other better. Don't wait to be an expert to join a conversation about your tools. A caveat, when I tell people my advice to be joyfully imperfect in public, I usually mean it a little bit glibly.

Like in the sense of, but obviously not things that are core to your central identity. That would be terrible. No, like I can take up watercolors and show people that I'm an amusingly bad artist, or take up Chinese and let people laugh. When your skill at something is core to your identity, being mediocre in public is like doing a penance for a sin that you didn't even really get to enjoy committing. What I'm trying to do with every fiber of my being is to push this other skill, this meta skill of learning and adapting to change even deeper into my identity and recognizing that this squeaky, uncomfortable like, no, I'm terrible at this. It's like the lactic acid buildup the day after a workout. Is it comfortable? No, it sucks. It is the concrete feeling of getting better.

Some of you have been quietly bemused during this whole, here's how to not give up and survive section, because you are fully into learning the new thing. You are like, I am literally a core contributor on Gas Town, my good lady, what are you on about? This next section is for you. See, given the choice, I would rather dance than talk about the weather. I find it less awkward. Sorry, England. If I had absolute power, every awkward silence would just meld seamlessly into a dance break. Yet, I have not once committed the faux pas of grabbing some poor soul by the hand and dragging them onto the dance floor. I would never. Imagine this? You're sitting there at your linen-covered table trying to remember which wine was yours, and some absolute zealot comes and drags you by the hand onto the dance floor and then cheerfully bops away.

You're welcome. It's not ok. Unless you very quickly find your own groove, as soon as you can get away with it, you will moonwalk right back to the table straight past both glasses of wine because this time you're choosing a table much farther from these diehards who keep trying to force you into places where you don't think you fit. People who are happy on the dance floor need to make it more obvious that this is a good place to be and not just keep shouting that all of the non-dance floor is lava and we're getting left behind. Another aspect of bringing people with you. A few months ago, I used an AI agent to help me strategy out decluttering my basement. I described the state of years of kid clutter accumulation, and listed off a couple sample starting ideas like disassembling the massive tower of cardboard box sculptures my kid had made, or sorting and condensing the various containers that were half full of miscellaneous.

According to recent reports, cursor came back with a useful blueprint and some excellent advice, which included, do not start with the miscellaneous bins. They will just exhaust you. Better to focus on low-decision weight, high-impact tasks. You all sighed with relief along there with me. Like, "Low-decision weight, high-impact? Yes, this plan will work. It's going to feel so good and productive." It did. I got the tower out. I got rid of expired food and old toiletries. I made so many easy decisions, and I wrapped up the day feeling tired but satisfied and a good day's work. Then I go to work the next day, and the AI agents are like, "Good, you're back. I saved all these high-decision weight tasks for you. You're welcome." It turns out I'm not the only one who's had this, hold up, I feel like I'm doing more work now. We're working harder. Birgitta mentioned this too.

We are tired. Please keep in mind that when you're telling people how great this tool is, it is not zero cost. It is free as in puppy. You can't just drop it on people's doorsteps. If you're walking around insisting that everyone adopts one, you've got to provide material support. One specific practice, Photoshop's strongest AI tooling advocates host weekly office hours. We're constantly re-explaining to each other how to export the right environment variables this week. The support is critical because you're asking people to work harder. If you're patient when you're asking someone if they've sourced their, Oh My Zsh config recently, they're more likely to keep trying your next, "You'll like this one, I promise." They're more likely to try that idea.

I know that some of you are very worried that some of us aren't fully embracing how different our jobs will be in five years. I actually said that to troll you a little because I know it's an order of magnitude faster. Remember that a source of denial can be a lack of certainty that we have the skills to deal with the change. The more you remind your teams and your colleagues that they have done hard things before, that they can learn and grow, that neuroplasticity is real, the more they can loosen their hold on denial. The more we all believe that we do have the skills to face it, the more likely we are to engage in real protective behaviors. My favorite researcher, Cat Hicks, again, if our teams have a culture of learning, we report more productivity. This next part is me, non-professional scientist, extrapolating, but I think if you have a choice between a team with one expert tool user and a team who believes that they can learn and has faith in the organizational support behind it, choose the team that identifies as learners, the team that thinks they can't use the tool yet.

Recent findings suggest that why are we here? This is a question whose spiritual pay grade is much higher than mine. I'm going to narrow it to something that I'm actually qualified to speak to, how did we get here? First, approximately one lifetime ago, a lot of people suffered through a lot of months of pregnancy. Some number of years ago, we went from not knowing technology to being paid to be good at it. Some number of weeks ago, we all decided it was a good use of three solid days of our time to sit at a tech conference, and then every single person got it together and left their home. If we had heads-up displays showing each of our logistical contortions we used to get here, we would be high-fiving and pouring each other pints all day. We all decided that, yes, it's worth it to take that skeptically optimistic next step to learn a new thing from a stranger rather than chatting up friends in the hall.

It has been revealed that we've been through a lot to get here, and it's all been in the mad hope of finding that next good thing. We got here, and here and now is oddly harder than anything our industry has encountered, and even this is just a practice round for the next. The beginner's mindset that you're dusting off, the resilience that you did not want to have to shore up, and the communities that you're building now, this is not the last time you'll be calling on them. We're all just brains in training for the next swell, so if you usually avoid things that make you feel like a December-born horse, take a minute to practice being latest at things. Start with watercolors if you want, but also today you could go to a talk whose topic intimidates you. If a popular or mandated tool is giving you blisters, you can say so.

Talk to your peers to commiserate, to your juniors so they know it's not just them, to your management if you've got some political capital burning a hole in your Slack drafts. This is what leadership looks like in this world where everyone's a beginner. It looks like being unafraid to say, don't you know who I am? Yes, I'm someone who learns out loud.

Cloudflare Releases Automatic Website Search for AI Agents

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cloudflare launched Search for Agents on November 25, 2026, making the beta feature available on every initiative, including Free.
  • In a recent development, previously, customers had to manually create and configure an AI Search instance, integrate its search endpoints with their domain and tell agents where to find the index.
  • It has been revealed that cloudflare advertises the endpoint on every page.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cloudflare launched Search for Agents on November 25, 2026, making the beta feature available on every initiative, including Free. A dashboard toggle or API control now automates website indexing and exposes an API that AI agents can discover under the site’s own domain.

In a recent development, previously, customers had to manually create and configure an AI Search instance, integrate its search endpoints with their domain and tell agents where to find the index. For a domain already onboarded to Cloudflare, activation creates the instance and starts crawling and indexing; once indexed, content is searchable at /.well-known/search. The setup documentation instructs customers to index only content they intend to make publicly searchable.

It has been revealed that cloudflare advertises the endpoint on every page. HTML responses carry metadata in their containing agent instructions, the endpoint, the GET method and a documentation link. Sites that also enable Markdown for Agents provide equivalent YAML front matter to agents requesting Markdown. An agent can therefore discover the search capability from a page instead of needing prior knowledge of the site’s index.

Industry observers note that agents submit keywords or natural-language questions through the GET q parameter. Responses contain retrieved Markdown with source references and relevance scores, not an answer generated by another model. Cloudflare’s design leaves synthesis with the agent’s own model and user conversation, so the website supplies source material rather than taking over the response.

Sources indicate that cloudflare’s OpenCode demonstration highlighted an agent discovering the endpoint on the company’s developer-documentation homepage, asking about Cloudflare Artifacts and returning a correct answer a few seconds later. Access remains subject to the domain’s bot-management, AI Crawl Control and Web Application Firewall settings, so the discovery metadata does not bypass existing security controls.

It has been revealed that new instances use Discover crawling, which finds pages through sitemaps and links without requiring a sitemap. The defaults crawl five link hops deep, synchronize every 24 hours and exclude subdomains. Search combines vector and keyword retrieval using the @cf/qwen/qwen3-embedding-0.6b embedding model, returns up to 10 chunks and starts with reranking and query rewriting disabled. Similarity caching is enabled for 48 hours.

The embedding model and data source are fixed when the instance is created, though other configurable settings can be changed later. Because the feature uses a standard AI Search instance, owners can also enable public REST or MCP endpoints, access it through a Workers binding or embed search components for human visitors. Those additions are separate and are not required for agent search.

According to recent reports, alongside GET, the endpoint accepts HTTP QUERY requests containing either UTF-8 plain text or a JSON object with a q field. RFC 10008, published in June 2026 and coauthored by Cloudflare’s James M. Snell, defines QUERY as a safe, idempotent way to put query criteria in a request body. Unlike POST, it can be automatically retried without concern for partial state changes, and its responses are cacheable.

It has been revealed that usage is metered across content ingestion, index storage and queries. AI Search billing begins December 1, 2026, and the limits and pricing documentation lists monthly account allowances of 5 million ingestion tokens, 10 GB-month of storage, 1,000 semantic queries and 1,000 full-text queries. Overage rates are $0.75 per million base-ingestion tokens, $2.00 per GB-month of storage, $0.75 per 1,000 semantic, vector or hybrid queries, and $0.10 per 1,000 full-text queries.

Crawl allowances add another constraint. Discover crawling accepts up to 100,000 pages, but per-instance file limits and daily crawl ceilings also apply; the lowest applicable limit determines the resulting page count. On Workers Free, the daily ceiling is 500 pages, making it the binding constraint despite the larger crawl allowance.

The launch makes website retrieval part of Cloudflare’s network configuration instead of a custom integration. Its practical value depends on agents acting on the discovery metadata and on site owners aligning public-content, access and crawl settings. Those choices determine how much useful material an agent can retrieve without crawling pages individually.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we have implemented KV Caching from scratch in our nanoVLM repository (a small codebase to train your own Vision Language Model with pure PyTorch).
  • Sources indicate that autoregressive language models generate text by sampling one token at a time.
  • This step-by-step generation is inherently sequential:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we have implemented KV Caching from scratch in our nanoVLM repository (a small codebase to train your own Vision Language Model with pure PyTorch). This gave us a 38% speedup in generation. In this blog post we cover KV Caching and all our experiences while implementing it. The lessons learnt are general and can be applied to all autoregressive language model generations. Implementing from scratch on a small codebase is a great learning experience, come along for the ride!

Sources indicate that autoregressive language models generate text by sampling one token at a time. During inference, the model processes a given input sequence, predicts the next token, appends it to the sequence, and repeats this process until some stopping criterion:.

This step-by-step generation is inherently sequential:.

This repetition also leads to computational redundancy. In this post, we explore KV Caching, an optimisation technique that mitigates this inefficiency.

Before diving into caching, let’s revisit how attention operates in transformer models. A Transformer language model consists of stacked layers, each composed of:.

To understand where KV Caching helps, we focus on the self-attention mechanism, specifically within a single attention head.

Let’s walk through a simple PyTorch implementation to visualise the key computations.

For a sequence of T T T input embeddings represented as X∈RT×D X \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times D} X∈RT×D, self-attention is computed as:.

Attention(X;Q,K,V)=softmax(QK⊤⋅Mdk)V \text{Attention}(X; Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left( \frac{QK^\top \cdot M}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right)V Attention(X;Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QK⊤⋅M​)V.

Here’s a minimal PyTorch equivalent using a causal mask:.

It has been revealed that in autoregressive generation, the model generates one token at a time. With each step, it recomputes Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V for the entire sequence, even though the earlier tokens haven’t changed.

These checks show that for all but the newest token, K K K and V V V are identical to previously computed values.

Most of the attention computation is repeated needlessly. This gets more expensive as sequences grow.

To eliminate this inefficiency, we use KV Caching:.

This changes generation from full-sequence re-computation to a lightweight, incremental revision.

✅ In practice, this cache is a per-layer dictionary with keys "key" and "value", each of shape (batch_size, num_heads, seq_len_cached, head_dim).

This is the foundation of how modern LLMs can generate long outputs efficiently.

Now that we understand the theory behind KV Caching, let’s see how it’s implemented in practice inside our nanoVLM repository. This is an ideal testbed, as it's a super concise and self-contained codebase.

KV caching is enabled across three key components in our model:.

In the LanguageModelGroupedAttention class, we modify the forward function to accept and update a cache of keys and values (block_kv_cache).

Previously, the model recomputed K K K and V V V at every generation step. Now we only compute Knew K_{\text{new}} Knew​, Vnew V_{\text{new}} Vnew​ for the current token, and append them to the cached values.

In the LanguageModel class, we introduce layer-wise cache tracking. The start_pos argument helps the model compute correct rotary positional encodings for newly generated tokens.

The biggest architectural change is in the generate() method of the VisionLanguageModel.

We split generation into two stages:.

By separating these phases, we avoid redundant computation and dramatically speed up inference, especially for long prompts.

KV caching eliminates unnecessary computation during autoregressive generation, enabling faster and more efficient inference, especially in long sequences and real-time applications. This is a trade-off between speed and memory, and its drawbacks can be more complex code and restricting fancier inference schemes, like beam-search, etc. KV caching is a popular method for speeding up LLM inference, making it possible to run them on consumer hardware, and now you know how it works too!

ScreenSuite - The most comprehensive evaluation suite for GUI Agents!

📅 06 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past few weeks, we’ve been working tirelessly on making GUI agents more open, accessible and easy to integrate.
  • We are very excited to share it with you today: ScreenSuite is the most comprehensive and easiest way to evaluate Vision Language Models (VLMs)across many agentic capabilities!
  • In short, an AI Agent is a robot that acts in the virtual world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past few weeks, we’ve been working tirelessly on making GUI agents more open, accessible and easy to integrate. Along the way, we created the largest benchmarking suite for GUI agents performances 👉 let us introduce ScreenSuite.

We are very excited to share it with you today: ScreenSuite is the most comprehensive and easiest way to evaluate Vision Language Models (VLMs)across many agentic capabilities!

GUI Agents in action - courtesy of OSWorld.

In short, an AI Agent is a robot that acts in the virtual world. (more thorough definition here).

It has been revealed that in particular, a “GUI Agent” is an agent that lives in a GUI. Think “an agent that can do clicks and navigate on my desktop or my phone”, à la Claude Computer Use.

This means in essence that the AI model powering the agent will be given a task like “Fill the rest of this Excel column”, along with screen captures of the GUI. Using this information, it will then decide to take action on the system : click(x=130, y=540) to open a web browser, type(”Value for XYZ in 2025"), scroll(down=2) to read further… To see a GUI agent in action, you can try our Open Computer Agent, powered by Qwen2.5-VL-72B.

Industry observers note that A good GUI agent will be able to navigate a computer just like we would, thus unlocking all computer tasks : scrolling through Google Maps, editing a file, buying an item online. This involves a variety of capabilities that can be hard to evaluate.

The literature, for instance Xu et al. (2025) or Qin et al. (2025), generally splits GUI agent abilities amongst several categories:.

So our first contribution is to gather and unify a comprehensive suite of 13 benchmarks spanning the full range of these GUI agent capabilities.

According to recent reports, if you look at the last category listed above, evaluating Multi-step agentic capabilities is especially challenging as it requires virtual machines to run the agent’s environment, be it Windows, Android, Ubuntu... To address this, we provide support both for E2B desktop remote sandboxes, and we created from scratch a new option to easily launch Ubuntu or Android virtual machines in Docker!

In a recent development, we’ve carefully designed our benchmark suite with modularity and consistency in mind, ensuring strong alignment across tasks and environments. When required, especially for online benchmarks, we leverage smolagents as framework layer to streamline agent execution and orchestration.

To support reproducibility and ease of use, we’ve built custom Dockerized containers that allow local deployment of full Ubuntu Desktop or Android environments.

Unlike many existing GUI benchmarks that rely on accessibility trees or other metadata alongside visual input, our stack is intentionally vision-only. While this can result in different scores on some established leaderboards, we deem that it creates a more realistic and challenging setup, one that better reflects how humans perceive and interact with graphical interfaces.

– All agentic frameworks (Android World, OSWorld, GAIAWeb, Mind2Web) use smolagents and rely solely on vision, without any accessibility tree or DOM added (in contrast with evaluation settings reported in other sources). – Mind2Web (Multimodal) originally used element-name-based multi-choice selection based on the accessibility tree and screenshots, but was later adapted to click precision within bounding boxes using vision only, which significantly increases task difficulty.

We’ve evaluated leading VLMs on the benchmark.

Our scores are in general agreement with the scores reported in various sources! With the caveat that we evaluate on vision only, causing some differences, see implementation details above.

Sources indicate that 💡 Note that ScreenSuite does not intend to exactly reproduce benchmarks published in the industry: we evaluate models on GUI agentic capabilities based on vision. As a result, on benchmarks like Mind2Web where other benchmarks gave the agent a view of information rich context like DOM or accessibility tree, our evaluation setting is much harder, thus ScreenSuite does not match other sources.

The multistep benchmarks requires a bare-metal machine to run and deploy desktop/mobile* environment *emulators (see README.md).

Running consistent and meaningful evaluations easily allows the community to promptly iterate and make progress in this field, as we’ve seen with Eleuther LM evaluation harness, the Open LLM Leaderboard and the Chatbot Arena.

We hope to see much more capable open models in the coming month that can run a wide range of tasks reliably and even run locally!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nexent Capital IFSC Private Limited said in a November 25, 2026 announcement that it had launched Nexent Capital ADGM Fund I, a closed-end fund targeting US$1 billion in capital commitments for quantum-ready AI infrastructure and advanced energy, with a US$20 million anchor commitment from the Tyagi family office.

Sources indicate that the target is not capital already raised. The fund can expand to a US$1.6 billion hard cap and is aimed at institutional and family-office investors, with a minimum investment of US$500,000.

According to recent reports, the mandate spans five strategies: infrastructure private equity in AI and data-center assets; private credit and structured capital; special-situations mergers and acquisitions; growth equity and private investments in public equity, or PIPEs; and liquid public-equity exposure within the AI and data-center value chain. The mandate consequently covers the financing and ownership of physical infrastructure as well as investments in companies across that value chain.

According to recent reports, nexent said it has line of sight to an identified pipeline across North America and India, including data-center and power assets sponsored by affiliates of the Nexent Capital and Tryfacta platform. These are pipeline projects, not acquisitions the fund has completed.

Director Abhimanyu Tyagi described the pipeline as drawing on relationships and projects the platform had developed for years, ranging from data-center conversions to gigawatt-scale energy campuses.

Managing partner Adesh Tyagi framed the investment case around AI’s physical requirements: “AI is being built on a foundation of physical infrastructure — power, land, and compute — that most capital isn’t positioned to finance at the scale or speed this moment demands.”.

Recent findings suggest that the structure comprises an Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM)-domiciled Qualified Investor Fund as the master fund, with a GIFT City-based Alternative Investment Fund regulated by IFSCA acting as its feeder. Nexent Capital ADGM Limited is being established as the licensed ADGM fund manager.

Nexent is working with an Abu Dhabi-based fund administrator that it says manages more than US$3.4 trillion in assets globally. Formal engagement of legal counsel and an auditor is progressing as part of the path to FSRA authorization.

The fund has not yet received that authorization. Nexent targets a first close approximately six months after FSRA authorization and a final close six months later, so neither closing has occurred.

The launch sets out a cross-border financing route aimed at the physical requirements of AI expansion. Its practical scale will depend on securing authorization, raising the targeted commitments and converting the identified pipeline into investments. For now, the announcement represents prospective infrastructure financing rather than upcoming operating data-center or energy capacity.

Today at GTC Paris, we are excited to announce Training Cluster as a Service in collaboration with NVIDIA, to make large GPU clusters more easily accessible for research organizations all over the world, so they can train the foundational models of tomorrow in every domain.

According to recent reports, many Gigawatt-size GPU supercluster projects are being built to train the next gen of AI models. This can make it seem that the compute gap between the “GPU poor” and the “GPU rich” is quickly widening. But the GPUs are out there, as hyperscalers, regional and AI-native cloud providers all quickly expand their capacity.

Recent findings suggest that how do we then connect AI compute capacity with the researchers who need it? How do we enable universities, national research labs and companies all over the world to build their own models?

This is what Hugging Face and NVIDIA are tackling with Training Cluster as a Service - providing GPU cluster accessibility, with the flexibility to only pay for the duration of training runs.

To get started, any of the 250,000 organizations on Hugging Face can request the GPU cluster size they need, when they need it.

To get started, you can request a GPU cluster on behalf of your organization at hf.co/training-cluster.

Training Cluster as a Service integrates key components from NVIDIA and Hugging Face into a complete solution:.

Once your GPU cluster request is accepted, Hugging Face and NVIDIA will collaborate to source, price, provision and set up your GPU cluster per your size, region and duration requirements.

The Telethon Institute of Genomics and Medicine - TIGEM for short - is a research center dedicated to understanding the molecular mechanisms behind rare genetic diseases and developing novel treatments. Training newly introduced AI models is a new path to predict the effect of pathogenic variants and for drug repositioning.

According to recent reports, AI offers upcoming ways to research the causes of rare genetic diseases and to develop treatments, but our domain requires training new models. Training Cluster as a Service made it easy to procure the GPU capacity we needed, at the right time.

-- Diego di Bernardo, Coordinator of the Genomic Medicine program at TIGEM.

Numina is a non-profit organization building open-source, open-dataset AI for reasoning in math - and won the 2024 AIMO progress prize.

We are tracking well on our objective to build open alternatives to the best closed-source models, such as Deepmind's AlphaProof. Computing resources is our bottleneck today - with Training Cluster as a Service we will be able to reach our goal!

-- Yann Fleureau, cofounder of Project Numina.

Mirror Physics is a startup creating frontier AI systems for chemistry and materials science.

Industry observers note that together with the MACE team, we're working to push the limits of AI for chemistry. With Training Cluster as a Service, we're producing high-fidelity chemical models at unprecedented scale. This is going to be a significant step forward for the field.

-- Sam Walton Norwood, CEO and founder at Mirror.

Training Cluster as a Service is a latest collaboration between Hugging Face and NVIDIA to make AI compute more readily available to the global community of AI researchers.

Recent findings suggest that access to large-scale, high-performance compute is essential for building the next generation of AI models across every domain and language. Training Cluster as a Service will remove barriers for researchers and companies, unlocking the ability to train the most advanced models and push the boundaries of what’s possible in AI.

-- Clément Delangue, cofounder and CEO of Hugging Face.

Integrating DGX Cloud Lepton with Hugging Face’s Training Cluster as a Service gives developers and researchers a seamless way to access high-performance NVIDIA GPUs across a broad network of cloud providers. This collaboration makes it easier for AI researchers and organizations to scale their AI training workloads while using familiar tools on Hugging Face.

-- Alexis Bjorlin, vice president of DGX Cloud at NVIDIA.

We are excited to collaborate with NVIDIA to offer Training Cluster as a Service to Hugging Face organizations - you can get started today at hf.co/training-cluster.

  • Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Vercel Rolled out Experimental Board to Coordinate Tasks Across Humans and Coding Agents.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

Vercel has introduced Vercel Board, an experimental, headless message board where people and coding agents coordinate tasks across tools and harnesses. Vercel says Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, eve, fx, Mastra, and LangChain can work on the same board as if they were a single harness.

Recent findings suggest that each Vercel team gets a default board, named General, organized into channels and threads. Developers and agents read and write through the `vercel board` CLI or the `@vercel/board` JavaScript SDK. A skill, installed with npx skills add vercel/board --skill board, teaches coding agents the CLI. Agents name themselves with --as or BOARD_PROFILE, but still act with the operator's or project's credentials.

Sources indicate that A task is a thread whose state the board keeps. A worker claims a ready task, posts updates, and completes or fails it. A claim is a lease of up to five minutes and must be renewed; if it expires, the task returns to the queue. When two workers claim the same task, one succeeds and the other fails with task_claimed. Tasks can declare dependencies, so a review waits until its fix completes while independent work proceeds in parallel. Watchers on a Vercel deployment can run when a reply is posted or a label changes, waking the deployment so no process has to stay running.

Sync, configured in the SDK and delivered through Vercel Connect, can attach a board channel to Slack, GitHub, or Linear. Slack and Linear sync both ways; GitHub imports pull requests and problems and does not write back unless the project sends those messages. Grants control who can read, post, and manage each channel. For an agent in a Vercel Sandbox, sandboxPolicy() can grant limited board access without putting a credential inside the sandbox. Vercel states it rebuilt v0's software factory on Board, and that the factory now merges over 50% of its pull requests.

Official documentation warns that Board grants do not apply on Slack, GitHub, or Linear, so a private Slack channel synced into an open board channel is readable by the whole Vercel team.

Austin King (@MadeWithOzten) replied to Vercel's announcement asking to.

Do this self-hosted and open source - Rust, Yjs Sync,.

then wrote that he had bought openboard.lol.

For a self-hosted open source Vercel board like thing.

Aaron Delz (@AaronDelz) stated he already kept a shared checklist with his agent, and liked that a Board task can be completed with the pull request attached:.

Same rule my agents run on: no saying 'done' without the evidence.

Similar coordination indicates up elsewhere. OpenCrawl is an open source, self-hostable board that also records agent sessions. GitHub Agent HQ can assign issues and pull requests to Copilot, Claude, or Codex. Linear's cloud coding agent turns scoped issues into draft pull requests with Claude Code or Codex. Claude Code agent teams coordinate multiple Claude Code sessions around a shared task list, and the Agent2Agent protocol standardizes delegation between agents rather than hosting a board.

Sources indicate that board remains experimental infrastructure on a Vercel team. Setup steps and the CLI and SDK references are in Vercel's Board documentation.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The IndiaAI Mission announced on November 25, 2026, that Ministry of Electronics and IT Secretary S.
  • According to recent reports, chariot is one of the first four teams selected by the mission to build sovereign foundation models.
  • IndiaAI reports three design elements: IndicShift, a shared alphabet for Indian scripts using 2.5 times fewer tokens on Indian text; Nested Training, which develops three model sizes in a single run with 62% faster training; and Mixture of Vocabularies, an approach delivering 38% faster training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The IndiaAI Mission announced on November 25, 2026, that Ministry of Electronics and IT Secretary S. Krishnan had inaugurated Chariot Artificial Intelligence’s Chariot-1 foundation models, developed from scratch in India and spanning English and 10 Indian languages.

According to recent reports, chariot is one of the first four teams selected by the mission to build sovereign foundation models. The unveiling took place at Chariot One, a launch and research showcase at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, bringing the government-backed programme together with a public demonstration of the lab’s speech research.

IndiaAI reports three design elements: IndicShift, a shared alphabet for Indian scripts using 2.5 times fewer tokens on Indian text; Nested Training, which develops three model sizes in a single run with 62% faster training; and Mixture of Vocabularies, an approach delivering 38% faster training.

It has been revealed that those choices address two distinct parts of multilingual development: how efficiently Indian text is represented and how much training work is required to produce different model sizes. They also indicate that Chariot-1 is intended as a reusable model family rather than only a single speech product.

In a recent development, beyond text representation, the models support context-aware speech generation. IndiaAI reports more than 97% verbalization accuracy on the Async TTS Pronunciation Benchmark, which measures whether written expressions receive an acceptable spoken interpretation. That capability matters because applications must read currencies, dates, abbreviations and symbols appropriately, rather than merely pronounce individual words.

The inauguration follows two public speech releases from the lab. Chariot’s November 12, 2026 release describes Chariot-1-TTS-Multilingual as generating speech in 11 Indic languages and English, with more than 50 voices, language mixing within sentences and voice cloning from a few seconds of reference audio. It also interprets prices, dates, abbreviations and symbols in context, reducing the need for custom text-normalization rules.

In Chariot’s own November 11, 2026 evaluation, the model ranked first among the configurations compared on three measures: a 7.60% Hindi character error rate, 93.78% English verbalization accuracy on its English suite and a 4.901 NISQA score, an automated estimate of audio quality. Those measurements address different parts of speech generation: intelligibility, interpretation of written text and estimated sound quality.

The earlier Chariot-1-ASR Realtime release, dated October 22, 2026, added streaming speech recognition in 10 Indian languages and Indian English. Chariot reports that it had the lowest word error rate in every language against every streaming API and batch model tested, and that its 10-language average had 26% fewer errors than Google Gemini 3.5 Transcribe’s batch API.

The release describes the system as the Chariot-1 speech-reasoning backbone post-trained for one task, rather than a model built exclusively for recognition. That makes it a public example of how the foundation model can be adapted to a specific task.

Chariot is headquartered in Delhi and led by co-founders Parth Sarthi and Suvrat Bhooshan. Its research roadmap calls for a speech-native model that reasons across meaning, delivery, timing and action, rather than dividing conversations among separate transcription, synthesis, dubbing and voice-agent pipelines. The current TTS and ASR systems are the first public steps, with developers able to generate and stream speech through the Chariot platform and API.

The inauguration connects India’s sovereign-AI policy with a specific technical approach: build shared multilingual foundations, then adapt them to individual speech tasks. The next substantive test is whether Chariot can extend that approach from generation and recognition into the broader reasoning system it describes while retaining the efficiency and accuracy gains reported for the initial models.
