📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plus WebAudio nodes, image inputs, and more!

Servo 0.8.0 contains all of the changes we landed in October, spanning 588 commits (a newly introduced record)!

Servo now renders subtitles and captions over elements (@TimvdLippe, #48809)!

We’ve shipped newly introduced web platform features:.

In a recent development, flutter web content no longer hangs now that we fixed a serious performance problem with typed arrays (@jdm, #48640). Example.

Sources indicate that we’re interested to hear how well your favourite websites run in Servo! Report successes in this Zulip thread or this Github discussion, and failures in our GitHub issues.

Sources indicate that with respect to accessibility in Servo, we report many more ARIA roles for DOM elements (@alice, @mrobinson, #48839). These can be inspected with the Get Computed Role WebDriver command (@lolaodelola, #47339). Accessibility integration can be turned on with the accessibility_enabled preference.

Sources indicate that webGL2 support received lots of attention this month, with fixes to getParameter(), drawBuffers(), readBuffers(), vertexAttribIPointer(), DEPTH_STENCIL_ATTACHMENT, getUniformLocation(), vertexAttrib4x(), pixelStorei(), texStorage2D(), texStorage3D(), texImage3D(), getInternalformatParameter(), blitFramebuffer(), and texSubImage2D() (@mxmgorin, #48651, #48620, #48678, #48689, #48751, #48681, #48911, #48972, #48590, #49201, #49289, #48560, #48571). The feature remains gated behind the dom_webgl2_enabled preference.

Reading and writing mapped WebGPU buffers got a significant speed increase (@sagudev, @jdm, #48372). WebGPU can be enabled with the dom_webgpu_enabled preference.

Industry observers note that JS script compilation can now occur off the main thread when the dom_script_asynch preference is enabled (@Gae24, #45687). Right now this only applies to non-module scripts.

Sources indicate that initial support for the backdrop-filter property has merged (@shubhamg13, #48829). This can be enabled with the layout_css_backdrop_filter_enabled preference.

ServiceWorkers now fire the statechange event when changing states during initialization (@gterzian, #48749). ServiceWorkerContainer can listen for message and messageerror events (@gterzian, #48680). Service Workers remain gated behind the dom_serviceworker_enabled preference.

The Geolocation API has been implemented (@webbeef, #48406). No platform-specific backends to provide the device geolocation data have merged yet, so it remains disabled behind the dom_geolocation_enabled preference.

According to recent reports, DOM interfaces for MathML elements now exist, gated behind the mathml_core_enabled preference (@tannal, #48631). There is no MathML-specific layout implemented yet.

It has been revealed that A new, native SVG implementation is in progress (@mu-mostafa98, @jdm, #48467). This work is still in the early stages, but is intended to replace Servo’s dependency on the resvg crate to better integrate with page styling and animations.

Recent findings suggest that indexedDB cursors now support the update() and delete() methods (@kuntal-devrat, #48402). The feature can be enabled with the dom_indexeddb_enabled preference.

According to recent reports, support for LargestContentfulPaint performance timing improved, with image URLs (@shubhamg13, #48668), the loadTime value (@shubhamg13, #48676), ignoring non-paintable elements (@shubhamg13, #48856, #48898), video URLs (@shubhamg13, #48931), and following containing blocks (@shubhamg13, #48551). This work is behind the largest_contentful_paint_enabled preference.

We added support for a upcoming performance timing metric: ContainerTiming (@jasonwilliams, #46966). This can be enabled with the container_timing_enabled preference.

It has been revealed that our support for adoptedStylesheets improved along with a latest implementation of the ObservableArray specification concept (@jerensl, @arihant2math, #48506). This is currently hidden behind the dom_adoptedstylesheet_enabled preference.

Recent findings suggest that the Android Compose migration is complete, and embedders now only need to interact with the Servo library component (@veyndan, #48592, #48601, #48595, #48574, #48609, #48778, #48780, #49266). Embedders no longer need to trigger the soft keyboard display; this is controlled by a parameter to the Servo component (@veyndan, #48757).

There’s a newly introduced API method to report the network status of the embedder: NetworkManager::set_online_state (@xbwwj, #47568). This data is exposed via the onLine property of the Navigator interface in web content.

In a recent development, embedders can now disable all support for developer tools, which can reduce the size of the final binary (@janeoa, #47255). This is controlled by the devtools feature and enabled by default; it is also part of the latest default_tooling feature.

Consumers of the C API can set preferences that accept f64 and f64 array parameters (@fran6co, #49325), as well as the HiDPI scale factor for each WebView (@fran6co, #49327). WebViews can also be resized via the C API (@fran6co, #49326).

It has been revealed that the layout_grid_enabled preference has been removed, since CSS Grid now defaults to enabled (@Loirooriol, #48718). Several preferences were renamed (@nicoburns, #48915):.

Double and triple clicking on selected text will extend the selection to the current word and line, respectively (@mrobinson, @SimonSapin, #48767).

Clicking a link with the middle mouse button now opens up the link in a new WebView (@SteveSharonSam, @mrobinson, #46000).

Range inputs can be dragged with the mouse (@webbeef, #48342).

Command+delete on macOS will delete the preceding line in a text control (@dzfrias, #48781).

The developer tools continue to improve:.

We improved exception error messages related to the XMLHttpRequest, History, Range, Selection, Element, CharacterData, and DOMTokenList interfaces, and namespaces and attributes (@gabrielecabrini, #49146, #49145, #48786, #49102).

Media elements that start playing outside of a document will no longer be garbage collected until playback finishes (@sabbCodes, @jdm, #49367, #48979).

Pinch zoom operations no longer have to rebuild a full display list, making zooming complex pages much smoother (@stevennovaryo, @mrobinson, #43561).

We improved performance in many small and focused ways by doing less work during restyling and layout (@SimonSapin, @webbeef, @nicoburns, @mrobinson, #49137, #49100, #48485, #48968), reducing GC interactions (@mrobinson, @jschwe, #48984, #49140, #49195, #49425), and delaying work on disconnected trees (@SimonSapin, #49098). We also fixed instances of quadratic layout with deep nesting (@nicoburns, #49148) and missing caching (@mrobinson, @Loirooriol, #49164, #49073).

We fixed some intermittent GC panics when notifying ResizeObservers (@mrobinson, #49189), introspecting keyframes (@MohamedAli00949, #48546), setting timers (@jdm, #48548), using writable streams (@jdm, #48656), and scrolling iframes after removing them (@mrobinson, #49230).

We also fixed numerous other panics and crashes in scrollable and incremental layout (@mrobinson, #49230, #49283), moving nodes around (@mrobinson, #49226), using WebGPU from opaque origins (@gabrielecabrini, #49207), stringifying some WebIDL types (@mrobinson, #49374), using readable streams (@Narfinger, @mrobinson, #49311), clicking disabled file controls (@mrobinson, #49379), rendering giant SVGs (@sabbCodes, #49264), unminifying JS (@jdm, #48567), measuring text (@mxmgorin, #48621), rendering text tracks (@TimvdLippe, @mrobinson, #48827), preparing dialogs (@lukewarlow, #49431), and running delayed tasks in destroyed documents (@mrobinson, @jdm, #49399, #48714).

Sources indicate that many small-to-medium improvements to reduce allocations were merged (@yezhizhen, @Narfinger, @Taym95, @mrobinson, @Loirooriol, @CynthiaOketch, @sabbCodes, @mxmgorin, #48549, #48558, #48568, #48598, #48615, #48565, #48646, #48654, #48569, #48562, #48588, #48650, #48702, #48675, #48589, #48720, #48721, #47720, #48745, #48703, #48750, #48770, #48789, #48754, #48828, #48838, #48836, #48841, #48843, #48867, #48882, #48842, #48881, #48840, #48899, #48924, #48904, #48949, #48953, #48980, #49028, #48885, #49035, #49038, #49084, #49131, #49125, #48951, #49154, #49160, #49198, #49202, #49194, #49219, #49258, #49275, #49295, #49298, #49300, #49320, #49323, #49313, #49373, #49380, #48969, #48991). We also reduced memory usage by shrinking some types (@Narfinger, @webbeef, #48954, #48082, #48906).

Memory leaks received a lot of attention this month, covering everything from network requests, to JS modules, to timer tasks, and more (@mrobinson, @SimonSapin, @jschwe, #48952, #48957, #49032, #49049, #49092, #49134, #49139, #49132, #48747, #48752).

We continue to work towards preventing certain sources of memory leaks with static analysis and the Rust type system (@Gae24, @Narfinger, @jdm, #48147, #48360, #48832, #48887, #48913, #48903, #48965, #48905, #48834, #48855, #49083, #49082, #49081, #49096, #49135, #49130).

We fixed bugs related to the CORS preflight cache (@sabbCodes, #49055, #49252), fetch metadata (@TimvdLippe, @mrobinson, #48793), HTTP cache revalidation (@mrobinson, @jdm, #48927), image load timing (@mrobinson, @TimvdLippe, #48902, #48790, #48599), touch events (@yezhizhen, #48671, #48699, #48701), cloning and moving input elements (@skyz1, @mrobinson, #48845, #48069), the :indeterminate pseudoclass (@skyz1, #48070), stylesheet introspection (@mrobinson, #48935), mutating ranges (@gabrielecabrini, #49072), blob URLs (@rogerkorantenng, #49074, #48989, #49206), form controls (@mrobinson, @lukewarlow, @jdm, #49163, #49225, #48513), the mapping property of Gamepad (@msub2, #49381), beforeinput events (@dzfrias, #48825), image dimensions (@TimvdLippe, #49085), table appearance attributes (@Loirooriol, #49120, #49108, #49156, #49150), IME events (@dzfrias, #48690), reconnecting IntersectionObserver (@shubhamg13, #48581), and root elements (@TimvdLippe, #48514).

We also addressed layout challenges related to soft wrap line breaks (@mrobinson, @Loirooriol, #48564), grid and flex layouts with indefinite dimensions (@RichardTjokroutomo, @rayguo17, @nicoburns, #48670, #48644, #49232), hanging whitespace (@mrobinson, @Loirooriol, #48591, #48753), preserve-3d (@mrobinson, #47933), inline block splits (@Loirooriol, #46445), video controls (@rayguo17, #44956), display: contents (@Loirooriol, #48784, #48785), justify-contents (@yezhizhen, #48746, #48988), absolute positioning (@mrobinson, @Loirooriol, #48846), (@Loirooriol, #49143), text-transform: capitalize (@jschwe, #48901), incremental table layout (@Loirooriol, #49176), width: stretch (@Loirooriol, #49239, #49237), backface visibility (@mrobinson, #49196), flex gaps (@yezhizhen, #49335), perspective (@mrobinson, #49174), quirks mode (@Loirooriol, #48942, #39869, #48978, #49211), SVG viewboxes (@leowatts, #48556), ISO-8859-8 documents (@TTyChud, #48444), and table borders (@adoublebarrel, @mrobinson, #47684).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NVIDIA Isaac GR00T (Generalist Robot 00 Technology) is a research and development platform for building robot foundation models and data pipelines, designed to accelerate the creation of intelligent, adaptable robots.

Sources indicate that today, we announced the availability of Isaac GR00T N1.5, the first major enhancement to Isaac GR00T N1, the world’s first open foundation model for generalized humanoid robot reasoning and skills. This cross-embodiment model processes multimodal inputs, including language and images, to perform manipulation tasks across diverse environments. It is adaptable through post-training for specific embodiments, tasks, and environments.

In this blog, we’ll demonstrate how to post-train (fine-tune) GR00T N1.5 using teleoperation data from a single SO-101 robot arm.

Technical Blog for GR00T N1.5: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/gear/gr00t-n1_5/.

Now accessible to developers working with a wide range of robot form factors, GR00T N1.5 can be easily fine-tuned and adapted using the affordable, open-source LeRobot SO-101 arm.

This flexibility is enabled by the EmbodimentTag system, which allows seamless customization of the model for different robotic platforms, empowering hobbyists, researchers, and engineers to tailor advanced humanoid reasoning and manipulation capabilities to their own hardware.

Before proceeding to installation, please check if you satisfy the prerequisites.

In a recent development, users can fine-tune GROOT N1.5 with any LeRobot dataset. For this tutorial, we will be using the table cleanup task as an example for fine-tuning.

It's key to note that datasets for the SO-100 or SO-101 are not in GR00T N1.5's initial pre-training. As a result of this, we will be training it as a new_embodiment.

According to recent reports, for this tutorial, you can either begin by creating your own custom dataset by following these instructions (recommended) or by downloading the so101-table-cleanup dataset from Hugging Face. Industry News: AI Is Speeding Up Security Disclosures. Patches Still Move at Different Speeds

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (756 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that software vendors can find and disclose more vulnerabilities with AI-assisted research, but companies that rely on those vendors still have to wait for fixes that work on their equipment.
  • According to recent reports, fortinet accounted for 89 advisories that day.
  • An infrastructure product can contain code written by its vendor alongside firmware, libraries, and other components supplied by outside companies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that software vendors can find and disclose more vulnerabilities with AI-assisted research, but companies that rely on those vendors still have to wait for fixes that work on their equipment. Eclypsium’s November InfraTrust Pulse report illustrates the gap. It tracked 373 advisories from 23 infrastructure vendors over 36 days, covering 3,880 distinct vulnerability identifiers. More than half the advisories in the period appeared on a single day. The report follows network equipment, servers, chips, firmware, and the controllers that let enterprises manage hardware remotely.

According to recent reports, fortinet accounted for 89 advisories that day. According to Eclypsium, 82 credited Fortinet’s product security team working with frontier AI models. The number of advisories was nearly eight times the vendor’s earlier average per release day that year. That is a striking example of how AI can assist a security team, but a single release day cannot establish how much of the increase came from AI, whether the pace will continue, or whether there are more underlying flaws. An advisory is also not the same thing as a newly discovered vulnerability: one advisory can cover several findings, and several vendors can issue advisories about the same flaw.

An infrastructure product can contain code written by its vendor alongside firmware, libraries, and other components supplied by outside companies. When the underlying component has a vulnerability, multiple manufacturers may have to determine which products include it, which versions are affected, and how to deliver a fix. Eclypsium counted 40 advisories arising from just six shared-component flaws. That helps explain why a month’s advisory totals can look much larger than the number of underlying complications that teams need to understand.

This is where a software, hardware, or firmware bill of materials can help. A conventional asset inventory tells a organization which devices it owns. A component inventory can help answer a different question: which of those devices depend on the same piece of code? Eclypsium’s supply-chain guide describes mapping those components to products. The quality of that inventory matters as much as its existence. A stale inventory, or one that does not record the version of a component in the equipment actually deployed, can still leave a security team waiting for vendor confirmation.

The report describes a case in which a component enhancement was already available in October, but projected fixes for some products extended to June 2027. For a downstream vendor, integrating a fix can mean validating it across hardware revisions, testing whether it breaks management functions, and producing firmware packages for each supported device. Customers then have their own installation and validation windows. The latest target date in the report is not a prediction for every vendor or device, but it illustrates how long the distance from upstream fix to customer deployment can be.

For defenders, the practical lesson is to track exposure and available fixes separately. A burst of AI-assisted disclosures makes it more vital to reconcile duplicate advisories and prioritize affected equipment. CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog provides one input to that judgment, alongside what an organization actually runs and which fixes it can deploy. Where a fix is not yet available, teams can document what is exposed, track vendor guidance, and reassess the risk as new information arrives. Faster discovery helps, but the more consequential measure for operators is how long a known exposure remains in their own environment.

Industry observers note that the next rust trait solver, a large subsystem of the rust compiler that we've been trying to replace, will finally land in rust 1.102.0. In the last stages, before stabilizing it, its performance was a major blocker. But what is "a trait solver"? And why is its performance a problem? My goal for this blog post is to answer those questions in a way where you don't need any prior knowledge. I think discussions of the trait solver can quickly become quite involved, and daunting. So today, we'll start from the very basics!

This is a writeup of my eurorust 2026 talk of the same name, that I gave on October 15, 2026.

And if you'd rather watch than read this talk, you can do so here on youtube:.

Industry observers note that the new solver is the codebase I work on daily, and I've done so for about a year full-time. I'm not the main person driving its stabilization though, that would be lcnr , who's worked on it for far longer than I've been around in the Rust project. My main focus has been optimizing the new solver's performance.

In a recent development, many people have worked avery hard, for years, to make the new solver a reality. You can find some of them here, and here.

Industry observers note that my work here is only possible because of Hexcat and RustNL paying me and others to work on rust compiler development. Consider whether you or your company could sponsor Hexcat or the RustNL maintainer team.

According to recent reports, on the 15th of May, 2015, Rust reached a major milestone. The very first stable version of rust was released. Version 1.0.0. Just 72 days later, on the 24th of July, work started on a new trait solver. Or well, that's when the Chalk project got its first commit. It seems the initial goal was to formalize the trait system so we could prove its correctness. One reason that didn't work well is because the trait system wasn't very correct at all.

Sources indicate that chalk is, according to its github description, "An implementation and definition of the Rust trait system using a PROLOG-like logic solver". The fact that it's "PROLOG-like" we'll come back to in a few paragraphs, it's quite interesting! However, Chalk isn't around anymore. Its README.md states it has been "sunset in favor of the newer next-generation trait solver". In October 2022, this project was officially started to turn the lessons learned from Chalk, into an actual latest subsystem of the rust compiler, that, once finished, could replace the code of the old trait solver.

In a recent development, the goal of the newly introduced trait solver is to make sure we wouldn't have as many correctness bugs in the trait system. We now call this project "project zero", referring to the number of soundness bugs we'd ideally like to have in our type system. There have been several very long standing bugs in Rust's (old) trait solver. Like this one, that has been open since May 28, 2015 (just 13 days after Rust 1.0!). It abuses something called "implied bounds" to convince the Rust compiler to turn a short lifetime 'a into a 'static lifetime, allowing you to use a reference after its already freed. Some of these bugs were fundamentally impossible to fix with the way the old trait solver worked.

Note: Chalk and the fresh trait solver aren't the same thing. Chalk came first, and learned a lot of lessons incorporated in the new solver.

But what is a trait system? And how does a trait solver solve it?

Industry observers note that the first place to look for documentation about the Rust compiler is the "rustc dev guide". It says "The goal of the trait system is to check whether a given trait bound is satisfied. Most notably when typechecking the body of - potentially generic - functions.". But I promised I'd start at absolute zero, so what's a trait?

In a recent development, some types act in similar ways. They share certain properties. For example, a lot of different types can be cloned, or copared for equality. To codify these properties, we can use traits. In other words, a trait is a property of a type.

Industry observers note that notably, you can associate behaviors with these properties. The standard library's definition of Clone also includes two methods that can be called to perform this cloning operation.

Industry observers note that to check whether the code you wrote is correct, the Rust compiler sometimes has to check that these properties hold. If you're trying to clone a value, the compiler has to check whether that value can be cloned.

Prolog is a cool programming language that works and looks very differently to what you may be used to. However, it is just as powerful (i.e. turing complete) as any other. The way it works has strong parallels to our trait system, let me show you. Here's an example:.

A Prolog program consists of a set of statements, called "facts", as well as relationships between facts. In the above program, there are two facts: u64 has the property Copy, String has the property Clone, And there's also a relationship between these two properties. If some variable x has the Copy property, it also has the Clone property.

Industry observers note that finally, we can ask the prolog program some questions. For example, Does the type u64 have the Clone property? To answer that question, the runtime of a prolog program has to analyze all the known facts and relations. In this program we haven't said that u64 has the Clone property. However, we have said that it has the Copy property. And by using the relationship between Copy and Clone, the solver can derive that both questions (starting with ?-) are true!

The reason Chalk was using a "prolog-like" solver, is because as you can see, the trait system is extremely similar to a logic solver. Both "facts" and "relations" can be written using impl blocks. In fact, I can write the above program as a Rust program:.

According to recent reports, neither the new solver or the old solver state as plainly as chalk does that they're using a "prolog-like solver". However, given the similarities, both the old solver and the new solver really aren't so different from how you'd implement a prolog runtime.

Industry observers note that trait solving is not the same as type inference. This is a common misconception. Inside the Rust compiler, the two are completely different subsystems. Type inference is the process of replacing blanks with types. Throughout this text I'll refer to some the following example code (with slight variations):.

Industry observers note that we use type inference to determine that the type of the variable a is an integer. The same for b.

Having remarked that, sometimes during type inference we do have to ask things about traits, and will call into the trait solver. Furthermore, the trait solver sometimes "unifies type variables", which means that while Rust makes a query about traits, we might make some progress on figuring out what the types of some variables are.

It has been revealed that in the example code, one place where the trait solver comes into effect is when we call weird_add. On the function there's a where bound. A where bound is a requirement that the Rust compiler must check before allowing a call to that function. In this case, Rust has to make sure that i32 (a type we found through type inference) implements the Add trait. To do that, the solver can use one of a couple of strategies, and we'll look at each. In this case, we'll be looking for an impl block that mentions the i32 type, and we'll find one of those in the standard library!

Once the trait solver finds this impl block, it acts as an answer to the question "does i32 implement Add?". We somtimes refer to this answer as a a proof that the statement holds.

Industry observers note that the example code contains several more calls to the trait solver. One you may not have thought about is that all local variables in Rust have to implement the Sized trait to be allowed on the stack. The Sized trait codifies that the compiler knows how many bytes of memory the value takes up, so it can be allocated on the stack. So, there will also be a query to the trait solver asking "does i32 implement Sized?".

The proof for this statement doesn't come from an impl block though. I did say that the compiler has several stratagies to derive proofs. In this case, the fact that some primitive types implement Sized is built-in to the compiler. i32 is inherently Sized, and there is no impl block anywhere that says so.

It has been revealed that answering Sized queries in general turns out to be quite hard because of the shear volume at which it occurs. To compile rust's standard library, we'll ask "does type implement Sized?" about 800 000 times! Additionally, answering it isn't always this simple. Let's take a slightly more involved example:.

To prove Kitten: Sized, a recursive process takes place. Both fields have to implement Sized too. So in the process of answering this question, the trait solver will produce more questions to be answered. Kitten: Sized leads to String: Sized & f64: Sized. f64 luckily is trivial again, and built into the compiler. String isn't though, and we go one more layer deeper to Vec: Sized, etcetera.

Sources indicate that in Rust, generic functions can be type checked standalone. The example using weird_add doesn't need a main function to be checked, and may emit its own type errors.

This is where the trait solver actually does the most work. For example, to type check weird_add, we have to prove that a + b is valid. a + b desugars to a.add(b), and when finding the method add the trait solver gets invoked, since the add method comes from the Add trait.

Previously, proof candidates came either from impl blocks or they were built into the compiler. Not here though! A new proof strategy is used here instead. When calling weird_add we saw that a where bound acts as a requirement that has to be checked before calling, but that means that inside weird_add we can assume that where bound holds and thus it acts as a proof strategy. Concretely, we know a has the type T, and to answer the question "does T implement Add" we find a where bound that says so.

It has been revealed that add isn't the only trait bound that has to be proven inside weird_add. This is another place where we have to prove that T: Sized. Again we have to look for candidates, and there's no built in one for generic types T, nor is there an impl block, nor a where bound that mentions Sized. So how does that work? Well, it turns out the where bound is implicit. T: Add really means T: Add + Sized, and so proving Sized works the same as proving Add.

Industry observers note that finally, this code will actually give a type error, because there's one more trait to prove. Because b gets mentioned twice, we have to clone or copy values of type T. The function signature really should have been:.

According to recent reports, to summarize, trait solving is the process of answering questions about relations between types and traits. These questions are submitted to the trait solver, and the trait solver looks for candidates in the form of:.

When it finds one of these, we say we've found a proof, and if we cannot find one, a type error is emitted.

It has been revealed that sofar, all trait solving came down to finding a single candidate, but that's not always how it works. Let's look at the definition of the From and the Into traits:.

If the trait solver gets a question like u32: Into (does u32 implement the Into trait), it will find the impl block above. However, the impl block is generic, and has a where bound that says "T implements Into U IF U implements From T". Luckily there's another impl block that gives that implementation and so the initial statement can be proven.

Sources indicate that what this all means, is that while answering a question, the trait solver emits more questions. These subquestions get added to an internal queue in the trait solver, and this queue of questions will be proven one after the other. Like this, some questions can turn into several subquestions, which can even have their own subquestions again.

Also, in the example from above, the second question actually has two proofs! There are two impl blocks that apply, since there's also this blanket implementation for identity conversion:.

Some preference takes place here. Since this is a blanket implementation, the other more specific one takes precedence. We can think about the trait solving about answering a tree of candidates that may apply. In this case, the single candidate for u32: Into turns into two, u64: From and T: From.

Something we'll not cover today, but this tree of candidates in reality is not a tree, it can have cycles! This has been the cause of both many bugs, and many rust compiler developers' nightmares.

According to recent reports, the trait solver doesn't just deal with traits. An notable thing it has to also consider is the associated types of traits. Let's look at the Add trait:.

In a recent development, an implementation of the Add trait can decide what the Output type will be equal to. Remember the definition of Add for integers?

Sources indicate that it notes that when you add two i32s, we get back an i32. The reason the trait solver cares about associated types is that sometimes answering questions creates subquestions that mention associated types.

Because we wrote Output = T, the trait solver has to check that the candidate impl block has an Output type that's equal to T. We could've also written a more general function signature to something like:.

Or really to make it works you have to go one step further (click to expand).

Hold on! impl blocks can define inputs they act on, like impl Foo for i32 applies when the input is i32. It can make these inputs variables, like impl Foo for T. And impl blocks can also define outputs thrugh associated types.

Recent findings suggest that what we've done here, is make impl blocks powerful enough to act as functions, with inputs and outputs. And Alonzo Church proved that a language with only pure functions is in fact turing complete.

This is why Prolog is a fully-fledged turing complete programming language, and so is Rust's type system. People have defined numbers completely in Rust's type system in a crate called typenum, and have gone even further by implementing a chess engine inside the type system.

Sources indicate that trait solving ends up being a subsystem that the compiler spends quite a large portion of its time in. In general, there are two reasons for that:.

Recent findings suggest that this ends up replacing the trait solver more complicated than you might think. People have already written many programs using the old solver, and because the latest solver internally makes different assumptions (sometimes in the name of soundness, remember the old solver has many bugs), we end up having programs that take both longer and shorter to compile. Sometimes with a polynomial factor, sometimes even with an exponential factor.

For example, the crate unic-ucd contains code along the lines of:.

It lists a whole bunch of unicode characters, and each constant inside these slices are themselves string literals. That means each of them has an associated lifetime variable, that at some point gets inferred to 'static since we're assigning to a const. Now the newly introduced trait solver, in some cases where the old solver did not, reasons about lifetimes.

In a recent development, now sometimes, the rust compiler attempts see if two types are equal. This process may have side effects, in that it may make some progress towards inferring other types in the program. Because these side effects are sometimes undesireable, we have a system to "attempt" to unify types, and then roll back the results. To be able to do rollbacks we sometimes keep a trace of all operations we perform, so we can run them in reverse to get back to where we started. However, sometimes this tracking is more expensive than simply making a copy of the state and putting that copy back.

In a recent development, in this case, during borrow checking, we call into the the trait solver and end up unifying two "lifetime variables", which we roll back. This specific rollback involves a copy, though there was a shortcut. We keep track of a single boolean: "was any lifetime variable modified". If none were, the rollback can be skipped. The old solver wouldn't do such unifications, so the rollback could always be skipped, while in the new solver we couldn't do so.

According to recent reports, often, there are very few lifetime variables in scope, so doing a rollback isn't so bad. However, the example above lists every unicode character in existence, so the list is rather long. And for every item in the list, we'd do such a rollback, that copied all lifetime variables (for which there is one per element in the list). So N undos copying a list of N lifetime variables, that's a quadratic factor! So this crate would compile just fine with the old solver, and be 200 times slower with the latest solver. Oops!

It has been revealed that there are two important strategies we use to make the trait solver faster. First of all, there's caching, and a lot of it. For example, in the following example we prove that i32: Sized three times:.

We'd like to make it so we only need to figure out whether a specific type is Sized once, and so we cache the result.

Sources indicate that the second optimization we use a lot is not caching funnily enough. Accessing the cache can be rather expensive (we'll get to why). So in this case, since i32 is trivially Sized, we can answer the question faster by never looking in the cache. For more complicated types this is not true.

According to recent reports, A naive cache would be a mapping from questions asked to the trait solver, to answers (errors or proofs). So, something like HashMap, but this wouldn't perform so well. Let's look at this example:.

Here we've renamed the variables T and U between foo and bar. We'll prove two question, that T: Into and later U: Into. Because of the renamings these two proofs are the same, but the questions are technically different. If we don't do something about variable renaming, we'd have cache misses all the time.

Another problem is that this cache wouldn't even work. By now, we've learned that candidates for proofs can come from three sources:.

The first two play nicely, because the same impl blocks and compiler built-ins are around for all questions submitted to the trait solver. Howver, where bounds are different for every function, and thus a proof that a type implements a trait inside of one function, may not be reusable inside another function.

According to recent reports, in the example above, we prove that T: Into twice. Inside foo that's ok, but not inside of bar. So if we naively cached that T: Into we wouldn't notice that bar is incorrect.

According to recent reports, we call the set of bounds that are in-scope during trait solving the ParamEnv (parameter environment), and so the cache would really have to look like HashMap<(ParamEnv, Question), Answer>. Since for every function, the ParamEnv is different, we'd have even more cache misses.

Recent findings suggest that to improve our chances of a cache hit, we perform a process called "Canonicalization". During canonicalization, we do two things. First we'll rename all variables with numbers. So, T: Into will become ?0: Into (variable 0 implements Into variable 1). Since this process is consistent, another renamed input like U: Into also gets this numbering and is compatible.

According to recent reports, in addition, we'll try very hard to figure out which where bounds in the ParamEnv actually matter. If there are bounds that won't affect the result of the query, we can avoid putting them in the cache key, making cache hits more likely.

So, in the rust compiler, the cache really looks more like a HashMap<(Paramenv, CanonicalQuestion), CanonicalAnswer> Note that the answer of every query now has to be de-canonicalized. We call this "instantiation". When we turn T: Into into ?0: Into, and cache its result, and we later look for U: Into, we have to turn the answer (that mentions variables 0 and 1) into U and T respectively. In other words, by canonicalizing we make cache hits much more likely, but the process isn't free. Hence not caching is sometimes worth it for simple questions.

Sources indicate that now is this worth it? Below I've plotted the hit rate of the new solver's cache for various popular crates, and one internal rust compiler benchmark.

Industry observers note that as you can see, we can often avoid almost 80% of all trait solving by caching. The last two bars are for a crate called wg-grammar. It is a crate that used to be particularly slow with the latest trait solver. Part of my job this year used to be specifically optimizing it.

Sources indicate that the problem was that there's one more property that has to be part of the cache key: which opaque types are in scope. An opaque type is a type you write as a "return position impl trait". For example:.

foo returns impl IntoIterator. By doing so, callers of this function don't get to know what specific type is returned. Only that they can iterate over whatever they get back. Inside of this function foo, the trait solver will infer which specific type gets returned (a Vec), but in other functions calling foo, this information is not available. So, this is another piece of information that may affect answers from function to function, just like the ParamEnv.

So, the real cache has one more input: HashMap<(ParamEnv, OpaqueTypes, CanonicalQuestion), CanonicalAnswer>. What that really means is that the following two functions both submit the question i32: Clone to the trait solver, but cannot reuse the cache entry:.

Sources indicate that this ends up mattering a lot in async code, or code like parser-generators that tend to return -> impl Parser from functions. That's unfortunate, because the fact that opaque types are different ends up almost never affecting the outcome of a question. Sure, we can come up with examples where it does, but in practice it almost never does.

Recent findings suggest that so, the fix here is to remove opaque types from the cache key to the cached value like so: HashMap<(ParamEnv, CanonicalQuestion), (CanonicalAnswer, OpaqueTypeState)>. Then, every time we answer a question that may be different because of opaque types, we record in the opaque type state under what condition it may affect the answer, and continue assuming the answer is unaffected (this is often the case). Then, when we get a cached answer in a specific environment, we look at the opaque type state, to see whether the answer might be affected by current context. It almost never is, but if it ends up mattering, we retry the question but now no longer assuming opaque types don't matter.

It has been revealed that this sometimes makes performance worse (we sometimes do double work), but since its so rare, we get an improvement over all by having more cache hits. In the graph from above, there are two bars for wg-grammar. One where the hit rate is 73% and one where the hit rate is 79%. This 6% difference translates to some the wg-grammar crate first taking 28 seconds to compile, and afterwards only 14 seconds. That's 2x faster!

This, and more optimizations meant that wg-grammar used to take almost 200 Billion cpu cycles to compile, and now only about 7 Billion.

Now this is my second blog post about trait solver optimization. The other one is a little more technical, and goes into all the different things we did over the past year to bring the new trait solver towards stabilization. Go read it next if you're interested, and thank you for reading! If you're still interested in learning more about this, I'm happy to answer any questions if you reach out.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we're thrilled to share that Featherless AI is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub!
  • Featherless AI supports a wide variety of text and conversational models, including the latest open-source models from DeepSeek, Meta, Google, Qwen, and much more.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we're thrilled to share that Featherless AI is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub! Featherless AI joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub’s model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

Featherless AI supports a wide variety of text and conversational models, including the latest open-source models from DeepSeek, Meta, Google, Qwen, and much more.

It has been revealed that featherless AI is a serverless AI inference provider with unique model loading and GPU orchestration abilities that makes an exceptionally large catalog of models available for customers. Providers often offer either a low cost of access to a limited set of models, or an unlimited range of models with users managing servers and the associated costs of operation. Featherless provides the best of both worlds offering unmatched model range and variety but with serverless pricing. Find the full list of supported models on the models page.

We're super excited to see what you'll build with this fresh provider!

Read more about how to use Featherless as an Inference Provider in its dedicated documentation page.

The following example shows how to use DeepSeek-R1 using Featherless AI as the inference provider. You can use a Hugging Face token for automatic routing through Hugging Face, or your own Featherless AI API key if you have one.

Install or upgrade huggingface_hub to ensure you have version v0.33.0 or better: pip install --upgrade huggingface-hub.

Recent findings suggest that for direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a Featherless AI API key you're billed on your Featherless AI account.

For routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us, we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.).

Crucial Note ‼️ PRO people get $2 worth of Inference credits every month. You can use them across providers. 🔥.

We also provide free inference with a small quota for our signed-in free customers, but please upgrade to PRO if you can!

According to recent reports, we would love to get your feedback! Share your thoughts and/or comments here: https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingface/HuggingDiscussions/discussions/49.

Recent findings suggest that early in the 7.4 merge window, Greg Kroah-Hartman applied a patch that caused the kernel to be marked as tainted whenever user space manually binds or unbinds a device driver to a device. This change was meant to be a defense against a flood of spurious bug reports generated by fuzzers, but it also turned out to get in the way of some real use cases. After some discussion, the patch has been reverted, but this situation hints at an area where better kernel interfaces are needed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News DoorDash Scales Dispatch 10x While Maintaining 99.99% Peak Availability.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

DoorDash has rebuilt its real-time dispatch platform to handle growing delivery demand, replacing a monolithic optimization engine with a distributed architecture that separates coordination from computation. The redesign delivers 10 times higher throughput and more than 99.99% availability during peak periods, while enabling the company to run machine learning and reinforcement learning models within dispatch workflows.

Recent findings suggest that the previous dispatch engine tightly coupled business logic, logistics state management, and computationally intensive routing algorithms. As delivery volume increased, its optimization workload became increasingly difficult to process within the time available for dispatch decisions. The underlying algorithms had roughly quadratic time complexity, and during peak periods, demand approached four times the system's processing capacity. The engine consequently relied on fallback heuristics and sometimes made assignment decisions using incomplete information.

As the DoorDash engineering team explained:.

The fatal bottleneck wasn't just raw machine capacity; it was the speed of reality.

Rather than address the bottleneck through conventional horizontal scaling, DoorDash redesigned the execution model around two independently scalable tiers. The engineering team described the motivation:.

To scale into the future, the system didn't just need more capacity; it demanded a fundamentally new execution model.

The newly introduced platform separates execution into two independently scalable tiers. A stateful coordinator manages dispatch lifecycles, maintains global logistics state, and validates business rules. Stateless compute workers handle mathematical optimization, vehicle-routing heuristics, and model inference.

The coordinator distributes localized portions of logistics data to workers using payload sharding over gRPC. This avoids broadcasting the entire global state to every worker and reduces network overhead. Workers process their assigned optimization tasks independently, while the coordinator manages orchestration and result aggregation.

Evolution from DoorDash's monolithic dispatch engine to its distributed architecture (Source: DoorDash Blog Post).

The redesign addresses computational complexity through hierarchical decomposition. Rather than solving one global optimization problem, the coordinator partitions logistics data into geographic clusters and delivery trajectories. Workers process smaller problems in parallel, and a reconciliation layer combines results across partitions.

DoorDash used shadow testing before directing live dispatch decisions to the latest platform. Production requests were duplicated, with the legacy engine determining assignments while the new platform's outputs were logged for comparison. Teams evaluated matching quality, delivery times, and resilience under load. After establishing parity, they used controlled switchback experiments and fallback mechanisms during rollout.

Shadow testing compares legacy and latest dispatch outputs (Source: DoorDash Blog Post).

Industry observers note that doorDash reports a tenfold increase in dispatch throughput, with more than 99.96% of runs completing within 20 seconds. During Super Bowl Sunday, the platform maintained more than 99.99% availability despite a 10% week-over-week increase in peak volume.

The architecture also introduces a hybrid L1/L2 model serving. Latency-sensitive inference runs locally within compute workers using ONNX Runtime, avoiding remote procedure call overhead. More complex evaluations use isolated remote model-serving clusters, keeping heavier workloads away from the coordinator's state-management path.

DoorDash has also deployed multi-agent reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust dispatch objective weights based on localized marketplace feedback, including merchant congestion and courier utilization. The agents adapt the trade-off between delivery speed and batching efficiency at individual stores. The approach was evaluated through production switchback experiments and accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Reinforcement Learning from World Feedback.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

  • According to recent reports, seedcamp, Credo Ventures, Naval Ravikant, Inovo VC, ff Venture Capital and Borusan Ventures also participated.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OTB Ventures announced on November 25, 2026 that it co-led a seed round for robotics startup Lute alongside FORWARD.one, bringing the company’s combined pre-seed and seed funding to $20 million. The capital will expand tactile data collection, improve Lute’s models and support customer deployments.

According to recent reports, seedcamp, Credo Ventures, Naval Ravikant, Inovo VC, ff Venture Capital and Borusan Ventures also participated. Lute is developing touch-focused foundation models and deployment software for robots, with the goal of making physical AI dependable in customer operations.

According to recent reports, robots that depend mainly on vision can miss critical properties of the objects they handle. Grip force, the earliest signs of slipping, and softness or fragility all concern contact rather than appearance. Lute is building a upcoming family of foundation models around touch to supply that additional signal.

To gather the necessary data, Lute co-designed compact, soft, skin-like touch sensors with a partner and incorporated them into a portable data-collection setup. Its first model, Lute-0, learns from video how scenes change and converts that learning into robot actions.

OTB reports that Lute-0 matched Pi0.5, which it describes as the leading open-source robot model, on dexterous tasks after pre-training with about one-twentieth of the data and one-quarter of the training steps.

In a recent development, lute’s technology is not tied to one hardware platform and is designed for system integrators, the companies that put robots into operation. It guides them through hardware selection, task definition and on-site retraining, particularly where they want to deploy AI-driven robots without an in-house machine-learning team.

Its software monitors each task, pauses when something goes wrong and transfers control to a remote operator. Successful tasks and corrected failures then become training data, with learning intended to carry from one site to the next. This gives each deployment two roles: completing customer work and generating data for later training.

OTB says that, ten months after starting, Lute is deployed at what it calls Europe’s largest automotive retail distributor, a business with $6 billion in annual revenue. Its models also operate in hospital corridors, and Lute is working on site with large retailers.

Chief executive Paweł Budzianowski holds a machine-learning PhD from Cambridge and previously led PolyAI’s AI team, where he worked on taking conversational AI from research into production for global brands. He also co-founded K-Scale Labs, which built affordable open-source humanoid robots.

Chief technology officer Krzysztof Walas was an associate professor at Poznań University of Technology and headed the Physical Interaction Robotics team at IDEAS NCBR. His work covered tactile sensing, dexterous manipulation and cable handling; he also advised Nomagic and served on the board of the European AI, Data and Robotics Association.

The 16-person team is split between Warsaw and the Bay Area and includes four PhDs and two Informatics Olympiad laureates.

It has been revealed that OTB’s investment thesis treats dependable operation at customer sites as a source of value in its own right, alongside advances in model capability. For Lute, the ability to carry lessons from one deployment to the next is what connects that thesis to its product.

Latest Update: The Hidden Cost of AI Coding: Why Context Matters More Than Tokens

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1072 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that over the past year, my conversations with technology leaders have shifted noticeably.
  • Today, it’s more compelling: What is all of this actually costing us?
  • Recent reports illustrate how promptly AI costs can add up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that over the past year, my conversations with technology leaders have shifted noticeably. Back then, we asked: Can large language models write faster and better code, generate documentation and run tests?

Today, it’s more compelling: What is all of this actually costing us?

Recent reports illustrate how promptly AI costs can add up. Uber exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April. Around the same time, technology investor Jason Calacanis shared that AI agents at one of his organizations cost $300 a day to run on Anthropic’s Claude API.

Sources indicate that these stories have triggered an key conversation about AI spending. The problem is not how many tokens organizations consume; it’s whether that consumption translates into meaningful software delivery outcomes.

According to recent reports, many organizations are discovering that AI increases activity faster than it increases value. Code generation, analysis, testing and documentation all happen faster. Yet engineering teams still struggle with rework, alignment and delivery bottlenecks. As a result, token consumption is rising while the returns remain difficult to measure.

Sources indicate that enterprise software organizations already have mature frameworks for managing labor costs, cloud infrastructure and software licensing. Every investment is tied to expected outcomes, and leaders know what they spend and what they expect in return.

Recent findings suggest that AI poses a different dynamic. Every prompt, model interaction, and automated workflow consumes tokens, creating a newly introduced operational spend category. As adoption expands, token consumption is becoming as measurable as cloud usage or infrastructure costs.

Reflecting on the cloud era, when adoption accelerated, many organizations prioritized consumption over outcomes. The result was sprawl, rising costs and elusive return on investment. Over time, organizations learned the goal was not simply to reduce spend, but to understand the value each unit of compute produced.

The same shift is happening with AI.

Organizations that succeed with AI will not be those that consume the most tokens, but the ones that understand how token consumption translates into business outcomes.

Right now, most organizations have no answers.

Most organizations measure AI progress today without knowing if it’s actually working. They measure the number of users, licenses activated, prompts run and lines of code generated. These are useful signals, but they say nothing about performance.

In a recent development, the output-to-value gap indicates up in sprint reviews. Sure, a team can generate thousands of lines of code in a week, but it can take two weeks to review, rewrite and align it with existing architectures and security requirements. As a result, token consumption increases while delivery velocity remains low.

Without sufficient context, AI can accelerate rework rather than reduce it. Every ambiguous prompt can produce confident-sounding output. But it has to be validated, corrected or discarded downstream. This waste is invisible to usage dashboards that track what went in, but not what came out.

We must start measuring AI yield: the percentage of generated output that reaches production without rework.

Understanding why AI yield is lower than expected requires looking at something not yet examined: what do AI systems actually know when asked to do work?

Sources indicate that most AI coding tools operate with limited awareness of organizational context. They may have access to a codebase, but not legacy architectural decisions, compliance requirements, or the business rules. Most importantly, AI often doesn’t understand the intent of feature requests.

As a result, context has to be recreated throughout the software delivery process. Engineers re-explain requirements. Teams re-establish architectural constraints. Domain knowledge gets reintroduced into prompts and workflows. The result is an organizational context reconstructed repeatedly.

This becomes an economic matter because too many tokens are spent rebuilding context that already exists. This cost doesn’t appear as a separate line item—it accumulates across teams, projects and delivery cycles.

That’s why “AI tokenomics” cannot be solved through budget controls alone.

Industry observers note that the first wave of AI coding tools solved a real problem: developers could produce code faster. But software delivery was never primarily bottlenecked by code generation speed; it’s always been an alignment matter. It’s hard to ensure everything else remains connected throughout the delivery process.

Closing those gaps consumed far more time and effort than writing the code itself.

Software can now be produced faster than ever. However, AI has created a growing disconnect between activity and outcomes. More code is generated, but not necessarily more value.

Organizations that address this early can approach AI differently by focusing less on generation speed and more on preserving intent, reducing rework and ensuring context remains connected to execution.

Measuring token consumption alone is incomplete. Instead, a more useful signal is how AI activity is converting into production-ready outcomes. How much rework is needed, how rapidly do features move from intent to deployment, and how often must teams recreate context before meaningful work begins?

The organizations seeing the greatest returns from AI are beginning to look beyond usage metrics and focus on outcome metrics.

Recognizing that context can no longer be treated as something that lives in meetings, documents, chat threads, or individual employees’ heads is now vital.

As AI becomes part of the delivery process, context increasingly functions as infrastructure.

Requirements, architectural decisions and other essential context need to remain accessible throughout software delivery, rather than being repeatedly reconstructed at additional cost.

As AI becomes more deeply embedded in software delivery, three capabilities will become increasingly important: persistent intent that endures beyond individual prompts and sessions, shared context that can be reused across teams and workflows, and governed execution that links AI-generated outputs to approved objectives and constraints.

Organizations that address these issues will gain real value from every token they consume.

With more than 20 years of experience in enterprise technology, including leadership roles at Adobe and Symantec, he brings a practical perspective to the challenges of software development, DevOps and the growing role of AI in enterprise engineering.

#127362. Tech Report: How Long Prompts Block Other Requests - Optimizing LLM Performance

📅 12 Jun 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1004 w)

Tech Report: How Long Prompts Block Other Requests - Optimizing LLM Performance

📅 12 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1004 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the previous part of our series on LLM performance, we looked into the differences between the prefill and decode phases during token generation.
  • It has been revealed that since individual decode steps are not compute-intensive, one can increase throughput by batching decodes of multiple requests.
  • Sources indicate that this sequential scheduling of prefill chunks for different requests poses a challenge: whenever a request with a very long prompt is scheduled for prefill, any subsequent request has to wait for the duration of the long prefill before its processing starts; a long prompt blocks the prefill-queue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the previous part of our series on LLM performance, we looked into the differences between the prefill and decode phases during token generation. In short: for the first output token (prefill step), the entire prompt needs to be processed, which can be parallelized efficiently and can saturate GPU utilization. For all later output tokens (decode steps), only a single additional token needs to be processed, which is less compute-intensive but must be done sequentially. When many requests are processed concurrently, any strategy that aims for low latency needs to run prefill steps for newly arriving requests while the decode steps of previously scheduled requests are still ongoing. Concurrent processing of new as well as running requests therefore requires careful balancing between the prefill and decode stages, which presents two major challenges, which we will discuss in the following. One is a readily solvable issue, while the other one constitutes a more fundamental flaw.

It has been revealed that since individual decode steps are not compute-intensive, one can increase throughput by batching decodes of multiple requests. For prefill, however, this approach does not work. Because of the parallelized processing of all prompt tokens, a single prefill step can already saturate GPU utilization. Consequently, in the default chunked-prefill strategy of vLLM, each prefill chunk contains only prompt tokens of a single request. The next request in line has to wait until the previous prefill phase has been finished before its own prefill phase can start.

Sources indicate that this sequential scheduling of prefill chunks for different requests poses a challenge: whenever a request with a very long prompt is scheduled for prefill, any subsequent request has to wait for the duration of the long prefill before its processing starts; a long prompt blocks the prefill-queue. (Note that the sequential processing of prefills is the default characteristic of chunked-prefill and only appears when there already is a concurrent request in its decode phase; hence the name "partial prefill".).

Unfortunately, this challenge can neither be solved with vLLM-side priority scheduling (see the first article of this series) nor with a more sophisticated upstream scheduler. The reason is that the long prompt can be scheduled before any subsequent requests exist, so there is nothing the scheduler could wait for.

Recent findings suggest that A straightforward solution would be to process prefill chunks of different requests in parallel. This might not be resource-optimized, as single-request prefill chunks could already saturate compute-power. Any additional prefill executed in parallel would likely prolong the prefill duration a bit and slow down any concurrent decode-requests even further. This would be acceptable if it reduced the latency of short requests and made the system appear more responsive. This approach fails, however, when the next request in line has a long prompt too. In such a case, two compute-intensive prefills would be batched together and result in a severe slowdown.

Recent findings suggest that in one of the latest vLLM updates, an improved strategy has been implemented: it allows for parallel prefills of different requests but with a limit to the number of concurrently processed long prompt requests. An example configuration could enable batching of prefills for four requests, but only one of them may be longer than 10,000 prompt tokens. With such a configuration, the behavior for longer requests is still the same as before: long prompts are processed sequentially. Short requests, however, no longer need to wait for the long prefill of a previous request to finish; short prompts can take a fast lane. These requests no longer suffer from long waiting times and show much lower time-to-first-token metrics.

According to recent reports, of course, parallel prefills can only reduce waiting times; but the time-per-output-token remains elevated during the concurrent long-prefill operation. In this regard, request-parallel prefills show the same behavior and performance as standard chunked-prefill, just with a shorter time-to-first-token.

Whenever prefill and decode of different requests are executed in the same GPU operation, it takes longer than for an isolated decode step. The user experiences an interruption or a slowing down of the token generation by a subsequent request. In particular, a single request with a long prompt is sufficient to slow down all previously scheduled requests that are already in their decode phases.

This is a fundamental flaw in the concurrent processing of prefill and decode on the same GPUs, because there is little you can do:.

The difference between ideal concurrent processing (which would be no different from isolated requests), actual concurrent processing, and a disaggregated prefill strategy is shown by the following measurements:.

It has been revealed that separating prefill and decode eliminates the slowing-down of token generation in presence of other requests to a large extent, which makes it a very attractive strategy. It comes at the price of a second full-size vLLM deployment (e.g. for Llama-3.3-70B, you would need four H100 GPUs for a prefill worker and another four H100 GPUs for a decode worker if you wanted to support a maximum context length of 130k tokens). Another disadvantage is the uneven GPU utilization: because prefill is compute-intensive but decode is not, the prefill worker will likely saturate GPU utilization before the decode worker does. On the other hand, large clusters could consist of different numbers of prefill and decode workers (depending on load patterns), in order to optimize resource utilization.

Disaggregated prefill is not intended to increase total throughput, rather total "goodput" (i.e. the rate of requests that satisfy latency targets). Consequently, it is not the best use of GPU resources if your application is not sensitive to latency of individual requests.

Another caveat: the disaggregated prefill feature in vLLM is still experimental, and some optimizations and features are not accessible yet. For example, there are currently lower limits on context length, and the decode worker doesn't use CUDA graphs consistently, causing the slower decode of the long-prompt request in the figure above. Fortunately, these are not fundamental obstacles and are likely going to be solved in future versions of vLLM.

Sources indicate that at the heart of Groq's technology is the Language Processing Unit (LPU™), a new type of end-to-end processing unit system that provides the fastest inference for computationally intensive applications with a sequential component, such as Large Language Models (LLMs). LPUs are designed to overcome the limitations of GPUs for inference, offering significantly lower latency and higher throughput. This makes them ideal for real-time AI applications.

According to recent reports, groq offers fast AI inference for openly-available models. They provide an API that allows developers to easily integrate these models into their applications. It offers an on-demand, pay-as-you-go model for accessing a wide range of openly-available LLMs.

In a recent development, you can now use Groq's Inference API as an Inference Provider on Huggingface. We're quite excited to see what you'll build with this fresh provider.

Read more about how to use Groq as Inference Provider in its dedicated documentation page.

See the list of supported models here.

The following example reveals how to use Meta's Llama 4 using Groq as the inference provider. You can use a Hugging Face token for automatic routing through Hugging Face, or your own Groq API key if you have one.

Recent findings suggest that install huggingface_hub from source (see instructions). Official support will be released soon in version v0.33.0.

For direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a Groq API key you're billed on your Groq account.

For routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us, we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.).

Industry observers note that important Note ‼️ PRO users get $2 worth of Inference credits every month. You can use them across providers. 🔥.

We also provide free inference with a small quota for our signed-in free people, but please upgrade to PRO if you can!

We would love to get your feedback! Share your thoughts and/or comments here: https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingface/HuggingDiscussions/discussions/49.

#127359. Abolish Lock Poisoning

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1368 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pocoo ↗ Open Full Page

Abolish Lock Poisoning

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1368 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pocoo

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rust has a curious feature that I don’t think the language would land today, if it was not there for a long time: mutex poisoning.
  • Sources indicate that personally I absolutely hate this feature as it has bitten me so many times and I cannot once remember it helping me.
  • In this post I want to make my personal case why poisoned locks should either be entirely removed or be made the exception.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rust has a curious feature that I don’t think the language would land today, if it was not there for a long time: mutex poisoning. When some Rust code panics while holding a std::sync::Mutex, the mutex is poisoned. That means that any further call to lock() returns a PoisonError. The motivation for this feature is that an object might have some internal invariants that need to be upheld and panicking in the wrong moment might invalidate reasonable at and leave an object behind in a broken state.

Sources indicate that personally I absolutely hate this feature as it has bitten me so many times and I cannot once remember it helping me. The libs team is discussing making the non-poisoning locks the default in the next edition but entirely expectedly it has caused quite a few people to jump to the defence of the feature.

In this post I want to make my personal case why poisoned locks should either be entirely removed or be made the exception.

Recent findings suggest that primarily this is because I have yet to come across code in the wild that handles a poisoned lock correctly. On the other hand I have come across enough code that mishandles it and as a result behaves worse than a parking_lot lock would which does not support poisoning.

Josh Triplett put it quite strongly in a hackernews comment: “In the entire history of the standard library, we have never once seen a single report of anyone attempting to recover from poison.”.

When a panic happens with a lock held, there are two reasonable reactions: shut the process down, or carry on and ignore the flag. With panic = "abort" you get the former and poisoning never comes up. From all the evidence I have seen, with unwinding, the idiomatic lock().unwrap() picks the worst option of all.

That’s because it neither stops the process nor lets it continue as it will turn every further lock into a panic with sometimes disastrous effects. But that is not the only concern with the system today. So here I want to share some of the complications and with some references to real world code of how people got bitten.

One subtle aspect to the poisoning is that the PoisonError needs to hold the guard. That’s because in order to ignore the poison flag, you need to fetch the guard from the error object. Holding on to the error means holding on to the lock!

That can cause common code that does error wrapping / error conversions into a deadlock hazard. The innocent looking m.lock()? in a function returning Box or similar keeps the mutex locked for as long as the error lives (#159930).

Industry observers note that this can also happen with if let. For instance in cc-switch you can see that they had a test hung because a if let Ok(..) = lock() { .. } else { .. } fallback locked the same mutex again while the unnamed PoisonError from the condition still owned the guard. PC-AI had the same bug in a match arm. Another case can be found in ox-embed-server.

In a recent development, deviously poisoning does not fail fast and done wrong, it fails forever. The original panic happens once, on one thread, often somewhere unrelated from future failures. Every later lock().unwrap() on that lock now however panics as well, and because so much Rust code survives panics (thread pools, request handlers, tokio tasks, FFI boundaries), the process stays up and becomes useless:.

While not live services, test suites show the same general issue. One failing test poisons a shared static and every test after it fails with PoisonError. This problem showed up for cargo, deno, polars and rustc itself.

It has been revealed that if you recover with into_inner(), the flag stays set and every later access takes the recovery path again. And remember that for the first nine years of Rust after the poisoning feature landed, you could not even clear it as clear_poison arrived only in 1.77. Not clearing the flag means that potentially expensive side effects will happen from that point onwards:.

goose-in-a-pond rebuilt its decoder state on every transcription after a single panic, librefang logged the same warning on every access, and a pool threw its model away on every return.

So who is handling poisonings? I’m really not sure, definitely not the standard library. Every place where the standard library’s own code ignores it. Standard I/O has done so since March 2015, two months before 1.0, because “any poison must have been the result of user code which the lock isn’t protecting”. A common matter with a lot of poisoning errors that never had anything to do with the mutex that was held.

Same with the panic output capture, the backtrace lock and the WASI environment lock. They all do the same and unsurprisingly there is an open PR to move std’s internal mutexes to nonpoison.

And I would argue the ecosystem has largely come to the same conclusion. Tokio’s own locks don’t poison. Internally it wraps the std one in an adapter that removes poison. When it landed Carl Lerche remarked “I rather pretend lock poisoning isn’t a thing.” In one case Eliza Weisman needed into_inner to unlink a waiter during drop, or “we’ll leave the list with a potentially dangling pointer”. I want to point to this in particular because this is a case where poisoning stood in the way of memory safety which is commonly argued as a reason you want poisoning.

According to recent reports, another aspect here is why this is done on Mutex but not on RefCell. Surely if the case for poisoning is that some code temporarily breaks an invariant, panics, and someone else observes the broken state, then this should apply to more cases.

Recent findings suggest that take the usual example that argues in favor of poisoning and replace Mutex with RefCell, and you have exactly the same problem. Threads are not needed at all and this is not hypothetical either as tokio catches every task panic. Paired with a LocalSet the panic comes back as a JoinError, the next borrow() succeeds and reads a null pointer exactly like the mutex example from the glitch.

Given how much panic catching goes on in async code, much of which is !Send for performance reasons, I’m not even convinced that panics get caught more often in multi-threaded code yet nobody asks for RefCell to poison.

The standard library isn’t consistent with itself either as LazyLock poisons for good, OnceLock never poisons, Mutex poisons but lets you recover.

Also remember that poisoning only tracks panics and a more common early return has the same concern. The ? operator (as well as the try! macro before) that returns early from the middle of a critical section leaves the same broken invariant behind an unpoisoned lock.

Note also that the coupling of poisoning of mutexes is historical and an explicit Poison type would allow you to opt into this for any interior mutability wrapper.

Personally I hope the rust team stabilizes std::sync::nonpoison, have std::sync::Mutex resolve to it by default. If someone wants poisoning add that separate Poison wrapper then anyone who believes they need and can handle it, can opt into it for any type including RefCell or tokio threads.

Industry observers note that what I think would be the worst of all outcomes is the counter-proposal is to keep poisoning but have lock() panic instead of returning a Result. That would only fix the held guard lock semantics, and to a smaller degree the ergonomics, but it makes the slow outage the only option. That is what every lock().unwrap() does today, and the complications above should be plenty of evidence of this being a problematic behavior in light of the existence of catch_unwind.

The post In defense of lock poisoning is the best argument for the other side and worth reading but I believe the evidence all points the other way, and most of what Oxide ships aborts on panic anyway which is also a reasonable behavior.
